name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Running on empty:  Tennessee Democrats pinning high hopes on uninspired campaigns
description: October means rounding the clubhouse turn on eagerly anticipated midterm elections. Sadly, even in a big-change-brewing year, the “eagerly” part of that sentence gets little traction in Tennessee, where the dense red fog of GOP political domination seemingly never lifts, keeping the election night suspense meter pinned near zero. But perhaps this year is dif[...]
text:
Tennessee Democrats are running congressional candidates with solid money and high profiles, but lackluster messaging. (Art: Getty Images)October means rounding the clubhouse turn on eagerly anticipated midterm elections. Sadly, even in a big-change-brewing year, the “eagerly” part of that sentence gets little traction in Tennessee, where the dense red fog of GOP political domination seemingly never lifts, keeping the election night suspense meter pinned near zero.
But perhaps this year is different, given accumulating political chatter about a blue wave washing ashore in otherwise unreachable red states. In this kind of political climate might some Tennessee surprises be in the offing? 
Tennessee Republicans went nuclear back in May redrawing themselves into majorities in every congressional district in the state, but that hasn’t stopped Democrats from fielding plausible contenders waging kinetic bids for several seats. 
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder in the 5th District and state Rep. Justin Pearson in the 9th District have both raised the money and the public profile needed to wage credible campaigns in open-seat races. And both have found their way into national visibility, snagging coveted spots on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s Red-to-Blue list, which targets potentially flippable GOP-leaning seats for strategic guidance, staff resources and fundraising help. 
Molder and Hatcher discuss positions on renewable energy, nuclear power ahead of November election

Also in the realm of blue congressional plausibility sits Darden Copeland in the 7th District challenging GOP Rep. Matt Van Epps, who has scarcely warmed the seat since taking it in ahotly contested special election last December. 
Copeland projects a normie moderate profile that could play in the sort of largely rural and exurban district the legislature drew for Van Epps, and the Copeland campaign recently shared some optimistic internal polling numbers, but unlike Molder and Pearson he hasn’t (yet) managed to draw the DCCC’s affectionate gaze. 
With national midterm momentum seeming to tinge a little bluer with each passing week and each new poll, it’s fun for Volunteer State Democrats to imagine the possibilities. For my part, while it’s encouraging to see blue team congressional hopefuls mounting serious bids, it is disappointing to report that the races they are running feel insipid, almost lifeless. Scanning the choices they are making about crafting and spreading their messages through legacy communication channels as well as social media, it all feels very conventional, very same old same old.
Take Molder, for instance. His social media content is thoughtful and crisply produced. His TV spots scream “I hired political media pros.” But it’s mostly anodyne unreconstructed talking points, offending no one (not a bad thing) but arguably inspiring no one either (not such a good thing). 
Copeland has an incumbent opponent who long ago superglued himself to Donald Trump, and we can see Copeland capitalizing on the socials, but the messaging, while apt on the merits, is flat. 
Democratic nominee for the 7th Congressional District, Darden Copeland is challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Matt Van Epps. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Pearson offers more varied and engaging social media content,  though the production values are often lacking, and the TV spot of his I’ve seen has a county-sheriff-candidate level of polish. 
Everyone understands that the current political environment, like the rest of our information economy, is built on a foundation of attention: grabbing it, holding it and using it to advantage. Each of these candidates is running a competently organized and well-intended campaign, but it’s hard to fathom how any are breaking through in an attention-getting way. There is little mainstream media coverage of these races because none are making news and there is little to cover. 
To be sure, these candidates and their staffs are working their tails off every day on an exceedingly difficult quest in a challenging political context. But at the risk of further torturing the maritime metaphor, it feels like they’ve set up campaign shops on rafts floating offshore, relying on the forces of nature, which is to say 2026’s building wind and wave, to pick them up and carry them home. 
Granted, none can win without the wave, and it will have to be a genuine biggie to splash all the way into Tennessee. We hear the term “tsunami” thrown around from time to time in political conversations about this year’s Democratic momentum, but metaphorically speaking that overstates. By definition a tsunami is a large wave typically caused by an undersea earthquake. 
Dems don’t need the full weight of a thoroughgoing national political earthquake to start turning Tennessee back in a blue direction. But floating competently in the red fog waiting for a big wave, while understandable, feels like not enough.

title: Alabama amendment would authorize county school board mergers
description: Voters next month will decide whether to approve a constitutional amendment that would give county school boards the option to consolidate. HB 380, sponsored by Rep. Terri Collins, R-Decatur, passed the House of Representatives 96-2 and unanimously in the Senate this spring. The measure would give two or more county school boards the opportunity to […]
text:
Students at Brantley Elementary School take part in a STEM activity during a visit from Dallas County Schools Superintendent Anthony Sampson on Monday, June 30, 2025. Amendment 2 would allow county boards of education to pursue mergers after a State Board of Education assessment and if local voters approve.  (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)Voters next month will decide whether to approve a constitutional amendment that would give county school boards the option to consolidate.
HB 380, sponsored by Rep. Terri Collins, R-Decatur, passed the House of Representatives 96-2 and unanimously in the Senate this spring. The measure would give two or more county school boards the opportunity to merge should voters approve it.
Collins said in an interview Tuesday that the board could explore consolidation to save money.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“What this would allow them to do is not to lose their system, it would allow them to combine their board with other county boards, particularly some of our small counties that are less than 1,000 students in the whole county,” Collins said in an interview Tuesday. “Therefore, they could put less money in administration.”
Lawmakers approved a separate bill that applied the same principle to schools within a city. A constitutional amendment is needed to allow consolidation of school boards outside municipalities.
If two county boards of education wanted to merge, each would approve merger resolutions, with details of consolidation — such as debt obligations, timelines and operations — left to the boards.
At least 30 days before the county school board votes on the consolidation, the State Board of Education would publish the results of a study that evaluates its impact on students, families, programming staff and the different operations of the school district at least 30 days before the resolution is adopted. Under the bill, the Board would not have any other powers on consolidation.
If 25% of registered voters submit a written protest within 30 days of the school boards authorizing the merger, then the affected districts will convene a referendum.
In that situation, a consolidation could take place if a majority of voters in each county approve it, as well as an overall majority of voters in the affected counties.
Two education groups have declined to take a public position on the amendment.
“I think if there was not the local decision-making in the process, we might have a stronger position one way or another on that, but the parameters are in place only to allow that to happen if it is in the best interest of the local area, and that would have to involve several entities agreeing that is what is in their best interest before that would happen,” said Allison King, government relations manager with the Alabama Education Association.
The Alabama Association of School Boards is also staying neutral on the proposal.
“We are not aware of any county school system that is currently considering consolidation,” said Chad Holden, executive director with the Alabama Association of School Boards.
Holden said consolidation could reduce administrative costs, but other expenses should also be considered.
“Things like transportation costs might actually increase,” Holden said. “Whereas you might save money on one hand, but there could be increased costs for others. All those costs would have to be taken into consideration.”
The League of Women Voters of Alabama opposes the amendment, citing the high threshold to set a referendum.
“The threshold is 25% of electors, which many times, you don’t even have that many people come out to vote,” said Kim Bailey, president of the League of Women Voters of Alabama.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Regulators fined state, local government offices $125,150 for workplace safety violations
description: State regulators issued $125,150 in civil penalties to state, county and local governments over an eight-month period for failing to adhere to workplace safety requirements, lawmakers were told Wednesday.
text:
Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery), right, asks a question during Wednesday's briefing on the Davis Martinez Act for the Joint Committee on Fair Practices and State Personnel Oversight. Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) listens. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)State regulators issued $125,150 in civil penalties to state, county and local governments over an eight-month period for failing to adhere to workplace safety requirements, lawmakers were told Wednesday.
The penalties were issued by Maryland Occupational Safety and Health as part of the Davis Martinez Public Employee Safety and Health Act, which took effect Oct. 1, 2025. The act, named in honor of a slain parole agent, aims to toughen enforcement of safety rules for state and local government workers.
Representatives of the Maryland Department of Labor, which houses MOSH, told members of the Joint Committee on Fair Practices and State Personnel Oversight on Wednesday that the law has allowed for gains in workplace safety. But they said the situation could be improved even more with more resources.
“We were not given any additional enforcement resources to do additional public sector work as part of the [Davis Martinez] law,” said Christopher Williamson, assistant commissioner with MOSH, during a two-hour briefing on implementation of the law.
Maryland Division of Labor and Industry Commissioner Devki Virk, left, testifies with Christopher Williamson, assistant commissioner with Maryland Occupational Safety and Health. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Davis Martinez was doing a routine home check on a parolee in Silver Spring in May 2024 when he was stabbed to death, becoming the first parole agent killed in the line of duty.
Subsequent investigation into his death revealed a series of workplace safety shortcomings. Those included his supervisors’ failure to check up on him for hours after he went missing. It wsa only after co-workers noticed he was missing and called police that his body was discovered. The parolee he was checking on, Emanuel Edward Sewell, has been charged with first-degree murder in Martinez’s death.
Besides requiring civil penalties against government bodies that violate workplace safety rules, the law also requires an annual report on workplace-related deaths, injuries and illnesses.
The first report, a 28-page document submitted in July to the General Assembly, said there were 40 inspections of government workplaces from Oct. 1, 2025, through May 31 of this year that resulted in penalties. The report said regulators issued civil penalties “if there is a substantial probability that death or serious physical harm could result from a condition that exists.”
It said 30 of the 40 inspections have been settled and closed, but that about $104,00 of the civil penalties are still owed.
In December, for example, about $19,000 in initial penalties were issued against the state Department of Transportation, but those were reduced to $12,778 after formal settlement agreements were reached. Penalties of $3,400 issued the same month against the town of Brentwood were decreased to $2,600 after a settlement.
While they were pleased that some progress has been made, committee members said one statistic showed more work is needed. Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor and Statistics showed that that for every 10,000 state workers in Maryland there were 66.9 violent acts, compared to a national average rate of 37 violent acts per 10,000 full-time state workers.
“I’m just dismayed looking at this chart,” said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery), the Senate co-chair of the committee.
Family, loved ones of Davis Martinez honored during final bill signing of 2025

Williamson said one potential reason could be more reporting in Maryland. Although there was not data from other state to compare, he noted that some states don’t have their own agencies to do workplace safety inspections. West Virginia’s Division of Labor has a program, for example, but officials with the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration conduct workplace inspections.
Hester agreed that while “Maryland is a unique state, I also don’t want us to settle for the status quo.” She said the state should look to polices in other states “that we can learn from.”
“That is a task worth doing,” said Devki Virk, commissioner with the Maryland Division of Labor and Industry, “but also one is not easily housed within our current structure within MOSH.”
Virk said most of the department’s resources are tied up doing the day-to-day enforcement work.
The state budget funds 97 positions this year for the state’s occupational safety agency. But the agency had as many as 200 positions at one point, said Christian Gobel, legislative and political coordinator for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) Maryland Council 3.
“We feel that needs to be significantly raised,” Gobel said of staffing levels for inspectors. “We just need many more resources at MOSH so that they can fulfill their important mission.”
The committee also received updates on workplace violence prevention and heat standards.
Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) said reviewing those and other standards doesn’t help when there aren’t enough workers to ensure they’re being adhered to.
“If there’s not the folks that would go in and do the inspections and have the enforcement piece of that, you’re kind of losing a lot of the momentum that would otherwise be there for implementing these new standards,” Lam said. “So that leaves us a little bit short if we’re putting in a new policy, but then no one’s enforcing it.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Republicans navigate Trump’s unpopularity
description: In 2024, Gabe Evans put a huge banner on his campaign website highlighting Donald Trump’s endorsement of his run for Congress. Then a Republican state representative, Evans was running to unseat the Democratic incumbent in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District north of Denver. Trump went on to win the presidency for a second time, and Evans […]
text:
Then-candidate Gabe Evans speaks during a rally for President Donald Trump in 2024 at the Gaylord Rockies Resort in Aurora. Evans, now a member of Congress running for reelection, no longer has a banner on his campaign website touting Trump's endorsement. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)In 2024, Gabe Evans put a huge banner on his campaign website highlighting Donald Trump’s endorsement of his run for Congress. Then a Republican state representative, Evans was running to unseat the Democratic incumbent in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District north of Denver. Trump went on to win the presidency for a second time, and Evans got a promotion to the U.S. House.
The environment for Republicans is dramatically different this election cycle.
Voters throughout the country, including many who supported Trump two years ago, don’t like the way he’s running the country. The cost of living is high and increasing. Trump started a war of choice in Iran that most Americans oppose. His administration throttled release of the full Epstein files. His immigration enforcement program is out of control. Corruption throughout his administration is brazen and massive.
Some Republicans like Evans appear to have taken note. He’s running for reelection in one of the nation’s handful of toss-up districts. But there’s no more Trump banner on his website, even though the president in April announced Evans has his “Complete and Total Endorsement.” In fact, there’s no mention at all of Trump’s endorsement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trump has endorsed all four members of Congress from Colorado, but they have responded to that support in various ways.
Rep. Lauren Boebert is running for reelection in Colorado’s most conservative district, the 4th, which covers the Eastern Plains. She’s been an outspoken MAGA adherent from her first run for Congress in 2020 and helped Trump spread election lies as he tried to overturn his loss that year. The endorsements page on her website features a banner that touts Trump’s endorsement of her, just like it did in 2024.
Rep. Jeff Crank is a slightly different story. The incumbent in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, which covers Colorado Springs, in 2024 had an “endorsements” link to a page that cited Trump’s support. The website looks largely the same this year, except for several notable alterations. In 2024, the site’s headline was “A Strong Colorado Conservative to Fight for Us.” Now the “conservative” label is gone, replaced with “A Strong Fighter for Southern Colorado.” And the link to the endorsements page has been removed. On social media, Crank highlighted Trump’s endorsement of his reelection campaign, but that was more than a year ago, before many of the developments that have tanked Trump’s approval rating.
Rep. Jeff Hurd, who represents much of the Western Slope, has long had an uncomfortable relationship with Trump. The president endorsed a primary challenger in February, after Hurd voted to repeal Trump’s tariffs on Canada. Perhaps persuaded by an adviser that this juvenile act of retaliation could hurt the GOP prospects in November, Trump endorsed Hurd the following month, and Hurd highlighted the president’s support on social media. The endorsements page on his campaign website makes no mention of Trump’s endorsement, but neither did it in 2024.
To whatever degree Colorado Republicans distance themselves from Trump, their wariness aligns with a national trend. Reuters reported this week that “two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive U.S. House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him … as his unpopularity threatens the party’s hold on Congress.” Few Republican candidates are in a more competitive House race than Evans.
Trump’s unpopularity is at historic levels. A polling average this week showed that just 37% of Americans approve of him. This reflects disapproval even among his base. A poll of Colorado voters in April showed similar results — for the first time, the percentage of respondents who had a favorable view of Trump dropped even among Republicans.
But even if any of Colorado’s House Republicans refrain from broadcasting the president’s support, all four of them are strongly aligned with Trump’s agenda. All four voted for H.R. 1, Trump’s signature 2025 bill, which did so much to cut healthcare and food assistance, and to benefit wealthy Americans. All four voted against reining in Trump’s war powers in Iran, even as Republican colleagues helped pass a measure that would do so. Evans this year has appeared at events in Colorado with Chris Wright, Trump’s Energy secretary, and Markwayne Mullin, Trump’s Homeland Security secretary.
“The President and I share the same goals,” Hurd said in March.
Any one of Colorado’s four House Republicans could say the same.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: We need more Kentuckians to understand what domestic violence looks like
description: “Nobody else would put up with you.”   “You know exactly how to make me act this way.”   “You don’t want to see what happens if you leave me.”   Unfortunately, many people will recognize these words from personal experience. They may have heard them from a partner in years past or just this morning. A single […]
text:
Gov. Andy Beshear  signed a proclamation in the Capitol Rotunda making October 2024 Domestic Violence Awareness Month in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd) “Nobody else would put up with you.” 
 “You know exactly how to make me act this way.” 
 “You don’t want to see what happens if you leave me.” 
 Unfortunately, many people will recognize these words from personal experience. They may have heard them from a partner in years past or just this morning. A single angry or hurtful comment does not necessarily mean someone is experiencing intimate partner violence. But when statements like these are routinely used to intimidate, isolate, demean, or control a partner, that is abuse.  
October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and ZeroV wants survivors of intimate partner violence across Kentucky to know that we see you, we hear you, and we are here for you.  
 Abusive people want to make you feel small and powerless. They minimize your experiences to undermine your sense of reality. They manipulate and coerce you into doing what they want. And they isolate you from friends, family, and other support systems that could remind you that you are loved and worthy of safety and respect.  
 Intimate partner violence takes many forms and can be difficult to recognize. It can include physical abuse, emotional abuse, financial abuse, weaponization of social stigma, threats to harm children or pets, stalking and intimidation, sexual and reproductive coercion, and sabotage of career and education.  
 People outside of a relationship may dismiss individual incidents as an argument or a relationship problem because they don’t see everything that happens. But when you call a ZeroV domestic violence program, the advocate on the other end of the line will understand what you’re going through, listen without judgment, and support you in choosing the path to safety that works best for you. 
 In just the first half of 2026, advocates at ZeroV member programs across the state answered their crisis lines nearly 10,000 times. Many advocates are survivors themselves, giving them a deeply personal understanding of the complexities survivors face. Navigating a path to safety while experiencing abuse is no easy task. When survivors are ready, our advocates are here to walk alongside them.  
 However, advocates can’t meet the need on their own. In the same six months that we answered nearly 10,000 crisis calls, we were unable to meet 719 requests for shelter. We also know that not everyone experiencing domestic violence feels safe enough to reach out, meaning the need is likely much greater than what we can track. 
 It’s time to learn
This month, we’re calling on all Kentuckians to join advocates in taking action to support survivors. The first step is researching what intimate partner violence can look like, understanding the nuances that make it difficult to flee, and unlearning the social norms that make this widespread problem so difficult to root out. This Domestic Violence 101 webinar from the National Resource Center on Domestic Violence provides a comprehensive overview. If you prefer to learn by reading, you can start with ZeroV’s website. 
 The next step is practicing supportive skills. If you’re concerned someone may be experiencing abuse, the best thing you can do is check in with them. You can say something like, “I’ve noticed you seem different lately, and I’m worried about you. How are you doing?” If they decline to share, that’s okay. The act of extending care and compassion lets them know you’re there if they need you. That in itself can be lifesaving. 
 If they do share that they are being abused, the actions you can take to support them are like what you might do for a friend having a hard time. You can invite them out for coffee, giving them a chance to talk outside their partner’s earshot. You can offer to be a reassuring presence when they take a step toward safety, such as calling a crisis line or filing a protective order. You can store some of their belongings if they need to move out but cannot immediately find new living arrangements. 
 Whatever you do, be sure to ask the survivor about it first. Your role isn’t to tell survivors what to do but to help them navigate their options. You can learn more about supporting survivors from the National Domestic Violence Hotline. And if you’re wondering whether you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, ZeroV advocates are just a phone call away to talk it through. 
 We all have the power to support survivors and end domestic violence. No matter what a partner might say, our actions can help overcome messages of abuse by affirming that survivors are worthy of safety and respect. This month, join ZeroV in showing survivors that their community is here to walk alongside them.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Constitutional: The amendment that could safeguard same-sex marriage in Virginia
description: Rachel Leyco had to adopt her biological sons.  As she and her wife Jenn Jackson sat in their Chesterfield County living room recently, the couple recalled how their marriage and parenthood journey was complicated by state and federal legal landscapes. Their love story is why they are backing an effort to enshrine same-sex marriage protections […]
text:
Rachey Leyco and Jenn Jackson sit on the porch of their Chesterfield County home with their sons in the summer of 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Rachel Leyco had to adopt her biological sons. 
As she and her wife Jenn Jackson sat in their Chesterfield County living room recently, the couple recalled how their marriage and parenthood journey was complicated by state and federal legal landscapes. Their love story is why they are backing an effort to enshrine same-sex marriage protections into Virginia’s constitution. 
“When I tell people I literally had to adopt my genetic children, they’re like ‘what!’” Leyco said. 
The couple first met in 2009, three years after Virginians voted to place a ban on same-sex marriage in the state constitution. Their 2010 vows made in front of family in Richmond’s Forest Hill Park were not legally binding.The couple had a second ceremony the following year while visiting Vermont. 
They wanted to “just have what someone considers a legal marriage somewhere,” Jackson said.
Should the majority of Virginians approve a ballot referendum this fall, the state could remove its 2006 ban and enshrine same-sex marriage protections in the constitution. 


Proposed Constitutional Amendment 2
Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) remove the ban on same-sex marriage; (ii) affirm that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race; and (iii) require all legally valid marriages to be treated equally under the law?


If Virginia had already protected gay marriage, Jackson and Leyco’s parenthood journey would also have been easier. 
In the lead-up to their first son, Eli’s birth in 2013, the wives endured the hardship of miscarriages in their quest to become mothers. Eventually, they paired Leyco’s eggs with a donor’s sperm for Jackson to carry. But this also meant that as the birthing parent Jackson was established as Eli’s mother, while Leyco was not formally recognized as his other parent. 
The couple navigated legal proceedings and traveled between Richmond and Washington D.C. before Eli’s birth. It shouldn’t have been so complicated, they said, but are grateful that they could afford their path to parenthood.
By the time the couple had Lucas in October 2015, they not only had the procedures memorized, but the U.S. Supreme Court Obergefell v. Hodges ruling on June 26 of that year made same-sex marriage legal nationwide — and rendered Virginia’s ban moot. 
“There was still a lot of uncertainty,” Leyco said. “So we still went through the extra hoop, even though our marriage was suddenly legal just to make sure.” 
That uncertainty about their family’s future returned in 2022 when Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that he would like to revisit Obergefell in his concurring opinion in the court’s overturn of federal abortion protections. 
Thomas’s statement prompted Virginia’s state lawmakers to craft and advance a constitutional amendment that could protect same-sex marriages.
Amid the rise in anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric in recent years, Leyco and Jackson said they’ve had frank conversations with their sons, now 11 and 13, about how states and courts have upheld and torn down civil rights. 
“This has brought back a lot of fear that had not been part of our day-to-day lives for years,” Jackson said. 
It’s what inspired the couple, with the backing of their children, to share their story with the Virginia Mercury.
Otherwise, their day-to-day lives are filled with both the excitement and the mundane that comes with married life and parenthood: picking up kids at school and dropping them off, spending time outdoors, cheering on student athletic events, making sure homework gets done and sharing family meals. 
Jackson and Leyco stressed that they also try to role model a healthy marriage to show their sons what a loving and supportive relationship can look like.
With a grin Jackson said “we always joke that’s the ‘gay agenda’ — raising kids to be decent human beings.” 
Virginia’s marriage equality amendment, which is among three civil rights proposals on statewide ballots this year, has bipartisan support. Seven Republicans voted in favor of the Democrat-led measure between the House and Senate chambers this year. 
Other proposed amendments include restoring voting rights for people with felony convictions as long as they’ve completed their sentences and a proposal to protect contraception, fertility treatments like in vitro fertilization and abortion access. 
The voting rights amendment saw a narrower show of bipartisan support while the reproductive rights amendment only advanced to ballots because of Democratic majorities in the legislature. 
Jackson and Leyco, who intend to vote in favor of all three amendments, emphasize the role reproductive rights played in their ability to start a family. 
Jenn Jackson’s father officiates his daughter’s “spiritual ceremony” to Rachel Leyco in Richmond. (Image courtesy Rachel Leyco)
But both the marriage and reproductive amendments have opponents.
Former Lt. Gov. Winsome Earle-Sears launched a “Life and Marriage” tour to campaign around the state in opposition of both amendments.   
Family Foundation, one of the state’s most prominent Christian lobbying organizations, has also opposed both the proposals. 
The Foundation’s pending lawsuit seeks to tear down the reproductive rights provision if the majority of Virginians approve, by arguing the ballot language is misleading and that legislative procedural steps for the amendment were not properly followed. 
Josh Hetzler, a lawyer with the Foundation, said over the summer that his organization doesn’t have a stance on the voting rights amendment but that it “might have incentive to file a lawsuit challenging the marriage amendment,” depending on how the reproductive rights challenge goes. 
For now, Family Foundation president Victoria Cobb said that the organization has staff participating in campaign events and doing door-knocking. 
It wouldn’t be the first time opponents have sought to undo marriage protections and undermine Obergefell in recent years. But those efforts have not been successful. 
A handful of Republican-led states have introduced symbolic resolutions opposing such unions, while the Supreme Court rejected a petition late last year to revisit Obergefell. Additionally, Congress’ Respect For Marriage Act of 2022 offers another layer of federal protection for now. 
This means that removing Virginia’s ban would be symbolic in nature for now, but could prove protective in the future. 
Jackson reflected on the dignity of love and the contrast between her family’s story and that of Jim Obergefell and his husband John Arthur. The Ohio couple at the center of that case had married out of state, but Obergefell was not recognized as Arthur’s surviving spouse on his death certificate following his battle with terminal illness. 
“It tears my heart out,” Jackson said. “Our story has the beginning of our children’s lives, but his story has his husband on his deathbed. I don’t want there to be any chance that when one of us passes, that we are not treated like any other married couple.”
Read part one of the Constitutional series here; the final part will be published Friday.

title: Roanoke region remains in emergency drought conditions despite rain in other areas
description: Despite cooling temperatures and repeated rain storms in central and northern portions of Virginia that have eased the drought conditions that were pervasive in the late spring and summer, Roanoke and the surrounding region is still experiencing emergency drought conditions.   According to the latest drought indicators, Campbell, Halifax, Charlotte, and Pitt[...]
text:
A map shows the Roanoke region of Virginia in emergency drought conditions in October 2026. (Department of Environmental Quality)Despite cooling temperatures and repeated rain storms in central and northern portions of Virginia that have eased the drought conditions that were pervasive in the late spring and summer, Roanoke and the surrounding region is still experiencing emergency drought conditions.
Map shows Roanoke region of Virginia in emergency drought conditions in October 2026. (Department of Environmental Quality)
 
According to the latest drought indicators, Campbell, Halifax, Charlotte, and Pittsylvania counties are in the red emergency category for precipitation, groundwater, reservoir levels, and streamflow. Some water systems in the area have had to implement voluntary and mandatory water restrictions to preserve accessible drinking water.
Two key reservoirs in the area provide the starkest picture of the situation. The Carvins Cove Reservoir in Botetourt County is 21.4 feet below full pond, leaving about 52% available. In Roanoke County, Spring Hollow reservoir sits at 27.5 feet below full pond level leaving about 67% available.
The Western Virginia Water Authority that oversees the reservoirs has contingency plans dictating when to implement stricter restrictions in the communities that rely on the water. Both reservoirs are almost low enough to enter the plan’s mandatory restrictions category.
 
Chart detailing different stages of drought policies for the Carvins Cove Reservoir. (Chart by Western Virginia Water Authority)
“They’re doing all they can to maintain all the necessary allocations for drinking water for the folks they supply down in North Carolina, as well as out towards Virginia Beach,” said Weedon Cloe, office of water supply manager with the Department of Environmental Quality.
In July, Gov. Abigail Spanberger supported Roanoke area officials’ request for the public to curb non-essential water use and for industrial water users to reduce their withdrawals. Conditions have not noticeably improved since then.
Virginia Secretary of Natural and Historic Resources David Bulova said that these conditions are reminiscent of the 2002 drought, which led to some smaller towns in the state to completely run out of water. That drought triggered the state’s revamp of its water resiliency plans and expanded water reserves.
“We learned a lot from the 2002 drought, and it has allowed for a number of our utilities to be more resilient,” Bulova said. “That doesn’t mean that they aren’t taking proactive measures in order to make sure that they are able to stretch out their supplies as long as possible.”
Bulova added that state and federal agencies have been coordinating with the region on how to best address water needs and monitor weather conditions. 
Earlier this year, over 80% of the state  experienced severe drought conditions. This was partly due to the commonwealth having a drier than normal winter that did not allow for groundwater sources to replenish as they typically would in the fall and winter months. 
There was also less precipitation this spring that led to deficiencies in hay supply, which drove Spanberger to sign an executive order that temporarily exempted over-width hay deliveries from certain transportation restrictions to allow farmers to feed their livestock more quickly.
The drought conditions in most parts of the state have eased with more frequent rain. But Roanoke and the nearby counties have missed many storms that have rolled through.
U.S. Drought monitor shows pervasive extreme drought conditions around Roanoke in October 2026. (U.S. Drought Monitor)
With the exception of the Roanoke area, Southwest Virginia is in the best shape statewide, with all drought categories back to normal. Groundwater levels for most parts of the state remain at emergency levels.
“It just takes a long time for that groundwater to be able to bounce back,” Bulova said. “While a reservoir can get filled up with a couple of key storms, you’re not going to see that with groundwater supplies. It’s going to take some long periods of sustained rainfall to do that.”
The National Weather Service is predicting an El Niño weather pattern this winter, meaning that warmer Pacific Ocean temperatures will be carried on jetstreams to the Gulf Coast and Southeast United States, increasing wet weather. If this pattern comes to fruition, it could help replenish Virginia’s groundwater levels. 
But if conditions remain dry, it could mean a tough year for some crops, especially in the Roanoke region.
“With respect to rain and snowpack over the winter … that will help to inform some of those early crops and whether this is going to continue to be a problem into 2027,” Bulova said.
Agencies remain ready to act if the reservoirs continue to drop and the predicted wet winter does not materialize. Things could turn around within the next few months, which was the case in 2002 when drought conditions had heavily ebbed by the new year.
“I can only hope that the El Nino pattern that’s supposed to come in comes in, and we can get that recharge that we need,” Cloe said.

title: Spanberger announces $1.3 million in scholarships and incentives for nursing students
description: Three hundred and fifty prospective nursing students around Virginia will be able to tap into $1.3 million in scholarships and incentives, new funding that Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Thursday.  The financial boost stems from the Virginia Nursing Workforce Center, which was created by state lawmakers this year to support the industry and was part of […[...]
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger speaks during a roundtable with healthcare organizations on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Three hundred and fifty prospective nursing students around Virginia will be able to tap into $1.3 million in scholarships and incentives, new funding that Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Thursday. 
The financial boost stems from the Virginia Nursing Workforce Center, which was created by state lawmakers this year to support the industry and was part of Spanberger’s legislative agenda. 
Last year, an analysis from George Mason University found that Virginia had a registered nurse shortage of 17,000. It mirrors a national trend, with the U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration projecting a shortage of 267,000 full-time registered nurses across the country by 2028.
Virginia is one of ten states with the largest projected registered nurse shortages by 2038, according to the federal agency. 
The new investments include financial awards between $500 and $5,000 per semester for licensed clinicians who can serve as nursing preceptors, or mentors, for nursing students that need hands-on training to earn their degree. Applications for those awards can be found here. 
Nursing students can also apply for scholarship awards up to $2,000 to help offset the costs of obtaining their degrees.
Registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, and certified nurse aids may also be eligible to apply for financial awards towards student loan repayments if they  commit to working in the state. 
Colleges, universities, hospitals and other healthcare providers can also apply for grant funding to support participation in a two-year program called Earn to Learn, where students can earn income while they complete their clinical training.
Eligible partnerships can receive up to $400,000, Spanberger’s administration said. 
The governor said nurses “are the heart of Virginia’s healthcare system.” 
“At a time when the federal government is cutting funding and putting access to healthcare coverage at risk, Virginia is investing in our healthcare workforce and making sure our nurses have the support they need to care for Virginians,” Spanberger added.
The nationwide nursing workforce challenge is spurred by multiple factors: retirements of older generations of nurses, a growing number of aging adults in need of nursing care with fewer workers to handle it, COVID-19-era burnout causing some to leave the industry, and educational bottlenecks. 
President Donald Trump’s administration also sought to exclude graduate nursing students from obtaining federal loans for their continued schooling, but a federal judge has temporarily blocked part of the policy. 
Additionally, a reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer also places 300,000 Virginians at risk of losing their Medicaid health insurance, which means small clinics and hospitals alike will absorb uncompensated care that nurses and other healthcare workers provide when uninsured patients need services. 
Some Virginian clinics have closed and hospitals have trimmed services over the past year, citing the reconciliation bill as part of the reason.
Investing in the workforce pipeline is not just critical to supporting workers, Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa said, but it also supports patients. 
When there are staffing shortages in clinics and hospitals, he said, patients “wait longer. They travel further. And the nurses who are already there are asked to carry even more.”

title: Rising prices may be here to stay, but poverty doesn’t have to be
description: For millions of Americans living in poverty, rising prices are a threat to their wellbeing and the wellbeing of our communities. These prices often result in painful choices — like rationing groceries, skipping meals, or not sending your children to extracurricular activities. Those choices are everywhere these days, with one recent poll showing that half […[...]
text:
The bipartisan Gateway to Careers Act, which has been referred to the U.S. Senate HELP Committee, would help expand access to workforce training programs and ultimately help families make ends meet. (Getty Images)For millions of Americans living in poverty, rising prices are a threat to their wellbeing and the wellbeing of our communities. These prices often result in painful choices — like rationing groceries, skipping meals, or not sending your children to extracurricular activities. Those choices are everywhere these days, with one recent poll showing that half of all Americans are struggling to afford gas and groceries.
The Padua program, an initiative of Catholic Charities Fort Worth, uses holistic, intensive case management services to address barriers faced by families in poverty. It’s launching a new site in Chicago this fall.
One participant described the hardships this way: “I’m only buying a small amount of food at the time. I am rationing items — things like milk. I stopped buying bacon altogether. It is so expensive now.” Another said: “I’ve had to hunt down the lowest gas prices near me more than ever to just afford the gas.”
Amid these challenging circumstances, researchers, service providers, and policymakers all play a critical role in expanding economic opportunity. We have evidence that can guide us, and we need to use it. In drawing on what works, we can head off an influx of families slipping into poverty and instead create the conditions for more families to thrive.
When prices rise, they rarely come back down. Instead, they simply stop rising as fast. While there may be some volatility among individual items — everything from gas to raspberries to electricity — once prices are up, they generally stay up. Given this, it’s critical to target our efforts toward poverty intervention, so fewer struggle when prices soar.
At the Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities at Notre Dame, we believe rigorous research in close partnership with service providers — like the Padua program — can identify the innovative, effective, and scalable programs and policies that help people move permanently out of poverty. Through our work, we’ve identified solutions that policymakers should consider in this economic moment. They should lean on our evidence so that fewer Americans are faced with the painful choices that come with living in poverty.
Inside Meta’s Indianapolis bootcamp for data center technicians

For example, we studied the Padua program and found it significantly improved labor market outcomes. It was particularly effective for those who were unemployed at enrollment. For this group, Padua led to a 67% increase in the probability of working full-time and 46% increase in monthly earnings. Those who lacked stable housing before enrolling saw a 64% increase in housing stability. Due to its success, Padua has been replicating nationally, including to Indiana, Michigan and, starting this fall, Illinois.
We also studied the Goodwill Excel Center, a tuition-free, charter high school in Indianapolis for adults. Goodwill of Central and Southern Indiana noticed that most of its job training program clients lacked a high school diploma. Building this school was a direct response to that — it offers flexible schedules, free on-site childcare, transportation assistance, and a life coach. Graduates saw a nearly 40% increase in earnings within five years — roughly $80,000 more in their pockets in their lifetime. The program has expanded to 12 states and Washington, D.C.
Those are just two examples of replicable, rigorously researched interventions that policymakers can consider as they work to cope with the impacts of rising prices on their constituents.
And fortunately, some are already making strong steps forward. Indiana U.S. Senator Todd Young, Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), Susan Collins (R-Maine), and Tim Kaine (D-Va.) reintroduced legislation to help Americans advance in the workforce.
The bipartisan Gateway to Careers Act, which has been referred to the U.S. Senate HELP Committee, would help expand access to workforce training programs, which we know is one avenue to help families better make ends meet. It would provide grants to support partnerships between community or technical colleges and workforce development partners — like the promising work happening at Goodwill Excel Center and Catholic Charities Fort Worth.
Rising prices may be here to stay, but poverty doesn’t have to be. By investing in proven, scalable interventions  — whether that means providing holistic, intensive case management services or offering flexible adult education to boost lifetime earnings — we can shift from managing the symptoms of financial stress to solving them.
There is evidence to help us do this. Our leaders should look at the data, invest in what works, and scale these solutions. If we want families to do more than just tread water in a high-cost world, we must expand opportunity, backed by evidence and designed to help more struggling families thrive.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Inside Indiana’s state surplus warehouse
description: There’s a saying at the Indiana Department of Administration: One man’s trash is another man’s treasure. The stack of broken chairs in storage at the IDOA State Surplus Warehouse may be useless to the 30,000 state employees who once sat in them, but the chairs are a popular item with recyclers. IDOA routinely redistributes state […]
text:
Kitchenware confiscated or abandoned at the Indianapolis International Airport is transported to the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse for storage. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)There’s a saying at the Indiana Department of Administration: One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.
The stack of broken chairs in storage at the IDOA State Surplus Warehouse may be useless to the 30,000 state employees who once sat in them, but the chairs are a popular item with recyclers.
IDOA routinely redistributes state property to other agencies, saving Hoosier taxpayers an estimated $571,000 in the past three years alone.
Local governments are next in line for this surplus property.
Any remaining unwanted property is then auctioned off to the public, who can bid on used vacuum cleaners, printers, lawn mowers, vending machines, television sets — even air compressors once used by divers at the Department of Natural Resources.
The state raised just shy of $2 million in revenue through those auctions in the past three years, averaging $252 apiece for products sold on govdeals.com.
“We like to think we’re the Fred Sanford of the state,” said state surplus Director Marshall Tullos, referring to the fictional junk dealer from the 1970s sitcom “Sanford and Son.”
Surplus chairs in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse in Indianapolis. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)An Indiana Integrated Public Safety Commission lectern in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Surplus desks, chairs, filing cabinets and office supplies in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Surplus metal detectors and metal chairs in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)Unwanted furniture from the Indiana Governor's Residence sits in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Pallets of unwanted outdoor furniture once on display at the Indiana Governor's Residence is kept in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A vending machine, refrigeration management system and television set stored in the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)NOT FOR SALE: The autopen desk once used by Indiana governors to automate their signatures. The desk is now in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Kitchenware confiscated or abandoned at the Indianapolis International Airport is transported to the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse for storage. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)Magazines confiscated at the Indianapolis Airport were transported to the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse for storage. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)A box of brass knuckles confiscated from passengers at the Indianapolis International Airport is now in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)The Indiana Department of Administration redistributes used state property like office supplies. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
A broken vending machine can be stripped for parts by recyclers or resellers, whom Tullos said are the surplus program’s primary customers. “There are good parts in there,” he said.
The surplus warehouse is brimming with unexpected finds: corkscrews, drill sets, brass knuckles, rolling pins, cast-iron skillets and a snake-engraved dagger confiscated by TSA agents at the Indianapolis International Airport.
Boxes are filled with forgotten car keyfobs, jewelry, belts, cellular phone chargers and sunglasses left behind at the airport.
Outdated security cameras, printers, snow blowers and a wardrobe-sized safe are in storage awaiting auction.
So too are metal detectors, vending machines and microscopes.
There’s a dresser filled with envelopes of every conceivable size.
Nearby is an old lectern used by the Indiana Integrated Public Safety Commission available for state employees to repurpose.
Not for sale is the gubernatorial autopen desk where Indiana governors once sat to automate their signature.
The desk is cordoned off in a section of the warehouse where governors and first ladies temporarily dispose of unwanted furnishings from the Governor’s Residence until the next family moves in.
NOT FOR SALE: The autopen desk once used by Indiana governors to affix their signature to documents. The desk is now in storage at the Indiana Department of Administration surplus warehouse. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Law enforcement agencies in need of supplies can browse through used police sirens, radios, flashlights, ballistic vests and holsters no longer needed by Indiana State Police or DNR.
IDOA also facilitates redistribution of surplus military vehicles and ammunition from the U.S. Department of Defense, though equipment is shipped directly from DOD to police departments.
More than 150 Indiana law enforcement agencies acquired equipment through the federal surplus program, which IDOA estimates saved a collective $4 million in the last three years.
The warehouse itself is neatly organized, with items for auction kept separate from office supplies and law enforcement equipment still available for internal redistribution.
Most items up for auction sell within three weeks, Tullos said.
Shipments go out daily, with anywhere from 40 to 80 items sold in a typical week.
In the past three years alone, IDOA coordinated 451 pickups and deliveries and auctioned off 7,531 items the state could no longer use.
“People think of surplus as being junk, and we don’t,” Tullos said. “We think that there’s a resale value for everything.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Why the Louisiana Democratic Party switched its endorsement in 5th District race
description: After first giving its official support to state Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the Louisiana Democratic Party is now backing Antonio Wilson of Tallulah.
text:
The Louisiana Democratic Party has endorse Antonio Wilson of Tallulah for Congress in the 5th District after initially endorsing state Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe for the same seat. Party leaders said the initial endorsement was made by mistake. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)More details have emerged behind the Louisiana Democratic Party’s decision to rescind its original endorsement for the open 5th Congressional District seat. After first giving its official support to state Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the party is now backing Antonio Wilson of Tallulah. 
State Party Chairman Randal Gaines said in an interview Wednesday the initial endorsement of Moore at an Aug. 30 meeting of the Democratic State Central Committee was an error. Party leaders initially thought Moore had won a majority of the endorsement votes from the committee at the meeting. Gaines said they later realized she had won the most votes — but not the majority needed — because a few committee members had voted not to endorse anyone in the 5th District race. 
“The initial endorsement of Pat Moore was premature based on the fact that four people voted to not endorse, and she didn’t get 50% of the votes,” Gaines said. 
When the committee vote was retaken with only Moore and Wilson as options, Wilson emerged as the victor. The second endorsement vote was conducted remotely, Gaines said. 

Wilson’s campaign announced his endorsement Sept. 16, more than two weeks after the party’s initial announcement about Moore receiving its backing. 
“The party understands that they made a mistake and they corrected the mistake,” Wilson said in an interview this week. 
A third Democrat in the race, Bunkie resident and attorney Dan McKay, also sought the party’s endorsement but did not advance to the runoff round of voting with Moore or Wilson. 
Moore typically would have had an advantage over Wilson in the endorsement race because she has been an elected official for several years. She has served in the Louisiana House of Representatives since 2019 and was a member of the Ouachita Parish Police Jury from 2007 to 2019. 
Wilson, who owns a construction company, has never held an elected government office but has attempted three times to run for mayor in Tallulah, he said. 

Yet Moore has taken stances as a legislator that are unpopular with the Democratic Party. She has voted for legislation to prevent transgender people from participating in school sports, and she has opposed exceptions to Louisiana’s strict abortion ban to allow women to terminate a pregnancy that resulted from rape or incest. 
Moore said  she finds it difficult to support the abortion ban exceptions for rape and incest because she was conceived as the result of a rape. Her mother was 14 when gave birth to her and couldn’t parent Moore after the trauma, she said in an interview Wednesday. 

“She could not have a relationship with me. She couldn’t love me, touch me and name me but she gave me life,”  Moore said. “She let my great grandmother raise me.”

But Gaines said many members of the Democratic State Central Committee are unwilling to support a candidate who does not support abortion rights and transgender rights. 
“My party members are typically very consistent with standing behind and supporting the national party platform,” he said. 

Moore said the endorsement process has left voters confused about who the party is backing in the race. 

Wilson also has had his own issues that should give voters pause, she added. 

Wilson has been kicked off the ballot twice after his residency was challenged in the Tallulah mayoral elections in 2019 and again this year. In both cases, judges said Wilson failed to provide evidence he had lived in the city long enough to run for the office. 

In an interview Wednesday, Wilson said he is a full-time resident of Louisiana and lives in Tallulah. He showed a reporter a copy of his driver’s license and utility bills for a Tallulah address. 

Wilson said no one has challenged his residency in the 5th District race. He said the confusion arises from the fact that his construction company is still based in Alabama even though he moved back to Tallulah. 

Tallulah officials challenged his residency in the mayoral races because he was in a dispute with several of them over the ongoing drinking water crisis in the city, Wilson said. 
Moore said Democratic State Central Committee members should have considered Wilson’s previous residency issues before he received the party’s backing.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: National
title: Aging workforce, immigration crackdown are depleting skilled workers
description: A perfect storm of harsh immigration enforcement, aging journeymen and a building boom for data centers is wreaking havoc on the nation’s supply of skilled trade workers.  Automakers and construction contractors say they need more access to workers through accelerated training, steady immigration and a cultural shift to encourage young people to do the hard,[...]
text:
A construction worker wields a hammer on the job at the Mill Creek Residential project in Paramus, N.J., in May 2026. The supply of skilled workers in construction and other trades is under pressure from aging, immigration enforcement and a rush to build data centers.  (Photo by Tim Henderson/Stateline)A perfect storm of harsh immigration enforcement, aging journeymen and a building boom for data centers is wreaking havoc on the nation’s supply of skilled trade workers. 
Automakers and construction contractors say they need more access to workers through accelerated training, steady immigration and a cultural shift to encourage young people to do the hard, dirty work of skilled trades. They’re looking for plumbers, electricians, carpenters, machinists and technicians — specializations increasingly in short supply. 
Worker shortages are the top reason for construction project delays, a September survey by the Association of General Contractors of America found. Applicants are there, but half of the contractors who were surveyed said too many job candidates are unqualified and need more training. 
The association cited both the demand for workers building data centers and tougher immigration enforcement as contributing causes for the shortage.  
“Over 50 percent of craft workers are born outside the United States. We don’t know that they’re illegal but frankly DHS (the Department of Homeland Security) is not being that discriminating in whom they pick up or who feels threatened by them,” said Ken Simonson, the chief economist for the Association of General Contractors of America. One answer is for the government to allow more worker visas for construction and other trades, he said. 
“We’ve been stymied for 20 years or longer trying to get construction treated similarly to agriculture, where if you can demonstrate that there isn’t enough Americans interested in a job you can bring in somebody,” Simonson said. 
Pay is rising for the skilled trades, but it’s hard to say how soon higher wages would attract more people. On social media, trades workers complain of long commutes to work sites, long waits through low-paid apprenticeships and a feeling they’re not valued as much as office workers.
“Getting up at 4am-5am. Driving 50 plus miles to random job sites. Obviously the dirty part which is construction sites and inhaling dust and dirt all day. Seeing people in corporate jobs in nice clothes while I’m dirty going on lunch break,” wrote a 30-year-old on a Reddit social media post in July, concluding that they should have finished a college chemistry degree.
Thousands agreed, including a 31-year-old tradesperson from Michigan who said top pay in their field, plumbing and HVAC, is attractive but that many make less than $70,000. 
“Been in the trades since I was 16 and recently started going back to college,” the person wrote. “Everybody I know who chose a degree over an apprenticeship is starting to outpace me in life buying houses and having kids while we’re check to check and getting less healthy by the day. “
Today’s children could prosper in tomorrow’s shortage of young workers

These are the concerns employers have to address if they’re going to find enough workers to build homes, cars and data centers for artificial intelligence. Ford Motor Company and the Ad Council announced a publicity campaign to bring more young people into the trades, with a video declaring “millions of skilled trade jobs are waiting for people ready to do something, with great pay, job security and work you can take pride in.” 
Ford and the alliance didn’t mention immigration enforcement as an issue, but the Association of General Contractors and an unrelated survey of roofers both mentioned it as a prominent factor in reducing the supply of skilled workers. 
John Burns Real Estate and Consulting, an independent housing research company, reported that many of the roofers it surveyed earlier this year saw immigration enforcement as hurting their business. 
“There are no American kids willing to install roofs in Central Texas,” said one roofing contractor in anonymous quotes published by the group. 
“Tough immigration reform and not enough Americans to fill the void,” said another. 
“A lot of these people have been deported. The next generation is complacent and does not want to do physical work,” said a Florida roofer. 
Elizabeth LaJeunesse, vice president for building products research at John Burns, said the vehemence of responses about immigration was surprising. 
“They used terms like ‘They’re hunting our workforce.’ They’re describing disappearing workers,” LaJeunesse said. “Most of these firms are pretty conservative, so this is a real phenomenon we’re picking up on, that level of concern over immigration enforcement.” 
If Trump wants more deportations, he’ll need to target the construction industry

Duane Musser, vice president for government relations for the National Roofing Contractors Association, said the responses are typical of what he hears from members. Immigration as well as better trade education are critical to roofing, he said. 
“Advocating for solutions to workforce shortages, including expanded career and technical education programs and bipartisan immigration reform, is a top priority,” Musser said. 
The DHS told Stateline in an unattributed statement that “those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear” and that “we will continue to enforce our nation’s laws and remove illegal aliens from American communities.” 
In September a Trump-appointed federal judge stayed a federal practice of entering construction sites without a warrant to investigate immigration status. One construction worker of Mexican descent in Alabama complained that he had been detained three times since 2025 despite showing a state driver’s license demonstrating that he was a citizen born in Florida. 
Immigrant workers make up a majority of roofers, painters and stucco masons, according to a Stateline analysis last year.  
The nation will need 1.7 million new skilled trade workers every year through 2035, according to a September report by Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, a trade group including Ford Motor Company, toolmakers and other businesses. Training programs produce just more than half the numbers needed, and only half of those who enroll in skilled training programs finish, the report found.   
Nine states were identified by the alliance report as having high demand but low supply of skilled labor: Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. 
Florida ranks first for demand for skilled workers, but last for supply, with not enough new workers coming online as building in the state booms and current workers near retirement age. The state’s Association of General Contractors’ chapter hopes the advancements in workforce AI will drive more young adults into construction jobs since those can’t be replaced by chatbots.



Quotation







You can’t hide lower skills in a trade, whereas middle management and white collar jobs are protected by the vagueness of the job.


– Shoua Thao, a machinist in Minnesota


Other states have the opposite issue: ranking high for new workers but low in demand for them, based on recent hiring and future projections. 
In the top 10 for worker supply but bottom 10 for demand: Indiana, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Wyoming. 
The alliance report suggested employers themselves need to help train future workers. The companies building data centers, in particular, want those tradespeople.
“America needs hundreds of thousands of electricians, welders and fiber technicians to build AI infrastructure,” said Dina Powell McCormick, president and vice chairman of Meta, in a statement, adding that the alliance is “paying for the training, removing the barriers that keep people from stepping into these careers, and guaranteeing a job at the end of it.”
Shoua Thao, 40,  is straddling the line between trades and AI as a machinist in the computer-assisted manufacturing business known as CNC machining, which uses computer code to control production. The son of Hmong refugees in the Twin Cities area of Minnesota, Thao is now experimenting with AI production techniques. 
“Trades are the one career path that doesn’t lie,” he said. “You can’t hide lower skills in a trade, whereas middle management and white collar jobs are protected by the vagueness of the job.”
Eventually trades could become a more valued career path than college, Thao said, though he has been discouraged at times by low pay and long hours that take time away from family.
“I think it will be a slow process but eventually, sometime in the future, maybe my children’s future, trades will take over,”.Thao said. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.
