title: New Hampshire needs more childcare. New programs face hurdles in filling the void.
description: Madison Fisher, a social worker and mom of four, decided she wanted to start a childcare program after she got custody of her young niece. With children ranging from infant to elementary age, she wanted somewhere everyone could be cared for in one place, instead of all over town.  “I had two of my kiddos […]
text:
Madison Fisher walks with two of her children, Lila and  Cooper, in The Willow Center in Hampton on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)Madison Fisher, a social worker and mom of four, decided she wanted to start a childcare program after she got custody of her young niece. With children ranging from infant to elementary age, she wanted somewhere everyone could be cared for in one place, instead of all over town. 
“I had two of my kiddos in an at-home center with a relative, and then I had my niece, who I got guardianship of and worked on adopting, in a center,” she said. “It was so hard just to figure out (and) piece together childcare.”
She drafted her plan during her lunch breaks at her former job, and eventually moved into a space in an office complex in Hampton she found with help from an old boss in January. After months of renovations, hiring and a couple of missed start dates due to roadblocks, The Willow Center opened in June. 
According to the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, there was a 14% decline in childcare programs in the Granite State from 2017 to 2025. 
Childcare availability issues have been a consistent concern for working families and politicians, but programs big and small are slowly popping up. In addition to Fisher’s program, a new Boys and Girls Club of Central and Northern New Hampshire program in Lisbon opened this year, and Easterseals has an early learning center under construction in a new housing development village in Londonderry.
These new programs are facing challenges parallel to those of existing programs: balancing business expenses with affordability, finding qualified staff, and gaining the support and trust of the community. 
Money, money, money
Every new business relies on capital to get started, and Fisher needed outside help as she is “not wealthy” and spent most of her career in social work and early learning. Through small-business aid organizations and business mentorship programs, she was able to get a $50,000 loan to start the program. 
“That’s all I could get. So I was determined to make that small amount work, which was a huge challenge in itself because nobody starts a business with that little amount of money,” she said. “I had to do a lot of learning because my background is not business.” 
The loan went toward rent, utilities and renovationg the program space to comply with state childcare licensing requirements, all before the program even opened for care.  
“There’s so many purchases we would love to do,” Fisher said. “I won’t be getting a paycheck for a long time.” 
Fisher said she wanted to make her program “accessible and helpful” to all families, and looked to state assistance programs to help make childcare more affordable for parents. Given Hampton’s position in the Maine-Massachusetts-New Hampshire seacoast triangle, she wanted to make sure she could take as much tuition assistance aid as possible. Her programs take New Hampshire and Maine childcare scholarships, as well as education freedom account dollars for her homeschool and summer programs. 
“The goal when I did research was, ‘What can we get?’ Like how can we make it more accessible because childcare is insanely expensive, and running a childcare business is so expensive,” Fisher said. 
In the few months since opening, Fisher is still figuring out how to balance her finances. To help with expenses and to keep costs for families down, Fisher also holds CPR and first-aid training classes in the center after hours. Her center has a dedicated multi-use space that she plans to rent to outside vendors in the future. 
Unlike Fisher, the Boys and Girls Club of Central and Northern New Hampshire and Easterseals relied on major fundraising efforts to get their new programs established. 
The North Country Clubhouse in Lisbon, run by the Boys and Girls Club, opened its new early childhood program in May. Around $2.5 million was needed to convert office space into classrooms in the program’s building in Lisbon, which only hosted an afterschool program. CEO Chris Emond said the money mostly came from private and community donors. 
The decision to open an early learning program in Lisbon, Emond said, came after he spoke with community members and realized there was a “serious need” for more early care in the North Country. The 16,000-square-foot building on North Main Street had the space, but would have to be repurposed. 
“We would never fill (the building) with school-age kids,” Emond said. “There just literally aren’t enough of them. So the thought kind of came up that maybe we can build an early childcare center there.” 
The renovations added 36 infant, toddler and preschool slots to the building; 20 have been filled as of September. In addition to construction funding, Emond said he wanted to raise enough money upfront when the program slowly “ramps up” care.
Easterseals’ new program, Technology Hill Early Learning Center, is being constructed along with a new apartment complex, The Village on Technology Hill, in Londonderry. Located near the Manchester-Boston Regional Airport, the complex has been advertised as a “work-life balance” community created with young families and working professionals in mind. Along with Easterseals’ on-site childcare, it will have a dog park, convenience store, children’s playground and fitness areas. 
Kristen McGuigan, chief programs officer of Easterseals, said the partnership with the developers came in part because of Easterseals’ reputation. The developers wanted to have childcare on-site available to families leasing apartments in the complex, and McGuigan said opening up a program there seemed like “a really natural fit” for the organization. 
“It’s so cool. It really shows when you can have funders, developers, community members, nonprofits come together, really cool things can happen,” she said. “When I think about young families and being able to get up in the morning, drop your kid off, grab a coffee and potentially go to work on that property, I think it’s so smart to be able to decrease stress factors for families.” 
The center is being designed from scratch to be licensed for more than 200 children. McGuigan said the organization was able to fund the project through donations and has a large team working to make sure everything runs smoothly so that the program can open in January. 
McGuigan also said the new program in Londonderry will help Easterseals balance finances for its two other programs in Manchester, which focus on early childhood supports and services. By serving families at all income levels, it will “continue to strengthen and utilize sustainability” for all of their programs. 
“Our program is designed to screen and assess children of all abilities coming in, and if they need higher levels of care, additional services, our model will allow us to make sure we’re meeting those kids’ needs, depending on the location of services needed as well,” she said. 
A play space within The Willow Center in Hampton. The program opened in June. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin.)
Finding qualified staff
As the number of childcare programs in New Hampshire has declined, so has the number of qualified early childhood professionals working in the field. 
According to the Fiscal Policy Institute, the state’s childcare workforce declined by 6%, representing a loss of about 330 educators and staff between 2023 and 2025. Analysis shows that professionals are leaving the field primarily due to low wages and lack of benefits such as healthcare and retirement (usually because many businesses cannot afford to offer them). 
When it came time to hire new staff, Fisher said she looked for teachers who would care for their students like their own and were qualified to do so. She used hiring websites like Indeed and, as of September, conducted more than 60 interviews. 
Her biggest issue was that not everyone who applied was qualified. Under state childcare licensing laws, early education teachers must have a certain level of postsecondary education and work hours to be left alone with children. 
“I got a lot of applicants who didn’t have childcare experience and kind of thought they had things that were similar, like being an LNA or things like that. It was a lot like going through interviews that maybe weren’t qualified to be lead associate teacher.”
Fisher was able to find staff that was not only qualified but “patient” with her through the uncertainty of her program’s opening date, which was pushed from March to June due to issues with the building’s fire alarm system. She is working with an apprenticeship program to find qualified staff, and has one teacher in a program right now. 
“Childcare is a field a lot of people end up in because they don’t have another choice, not necessarily because they want to be here, so finding the teachers who want to be here is a big challenge.”
Large organizations like The Boys and Girls Club and Easterseals have the funding to provide benefits such as healthcare, retirement and career movement opportunities, making them appealing to prospective employees. However, they are still facing recruitment challenges, just like the rest of the industry. 
Emond said that while staffing is a challenge for the program, it is less of a challenge for him now because this is not the first time the Boys and Girls Club has started a new early learning center in the region. He said he’s learned important lessons from past startups, including that hiring good teachers takes time. 
“The biggest thing I’ve learned is it could take nine months to a year to get fully staffed and fully enrolled, because you’ve got to take your time in finding the right staff,” he said. “Once you’re open, then the parents are counting on you. If you hired the wrong team, it’s this constant battle of culture and people calling out on Monday and people quitting, and you’re constantly trying to plug holes. You don’t want to be in that situation.” 
Katlyn Giragos, center director for the program in Lisbon, said she was getting “less applicants than expected.” She suspects it’s partially because the early learning program at Plymouth State closed. 
Giragos said a decent number of teachers came from the local Head Start program, which is for children 3 to 5 years old, because they want to work with infants and toddlers. 
Growing their community roots
Families may need childcare, but it does not mean they will immediately trust a program with their child. New programs try to establish themselves within the communities they serve to increase their enrollment and meet their goals. 
The Boys and Girls Club knew that because the program was new, it would have to build a reputation in the community. Before construction in Lisbon finished, Giragos gave families tours of the facility and introduced them to staff members so they could get a feel for the center. 
“I really got to know each family that came in,” Giragos said. She also helped organize open houses and events to engage with the community, and said they had a “huge turnout.” 
“It’s a scary thing to hand off your kid,” Giragos said. 
Her goal is to continue to build trust within the community so the program becomes better known for its early care offerings, not just its afterschool program. 
Because its center is still under construction, Easterseals has been working with the apartment complex’s leasing office and local companies to introduce the center to residents and employees. Discounts are being offered to prospective families, and McGuigan said the organization has created a lot of partnerships around “communication and collaboration” to ensure people in the community get first access to the center. 
They also plan to have longer operating hours in an attempt to accommodate more working families. Most childcare programs in New Hampshire close between 5 p.m. and 6 p.m., which can make pickup difficult for families who work outside traditional working hours or commute. 
“The extended time will look a little bit different, but we’re hoping it will be really supportive for families,” McGuigan said. “It makes staffing more difficult though.”
In the early days of her program, Fisher said she’s trying to be flexible as the needs of her families, teachers and community at large fluctuate. Already, she is opening another toddler classroom, as she is “constantly getting interest” for toddler care, which is sparse in the Seacoast. She has also opened up parts of the space to homeschooling programs as a way to generate conversation and get more parents in the space. 
Additionally, Fisher wants her center to be more than “just childcare” and has connected families with early support and service resources, as well as bringing some of those supports on-site. As a parent and former social worker, Fisher said she knows how hard it is for parents to manage childcare and other services. 
“Our society is not built for working families, so for mom and dad or grandma to come pick up at 5 o’clock and then have to go to speech or OT afterwards. … We’re trying to incorporate as much as possible into that child’s day here for them,” she said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Proposed Federal Scholarship Tax Credit rules fail to win over CT educators
description: The U.S. Treasury Department released its proposed rules for the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit. CT educators don't like what they see.
text:
Connecticut education leaders still aren’t happy with the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit.
On Friday, the U.S. Treasury Department released its proposed rules for the program, which provides a dollar-for-dollar tax credit of up to $1,700 to individuals who donate to scholarship-granting organizations, known as SGOs. The rules clarify how SGOs should operate, who qualifies for scholarships and what role states have in regulating the program.
But public school advocates in the Nutmeg State still don’t like what they see. Everything they’d feared the FSTC would enable, they say, remains in play.
“I think [the rules] solidified for me exactly what we always knew: that this was a program that is going to be designed to hurt public education and basically help the rich,” said Jan Hochadel, an outgoing state senator and the president of AFT Connecticut, one of the state’s two major teachers’ unions.
Public education leaders made it abundantly clear in May they did not want Gov. Ned Lamont to opt Connecticut into the FSTC. They argued the program lacks oversight, exacerbates inequality and will likely prompt cuts to core federal education programs like Title 1 and the Individual with Disabilities Education Act.
At the time, Lamont said he’d rather wait for the federal government to release additional guidance before making a decision. 
On Tuesday, he told reporters he’ll be asking the feds for further clarification this week.
“I want to make sure this does not discriminate in any way against public education,” Lamont said. He added it should be transparent and carefully audited “given all the back-and-forth we have about not-for-profits.”
“I think we’ll know within a month or so,” Lamont said.
Lamont’s Republican opponent in this year’s gubernatorial election, Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, was an early supporter of the FSTC, telling the Connecticut Mirror in May that it is “literally free money” for the state. The Connecticut Mirror reached out to Fazio for comment on the Treasury’s new rules this week, but he did not respond in time for publication.
The new rules from the Treasury have not won over the FSTC’s critics, who are still urging Lamont not to opt in.
What the FSTC actually does
The FSTC is a scholarship program signed into law by President Donald Trump as part of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Individuals can donate up to $1,700 a year to an SGO, or $3,400 per household; SGOs then award the money to students as scholarships for a wide range of potential services, including tutoring, afterschool programming and private school tuition. Donors, meanwhile, get their donations paid back in full as a tax credit when they file their returns at the end of the year.
In effect, the federal government is paying for scholarships, with several steps in-between. At the heart of advocates’ concern is where the money would actually end up, and what redirecting federal dollars in this way will mean for public schools.
According to the Treasury’s proposed rules, states that opt in cannot prohibit SGOs from offering private school tuition scholarships — almost guaranteeing that some federal dollars will flow to private schools as a result of the FSTC. That alone is a red flag for public school advocates like Hochadel, who fear the FSTC is a step toward privatizing education nationwide.
“The incentive is to have more students go to private institutions,” Hochadel said. 
There is an income limit on which students qualify for scholarships, but it’s high: 300% of the area median income, which includes an estimated 96% of all students nationwide. 
Hochadel said she expects most students who get private school scholarships to come from affluent families, “so all they’re doing is getting more tax dollars sent to the rich.” And she said if there are students “on the cusp” for whom those scholarships make private school possible, their departure would cost public schools directly, because state funding is tied to enrollment.
Even a small number of students leaving public schools for private schools is more than some districts can afford, she said, pointing to ongoing concerns about Connecticut’s school funding system.
There are some who argue states can still make the FSTC into a boon for public school students. 
They note scholarships can go to those students, too — not for core services offered by schools themselves, but for things like high-dosage tutoring and afterschool programs provided by third-party vendors. And they point out that governors who delay won’t stop the FSTC from happening — they’ll only prevent their own states from getting a cut.
Those proponents include Nicole Pollock, the president of Democrats for Education Reform, an advocacy group that favors greater school choice. She laid out a vision for how state governments might direct FSTC dollars toward public school students.
“The way I think about design is, you should have a statewide SGO, or a collection of public school-serving SGOs, that focus on a particular goal for the state” such as early literacy, Pollock said. “And then that organization partners with LEAs [Local Education Agencies] and raises money.”
She offered Colorado, one of the only states with Democratic governors to opt in yet, as a case in point. There’s now an SGO that partners with districts there to deliver “district-aligned interventions.”
Pollock said it’s also possible to get a state’s major employers in on the arrangement. For example, say an SGO forms around scholarships to give public school students access to technical career training.
“At that table sits your top 10 employers in the state, right? And part of their commitment is that they will be offering this [FSTC] program to their employees as a deduction program,” Pollock said. 
In other words, employees donate to the SGO automatically through payroll deductions, and the SGO gives scholarships to students to get workforce training. Because it’s a dollar-for-dollar tax credit, employees can lower their federal withholdings at the same time, ensuring they don’t see any change to their paychecks.
“It doesn’t require sophisticated systems to do that,” Pollock said. “Most payroll providers do wage garnishment or wage adjustments … like this all the time.”
But Fran Rabinowitz, executive director of the Connecticut Association of Public School Superintendents, said setting up an SGO for a public school isn’t as easy as it sounds.
“I’ve set up 501(c)(3)s. CAPSS became a 501(c)(3) about five years ago, and it cost quite a bit of dollars … and attorney time,” Rabinowitz said. “I created a 501(c)(3) with a foundation in Bridgeport, and that took nearly a year.” 
Considering the FSTC begins operating in January, that doesn’t leave much time for states to get everything set up.
Conversely, Rabinowitz said, “all of the private schools are very used to having 501(c)(3)s and setting up scholarship programs.” In effect, they’re starting the competition already ahead, she said.
Pollock acknowledged that the FSTC does create market competition for education resources, “and that is an uncomfortable place for a lot of folks … who are concerned about the movement around ESAs [Education Savings Accounts] and choice.”
However, she said the Treasury guidance “creates more of a regulated market … that makes it more possible and easier for high-poverty districts and students in high-poverty areas to participate.”
Among those regulations are safe harbor rules that reduce the administrative burden on SGOs serving high-need students. More specifically, SGOs don’t have to conduct income verification for students enrolled in certain social programs, residing in qualified census tracts or living in foster care.
“That’s like a market signal … to drive those resources administratively into more high-need districts or for high-need students,” Pollock said.
Rabinowitz said she doesn’t buy that. She expects families to donate primarily to SGOs that benefit their own students and communities — which, if true, would suggest more affluent communities with an abundance of disposable income will see more scholarships.
“You’re certainly not going to have as many families in Hartford as you might have in Simsbury who can afford to send up to $1,700 to an SGO,” Rabinowitz said. 
Connecticut Education Association President Kate Dias speaks alongside fellow union members at a press conference on Apr. 8, 2026. Credit: Theo Peck-Suzuki / CT Mirror
Other concerns
Ultimately, the FSTC will cost the federal government money. Exactly how much will depend on how many people donate to SGOs and claim the credit — estimates range from a few hundred million to tens of billions annually.
In theory, Congress will have to offset that lost revenue somewhere, and public school advocates are pretty sure they know how it will happen.
“Connecting the dots, they’re going to take it away from education,” Hochadel said — in other words, cutting core public education programs like Title I and the Individual with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA).
Connecticut Education Association President Kate Dias said many of those programs already aren’t funded as much as they should be. The federal government’s own goal is to fund 40% of IDEA; Dias said it currently funds closer to 14%.
“If you look at the dialogue in Connecticut around education funding, it is all about special education,” Dias said. “We are making up the difference.” Most special education costs fall on local districts, and the state does not weigh its contribution based on how many special education students a district has.
The problem will only get worse if federal funding shrinks further, Dias said. Connecticut towns may end up having to pay even more out of local property taxes to fund those services, she said.
Pollock pushed back on those concerns. She said it’s highly unlikely that the federal government — notorious for operating at a glacial pace — will do anything in response to the FSTC’s costs in the next two to three years. By then, she expects Democrats to once again be in control in Washington.
She also offered a different perspective on the $1,700 tax credit itself.
“If you proportionally thought about that $1,700 as if it was the federal budget for this country, less than 20 of those dollars would be going into K-12 education,” Pollock said. Viewed that way, sending $1,700 directly to education looks more like “supercharging” education funding.
Except, Rabinowitz noted, those dollars can’t go toward a public school’s core operations. “It can be used for tutoring and for afterschool programs. That doesn’t speak to staffing. That doesn’t speak to what goes on in classrooms all day long,” she said.
Rabinowitz also raised concerns about oversight.
“Yes, the governor has to approve that SGO, but they get to use 10% of whatever they collect for administrative costs. … And I’m just not so sure that all of that money and funding will go in the direction that we would want it to,” Rabinowitz said.
Dias was blunter. 
“We don’t have a great history with this kind of stuff in CT,” Dias said. “We have Kosta Diamantis who’s in Greece, we have an FBI investigation in terms of moneys being used improperly,” she said, referring to the former state budget official who oversaw school construction contracts, was convicted of extortion and bribery in connection with those deals, and is currently a fugitive in Greece.
“SGOs can go under, go to Greece, and … what’s the recourse?” Dias added.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: A peace plan for New Hampshire Democrats’ primary wars
description: The shooting war with Iran and the trade “war” with Canada are not the only conflicts roiling American political life these days. In our own backyard, the New Hampshire Democratic Party and the Democratic National Committee are waging a continuing battle over New Hampshire’s place in the queue of Democratic primaries for 2028. Because both […]
text:
New Hampshire Secretary of State Dave Scanlan takes questions from reporters in the State House visitor center shortly after announcing the date of the 2024 New Hampshire presidential primary. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)The shooting war with Iran and the trade “war” with Canada are not the only conflicts roiling American political life these days. In our own backyard, the New Hampshire Democratic Party and the Democratic National Committee are waging a continuing battle over New Hampshire’s place in the queue of Democratic primaries for 2028. 
Because both sides appear “dug in” to dubious positions, cooler heads must prevail.
The current dustup dates to the 2024 presidential primary season, when the DNC dropped New Hampshire from its traditional leadoff spot in favor of South Carolina. New Hampshire balked, citing its traditional “first in the nation” role and a state law that requires its primary to occur seven days or more before a primary in another state. 
Honoring that law, New Hampshire Democrats retained their preferred date, but President Joe Biden followed the DNC rule instead by declining to appear on the New Hampshire primary ballot. Ultimately, the DNC declined to punish New Hampshire for its transgression and even permitted the state’s delegates to be seated at the party’s national convention.
But the temporary fix did not resolve the conflict. 
In August the DNC denied New Hampshire the leadoff slot in the primary schedule for 2028, moving it to third in line, behind South Carolina and Nevada, two larger, more racially diverse states. Once again, New Hampshire Democrats are crying foul, while trumpeting their state’s capacity for evaluating presidential candidates because of its tradition of voters meeting them in small venues.
Neither the DNC’s concern for racial diversity nor New Hampshire’s reputed political skills justify the train wreck that will likely result from a standoff over the 2028 primary calendar. 
The Republicans who control the state’s government likely will not support a repeal of the law that requires holding New Hampshire’s primary first because, at least to date, repeal would help only the Democrats. As long as that law is in effect, though, Democrats face an unhappy choice between holding their primary on the DNC’s preferred date, hence violating state law and having to finance the election themselves, and holding it on their preferred date, thereby incurring the wrath of the DNC and possibly facing a candidate boycott. Furthermore, New Hampshire cannot assume that in 2028, the DNC will capitulate and seat the state’s national convention delegates, as occurred in 2024.
Happily, the train wreck is avoidable because both sides’ interests can be served without a major change to the primary schedule.
 The DNC can honor and reward racial diversity even if New Hampshire’s primary occurs first, so long as the South Carolina, Nevada, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia primaries follow soon thereafter. That arrangement would deviate only slightly from the schedule announced in August. And even if New Hampshire produces a quirky result, it could be countered by a succession of contrary verdicts in the other early primary states. 
One primary victory does not make a presidential nominee, especially in today’s nationalized, media-saturated electoral environment. Besides, letting New Hampshire go first would acknowledge the state’s continued value as a relatively inexpensive place to campaign that lets candidates meet voters face-to-face. 
Thus, in the near term, the DNC should tweak its 2028 calendar to put New Hampshire at the front of the line. In the longer term, especially if Democrats regain control in Concord, they should repeal the presidential primary law that threatens to make their state party a pariah in presidential politics. Then the DNC could devise a national primary schedule that alternates the leadoff position from among small states such as Delaware, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont, any of which would enable relatively inexpensive “retail” politics. That system would preserve face-to-face campaigning in a fairer way than the traditional “New Hampshire first” practice does. 
New Hampshire is important to the lineup, but it should not be the leadoff hitter every four years.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall keeps punching himself in the face. Kansans raise a bemused eyebrow.
description: Visualize a clenched fist, fingers tight and knuckles braced, pulled back to strike. Visualize that fist taking an unexpected turn, avoiding an opponent and instead circling back to slam into its owner’s face. I won’t describe the sights and sounds that follow, just know that the fighter for some unholy reason keeps clenching that fist […]
text:
U.S. Sen Roger Marshall pauses during the debate at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson on Sept. 12. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)Visualize a clenched fist, fingers tight and knuckles braced, pulled back to strike.
Visualize that fist taking an unexpected turn, avoiding an opponent and instead circling back to slam into its owner’s face. I won’t describe the sights and sounds that follow, just know that the fighter for some unholy reason keeps clenching that fist and striking his own face, over and over and over.
Visualize U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall’s recent moves in his re-election campaign.
Fresh attacks on his Democratic rival. the Rev. Adam Hamilton of Leawood, misfired after a New York Post story turned out to rehash Kansas Reflector reporting from months ago about abuse at a church camp. Don’t believe me? Look here and here for our coverage from May and July.
The Post even cited our reporting four times in that single article! Marshall’s staffers — and their out-of-state financiers — planned a juicy smear campaign against their opponent. I understand. But reanimating allegations that were extensively covered by local news media sure smells like desperation.
That wasn’t the end of the embarrassment. A Marshall ad about the allegations had to be revised after including footage from other Kansas camps. Visuals showing Linwood’s Tall Oaks Camp and Conference Center, along with Lacygne’s Valley Cabins, illustrated the attack.
Whoops! A little slip-up there.
Actually not so little, given that actual Tall Oaks campers appeared in the ad. I’m sure they won’t face any scrutiny or humiliation after being used as political props. You could describe Marshall’s campaign in many ways after this episode — just don’t use the words “careful,” “attentive to detail,” or “grounded in reality.”
Finally, Marshall himself felt the need to inflict damage on his efforts to secure another six years in Washington, D.C.
In an “exclusive” with the Washington Examiner — the favorite news source of at least two or three Kansans — Marshall proclaimed that Hamilton ““lives in a bubble. Johnson County is one of the wealthiest counties in the country.”
Wait, did I read that correctly?
Roger Marshall decided to badmouth the most populous county in Kansas? I would hope someone in the campaign explains to Marshall that you need more voters to cast their ballots for you than your opponent to win elections. It’s a fairly fundamental fact!
I understand that the incumbent wants to underscore his rural roots, but surely you could do that without insulting a huge swath of Kansans. Also, what’s wrong with being rich? Wasn’t Marshall building his wealth when he sued more than 700 patients? I’m reliably informed by the good doctor’s fans on social media that he deserved payment for his work.
Don’t Johnson County doctors and lawyers and dentists deserve the same opportunities?
We’ve watched Marshall’s team follow this dismal playbook before. Back in May 2025, his chief of staff Brent Robertson ridiculed residents who showed up for a feisty town hall: “Real Kansans overwhelmingly support President Trump’s DOGE initiative, shrinking the size of the federal government, and firing career bureaucrats. Local Oakley citizens had no clue who these people were and were embarrassed by the behavior.”
Note that term: “real Kansans.” Marshall has followed the example of his employee and divided the people of this great state into the deserving and undeserving, the virtuous and the sinful, the rural and the urban.
Division didn’t work out for him 19 months ago. I’m not sure why he thinks it will now.
Roger Marshall just cant stop walloping himself in the face.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: 7th CD candidates Republican Michael Alfonso and Democrat Fred Clark debate
description: Republican Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, and Democrat Fred Clark, a conservationist and former state lawmaker, faced off Wednesday night in the only scheduled debate in the race for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.  The district, which represents the Northwoods, is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Tom T[...]
text:
Wisconsin 7th Congressional District candidates Democrat Fred Clark, a conservationist and former state lawmaker, and Republican Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, faced off Wednesday night in a debate. (Screenshot via WDIO YouTube)Republican Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, and Democrat Fred Clark, a conservationist and former state lawmaker, faced off Wednesday night in the only scheduled debate in the race for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. 
The district, which represents the Northwoods, is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is running for governor. He was first elected in a 2020 special election after Duffy resigned the seat, saying he wanted to focus on his family. 
Duffy, who President Donald Trump appointed transportation secretary last year, has helped bankroll and provide support for his 26-year-old son-in-law’s campaign. 
Alfonso, who is married to Evita Duffy, has spent much of the campaign touting an endorsement from Trump and faced criticism about his lack of work experience. After he went to college, he worked for as a producer on Dan Bongino’s podcast in Florida for about a year. He said during the Republican primary that he has worked as an accountant for a church since moving back to Wisconsin.
Clark, a 67-year-old forester, is looking to flip the seat for the first time in 16 years, though it will be an uphill battle. Prior to Tiffany and Duffy, the seat was held from 1969 to 2011 by Democrat Dave Obey, the longest serving U.S. House member in Wisconsin history.
Wednesday’s debate covered an array of issues, including the cost of housing and gas, data centers, the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline and how northern Wisconsin can keep its residents from leaving. Throughout, Alfonso staked out positions that leaned towards cutting regulation and reducing government involvement, while Clark advocated for a balance of government investments and regulations.
One of the first topics was affordability as well as helping support residents in the 7th Congressional District. Alfonso brought up gas prices and argued that the U.S. needs to be more energy independent. 
“We cannot be relying on nations that hate us for stability in our oil prices,” Alfonso said. “Now, it’s very simple. We need to make sure that we are drilling here and that we’re producing energy here in a safe manner.”
Diesel prices have risen to record highs, in part due to the war in Iran launched by the Trump administration. Clark called for better foreign policy to help address the rising cost of fuel.  
“As Michael Alfonso pointed out, gas prices and diesel prices are through the roof high as a result of this administration’s war in Iran, which was started without a plan with no plan to get out, but the reality here is that oil prices are a global commodity, and what happens in the Middle East affects oil prices here at home, no matter how much we pump,” Clark said. “We’ve got to get smart about a trade policy and a foreign policy that reduces the risk and the chaos that we’ve been experiencing in the last 18 months.”
The war in Iran also came up later in the debate. 
Clark said that Congress needs to take seriously its job of deciding whether the country should go to war. 
Alfonso said that the U.S. needs to stop acting as the world’s “policeman” and needs to stop being involved in foreign conflict altogether — but then pivoted to defending Trump’s decisions in Iran. 
“We are not going to bring peace to the Middle East, but what we can do is stop them from having a nuclear weapon. Iran is a country that has hated us for decades. President Trump had the bravery to step in and make sure that these people do not have a nuclear bomb to use against us,” Alfonso said.  
One of Trump’s justifications for launching a war in Iran was to prevent it from developing a nuclear weapon. According to Reuters, there was no credible indication of Iran having a coordinated weapons program in the leadup to the beginning of the conflict, though Iran was enriching uranium.
Alfonso said that he supports Line 5, a 645-mile petroleum pipeline owned and operated by Enbridge that runs through Wisconsin. He criticized Clark for not being supportive of the pipeline.
“Line 5 is one of these things that brings costs down for every single family in Northern Wisconsin,” Alfonso said. “How can you not support it?” 
Clark said that he doesn’t want to shut down Line 5, but said there needs to be some federal guardrails on setting lines. In August, Line 5 had a leak that is the largest oil and gas pipeline spill reported in Wisconsin in more than 50 years.
“The risk of a spill in the Lake Superior watershed, in the river watershed and Lake Superior is extraordinarily high, and the environmental impact of that would affect this area for generations, but it also brings natural gas liquids here to Wisconsin and Michigan,” Clark said. “I’ve not called for it to be shut down, but we do need a law at the federal level to allow basically the opportunity to cite these lines. Right now, nowhere in federal law is there any law or any agency that oversees line setting where these things are placed, and we need that just the same way that we needed for transmission lines and other public utilities. I want to see that change.” 
Both candidates also discussed bringing down the cost of housing, though their approaches were starkly different.
Alfonso said the government should cut regulations on home building. 
“The number one thing we can do is cut red tape, especially around housing,” Alfonso said. “I worked in construction, and I know that it costs almost $50,000 before you can even break ground on a new home. If you want to make housing more affordable and have young families move back to the district, that’s a great step to take.” 
Clark said there needs to be programs to help people looking to buy their first home as well as support from the government and private sector that can make manufacturing more affordable, including by using wood from Wisconsin. 
“We need to be smart about it,” Clark said. “It isn’t just eliminating all the rules and regulations.”
Alfonso worked in construction while in school at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. During the debate, Alfonso criticized “these ridiculous public universities that do nothing but indoctrinate our students” and called for taking away funding from them and putting it towards trade schools, saying that that would help keep young people from moving away. 
“We need to be pushing our young people towards trade schools that will actually teach them a useful skill in sending instead of sending them off to a crazy wealth university that will do nothing but indoctrinate them and put them deeper into debt, so it’s even more difficult to buy your first home,” Alfonso said. “The best part about trade schools is the students that graduate from these trade schools stay in Wisconsin.” 
Clark said that he has heard from mayors and small town leaders from across northern Wisconsin that young people aren’t staying in their communities due to a lack of affordable housing, childcare and public investments, which “make people want to live in a place.” 
“Until we change that… our economies are not going to be able to thrive,” Clark said. “There is a smart role for government to do that. It doesn’t mean more regulation. It means the right investments in the right places. It means helping make housing more affordable. It means helping families afford childcare.” 
On the topic of education, Alfonso said he also supports eliminating the Department of Education, saying that he doesn’t think the agency should have any say over what is happening in local Wisconsin schools. 
Alfonso then pivoted the question to being about bathrooms. Alfonso has used the issue of bathrooms being used by transgender students as an issue throughout his campaign.
“So you know what the Department of Education is responsible for? Boys and girls bathrooms,” Alfonso said, mentioning the New Richmond school district, where the Department of Education had launched an investigation over its policies surrounding bathrooms. 
Alfonso asked if Clark supports the federal agency on that issue. 
“I don’t think the federal government needs to be deciding what bathrooms” students use, Clark said. “I trust teachers and school administrators and parents make that decision in their community schools.” 
The candidates also answered questions about data centers, which across the country have become major issues in political campaigns. 
Alfonso said that data centers should use “closed loop” water systems, that they should not raise energy costs and that local communities should have control over whether data centers are built. He said the federal government should not be stepping in to decide those matters.
“If you were to ask me, do I want a data center in Hayward, Wisconsin, where I live? Absolutely not, but I’ll tell you what the federal government does not have a role in stepping in,” Alfonso said.
In response, Clark asked Alfonso, “Are you willing to tell the president that he’s wrong to want to preempt states from having regulations around artificial intelligence and that he’s wrong to let Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos basically run the table wherever they want to when it comes to AI and data centers?”
A provision in Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” Law in 2025 that passed the U.S. House, but was removed in the Senate would have prevented states from being able to regulate AI for 10 years and limited states’ ability to restrict or tax AI data centers. Trump has also signed executive orders aimed at discouraging states from regulating AI. 
“President Trump was actually very clear with this. He said, if you’re a local municipality and you don’t want one, you don’t need one. President Trump truly listens to the people, I mean, we look at issues like the data center issue. It’s very clear people in northern Wisconsin don’t want it, but I can’t say the same for Kansas. I’ve never been there if they want one. It’s not the federal government’s job to step in and say, no, it’s the state or local government,” Alfonso said. 
Trump recently said that communities that don’t want data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.” 
In his closing statement, Alfonso said that the election would be about “common sense versus crazy.” 
“I support getting the government out of the way of business so that we can lower costs for Wisconsin families. That’s my number one priority,” Alfonso said. “I want to work to make sure that everyone in Wisconsin can afford healthcare. I want to make sure that every small business owner is able to grow, and I also want to make sure that the young people that are born in northern Wisconsin have a northern Wisconsin that they can come back to.” 
Clark said in his closing statement that northern Wisconsin has “everything we need to lead good lives with prosperous businesses,” and that its  farms, forests, water and tourism are assets.
“For that to work for all of us, we need a government that works that sets fair rules of the game, and that allows us businesses to grow and make the right investments to help make that happen,” Clark said. “We’re not going to see people moving back to Northern Wisconsin if that doesn’t happen. We’re not going to see businesses thrive and survive. There’s a partnership there that has to work.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Advisory group zeroes in on recommendations to regulate data center energy use
description: As the Maine Data Center Advisory Council begins drafting recommendations for the upcoming Legislature to regulate data centers, energy use is emerging as a key and contentious issue.  The council met Wednesday and began to refine its initial draft recommendations, which are due to lawmakers in a final report in January. Much of the discussion […]
text:
An explosion of data center facilities, including the one pictured here in northeast Oregon on May 18 have been built along the Columbia River Gorge during the last few years. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)As the Maine Data Center Advisory Council begins drafting recommendations for the upcoming Legislature to regulate data centers, energy use is emerging as a key and contentious issue. 
The council met Wednesday and began to refine its initial draft recommendations, which are due to lawmakers in a final report in January. Much of the discussion related to energy, which has been a key concern of communities across the country with the rapid expansion of large scale data center development. 
Celina Cunningham, acting commissioner of the Maine Department of Energy Resources, said the main focus of the energy recommendations was to ensure that the power costs “associated with large data centers should be borne by the data centers, not Maine people and businesses.” 
Patrick Scully, a member of the Maine Public Utilities Commission, said he was concerned that data centers could inadvertently drive up prices in Maine’s energy supply market, because of the increased consumption and demand. He compared it to Maine’s natural gas usage during winter heating. 
“Even if we have enough steel in the ground, we can see in the winter when demand gets really high that those energy market prices spike pretty dramatically,” he said. 
Scully said another issue the PUC is considering is the secondary impacts on grid capacity. Even if the regional power grid has the capacity for a data center to connect, it could max out the existing capacity.
And without that wiggle room, it raises prices for natural load growth or other new, smaller customers trying to connect.
“So you’ve lost the headroom because the data center came in and ate it up, and so those next customers coming along — that we might very well want to see — might be facing big costs to accommodate their interconnection, where those costs are really a consequence of the data center eating up the available headroom,” Scully said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Public Advocate Heather Sanborn also raised concerns about utilities and local communities making upgrades in anticipation of a data center that then never arrives. 
“We need to give some consideration to what happens if a data center comes in and there’s a lot of investment made in order to upscale infrastructure to meet the needs of that data center, and then the data center disappears,” Sanborn said. “This is a particular issue, not just for electric utility, but potentially for water as well.”
The 17 council members weren’t in agreement on all the recommendations, and disagreed on what to do about clean energy requirements. The preliminary draft recommends that the state require data centers to adhere to Maine’s existing clean energy laws and procure some amount of energy generated by renewable sources. 
Jack Shapiro, with the Natural Resources Council of Maine, suggested that the state should require data centers to procure more clean energy. 
“It feels to me like a simpler way to do it is to actually just create a requirement that that capacity and energy that is being procured by the facility would just need to be 100% clean because we’re only 14 years from that requirement,” he said, referring to the state’s commitment to reach carbon neutrality by 2040.
But Amy Turner, CEO of Fox Islands Electric Cooperative, pushed back and argued that Maine’s clean energy laws are aimed at utilities, not customers like data centers. 
“The prescriptive portion in this clean energy section could be like a de facto ban effectively on data centers, because it’s not going to be practical or feasible or economically possible for developers to work within these guidelines,” Turner said. 
Sanborn countered that the state can’t control all aspects of the broader energy market, but requiring data centers to bring their own clean energy is one way to protect ratepayers. 
“What we can do is say what these data centers have to do in terms of bringing their own clean energy and capacity, as a way of trying to ensure that those new entrants into the market aren’t disproportionately driving up costs for the rest of us,” she said. 
The question of mandatory requirements versus flexible recommendations was a recurring theme of the meeting. 
Cunningham noted that any regulations will need to be able to adapt as the industry develops. 
“We want to make sure that we continue to have ratepayer protections in place even as the data center market evolves,” Cunningham said. 
Michael Duguay, commissioner of the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development, argued such an approach would deter development. “I do think having something that’s prescriptive up front, sadly, as a default, creates more obstacles,” he said. 
But Shapiro noted that public sentiment about data centers is “dire” and the council should have stricter suggestions to make sure residents are confident in the regulations. Otherwise, he said, “we’re just going to see local moratoriums and opposition, and none of the projects will ever get built, which is the other side of the tightrope between it being sort of prescriptive. “
The council also discussed the initial recommendations focused on the environment and public health; and community and economic development. 
The group will continue to meet and discuss the recommendations, and a final draft will be shared for public comment later this year.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: A construction ban on data centers would be better for Ohio than the status quo, study says
description: Given the amount of data center construction already in Ohio, the best economic deal going forward would be to require all new ones to use 90% renewable energy, a new cost-benefit analysis has found. The next-best deal would be to ban new construction altogether, it said.  Ohio has the fourth-most data centers of any state, […]
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Given the amount of data center construction already in Ohio, the best economic deal going forward would be to require all new ones to use 90% renewable energy, a new cost-benefit analysis has found. The next-best deal would be to ban new construction altogether, it said. 
Ohio has the fourth-most data centers of any state, and after being forced to provide $2.3 billion in subsidies via tax breaks, taxpayers are questioning whether they’re really a good thing.
The centers have  more than doubled the state’s electricity consumption, they generate noise and air pollution, the AI they generate is causing serious social harms, leaders of the big AI companies warn of possible calamities, and they’ve predicted that their machines will take millions of Americans’ jobs.
With these concerns in the background, the Columbus firm Scioto Analysis undertook a straight dollars-and-cents look at future data center development in Ohio. 
The Buckeye State ranks only behind Virginia, Texas and California in the number of data centers. And the gargantuan facilities are poised to move into rural parts of Ohio and other Midwestern states in a big way.
“About 87% of current data centers in the United States are in urban areas, while 67% of planned data centers across the country are in rural areas, driven by the land and power requirements of modern hyperscale facilities,” the Scioto Analysis report said. 
“Data centers in the Midwest are expected to grow by the highest percentage: a projected 64% increase compared to current data centers. As of 2026, 38% of Americans live within five miles of at least one operational data center.”
One criticism of data center economics is that while they create initial construction jobs, once completed they only require a skeleton staff to make sure the machines keep running. 
The Scioto Analysis study credits data center development with 96,000 new jobs and $62 billion in social benefits to Ohio since 2013, but it also asks what new benefits they’ll create going forward.
A big factor in that is the huge electricity drain they’ll create and the social cost of all the pollution it will generate, the study notes.
“If every planned project comes online by 2028, the number of data centers in Ohio will increase by half, their annual energy draw will more than triple, and their annual carbon emissions will more than triple,” the cost-benefit analysis says. 
“In 2026, Ohio data centers use enough electricity to power 5.7 million homes, which is more than the 5.4 million homes in Ohio. By 2028, we predict they will use enough electricity to power about 3.5 times as many homes as there are in Ohio.”
Rob Moore, the principal of Scioto Analysis, said it’s important not to forget about the cost a business enterprise imposes on third parties — such as that which pollution imposes on the public.
“While data centers present a new category of high-intensity energy use in the state, they still present the same problems as transportation, manufacturing or power generation in general: emissions that are not priced will lead to local air-quality issues, lung and heart conditions and higher levels of carbon emissions,” Moore said in a text message.  
He and his team looked at five scenarios and ran 10,000 simulations of what would happen between 2027 and 2034 with different variables. 
The values the analysis arrived at are expressed in terms of “benefit-cost ratio.” Maintaining the status quo scored 1.04, meaning benefits only slightly outweighed costs.
Benefit-cost ratios for the other scenarios, in descending order of public benefit:

Data center generates its own power, 10% gas, 90% renewable — 2.9
Ban on new data center construction — 2.7
Data center generates its own power, 50% gas, 50% renewable — 2.5
Data center generates its own power, 90% natural gas, 10% renewable — 2.2

In other words, according to the analysis, forcing renewables to be used to generate power and an outright ban on new data center constructions would be the biggest improvement over what we’re doing now.
“A ban on construction produces a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than the status quo,” the report said. “This is because most employment benefits from existing data centers remain, while the cost of higher electricity prices to ratepayers falls. 
“A behind-the-meter requirement with 90% natural gas produces about the same net present value, but a lower benefit-cost ratio. A behind-the-meter requirement with 90% renewables produces both the highest net present value and the highest benefit-cost ratio.”
The analysis came with an important caveat, however. If data centers produce more jobs than expected, a ban or a heavy renewable requirement won’t look so good.
“Our results depend heavily on our employment assumptions,” it said. “If we are overestimating how much data centers raise employment and earnings, even a ban or a 90% renewables requirement could have a negative net present value. If we are underestimating these effects, every alternative looks much better. Across our other tests, the status quo is the alternative most likely to have costs that exceed its benefits.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Can Tom Tiffany survive ties to toxic Donald Trump?
description: It is still weeks until the Nov. 3 midterm, but the early returns are in for Donald Trump, who wants voters to pretend he is on the ballot.   Trump is at his lowest point ever in Wisconsin, with 60% of registered voters disapproving of him, 53% strongly, Marquette University polling says.  Yet Tom Tiffany, Trump’s […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, Republican candidate for Wisconsin governor, and President Donald Trump (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner and Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)It is still weeks until the Nov. 3 midterm, but the early returns are in for Donald Trump, who wants voters to pretend he is on the ballot.  
Trump is at his lowest point ever in Wisconsin, with 60% of registered voters disapproving of him, 53% strongly, Marquette University polling says. 
Yet Tom Tiffany, Trump’s endorsed candidate for governor and a 100% supporter of his policies — which almost all poll even worse than Trump himself — is virtually tied with Dem David Crowley.  A good chunk of the electorate has not yet made the Tiffany-Trump connection. That may be the deciding factor over the home stretch.
Trump’s Iran war and its impact on skyrocketing gasoline and diesel prices are widely unpopular, and Tiffany has repeatedly voted to support the war and to leave  Trump unchecked.  One new Crowley TV spot takes Tiffany’s voting record  head-on, calling Tiffany “loyal to Trump, not Wisconsin.”  Trump is toxic.  Crowley is not just  running against “three billionaires” who have bought Tiffany with over $45 million — the majority of the money raised by the Republican gubernatorial  campaign.  Diane Hendricks, along with Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, are Trump’s billionaires. 
When Trump lost the 2020 election, the Uihleins provided millions of dollars to political groups that helped organize and promote the events of Jan. 6, 2021. And prior to the violent insurrection that day, Trump accomplice Tiffany  signed on to a brief to overturn the outcome of the 2020 election, voted against certifying the election results in Arizona and Pennsylvania, and said he would have opposed the will of Wisconsin voters and invalidated our state’s electoral votes, too.
This week, in an interview with WLUK in the Fox Valley, Tiffany was asked if he’d be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump. Tiffany’s response: “They should check Tom Tiffany’s record.” 
Tiffany’s record in Washington is one of rubber stamping everything Trump has done to make things worse for Wisconsin. One hundred per cent of the time. Tiffany has supported Trump’s chaotic trade wars and reckless tariffs that have devastated farmers and raised the cost of groceries. He voted for healthcare cuts and rising insurance premiums for working families to pay for…you guessed it — tax breaks for Trump’s billionaires. 
Craig Gilbert, longtime Journal Sentinel political reporter who analyzes, interprets and explains polls, put it this way in his piece based on the latest MU poll: “Trump disapprovers” — those who disapprove of Trump — are a key voting bloc.
Tiffany now gets 11% of those voters.  Gilbert says he needs 15 to 20% to get to a majority on Nov. 3.  Crowley has a big lead among independent voters, but Tiffany is chipping away at that with his negative TV onslaught funded by the Trump billionaires. 
The MU poll shows 81% of independents disapprove of Trump, and even 62% of non-MAGA Republicans disapprove.  Those voters will be the target audience as Election Day approaches. 
As I was writing this, as if to underscore my point,  the Crowley campaign just launched a hard-hitting TV spot that makes the connection between Tiffany and Trump.  The subject line on a Crowley fund-raising email today is “100 percent of the time.” You can expect to hear a lot more about Tiffany and Trump between now and Nov. 3.
Voters don’t need to pretend Trump is on the ballot. For Wisconsin voters who will decide the outcome of the governor’s race, he is.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Woof! Animal welfare advocates want Georgians to know their state lawmaker’s record on pet issues
description: The dogs and cats in your life don’t get a vote on Nov. 3, so they’re counting on you to get it right. That’s the message from the Georgia Pet Coalition, a nonpartisan group of Georgia humans who advocate state and local governments on behalf of the state’s companion animals. “We do not endorse candidates, […]
text:
State Rep. Sharon Cooper models a shirt featuring her corgi, Maggie, named for former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. Cooper has sponsored pet-related legislation including a bill to protect pets in family violence proceedings. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThe dogs and cats in your life don’t get a vote on Nov. 3, so they’re counting on you to get it right.
That’s the message from the Georgia Pet Coalition, a nonpartisan group of Georgia humans who advocate state and local governments on behalf of the state’s companion animals.
“We do not endorse candidates, and we remain nonpartisan,” said Peggy McCarthey of the coalition’s board of directors. “But we do want to educate our voters about what the pertinent issues are.”
Dogs and animal advocates gathered at the GeorgiaCapitol in 2025. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
The coalition recently sent supporters legislative scorecards for the state House and Senate as well as a list of animal welfare-related questions to ask candidates at town halls and community events ahead of next month’s big midterm election.
McCarthey said speaking out on behalf of pets doesn’t have to mean lobbying lawmakers under the Gold Dome.
“It’s not even going to the Capitol,” McCarthey said. “It’s meeting with your local lawmakers, your city councils, your county commissions, making appointments, meeting them in person, and being polite and respectful and providing education and resources. And the same thing for state lawmakers.”
This year, McCarthey said six of the nine bills they supported passed with broad bipartisan support, and in 2025, that number was seven out of 10.
Pet coalition-supported bills that have passed in recent years have dealt with some weighty issues like adding protections for household pets in cases of family violence and establishing a database of animal cruelty offenders to prevent animals from being placed in dangerous situations.
McCarthey said it’s not hard to find animal lovers among Georgia lawmakers, and when she walks into committee rooms at the Capitol, it’s not uncommon for lawmakers to pull out their phones and proudly show off photos of their own pets.
But she said Georgia still has plenty of room for progress, especially when it comes to the number of homeless cats and dogs. Coalition data shows the number of dogs that died in Georgia public shelters grew to over 20,000 between 2021 and 2025, increasing by nearly 10,000 dogs during that timeframe.
“Even if you don’t care about animals and their well-being, lawmakers need to care about public health, and that does involve pet population management,” she said.
McCarthey said high numbers of stray animals in communities can mean diseases transmitted to humans, bite incidents, traffic accidents and higher cost for taxpayer-funded shelters.
“So by investing upstream in something like pet population management, which means access to affordable spay and neuter, now you prevent a large amount of these downstream consequences,” she said.
State Rep. Marvin Lim. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Norcross Democratic state Rep. Marvin Lim, who has sponsored animal welfare legislation and hosted pet vaccination, microchipping and spaying and neutering events in his district, said lawmakers largely agree about protecting animals, but a sticking point often comes during appropriations as lawmakers are looking to make the budget leaner.
The governor vetoed more than $300 million in new spending, including funding for domestic violence and sexual assault programs, this year to help pay for an income tax package that created a $1.3 billion deficit.
“When you have to balance the budget, as is constitutionally required here in Georgia, there wasn’t enough money for things like sexual assault centers, domestic violence centers,” he said. “So without even saying, ‘Oh, we would prioritize that over animal welfare or animal-related legislation,’ we are just seeing all sorts of things that are important being cut.”
Other issues, like proposed statewide bans on tethering dogs or cockfighting, have seen opposition on cultural grounds, he said. Georgia is the only state where cockfighting is not a felony.
“The closer you get to maybe farming practices or practices that have been generally accepted, particularly in non-urban areas, the more, I suppose, pointed or controversial it can be,” he said.
State Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republican state Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick of Marietta has sponsored animal welfare bills including one creating partial student loan repayments for veterinarians who work in shelters or sterilization clinics. She said there are several bills that have failed in the past that she hopes to see action on, including the cockfighting bill and one she sponsored to provide legal protections for people who damage property to rescue animals from hot cars.
“We’ve still got work to do,” she said. “We’ve still got puppy mills all over the place, and those create a huge burden on the rescue organizations and the counties who have to clean up the mess.”
“Everybody cares about animals, and they are a big part of many of our lives,” she said. “And people don’t like seeing animals being treated poorly, just the public doesn’t like it, and the legislators are people too, so they don’t like it either.”

text:
Republican U.S. Senator Bernie Moreno (right), Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and leaders from Bayer speak to the media. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Bayer is building a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in New Albany, Ohio, the company has announced.
This will create 1,500 construction jobs and 600 highly-skilled permanent jobs “focused on developing the compounds that make Bayer’s medicines work,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said. 
“This is an historic win for Ohio,” DeWine said. “It is by far Ohio’s largest international healthcare project and the largest German direct investment in Ohio history.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said this will “impact multiple generations.”
“The new site will be home to manufacturing expertise and a skilled workforce that will strengthen our ability to deliver innovative, high-quality medicines to patients both in the United States and abroad,” Anderson said. 
Anderson wouldn’t say what other cities were finalists for the plant. 
“We saw some really great sites, but the combination of the workforce, the proximity to important healthcare institutions, and research institutions, and frankly the attitude of everyone we worked with from JobsOhio, the state leaders, the federal leaders, it made a difference.” 
Anderson said he expects the new plant will mostly hire people from Ohio. 
“If we wanted people from someplace else, we would have gone there,” he said. 
The Ohio Life Science Training Center in New Albany, a $30 million building expected to open next year, will be used to prepare people for careers in pharmaceutical biomanufacturing and Bayer will build a production facility five miles away in New Albany. 
“In just a year, newly certified Ohioans will walk out of this training center, drive a few miles down the road, and go to work making the ingredients for medicines that will improve lives all over the world,” DeWine said. 
Bayer’s new plant will be close to Ohio’s seven major research universities. 
“We’re excited for Ohio State researchers to work alongside Bayer teams toward our shared goals, and we’re especially proud of the integral role that our university and Ohio higher education partners play in securing economic wins like this for our state, Ohio State University President Ravi Bellamkonda said in a statement.
The plant’s groundbreaking is expected next year and manufacturing is expected to start in 2031. A second module for drug product manufacturing is scheduled to follow in 2034.
Bayer, a German pharmaceutical company, has treated 4.5 million people in the United States with their prescription medicines in the last three years, Anderson said. 
“After a competitive global review, we’re happy to expand our production footprint here,” Anderson said. “We see a tremendous chance to build the biopharma ecosystem here and partner with your research institutions. What’s next in medicine will go through you, New Albany, Ohio.” 
Bayer’s U.S. pharmaceuticals headquarters is in Whippany, New Jersey and has other U.S. sites in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Berkeley, California; Cambridge, Massachusetts; Research Triangle Park, North Carolina; and San Diego, California. 
New Albany is home to other new biotech companies including drug manufacturer Amgen, telehealth company Hims & Hers and vitamin maker Pharmavite. 
“We’ve created an environment where businesses grow, where people can find meaningful careers, and where economic development strengthens the community and the region for generations to come,” said New Albany Mayor Sloan Spalding. 
The massive Intel chip plant near New Albany is years behind schedule. Factories were supposed to start production last year, but production has been pushed back to at least 2030.

title: Trump claims Ohio’s economy is ‘booming.’ The November election might show if Ohio voters agree.
description: In these surreal times that try men’s souls, Ohio has come to a moment of reckoning. Early in-person voting and absentee voting by mail has begun. The midterm elections are a month away. The Nov. 3 referendum, in the middle of a presidential term, is essentially a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on the status quo. You […]
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)In these surreal times that try men’s souls, Ohio has come to a moment of reckoning. Early in-person voting and absentee voting by mail has begun. The midterm elections are a month away. 
The Nov. 3 referendum, in the middle of a presidential term, is essentially a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on the status quo. You either like the way things are going or you don’t. 
The outcome of this off-year election will show as much about Ohio voters as it does the candidates on the ballot. What will it say about us in 2026?
In 2024, over 3-million Ohioans voted for Donald Trump giving him, as he boasted at a weekend rally in the state, “the highest vote total in the history of Ohio.” 
He returned to Vandalia, for first time since his 2024 campaign stop at the Dayton airport, to galvanize support for Ohio Republicans in tight races for the U.S. Senate and governor. 
His profanity-laced, hour-and-a-half speech at Butler High School was pointedly crude. So much for presidential decorum. 
His sales pitch (?) for electing appointed U.S. Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy “even if you hate” them was lousy. 
He promoted data centers with Husted and Ramaswamy under fire for them. Trump, who’s approval rating on the economy has dropped to an all-time low, told rallygoers Ohio’s economy is “booming” just days before a nearby truck factory laid off 1,400 workers. 
He derided Haitian immigrants down the road in Springfield, the same day the community buried one of its own, a 20-year-old college student who reportedly took his own life over the shame of wearing a conspicuous ICE ankle monitor. 
He singled out a female reporter again for personal attacks — as the approving crowd in the high school gym erupted in loud boos.
Rally attendees chanted “Deport!” when Trump made several false statements about Springfield’s Haitians, inferred that they ruined a “beautiful, idyllic” town, and promised that it will soon be better because “they’re all being brought back to their country.”  
(Most of the immigrants living and working in the metro Springfield area arrived legally through Temporary Protected Status, a humanitarian relief program for people fleeing countries unsafe from violence and disasters). 
The Trump administration abruptly ended TPS for Haiti — considered too dangerous for American travel due to extreme risks of violent “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care” — but apparently fine for terrified Ohio Haitians sentenced to a life-threatening fate. “Deport! Deport! Deport!”
While massive chants swept the Trump rally in a Dayton suburb, hundreds of Ohioans, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and his wife, grieved in Springfield and agonized over the inhumanity that had killed a promising young man. 
“This country needs people like Pierre Damas Bel,” said DeWine after Bel’s heartbreaking funeral. “We need people who are smart, hard-working, who seek their own version of the American dream. We need these people. We needed him.”  
But even after the 20-year-old died, as the news paralyzed his family and friends with fresh, unbearable pain, the anti-immigrant hostility expressed at the Trump rally appeared online. 
“One less plane ticket that we have to pay for” said one callous post on X. 
Yet as ICE activity has escalated dramatically across Ohio, following federal termination of TPS nationals from countries such as Haiti, Syria, and Yemen, recent polling in the state showed a majority of voters disapprove of brutal Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics (that brought down Bel) despite strong support for border security. 
Thumbs down to masked, armed thugs in unmarked vehicles indiscriminately targeting people with no criminal background (including American citizens) who have the wrong skin color but thumbs up to secure borders done right. 
A majority of Ohio voter also think their state is on the wrong track economically, regardless of Trump’s bluster. They give the state a fair/poor rating with Trump’s job approval at 35%. 
Affordability tops Ohioans concerns weeks away from the election as inflation outpaces income and costs climb on everything from childcare, utilities, housing, groceries, health care, and gasoline. 
A temporary gas tax pause, enacted in a day by state lawmakers as a pre-election gimmick, hardly puts anyone on easy street. 
Trump’s endless war of choice in Iran continues to drive up gas and diesel prices along with products you buy that now cost more to move and his reckless tariffs have hit families and businesses hard. 
He may draw cheers from his diehard fans about the “golden age” he has supposedly brought to Ohio, but many Ohioans aren’t feeling it. 
Polls also show most do not buy Trump’s upbeat spiel on Ohio’s rapid data center expansion — greenlit by state and local governments with zero transparency or community input.
Ohioans are sharing space with over 200 gigantic data centers that consume vast amounts of energy and millions of gallons of water daily while generating continuous noise pollution and air emissions from backup generators. 
They are subsidizing tech companies worth trillions with higher utility bills and insane tax breaks while AI giants strain grids and deplete local resources with no public guardrails or value benefit to the community in permanent jobs. 
But Trump dismissed data center concerns as he praised Husted, who once touted them, for a futile attempt to pass a “toothless” Senate bill with optional ratepayer protections that states would only be required to consider without any actual safeguards around paying for data center energy use. 
Ohioans have come to a reckoning. On all of the above. We know where the candidates land from rallies to funerals. But what will this election say about us?
