name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Lawmakers consider introducing recording to Oklahoma courtrooms to assist operations
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Lawmakers on Wednesday discussed taking another stab at modernizing Oklahoma courtrooms by introducing audio and visual recording technology.  At an interim study hosted by Sen. Christi Gillespie, R-Broken Arrow, and Rep. Derrick Hildebrant, R-Catoosa, lawmakers considered if a pilot program in a dozen courtrooms across the state could allevi[...]
text:
The Oklahoma County Courthouse in downtown Oklahoma City, pictured Aug. 15, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Lawmakers on Wednesday discussed taking another stab at modernizing Oklahoma courtrooms by introducing audio and visual recording technology. 
At an interim study hosted by Sen. Christi Gillespie, R-Broken Arrow, and Rep. Derrick Hildebrant, R-Catoosa, lawmakers considered if a pilot program in a dozen courtrooms across the state could alleviate strains left by court reporter shortages and improve transparency and trust in the state’s judicial system. 
“It is not livestreaming or broadcasting courtroom proceedings, although it does have that capability,” Gillespie said. “It does not replace court reporters with AI-generated transcripts. And when an official transcript is needed, a certified court reporter would still be responsible for certifying that record.”
Sen. Christi Gillespie, R-Broken Arrow, applauds during the governor’s State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
The two lawmakers last session authored Senate Bill 1386 which would have created the pilot program in 12 courtrooms to record proceedings for the record. The measure never passed off the Senate floor, but Gillespie said Wednesday that she’s planning to work on it again. 
“What we are studying is the use of permanently mounted audio and video technology to preserve a complete, accurate, and reliable record of courtroom proceedings, providing another tool for the transparency, accountability, and public confidence in our justice system,” she said. 
The three-year pilot program is estimated to cost $2.3 million, said Diana O’Neal, director of the administrative office of the courts. This includes $25,000 in technology upgrades and software licensing for each courtroom, plus the cost of two full-time IT officers and operators for the software during proceedings. 
Oklahoma Supreme Court Chief Justice Dustin Rowe said while the state’s high court currently offers audio and visual livestreams of proceedings, the matters before the panel are usually relevant to the entire state. This is not often the case in trial courts where matters can be more personal, he said. 
Legislators need to be wary of livestreaming proceedings if they can then be clipped, potentially manipulated and disseminated on social media, Rowe said. 
Oklahoma Supreme Court Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe sits alongside fellow justices during the governor’s State of the State Address in the House chamber of the state Capitol on Feb. 3, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
“We can’t lose the public’s respect for the rule of law and the judiciary,” he said. “It would be devastating. And so, whatever happens and whatever comes out of these discussions, I ask you to keep that at the forefront.”
Of the 198 court reporter positions in Oklahoma, 75 are vacant, Rowe said. There are some counties with a single court reporter trying to work with multiple judges which delays proceedings, he said. 
Laura Griffin has been a court reporter in Oklahoma for 37 years. The state should continue to improve the court system with technology, but audio and visual recording cannot replace what a court reporter offers, she said. 
Court reporters can ask for clarifications, for speakers to raise their volume or for parties to stop talking over each other, none of which a recording can do, Griffin said. 
“It’s not whether technology should assist the guardian of the record,” Griffin said. “They should not replace the guardian of the record. Those are two very different things, and very different issues.”
She said court reporters would not be able to certify transcripts produced by these recordings. 
Jeremiah Gregory, district attorney for Payne and Logan counties, said he would go further than what the interim study discusses and recommend livestreams and broader public access to recorded proceedings in an effort to prevent the spread of false narratives.
“I don’t believe that’s something that should be held private,” he said. “With the exception of the juveniles, the adoptions, the guardianships, the family and domestics. I think that should apply to where it’s only available to the judge, a court reporter, and the parties, for the obvious reasons of the people who are involved, are very vulnerable.”

title: Parents of cyclist who was killed in crosswalk file wrongful death lawsuit against driver
description:
"She loved to ride her bike," the teen’s father said Wednesday, after bringing the legal action against folk artist Douglas Knapp.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Parents of cyclist who was killed in crosswalk file wrongful death lawsuit against driver.
text:
Shiloh Skalka, 16, was killed in July in Burlington after she was struck by a vehicle while crossing a roadway on her e-bike in a crosswalk with warning lights flashing. Provided photo
The parents of a 16-year-old girl are suing a Burlington folk artist who already faces charges that he struck and killed her as she rode an e-bike in a crosswalk with warning lights flashing. 
Christian Skalka and Susan Skalka, the parents of Shiloh Skalka, filed the lawsuit against Douglas Knapp this week in Chittenden County civil court in Burlington. Knapp is a well-known Burlington folk artist using the name dug Nap.
The lawsuit comes about three months after the July crash and a little more than a month after Knapp, 80, was arraigned. He pleaded not guilty to a misdemeanor charge of negligent operation of a motor vehicle resulting in the death of Shiloh, who was a rising junior at Burlington High School.
“She was kind and loving to her friends, always supportive, and to us as well — to me, my wife, her twin brother,” Christian Skalka said Wednesday of Shiloh. “She always wanted to know how we were feeling and hear our thoughts.”
She excelled at school with strong interests in history and art, he said. She also loved animals and spending time with her friends, hiking, skiing and riding horses, her father said, adding, “She loved to ride her bike.” 

READ MORE

Her father recalled a video of his daughter when she was about 2 years old riding a bicycle with training wheels. “When she was older we would go riding together,” he said, calling her an experienced cyclist.
Shiloh went out on her e-bike on the afternoon of July 16 after returning home from working a shift at Starbucks. The crash occurred at the intersection of Pine and Locust streets. She was heading west on Locust Street when she stopped at a crosswalk, according to court filings. 
She activated the crossing signal, waited about 3 seconds, and began to cross the roadway, the documents stated. Shiloh, who was wearing a helmet, was struck seconds later in the crosswalk by a Dodge Grand Caravan going south on Pine Street, driven by Knapp. According to court filings, the warning lights had been flashing for 7 seconds when the crash took place.
The civil lawsuit asserts:  “Despite recognizing that he had hit Shiloh, as he stated to law enforcement, Defendant Knapp continued to drive his vehicle over Shiloh’s body and south of the crash before finally coming to a stop.”
Shiloh was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington and later died from multiple injuries.
According to the court filings, police estimated that Knapp was driving 28 mph in the 25-mph zone leading up to the crash.
“After a crash investigation and reconstruction conducted by law enforcement,” the lawsuit stated, “it was determined that had Defendant Knapp been paying attention to the roadway, even traveling at the speed of 28 miles per hour, he would have had adequate time to stop at the crosswalk allowing Shiloh to safely cross the intersection.”
Knapp could not be reached Wednesday, and it was not clear if he had an attorney representing him in the civil case. Austin Howard, an attorney who represented Knapp at his arraignment on the criminal case, could not be reached Wednesday for comment.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages.
“We cannot change what happened, but we can insist on accountability,” Brooks McArthur, an attorney for the parents, said Wednesday. 
The criminal case and the civil lawsuit are separate proceedings that serve different purposes, McArthur added. 
“The criminal case is brought by the state and addresses whether the defendant should be held criminally accountable,” he said. “Our civil case is brought on behalf of Shiloh and her family and seeks accountability and justice for the loss of her life.” 
The Skalka family has established a memorial fund in Shiloh’s honor through the Vermont Community Foundation. The fund, called Shiloh’s Memorial Fund for Kindness and Creativity, aims to support giving to local organizations and community programs aligned with her values.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Ingoglia seeks ‘transparency’ on property insurance payments to affiliates
description: TAMPA — Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia is calling for more transparency when it comes to payments made between property insurers and their affiliated companies. His comment came Thursday in a response to a story published jointly last month by the Orlando Sentinel and South Florida Sun Sentinel about an analysis commissioned by the Florida [[...]
text:
Florida CFO Blaise Ingoglia at the University of South Florida (USF) in Tampa on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia is calling for more transparency when it comes to payments made between property insurers and their affiliated companies.
His comment came Thursday in a response to a story published jointly last month by the Orlando Sentinel and South Florida Sun Sentinel about an analysis commissioned by the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation (OIR) in 2022.
The report revealed that between 2017 and 2019, insurers in Florida claimed $432 million in losses but paid fees to their affiliate companies amounting to $1.3 billion.
The consultant who wrote the analysis also found that 20 insurers made affiliate payments exceeding the benchmark for what was “fair and reasonable.”
“I think there should be more transparency in the way that money flows back and forth between those affiliated companies,” Ingoglia said Wednesday during a press conference on the University of South Florida campus in north Tampa.
“I know that there was a bill that passed through the House years ago that did not pass through the Senate, but at the time I was the Banking and Insurance chair and I was championing that we put it up,” Ingoglia added. “I voted affirmatively [and] I put it up as chairman because I think that it is that important.”
Legislation has been sponsored for several years by lawmakers to create a framework for oversight of affiliates and their transactions with property insurers.
A bill (HB 1399) in the Florida House during the 2026 legislative session by Pinellas Republican Rep. Kim Berfield would have required insurers to weigh whether payments to affiliates are fair and reasonable, and to provide factors for OIR to decide. It was approved overwhelmingly in the Florida House, 106-3, but its Senate companion (SB 234) never received a hearing.
That proposal, sponsored by Sen. Carlos Guillermo Smith, D-Orlando, capped payments to affiliates at 20%.
“Step one is to offer some transparency when it comes to that,” Ingoglia said. “The other stuff we can debate. Until we have the information and we know exactly what is going on, then everything should follow after that.”
The newspapers reported that after they received an unredacted version of the analysis this summer, attorneys for the Florida Senate threatened both with “civil or criminal legal implications” if they refused to immediately shred the evidence.
The editors with both publications insisted they had obtained the records “legally and appropriately through the state’s public records process” and would not allow the Senate’s “threats to prevent us from reporting.”
The Tampa Bay Times initially reported about the secret analysis in February 2025 following a two-year wait for public records. It led to state lawmakers holding a single committee meeting in March 2025.
Political issue
Property insurance has emerged as a top issue in the Florida gubernatorial race between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly. Donalds has provided his own proposal but also contends the Florida property insurance market has stabilized due to legislative reforms passed earlier this decade — a talking point Gov. DeSantis and other legislative Republicans have repeated.
Jolly told reporters late last month following the Sentinel-Sun Sentinel story that the state’s insurance regulation system is “corrupt” and that he would use executive action to cap amounts insurers can shift into affiliated companies.
Homeowners’ insurance premiums increased by 75% between 2021 and 2025, according to a May 2026 report by the Coalition for Insurable Future.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Forester, influencer and author Ethan Tapper on why ‘it’s our responsibility to carry hope for each other’
description:
Tapper’s new book, “The Forest Year: Finding Hope in a World Worth Saving,” explores the power of staying and paying careful attention to the environment around you.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Forester, influencer and author Ethan Tapper on why ‘it’s our responsibility to carry hope for each other’.
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Forester Ethan Tapper, author of the book “The Forest Year: Finding Hope in a World Worth Saving.” Photo by Corey Hendrickson
Ethan Tapper is a forester, philosopher, bestselling author and social media star. The chainsaw-toting, ATV-driving Vermonter has an audience of some 400,000 followers for his folksy and instructive videos on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook. His previous book, “How to Love a Forest: The Bittersweet Work of Tending a Changing World,” won the 2025 New England Book Award in nonfiction and was a regional bestseller.
The 37-year-old former Chittenden County forester lives in a 175-acre forest in Bolton that he calls Bear Island. It’s a central character in his writing. 
When Tapper purchased the forest in 2017, it was “some of the most degraded areas of forest that I’d ever seen,” he said. He began clearing brush, removing trash, planting trees and enabling new growth. 
Tapper and I walked through Bear Island in late September as it was erupting in fall color. He told me that he “just sort of gave this forest a chance. And as I find again and again and again, you give it a chance, and life finds a way.”
Tapper has a new book out this week, “The Forest Year: Finding Hope in a World Worth Saving.” In it, he explores the power of staying and paying careful attention to the environment around you. Tapper tells the story of how deepening a relationship with the natural world is a model for how to take care of oneself and others.
“I’ve chosen roots over wings,” he said as we hiked to a clearing with views of the surrounding peaks. Staying close to his forest has “given me the freedom to be here and to invest in this place and really live with the seasons, live with this forest.” 
His deepening awareness of his environment has had multiple benefits. “It’s also made me a better forest steward and a more curious and interested person.” 
Tapper has worked as a professional forester since 2012. He received a bachelor’s degree in forestry and a master’s in natural resources from the University of Vermont. After working as a county forester for the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation for eight years, he left to start his own consulting forestry business, Bear Island Forestry, in 2024. In his spare time, he dabbles as a rock star — literally — as the lead singer in a punk rock band called the Bubs.
We stood next to a pond that reflected the brilliant red, yellow and green around us. “The process of being here with Bear Island has been an extremely hope-filled process,” Tapper told me.
“Hope is a self-fulfilling prophecy, because when you feel hope and you give other people reason to feel hope, they do stuff. They take action. They make hard choices. They stand up. … 
“We live in this world which, despite centuries of degradation (and) exploitation, we’re surrounded by all of these species and all of these ecosystems that still work.”
He added: “It’s our responsibility to carry hope for each other. We hand this mantle of hope to other people and we change the world. And I think we have to.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Appeals court rules portion of Arkansas whistleblower law unconstitutional
description: The Arkansas Court of Appeals struck down a key part of a state law Wednesday protecting public employees from being fired for reporting wrongdoing or misuse of funds by a government agency. A three-judge panel of the court ruled that a provision of the 1999 Arkansas Whistleblower Protection Act violates the state Constitution. The stricken […]
text:
The Arkansas Justice Building on the state Capitol grounds in Little Rock on Jan. 14, 2025. The building houses the state Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals and the Administrative Office of the Courts. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Court of Appeals struck down a key part of a state law Wednesday protecting public employees from being fired for reporting wrongdoing or misuse of funds by a government agency.
A three-judge panel of the court ruled that a provision of the 1999 Arkansas Whistleblower Protection Act violates the state Constitution. The stricken provision allows employees who have filed a civil lawsuit claiming they were retaliated against to seek temporary reinstatement during the case. 
The provision says employees must be reinstated if  they demonstrate that “a reasonable person would conclude that his or her termination was a result of adverse action.”
The judges ruled that the Legislature did not have the authority to grant such a process.
“The Legislature overstepped its bounds by dictating pleading, practice and procedure” with the provision, Judge Casey Tucker wrote in the court’s decision.
The ruling reverses a Pulaski County judge’s decision granting a former Little Rock school district employee’s request for a preliminary injunction reinstating him as executive director of human resources.
The employee, Robert Robinson, was one of three human resources directors whose positions were consolidated into two during budget cuts in 2024. All three directors applied for the two new positions, but Robinson was not hired.
Robinson claimed the action was in response to him advocating that teachers whose contracts were terminated or not renewed were entitled to hearings and for telling the district it needed to increase a female high school principal’s pay.
A Pulaski County judge ordered the district to reinstate Robinson and place him on paid administrative leave until the conclusion of the case. 
Chris Heller, an attorney for the district, said he thought the decision was “a well reasoned and correct opinion.” An attorney for Robinson did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
Robinson’s attorneys argued in court filings the whistleblower protection being challenged didn’t violate the Arkansas Constitution because it didn’t create or alter procedural rules in court. The provision just set an evidentiary standard for reinstatement, the attorneys said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island state crime lab taking back more firearms cases
description: The Rhode Island State Crime Laboratory is sending fewer firearms cases to outside reviewers while accepting more gun evidence from local police departments thanks to progress rebuilding its in-house testing staff, its director said. Three forensic firearms examiners left the lab after 2024 testing error upended its operations and reputation. Soon after the[...]
text:
Shotgun shell casings at the Rhode Island State Crime Lab in 2023. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The Rhode Island State Crime Laboratory is sending fewer firearms cases to outside reviewers while accepting more gun evidence from local police departments thanks to progress rebuilding its in-house testing staff, its director said.
Three forensic firearms examiners left the lab after 2024 testing error upended its operations and reputation. Soon after the labs outsourced its toolmark exams to two former New York City police examiners with all work verified by two out-of-state labs.
In April, under a plan approved by the five-member commission that oversees the lab on the University of Rhode Island’s Kingston campus, 15% of cases needed verification from third-party contractors, a workload that has gradually scaled down to 10% this month.
State Crime Lab Commission approves plan to bring firearms toolmark testing largely in-house

By March 2027, that figure should be 5% assuming the lab’s new toolmark examiners continue demonstrating that they can reliably handle the work, Lab Director Dennis Hilliard said in an interview Wednesday.
“There were no issues in these first six months,” Hilliard said.
Hilliard is scheduled to update the State Crime Laboratory Commission Thursday on the toolmark section’s progress as it moves into the next phase of the action plan.
The lab temporarily suspended toolmark testing in August 2024, after discrepancies were found in test results for a pistol seized as evidence in a 2021 Pawtucket murder case. Cartridge casings were flagged as matching a different firearm in possession of the Boston Police Department.
Work was subsequently handled by two former New York City police examiners from STRIA Consulting Group. All verifications were performed by examiners at SCL Forensics in Texas and FoCoSS Forensics in New Hampshire. 
But in January, the lab began rebuilding its in-house staff, hiring a lead toolmark examiner who previously served as a lead examiner for Connecticut’s state crime lab. The lab has since filled its standard examiner position with an internal candidate who completed training through the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and passed competency testing.
That second examiner is now working under supervision on casework and is expected to be cleared to verify other analysts’ work within two to three months, Hilliard said.
The lab has left a third examiner position unfilled, Hilliard said, allowing it to use those funds to continue paying STRIA consultants for third-party verifications. Since the lab staffed up, consultants have come in on a weekly basis.
“It might step down to a monthly basis — depending on how many cases come in the laboratory” Hilliard said.
And Hilliard is expecting more cases as the lab begins accepting firearms evidence that police departments previously were told to hold onto.
Following the 2024 testing suspension, Hilliard said police departments were told to hold off on submitting cases when there was no suspect or firearm for comparison. Now, the lab plans to accept those cases and begin microscopic examination while investigators continue looking for a suspect or gun.
“Police chiefs have been notified that they can send any firearms cases that they want to,” Hilliard said.

title: Tybee Island secures funding to replenish beach sand
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Tybee Island has secured federal funding to replenish its beaches with sand after being denied the money earlier this year. Local officials say the beach renourishment project is critical for a rapidly-eroding beach. Barrier islands like[...]
text:
Portions of Tybee Island's beach and dunes are badly eroded from the tide and storms. A renourishment project this winter will replenish the sand. (Emily Jones/WABE)This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Tybee Island has secured federal funding to replenish its beaches with sand after being denied the money earlier this year. Local officials say the beach renourishment project is critical for a rapidly-eroding beach.
Barrier islands like Tybee should naturally accumulate sand from islands farther north; it’s called the sand-sharing system. But human activity — development on the island, building sea walls and jetties, creating shipping channels — has disrupted that process. As a result, Georgia’s barrier islands are constantly losing sand, and the beaches are constantly being washed away by the relentless tide.
To address the problem, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has, since the 1970s, been dredging up sand and depositing it onto beaches up and down the East Coast. 
On Tybee, which sits just south of the mouth of the Savannah River, the natural sand-sharing is further interrupted by the shipping channel that cuts between Tybee and its island neighbors to the north. The Corps typically replenishes sand there every seven years. But that cycle was nearly interrupted this year –  creating concerns for Tybee businesses, beachgoers and wildlife.
In the winter of 2019 and 2020, the Corps placed 1.3 million cubic yards of sand on the Tybee Island beach. More than half of that sand is gone now. On one stretch near the DeSoto Beach Hotel, the dune looks like it’s been chopped in half with a giant knife, ending in a five-foot cliff instead of a gradual slope.
“It’s extremely stark and startling to see up close and personal,” said city manager Bret Bell. “You can see the vegetation. It’s bisected in half. You can see the roots coming out of the dune system.”
It’s not just the dune grasses. In some places, the tide and storms have cut into sea turtle nests buried in the dune. 
Businesses are feeling the pinch too. The dramatic erosion has forced chair and umbrella rental operations off the beach in some places, Bell said, and the DeSoto has lost bookings due to the poor state of the beach in front of its doors. 
All told, the erosion puts the island itself — and the mainland — at risk. The sea level is rising about half an inch a year due to climate change.
“It is really our only protection against the encroaching oceans,” Bell said. “Storm surge would inundate our island if it weren’t for the mitigating effects of the beach and our dune system.”
Tybee Island is due for renourishment again this winter. Planning began when the last renourishment ended, Bell said, and the city of Tybee, Chatham County, and the state of Georgia have worked since then to set aside enough funds to cover 40% of the $20 million price tag — the required local match for the federal beach renourishment program. But Congress underfunded that program, according to Bell, and Tybee was left off the project list.
“All of a sudden, all of these beach communities started really competing for the limited amount of funding that there was,” he said.
City officials continued to lobby, residents launched a letter-writing campaign, and members of Georgia’s congressional delegation visited the island to see the stark beach erosion. 
Then, in September, came a development Bell called a “miracle”: Several beach nourishment projects in New Jersey came in under budget, so the Corps agreed to divert leftover funds to Tybee. Work is slated to begin this winter.
When it does, the Corps plans to try something new. When the agency dredges the Savannah River shipping channel, it will deposit that sand in the shallows off Tybee’s beach instead of pumping it farther offshore. The goal is to minimize the wave action that eats away at the beach and allow the sand to travel more like it naturally would without the interruption of the shipping channel.
“That really is expected to extend the life of our nourishment,” Bell said. “So instead of the next nourishment happening in seven years, it might be 10 years.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Lincoln University students, alumni sue Missouri over unequal funding
description: Current and former Lincoln University students are suing the State of Missouri for nearly $550 million to address what they allege are decades of inequitable funding that they say has hurt the college’s academic programs and facilities. In a complaint filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri, their attorneys […]
text:
Lincoln University in Jefferson City is the center of a U.S. District Court filing Wednesday, alleging the college has been historically underfunded (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Current and former Lincoln University students are suing the State of Missouri for nearly $550 million to address what they allege are decades of inequitable funding that they say has hurt the college’s academic programs and facilities.
In a complaint filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri, their attorneys claim the state has treated its two land-grant institutions — Lincoln University and the University of Missouri — unequally.
The lawsuit is part of a larger effort called the 1890 Project, which is seeking to draw national attention to funding disparities at historically Black land-grant universities. Its founder, Donald Calloway Jr., is a former Missouri House member who leads a law firm and strategic advisory firm.
Central to the lawsuit is a letter the United States Secretaries of Agriculture and Education sent in September 2023 to then-Gov. Mike Parson, outlining a funding disparity of $361.6 million between fiscal years 1987 and 2020.
Lincoln is one of 19 historically Black colleges and universities designated as a land-grant institution under the Second Morrill Act of 1890. At the time, states were required to either allow Black students to attend their existing land-grant universities established under the 1862 Morrill Act or operate a second college for Black students that would receive federal land-grant support.
A monument at the center of Lincoln University’s campus in Jefferson City commemorates soldiers of the 62nd United States Colored Infantry, who helped establish the institution in 1866 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Missouri is one of 19 states to choose the latter, designating Lincoln in Jefferson City as its 1890 land-grant institution. In 2023, federal officials wrote to 16 of those states, saying they had underfunded historically Black land-grant universities by billions of dollars over decades.
The Lincoln lawsuit focuses in part on how Missouri provided the state money needed to match federal funding for the university’s agricultural programs.
Each year the U.S. Department of Agriculture gives grant money to land-grant institutions to support agricultural programs and research with the expectation that states will match the investment. Waivers allow 1890 land-grant universities to pull their full federal grant without the full 1:1 match if they can put forward at least 50%.
From fiscal years 2000 through 2007, the state did not earmark any funds for Lincoln’s land-grant programs, according to the court filing. And from 2008 to 2021, the state gave anywhere between 11% and 51% of the required match.
To avoid leaving federal money on the table, Lincoln administrators diverted some of its core funding to grow its agricultural programs and obtain the full USDA grants, totaling $43.5 million between 2000 and 2016.
“Missouri’s failure to appropriate the required state match did not merely leave a gap in Lincoln University’s funding,” attorneys wrote in the lawsuit. “It forced Lincoln to cannibalize its own core institutional operating budget to survive.”
Missouri lawmakers push for study of Lincoln University funding inequity

In 2023, state lawmakers requested a study of the funding inequity, but their proposal to create a special committee was never approved by legislative leaders.
At the time, Lincoln President John Moseley told The Independent that the college’s buildings were suffering as a result of the diverted funds. He estimated that it would cost $87 million to make the necessary repairs.
Students and alumni who brought the lawsuit say the consequences extend beyond aging buildings, affecting their health, finances and quality of life.
One of the plaintiffs, Makhi Joseph Berinyuy Jaff, took photos, videos and interviewed other students during his time at Lincoln in 2023 and 2024. 
He described his experience in a presentation called “The Effect of Underfunding” that attorneys are presenting as evidence. In a handful of slides, Jaff shows photos of his “downtrodden” dormitory Perry Hall.
“Last year the pipes completely burst, leaving open feces to disperse. Perry smelled disgusting, and they still left this dormitory open. We had to live in the smell for several weeks,” he wrote alongside photos of a 1960s, communal-style bathroom.
Jaydan Monee Ware began attending Lincoln in 2025 and was placed in Tull Hall as her dormitory, “where the ventilation in her room was visibly dirty and where she experienced respiratory and allergic symptoms she had never before experienced,” the lawsuit says.
Other plaintiffs said problems with food in campus dining halls forced them to spend additional money eating elsewhere.
Ware has a cousin who attends the University of Missouri.
“I can see how much more funding they have than us,” she told her attorneys. If Lincoln received equal funding, she could “live somewhere where I don’t have to worry about eating, or mold in my vents.”
While Lincoln pushed off building repairs to be able to receive its USDA grants, the lawsuit says, the University of Missouri received its full match from the state.
Between 2011 and 2022, the University of Missouri received $191.7 million in federal grants with a state investment of $192.7 million, according to USDA data.
The lawsuit also takes aim at a performance-funding formula adopted in 2012 by the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education that determines state aid for universities based on factors like degree attainment and financial efficiency. The board is currently looking for a replacement to its current funding strategy.
Attorneys allege that Lincoln’s land-grant funding from the state is conditioned on the performance metric while the University of Missouri’s is not.
“This two-tiered system requires a historically Black institution to qualify for funds that are statutorily owed to it, while the predominantly white institution receives equivalent support automatically,” they wrote.
The plaintiffs argue that the differing treatment amounts to unconstitutional race discrimination and violates the Equal Protection Clause.
The lawsuit asks the court to oversee a remedial fund, for which the state would owe nearly $550 million, and ensure equal funding going forward.
Defendants include the Coordinating Board for Higher Education, Higher Education Commissioner Bennett Boggs, Gov. Mike Kehoe and University of Missouri President Mun Choi.
Following the announcement of the lawsuit, the Missouri Legislative Black Caucus released a statement in support of fair funding for the university.
“Lincoln University has served Missourians for generations, and its future matters to communities across our state,” said state Rep. Michael Johnson, a Democrat from Kansas City and chair of the Missouri Legislative Black Caucus. “We support the students and alumni and we welcome thoughtful, good-faith work toward a resolution that strengthens the university and benefits Missouri.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Labor commissioner candidates to tackle ‘red tape,’ Oklahoma inspector shortages
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Candidates for Oklahoma’s labor commissioner on the November ballot vary on how they’d handle staffing shortages, budget requests and dealing with “red tape.” With ideas ranging from privatizing operations to potentially asking the Legislature for more appropriations, the three men running to lead the Oklahoma Department of Labor have differi[...]
text:
From left to right, Democrat Kevin Dawson, Libertarian Mike Hall and Republican Kevin West will compete in November to be Oklahoma's next labor commissioner. (Photos provided)OKLAHOMA CITY — Candidates for Oklahoma’s labor commissioner on the November ballot vary on how they’d handle staffing shortages, budget requests and dealing with “red tape.”
With ideas ranging from privatizing operations to potentially asking the Legislature for more appropriations, the three men running to lead the Oklahoma Department of Labor have differing visions on how to tackle some of the agency’s biggest challenges and criticisms. 
Democrat Kevin Dawson, Libertarian Mike Hall and Republican Kevin West are set to face off Nov. 3 to be the state’s next labor commissioner. 
Voters will elect one to a four-year term. The current labor commissioner, Leslie Osborn, is term-limited and cannot seek reelection. 
Dawson, of Norman, said he’s the most qualified for the job because of his 43 years working in the railroad industry and 12 years in union leadership. He said he’s an advocate for the general public and the safety of Oklahoma workers. 
“We have to make sure that we are managing the industrial safety side properly so that the general public is given the safest opportunity to continue to function throughout our society and use our services,” he said. 
Hall, of Oklahoma City, said his experience as both a project engineer and manager qualify him for the job. He said he spent years problem-solving and finding efficiencies in projects which will translate well to a state agency. 
“I’m not associated with one of the major political parties, so I view that as an advantage for the taxpayers in some way,” Hall said. “I don’t answer to party bosses or anything like that so I would be able to work with the Legislature, Republicans or Democrats.”
West, of Moore, said his decade in the state Legislature and 40 years in commercial cabinetry make him the most qualified. He said his experience working with state budgets, administrative rules and the legislative process prepared him. 
“I think that combination is fairly unique, being somebody who’s actually worked out on these jobs sites,” West said. “You know what it’s like to hire people, know what it’s like to work on deadlines.”
‘Red tape’
The Department of Labor is charged with the regulation of certain industries, workplace safety and enforces labor laws. But some candidates said some of these regulations and rules can be overburdensome and need to be reevaluated. 
Dawson, 65, said while he is supportive of finding ways to streamline agency operations, safety needs to come first and he’s wary of “cutting red tape.”
“I’m not OK with doing away with something to the point where it’s going to be to the detriment of the general public,” he said. “I’m gonna put people before politics every day of the week.” 
Hall, 59, said the agency needs to reduce “regulatory bloat” that can prevent swift action. 
A lot of the “red tape” that could be cut comes from within the Oklahoma Department of Labor itself, he said. 
“I think a lot of it could be run leaner and smarter, perhaps,” Hall said. “So, streamlining internal processes and just cutting administrative waste, that is another kind of form of red tape that could be improved.”
West, 58, said one of the first things he’ll do if elected is review the department’s administrative rules to ensure everything is necessary, up-to-date and relevant to safety standards. 
“We’ve seen across many different agencies where over time, those administrative rules get outside of those boundaries that the Legislature put in,” he said. “And beyond that, it’s really working with the industry that it affects and making sure that it’s a safety issue and not a barrier to entry.”
Inspector shortages and budgets 
The Department of Labor in July told Fox 25 that there was a staffing shortage for elevator inspectors. The agency inspects things such as elevators, amusement rides and boilers. 
Dawson said to reduce staffing shortages, there may be a need to ask the Legislature for more money in order to fulfill the agency’s mandated responsibilities. 
“We can’t be out here advocating for continuing to freeze budgets and still have a mandate that things have to be inspected,” he said. 
There needs to be strict accountability for spending, but Oklahoma also cannot go without inspectors, Dawson said. Inspectors and other staff working for the agency need to be paid appropriately and competitively, he said. 
“So, in order to accomplish that, if that means that I have to go back to the Legislature and ask the Legislature to live up to their own duties and responsibilities and make sure that we are funded appropriately, I’m OK with doing that,” he said. 
Hall, on the other hand, said inspections could be outsourced to the private sector – specifically insurance companies. 
“I mean, nobody wants to use an unsafe elevator or an amusement ride or be in a workplace that has an unsafe boiler or anything like that,” he said. “… And so I really think the insurance companies make a lot more sense to provide the inspectors on things like that because they’re the ones bearing the financial risk, which can be pretty severe.”
Hall said he does not think the agency’s budget should grow and instead the department should be allocating its current resources better.  
“I do think we have to work around a leaner and smarter operation and allocate the resources to the parts of the department functions that are most essential,” Hall said.  
West also wants to contract with private sector inspectors in the short-term. 
“Ultimately, I think everybody would much prefer that they’d be full-time (state) employees,” he said. “But if we’re not able to keep up with demand, then rather than have elevators either possibly operating unsafely or being shut down, I would much rather go to some outside sources and make sure that the elevators keep running safely.” 
When it comes to offering a competitive salary to agency inspectors and staff, West said it’s important to look at what other states are paying. He said only a small portion of the agency’s “limited” budget comes from legislative appropriations and he’d like to keep this stagnant. 
“But if there’s a need that can be made to the Legislature and they agree, then that’s something that we can definitely look at,” West said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge dismisses Tameshia Shelton’s murder indictment
description: Tameshia Shelton's daughter Trinity, left, and niece Danyell Randle, right, embrace Shelton outside the Clay County Detention Center after her release on June 29, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WEST POINT — A Mississippi judge Wednesday threw out the murder indictment against Tameshia Shelton, putting an end to the case that has haunted the mother of four for nearly two decades.
Shelton, now 48, was slated to face a new murder trial in Clay County on Monday, but Circuit Judge James T. Kitchens canceled the trial and agreed with Columbus-area District Attorney Scott Colom that the murder indictment should be dismissed.
Shelton, who has maintained her innocence, served 11 years in prison after a jury convicted her of murder in the 2009 shooting death of her sister’s 21-year-old boyfriend, Danelle Young. Shelton was freed on bond in June, after the state Supreme Court upheld an appellate-court ruling overturning her murder conviction and ordering her a new trial. Young’s family could not be immediately reached for comment.
Tameshia Shelton beams at a crowd of family members after her release from the Clay County Detention Center on June 29, 2026. She walked out in a shirt from her niece, featuring a photo of her taken before she was sentenced to life in prison 11 years before.  Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
When Shelton heard Wednesday that the judge had dismissed her murder indictment, she said she felt ecstatic. “Now I can breathe,” she said. “God, thank you.”
The dismissal marks the end of the nightmare that began 17 years ago when authorities first accused her of murder, she told Mississippi Today. “It’s been a long time coming. It feels like a whole lot of weight has been lifted off my shoulders.”
She said her sister, Shenikia, told her, “Now, we can celebrate.”
The dismissal means this judicial district that covers Clay, Lowndes, Noxubeeand Oktibbeha counties has seen seven people freed from prison after courts overturned their murder convictions — the most of any judicial district in the state. All were prosecuted under the previous district attorney, Forrest Allgood.
Allgood has told Mississippi Today that just because people have their convictions tossed doesn’t mean they’re innocent. “Only God knows if a man is innocent,” he said. “That’s why we have no verdict of ‘Innocent’ in our law — just ‘Guilty’ or ‘Not Guilty,’ or, in Scotland, ‘Not Proven.’”
Last December, the Mississippi Court of Appeals ordered a new trial for Shelton, saying prosecutors failed to prove “beyond a reasonable doubt” she killed Young. 
Jurors never heard the apparent suicide note that Young wrote after Shelton’s sister decided against living with him.
“I have no life without her,” he wrote. “These are my last words. Bye, bye.”
Three jurors shown the note this year told Mississippi Today that Shelton deserved a new trial.
On June 1, Mississippi Today published its four-year investigation into Shelton’s case, showing how much of the evidence suggested that Young died from suicide. The pathologist who originally ruled the death a homicide reversed himself.
Days later, the state Supreme Court let stand the appeals court’s decision, clearing the way for Shelton to receive a new trial. The judge has now canceled the trial and dismissed the murder indictment.
“At last, this case that should have never been brought is over,” said Shelton’s lawyer, Sandra Levick. “Ms. Shelton was convicted of a murder that never happened at a trial that was not fair by a jury that never heard all the facts.”
She thanked Colom, who had directed Shelton’s family to the Innocence Project in 2018. “If he had not agreed to look into this case,” Levick wrote, “this day would never have come.”
She also said, “We are grateful as well to generations of law students at Ole Miss, to our many experts including Dr. (Liam) Funte who did the hard thing and admitted that he had been wrong.”
She also thanked her co-counsel Jake Howard from the MacArthur Justice Center, Tucker Carrington, director of the Mississippi Innocence Project, and “everyone else who helped claw back this injustice.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan set to open new $383 million psychiatric hospital in Northville
description: Dozens of state officials, healthcare providers and community members celebrated the completion of the new 406,000-square-foot, 264-bed Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville Wednesday.  The state-run hospital, which has been three years in the making, cost $383 million and was built on the former site of the Hawthorn Center, a children’s psyc[...]
text:
Grounds of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Dozens of state officials, healthcare providers and community members celebrated the completion of the new 406,000-square-foot, 264-bed Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville Wednesday. 
The state-run hospital, which has been three years in the making, cost $383 million and was built on the former site of the Hawthorn Center, a children’s psychiatric hospital. Patients at the Walter P. Reuther Hospital in Westland, which currently houses adult patients, will be transferred to the new facility starting later this month.
The new hospital, which has 192 adult beds and 72 youth beds, increases the state’s capacity to serve children and adults by 54 beds, bringing the total capacity to 730 beds statewide.
“It has been thrilling to watch this dream become reality,” Mary Clare Solky, the hospital’s director, said. “Providing compassionate, high-quality psychiatric care for adults, children and adolescents is not just our mission. It is our responsibility.”
The hospital will be the state’s only psychiatric hospital providing inpatient services to children, and according to acting Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Director Amy Epkey, it was completed on schedule and under budget. 
The department’s fiscal year 2027 budget allocates $33.8 million to begin operating the new hospital. To help lower costs, the facility is heated and cooled by 352 geothermal wells drilled 550 feet underground. Andrew Miller, a project executive at Christman Construction, said using this renewable energy will save at least $10,000 a month.
Mary Clare Solky, director of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville, at the facility’s opening on Oct. 7, 2026. Solky said she feels “incredibly supported that mental health care is being prioritized in Michigan.” (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
A connection to nature
Solky said on average, adolescents stay in these long-term care facilities for three to six months. She said adults can stay for up to a year or longer. The two age groups share common spaces, like courtyards, but remain separated. 
The hospital has 12 courtyards, a nondenominational chapel, a music room, art room, movement room, hair salon, group therapy rooms, dining rooms, a gymnasium and patient clinic. The patient clinic includes exam and minor procedure rooms, dental suites and optometry and dietitian offices. 
Adolescent patients will attend a school within the hospital during the day. The school includes classrooms, a media center, a computer center and workrooms. A library and adult education classrooms serve older patients. 
A dental suite at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
Adult patients who are getting ready to leave the hospital can stay in a studio apartment equipped with a kitchen and washer and dryer. 
Safety is a priority, with special door handles, hinges, ceilings and drinking fountains designed to reduce the risk of harm. 
Throughout the hospital, designers wanted to create a connection between indoor and outdoor spaces. David Giroux, senior vice president of Integrated Design Solutions, said the outdoor landscaping, windows and lights were all chosen to bring the outdoors in.
“There’s a lot of evidence to suggest having patients be outdoors or connected with the outdoors aids in their healing,” Giroux said.
This emphasis on the outdoors is evident on the building’s interior walls, which feature blue, orange, pink and purple indigenous flower designs. 
Patients also have the opportunity to interact with the outdoors through the hospital’s horticulture program. They can water, propagate and harvest plants, which include fruits and vegetables. They can also use the vegetables to make meals, such as fried green tomatoes. 
Courtyard at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
Mental health care challenges
While connection to the outdoors is a focus of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital, an employee at the Reuther facility claimed in 2023 that children weren’t allowed outside for months.
An audit published in 2025 by the Office of the Auditor General found that Michigan’s Office of Recipient Rights was not sufficiently protecting the rights of recipients of mental health services. 
“Almost 30% of sampled complaints alleging abuse, neglect, serious injury or death were not retrieved or actions initiated until between 2 and 12 days after the complainant-provided date,” stated the audit.
State psychiatric hospitals were also found to lack consistent video surveillance and audio recording.
While Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has increased funding for mental health services, as of 2025, Michigan ranked 47 in the nation for access to inpatient psychiatric beds. Federal cuts to Medicaid continue to threaten inpatient psychiatric services.
“We know that in our communities, mental health beds have been reduced,” Solky said. “So this is a step forward for Michigan.”
She said there is a need for more adult facilities like this one across the state. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she said, mental health providers became more aware of their patients’ needs. 
“Looking at how people maybe spoke up more about mental illness, maybe it kind of came out of the closet a little bit, and I believe it allowed our officials to help us prioritize that,” she said. 
The Walter P. Reuther Psychiatric Hospital opened in 1979, and the Hawthorn Center opened in 1965. Solky did not know what the state plans to do with the Reuther building once all the patients are transferred.
Playground at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)An independent living area at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)An inpatient bed at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)A mural photo at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Acting Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Director Amy Epkey speaks at the opening of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Mary Clare Solky, director of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville, speaks at the facility's opening on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Dr. George Mellos, senior deputy director for the State Hospitals Administration at the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, at the opening of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas education board allows local election to consider creating Sherwood School District
description: The Arkansas State Board of Education on Wednesday authorized an election allowing some Pulaski County voters to decide whether to establish a new Sherwood School District.  The measure, which will be decided during the annual school elections on March 2, 2027, would detach the new district from the existing Pulaski County Special School District.  The […]
text:
State Education Board member Randy Henderson (left) and Education Secretary Jacob Oliva (right) listen to public testimony during a state board meeting on Mar. 9, 2023.

(Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas State Board of Education on Wednesday authorized an election allowing some Pulaski County voters to decide whether to establish a new Sherwood School District. 
The measure, which will be decided during the annual school elections on March 2, 2027, would detach the new district from the existing Pulaski County Special School District. 
The election on the new district was proposed in a resolution by the Sherwood Public Education Foundation that the Pulaski County Special School District board adopted last month. The new district would be created by detaching territory based on the Sylvan Hills High School attendance zone. 
Devin Bates, a lawyer for the Pulaski County Special School District, said the detachment has been discussed for more than a decade, but officials couldn’t move forward because of a desegregation order.
A federal judge ended a 43-year desegregation case in February, ruling that the Pulaski County Special School District was now providing equitable facilities to students after years of court supervision. 
Federal judge ends decades-old Little Rock-area school desegregation case

Linda George, Sherwood Public Education Foundation board member, said was “thrilled” by the board’s decision. 
“After 100 years, the community of Sherwood will have the opportunity to make their voices heard and vote on what best represents the goals and vision of their community for their students,” George said in a statement.
The Pulaski County district, one of the largest in the state, has around 11,000 students and its boundaries wrap around the Little Rock and North Little Rock school districts. Under the proposal, about 4,600 students from the current district’s northeast quadrant would join the new Sherwood district. 
Scott Richardson, an attorney for the Sherwood Public Education Foundation, told the state education board Wednesday that he previously helped with the Jacksonville School District’s detachment from the Pulaski County School District. 
Supporters of Jacksonville and Sherwood detachments have cited concern that the Pulaski County Special School District is a large district with many different communities of interest, Richardson said. 
“And those communities of interest feel like their schools would be addressed if those communities could address the conditions they find there,” he said. “I would submit to you that has worked out well in Jacksonville. It’s all new facilities over there…and the schools are functioning well.”
State education board member David Peacock questioned how the split would affect student demographics.
“I spent a lot of time in the military, and you bring a lot of diverse communities together and as a result, the military’s a better organization because of it,” Peacock said. “I understand the desire to do this, but I think there’s also a loss associated with not being the melting pot that we once talked about pretty regularly.”
Jerrod Williams, a consultant for the Pulaski County Special School District, highlighted a feasibility study commissioned by the Sherwood Public Education Foundation that found racial demographics would be similar, with white students making up about a third of the population in both districts. The Black student population would increase from about 46% in Pulaski County to 49% in the new district, according to the report.
Peacock also asked for a breakdown of socioeconomic status.
“I just think it’s important that we look at all the different factors that impact the education, we shouldn’t just focus on race,” he said.
About 75% of students receive free meals at the Pulaski County Special School District, and that would increase to about 85% of students in the Sherwood district, according to the study. 
The March election will be open to voters who reside in the proposed district. If voters approve the detachment, the law allows a two-year transition period to stand up the new district, Williams said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ agency will conduct daily audits to prevent more voter registration errors, governor says
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill says new daily audits at the Motor Vehicle Commission will prevent any more ineligible people from being registered to vote.
text:
Thousands of people who identified themselves as noncitizens were registered to vote after visits to the Motor Vehicle Commission. Gov. Mikie Sherrill says new daily audits will prevent future mistakes. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission will automatically check new voter registrations against customers’ responses before transmitting them to election officials in a bid to prevent erroneous registrations, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Wednesday.
The new procedures come more than two months after Sherrill announced roughly 6,600 people who marked themselves as noncitizens were registered to vote during visits to the Motor Vehicle Commission as a result of what the administration said was a technical glitch.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
“Our investigation is ongoing, we will follow the facts wherever they lead, fix the problems we inherited, do it the right way, and hold those responsible accountable,” Sherrill, a Democrat, said in a statement Wednesday.
The voter registration gaffe elicited criticism from Republican officials here in New Jersey and nationwide who said it verified their claims of widespread voter fraud. Sherrill said about 340 noncitizens ended up casting ballots, and has noted that the problem arose before she became governor in January.
The new daily audit system Sherrill announced Wednesday will compare customers’ responses to newly created voter registration records to ensure the information is accurate and the voter is eligible.
The automated system, which is in the process of implementation, will flag incomplete or contradictory records for manual review. Under the plan, corrected records can only be released once commission staff confirms they match customers’ responses.
The governor said the ongoing review uncovered other registrations affected by a software error caused by Idemia, the vendor that oversaw the commission’s licensing systems, that registered some voters who marked themselves as too young to be eligible. Idemia has said it was not responsible for the erroneous registrations.
About 750 residents were registered after saying they were not eligible to vote because of their age, though all of them entered birth dates that would have made each of them at least 18 years old at the time, Sherrill said.
“No underage person voted as a result of this error,” Sherrill said. “They appear to have pressed the wrong button on the PIN pad by mistake.”
Still, many of those registrations may not be valid. The administration deleted about 380 registrations of voters who cast no ballots and were entered as a result of the age error. It sent another roughly 320 nonvoting registrants for county review.
About 50 people who registered after marking themselves age-ineligible subsequently cast ballots. Those registrations were deleted and forwarded to counties for review.
The review separately found about 340 individuals who were improperly registered at Motor Vehicle Commission prisoner reentry events dating as far back as 2016. Another 60 falsely attested to eligibility while imprisoned for a felony conviction. Their registrations were sent to counties for remediation.
“I said we were going to run a secure and fair election here in New Jersey and I meant it.  In just two and a half months, we conducted this review and are taking sweeping action to secure our voter registration processes and the integrity of our voter rolls, so that New Jerseyans can feel confident about their election system,” Sherrill said.
Sen. Anthony Bucco, the state Senate’s GOP leader, said Sherrill’s updates on the voter registration debacle create more questions than answers. The public should see a full report about the thousands of people improperly registered and the analysis that supports Sherrill’s conclusions, Bucco said.
“We now have even more evidence that there were serious weaknesses in New Jersey’s voter registration system but still do not understand the full story. It is past time to release that report and give the public the facts. We need to stop learning about new problems through piecemeal press releases and start getting real answers, with a legislative review that leaves no stone unturned and ensures New Jersey voters can have confidence in the integrity of their elections,” he said.

name: WyoFile
title: Sublette County deals surprise blow to billionaire developer Joe Ricketts’ resort plans
description:
Commissioners abruptly reverse resort zoning for luxury resort that TD Ameritrade founder has argued is akin to conservation. 
The post Sublette County deals surprise blow to billionaire developer Joe Ricketts’ resort plans appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Sublette County elected officials unexpectedly delivered a major blow Tuesday to billionaire TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts’ yearslong ambitions to transform the Upper Hoback River area into a destination upscale resort.
In a 3-2 vote, commissioners eliminated a 2021 zoning change that carved out 56 acres of Ricketts’ Jackson Fork Ranch in northwest Wyoming for the resort. 

TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts welcomes guests at the August 2026 Saving Yellowstone conference hosted at his ranch. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Last week, the public learned that the Nebraskan financier had renewed his efforts to bring spas and fine dining to Bondurant — the source of considerable consternation for the small community about halfway between Pinedale and Jackson. In 2024, Ricketts halted construction on the resort, citing high costs, after county commissioners declined to waive seasonal protections for elk and moose that prevented construction during the coldest 5.5 months of the year. 
The undoing of Rickett’s renewed plans came suddenly. The five-person Sublette County Board of Commissioners did not include an agenda item in its Tuesday meeting about the billionaire’s plans for an all-inclusive luxury resort. During an earlier iteration of the project, his agents likened the planned facilities to Saratoga’s Brush Creek Ranch, which charges over four figures per night.
The decision came after commissioners went into executive session, when they can discuss matters in private. They emerged toward the end of the daylong meeting, and Commissioner Doug Vickrey made a motion to “initiate the process of terminating” Ricketts’ zoning, and in turn notify the planning and zoning commission and the landowner. 
There was no discussion on the matter before Sublette County Commission Chairman Lynn Bernard and Dave Stephens submitted aye votes. With Commissioners Sam White and Mack Bradley opposed, the resort zoning was rescinded. 
It’s a decision that boiled down to Sublette County’s zoning and development regulations, according to Bernard. Those rules stipulate that property rezoned to accommodate resorts must undergo “substantial development” within two years or the zoning change “shall” revert.
“Because of that, it was revoked,” Bernard told WyoFile. 
Sublette County commissioners referenced language in Section 2 of the county’s zoning and development regulations in their decision to rescind the resort zoning for Rickett’s property that had been approved in 2021. (Sublette County)
In revoking the zoning change, Bernard said, commissioners de facto invalidated a building permit for a lodge, restaurant and bar, a wellness/spa center, 20 guest suites, and a nearly  50,000-square-foot underground parking garage.
That permit application had been submitted in July and was approved administratively in September, the Jackson Hole News&Guide reported.
A spokesperson for Ricketts, whose family owns the Chicago Cubs, provided WyoFile with a statement on Wednesday.
“Private property rights are a cornerstone of our state, and property owners deserve clear rules, a consistent process, and confidence that their rights will be upheld,” Ricketts’ spokesperson Jessica Jaubert said. 
A detail of the main 20-room guest lodge from a landscape plan submitted July 20, 2026, to Sublette County Planning and Zoning for a new development on Joe Ricketts’ property along the Upper Hoback River Road in Bondurant. (Courtesy)
Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich explained to commissioners earlier in the Tuesday meeting why the zoning change hadn’t already been rescinded. 
“Termination is not something that happens automatically,” he said. “It has to go through a public hearing process and everything else.” 
Around the time of their vote, commissioners did not discuss any hearing or public process. 
But Bernard told WyoFile on Wednesday that he “absolutely” believes the commission’s change was legally sound. 
“The time period on that zoning had expired,” he said. 
The setback for Ricketts comes after he received some positive publicity for his conservation-oriented work under a venture called Saving Yellowstone. The billionaire, who was also in the news recently after filing a federal lawsuit alleging he was bilked out of $34 million, has repeatedly argued that developing resorts and getting wealthy tourists to understand conservation are needed to protect the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. 
Bondurant residents who worry the businessman’s plans will run roughshod over their rural, wildlife-rich corner of Wyoming have criticized Rickett’s rationale. 
“The only people who seem to be buying it are some conservationists,” Upper Hoback resident Dan Bailey said, “and that’s just bewildering that those people would drink that Kool-Aid.” 
Bailey’s girding his loins for another prolonged fight over the 85-year-old Ricketts’ development ambitions. Two years ago, when construction was halted, he told WyoFile he was unconvinced that the fight was truly over, and he reiterated those views on Wednesday. 
“They’ll be back,” Bailey said. “We’re not done. That’s for sure.”
Ed’s note: This story has an updated description about the resort plans.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV lawmakers give Flock until Friday to answer questions
description: As West Virginia lawmakers consider how to reign in artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance technology with legislation during their upcoming session, they’ve given Flock Safety a deadline of this week to answer a series of questions to their satisfaction — or else they may use subpoenas or compel witnesses to answer them.
text:
A Flock camera is seen in a parking lot in Morgantown, West Virginia on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)As West Virginia lawmakers consider how to reign in artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance technology with legislation during their upcoming session, they’ve given Flock Safety a deadline of this week to answer a series of questions to their satisfaction — or else they may use subpoenas or compel witnesses to answer them. 
In a letter Monday, members of the House Committee on Government Organization gave Flock Safety until Friday to provide written answers to questions they sent in a letter dated Aug. 14. 
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, and a member of the committee, said Tuesday lawmakers will introduce legislation regarding the technology in 2027, but the committee is trying to gather as much information as it can before crafting “responsible safeguards.”
“The reality is that the technology continues to evolve, and so it creates all sorts of questions ranging from the technological, to, again, just what protocols they have in place to, again just the efficacy of the product altogether,” Leavitt said. 
Lawmakers’ original request included 19 questions from five categories: security incidents and unauthorized access, surveillance scope and data sharing, accuracy and false positive rates, internal oversight and employee access controls, and data governance and infrastructure. 
Delegates asked Flock, for instance, to provide the number of times when raw video footage has been accessed by unauthorized users for each year the company has existed, and what caused the security breach in each instance. 
In a 10-page response from Flock Safety on Sept. 1, Dan Haley, chief legal officer for Flock, wrote a broad response to each of the five categories of questions, but did not include specific answers to many of the questions lawmakers posed.  
“Flock Safety takes the security of customer data, including video and license plate data, extremely seriously,” Haley wrote, in part, under the heading regarding security incidents. “Because Flock operates technology used by thousands of public safety agencies and handles information associated with active criminal investigations, our security program is designed around continuous prevention, detection, testing, investigation and remediation rather than the unrealistic assumption that a system will never experience a security event.
State lawmakers wrote in a response that many of the answers were not sufficient. 
“A general description of your security program is not a substitute for the information we  requested about raw video footage from Flock devices being accessed,” lawmakers wrote in a response Sept. 3. 
Flock said that they would “welcome the chance to provide a briefing to the committee,” but Lawmakers said in a response that a briefing is not acceptable.
“Meeting behind closed doors is no substitute for providing written responses to questions of such clear  public concern — questions all the more relevant since new Flock camera hacking incidents have come to light,” the letter from Monday reads. “Six weeks after our initial August 14, 2026 request, you have failed to produce these answers. As our last letter clearly stated, we do not intend to sit for a briefing with you until Flock Safety has responded in full to our requests. “
The Oct. 5 letter is signed by Leavitt, Ryan Browning, R-Wayne; Patrick Lucas, R-Cabell;  and Committee Chair Chris Phillips, R-Barbour. 
Several West Virginia municipalities across West Virginia have either considered or contracted with Flock Safety to install surveillance systems, including automatic license plate readers and gunshot detection equipment. The American Civil Liberties Union says the technology is “tracking, logging and sharing your movements without a warrant.” 
Flock Safety has been the subject of privacy and constitutional concerns nationally. The Institute for Justice has reportedly identified more than 100 incidents of Flock abuse, including law enforcement stalking romantic partners, wrongfully pulling people over and other misconduct. 
The ACLU of West Virginia is suing the city of Huntington over its five-year contract with the company to provide the surveillance equipment for more than $2.1 million. A Huntington organization opposed to Flock is pursuing a ballot initiative that would require the city to void its contract with the company. 
Leavitt declined to mention what specific safeguards lawmakers are considering, but said he expects a “very robust discussion” during the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January.
“What has kind of united everybody from all different perspectives on these questions is that Flock needs to answer the requests that we’ve made so that we are best informed to make those decisions,” Leavitt said. 
The request comes about two months after Kevin Kane, director of government affairs for Flock, gave a presentation to the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization during the August legislative interim meetings. 
“You had, really, two different categories of challenges there,” Leavitt said of Kane’s testimony. “One is that a number of detailed questions they simply said ‘we’ll get back to you on that,’ and they clearly intimated they’d like to have a private meeting instead.”
Leavitt said lawmakers believe the information should be provided publicly because the issue has so much public interest, and public interest plays a role in how lawmakers legislate.
“The second real challenge is that there were several different areas where Flock’s representative provided certain information that then, on later questioning, really broke down, and rather gave the impression that he was trying to mislead the Legislature.”
Leavitt said many West Virginians have questions about Flock. Some people are adamantly opposed to the technology, while others are learning about it for the first time, he said. It’s important that lawmakers understand it before regulating it, he said. 
“We want to make sure that we don’t craft the law in such a way that it doesn’t really actually get at what all of the vulnerabilities and issues are,” he said. “So that requires us really honing the depths of this as much as we can, so that we make sure that we do as good a job as possible in the legislation that we pass.”
