name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gov. Laura Kelly backs Kansas Democrat for U.S. House, wades into Iowa governor’s race
description: Outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly endorses a Democrat in Kansas' 2nd District congressional race and she taunts the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Iowa.
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly, the two-term Kansas governor, endorses Democrat Don Coover in the 2nd District congressional race and declines to endorse Iowa gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn, a registered Kansas voter until October 2024. This June 26, 2026, image of Kelly is from a Kansas Reflector interview with the governor. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly issued the anticipated endorsement Wednesday of a fellow Kansas Democrat campaigning for U.S. House and unexpectedly ventured into the Iowa gubernatorial contest to oppose one of her “constituents.”
The two-term governor from Topeka urged voters Nov. 3 to support Don Coover, a U.S. Army veteran, veterinarian and rancher from Galesburg. He’s campaigning for the 2nd District seat held by Republican U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt.
“Kansans deserve leaders who work hard, listen to Kansans and show up ready to get to work on day one, and that’s Don Coover,” Kelly said. “He’ll put Kansans first, not special interests or big donors, and work with both parties to get things done.”
Coover said he was honored to receive Kelly’s blessing and admired her record of placing Kansans ahead of partisan politics.
“I’ll take that same approach to Washington,” he said.
Schmidt celebrated an endorsement by the Kansas State Lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police, which represents thousands of law enforcement officers. He was previously endorsed by Kansas Farm Bureau, Kansas Livestock Association and National Rifle Association.
“In Congress, I’ll continue working to give law enforcement the tools and resources they need, protect those who protect us and keep Kansas communities safe,” Schmidt said.
Meanwhile, Kelly took to social media to support Democrat Rob Sand, who is competing against Republican Zach Lahn in the race for Iowa governor. A point of contention has been a revelation that Lahn voted in Kansas elections during 2018, 2020 and 2022 before registering in October 2024 to vote in Iowa. Another campaign topic has been Lahn’s frequent trips to visit his children in Kansas.
“Imagine my surprise when I learned that one of my constituents is running for governor,” Kelly said. “Not here in his home state of Kansas, but two states over in Iowa. Now, generally, I support Kansans. I was even proud to see Zach Lahn voted here in ’18, ’20 and ’22. I hope he voted for me in the Kansas governor’s race. But in the Iowa governor’s race, I’m supporting the Iowan.”
“Zach, there are no hard feelings, but it is time to come back to Kansas,” she said. “As they say, there’s no place like home.”
Lahn graduated from high school in Iowa before attending college in Colorado and working on political campaigns in Colorado and Montana. During the gubernatorial race in Iowa, Lahn said his official residence was a farm near Belle Plaine, Iowa.
He moved to Wichita nearly a decade ago to help launch a private school financed by the son and daughter-in-law of billionaire Charles Koch. With millions of dollars from the Koch family and backing of Chase and Annie Koch, the school opened in 2018. Annie Koch and Lahn divorced their spouses and married each other, which coincided with signs of financial stress at the school known as Wonder. The Lahns loaned the school at least $4.5 million.
Lahn said he returned to Iowa in 2023, but children in his blended family stayed in Wichita. The Des Moines Register reported that Lahn, a licensed pilot, flew from Iowa to Kansas 37 times from October 2025 to May 2026.
During the Tuesday debate in Iowa between Lahn and Sand, the issue of Lahn’s residency was raised.
“I have a blended family, and they split time,” Lahn said. “And I’m gonna tell you right now, I am not going to be intimidated on this.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Lincoln Party puts out statement of principles, which foe calls ‘bare minimum’
description: After facing criticism for lacking any policy platform, Indiana’s fledgling Lincoln Party released Wednesday what it called a statement of principles.
text:
The Lincoln Party logo.After facing criticism for lacking any policy platform, Indiana’s fledgling Lincoln Party released Wednesday what it called a statement of principles.
The Lincoln Party’s platform is at issue because it will gain automatic statewide ballot access for its nominees if its secretary of state candidate, former Republican Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, tops 2% of the vote in this fall’s election.
Lincoln Party Chair Nathan Gotsch says the party’s creation is aimed at making it easier for independent candidates to run for office without having to gather petition signatures to appear on election ballots.
Gotsch, who is Ballard’s campaign manager, said in a statement that all Lincoln Party candidates and party officials will be required to sign and uphold the statement of principles.
Indiana Lincoln Party Chair Nathan Gotsch (Courtesy photo)
Those include broad strokes such as “ensuring that government protects the rights of all people equally” and meeting “standards for governing in the public interest.”
“The Lincoln Party will be built around principles, not a platform that tells candidates where they have to stand on every issue,” Gotsch said. “That doesn’t mean our candidates won’t have clear positions on issues. Quite the opposite. It will be their job to tell voters where they stand and what policies they want to advance to solve the problems facing their communities.”
Republican candidate Max Engling has faulted Ballard and the Lincoln Party for a lack of stances on taxes, social issues and other policies.
Engling’s campaign did not immediately comment Wednesday on the Lincoln Party’s announcement. 
He previously criticized the Lincoln Party as presenting voters a blank slate of future support for what it regards as “high-quality candidates” without any stated ideology.
“To me, that says nothing about what they stand for,” Engling said.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh’s campaign declined to comment Wednesday.
The Libertarian Party has retained automatic ballot access by topping the 2% mark in secretary of state voting every four years since 1994.
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings knocked the Lincoln Party statement as “establishing a bare minimum standard.”
“What the Lincoln Party released is a code of conduct,” Shillings said. “It’s nice, but it isn’t a policy platform, and I don’t think it’s news. Pretty much every political party, every elected or appointed official and anyone else who holds an office job already adheres to something very similar.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: US Wind pulls out of wind turbine manufacturing at Sparrows Point
description: US Wind, the company behind a proposed offshore wind farm off the coast of Ocean City, no longer plans to develop components for wind turbines at Sparrows Point — at least not for now — turning its lease over to Anduril Industries to build a shipyard there.
text:
US Wind CEO Jeff Grybowski outside the U.S. District Court in Baltimore on Dec. 10, 2025, after a hearing on the Trump administration's plans to reconsider the permit issued for its Maryland wind farm. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)US Wind, the company behind a proposed offshore wind development off the coast of Ocean City, no longer plans to develop components for wind turbines at Baltimore County’s Sparrows Point — at least not for now.
The Baltimore-based company turned over its lease at the Tradepoint Atlantic site in Sparrows Point to Anduril Industries, the shipbuilding company whose arrival was heralded on Tuesday by a visit from President Donald Trump (R).
It comes as US Wind’s only offshore wind project, planned for Ocean City’s coastline, continues to face legal headwinds and roadblocks from the Trump administration.
At the tail end of President Joe Biden’s (D) administration, the US Wind project received its last federal permit, but the town of Ocean City challenged it shortly thereafter. And after Trump’s inauguration, the federal government that once defended the permit permit for the project signaled its intent to revoke it, spurring a new round of legal wrangling.
Sparrows Point shipyard could bring thousands of jobs, promises billions in investments

In a statement issued Tuesday, US Wind CEO Jeff Grybowski said his company “jumped at the opportunity” to bring “near-term” jobs to the Sparrows Point site as US Wind faces delays. The site will be taken over by Anduril, which plans to invest $3.7 billion at the former home of Bethlehem Steel to construct a new shipbuilding facility, Arsenal-2, that is expected to bring an estimated 3,100 permanent new jobs to Maryland.
“Our offshore wind plans, like many other similar projects in the U.S., are delayed due to legal disputes and uncertainty created by federal agencies. So, we are shifting our focus to helping Anduril build a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility at Sparrows Point,” Grybowski’s statement said. “This new development ensures that job creation and economic development can proceed apace at [Tradepoint].”
The facility at Tradepoint had been expected to fabricate steel components for wind turbines, including towers and monopiles, and create hundreds of manufacturing jobs. Last year, the Trump administration pulled back $47.4 million in grant funding that had been awarded during the Biden administration for the steel facility, called Sparrows Point Steel, but US Wind said at the time that it planned to move forward with the steel fabrication site anyway.
In a statement on Wednesday, Rebecca Rehr, the director of climate policy and justice at the Maryland League of Conservation Voters, bemoaned the news about Sparrows Point Steel, calling it another negative effect of Trump administration policies on clean-energy companies.
“Maryland faces rising energy demand and electricity bills. We have been consistently disappointed that the Trump administration doesn’t see the value across the supply chain for the clean energy industry, and continues to single out wind when wind is working,” Rehr said.
“We are seeing job and growth opportunities across clean energy sectors, yet this administration continues to block these projects, which are the fastest and cheapest to deploy,” her statement said.

Van Ingram, the longtime head of Kentucky’s Office of Drug Control Policy, is retiring at the end of 2026, Gov. Andy Beshear announced Wednesday. 
Tara Hyde, the CEO of People Advocating Recovery who is in long term recovery, will step into the role of executive director. 
Ingram has been with the office since 2004, when Ernie Fletcher was governor of Kentucky. 
Before that, he worked with the Maysville Kentucky Police Department for 23 years, including six as chief of police, according to the Justice and Public Safety Cabinet. Ingram was named executive director of the office in 2008. 
“There are caring people all over state government, in every cabinet and every agency, that have worked to bring this problem under control, as well as the Administrative Office of the Courts, the General Assembly, have all played a big part in our success,” said Ingram. 
During Ingram’s time with the Office of Drug Control Policy, overdose deaths took a downward turn. The 2025 Drug Overdose Fatality Report showed overdose deaths are down nearly 23% from 2024, following a four-year downward trend. 
Tara Hyde. (Sam Foree)
“It’s this work that led governor after governor, both Republicans and Democrats, to reappoint him to this position,” Beshear said during a Wednesday press conference in Frankfort. 
Hyde, a longtime advocate for policy to help people in recovery, has herself been in recovery since 2011. 
“Since being in recovery and overcoming addiction, I’ve found a real passion for helping people, for getting people access to services and for creating new services when they didn’t exist,” Hyde said. “That’s why I’ve made it my life’s work to support recovery services as well as individuals who are actively seeking help.” 
She added: “I look forward to stepping into this role to support my fellow Kentuckians who are fighting addiction and going through substance use disorder treatment, recovery support services, looking for housing and gaining access to meaningful, passionate lives — because that’s what we all deserve.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s housing crisis needs bold answers
description:
Homelessness has become ordinary in Vermont. And that is extraordinary.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s housing crisis needs bold answers.
text:
This commentary is by David Bond, who taught at Bennington College from 2013 to 2026. He now runs the Center for Environmental Justice at Georgetown University. 
Vermont is not an easy place to be homeless. Winters are unforgiving, and this rural state has minimal infrastructure to support unhoused people. Shelters are few and far between, and most were built when the loss of housing was a temporary setback tied to house fires or fleeing domestic abuse.
Personal tragedy is no longer the trigger of homelessness in Vermont. Today, a social catastrophe rips all manner of residents from their homes with ruthless indifference. Yet our government seems incapable of reckoning with this unfolding disaster.
Last year, I taught a class on the housing crisis at Bennington College. My students and I read every report we could find and interviewed shelter staff, local journalists and housing advocates who all describe the same horror story: a system overwhelmed by desperation. 
Ten years ago, the median price of a home in Vermont was $200,000. Today, it’s $438,000. Home prices have nearly doubled over the past decade while salaries increased at half that rate, with most wage growth accruing on the higher end of the income ladder. A newly constructed home in Vermont now has a median price of $620,000, a sticker price out of reach for, by my calculation, 80% of the state’s population. 
Rents have also risen while the income of most renters has flatlined at $43,000. In some Vermont communities, the median fair market rent has almost doubled in the past five years. And today, half of all renters in Vermont have slipped into what the Department of Housing and Urban Development defines as cost-burdened as rent eats up more and more of their paychecks. 
The human wreckage of these numbers gathers in parking lots crowded with occupied cars each night, in tattered encampments in the woods and under the overpass, and in the long lines outside public libraries and recreational centers each morning waiting for the privilege of a bathroom: rural homelessness.
While the actual number of homeless people in Vermont may seem minor in comparison with states like California and New York, the rate of increase in homelessness in Vermont outstrips every other state.

READ MORE

And in contrast with those states, the homeless in Vermont are not pouring in from elsewhere nor willfully rejecting society. By and large, unhoused people have deep roots in the Green Mountain State. And a great number of them are working full-time or are seniors living on the fixed income of retirement.
In Vermont, housing costs have achieved escape velocity from the economic fundamentals of place. What working residents can afford is no longer a gravitational force holding mortgages and rents within the realm of reason.
For Vermonters losing their grip on housing, few accord the crisis any academic explanation. It’s a full-time job that no longer adds up. It’s a sickness that bankrupted a family. It’s retirement that never factored in inflation. It’s student loans when no one is hiring. It’s a divorce that cut a paycheck in half. It’s a minor setback that spirals into total loss.
Three converging trends offer a provisional explanation of the housing disaster in Vermont.
First, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many cooped-up residents in Boston and New York City bought second homes in Vermont. Many of those homes now operate as vacation rentals in a state with the second-highest share of seasonal homes in America. Vacation rentals limit housing available for residents and skew pricing away from local wages and toward weekend wealth.
Second, private equity has elbowed its way into single-family home markets. A recent study found that Vermont has witnessed a 60% rise in corporate investor purchases of single-family homes, catapulting the state into the top 10 for growth of private equity in residential markets. 
And third, global investors, having amassed more wealth than can be profitably held in checking accounts or stocks, now turn to U.S. real estate. Their outsized investments in luxury properties may have started in big cities, but their telltale signs ripple outward into rural areas: surging prices with high vacancy rates. 
This all shines a rather unflattering light on high-minded talk of supply and demand as the most sensible solution to the housing crisis. Simply unshackling private developers to build, build, build may only construct more vacation homes and investment opportunities for elites from elsewhere.
Vermont was founded as an armed animus to absentee landlords. Where are the bold visions now to meet this housing crisis at scale? Where are the radical policies and programs that can place housing costs back within reach of working Vermonters?
In my class, students brainstormed how Vermont might seize shuttered colleges and factories to remake public housing for the 21st century. We explored how Vermont might look to Red Vienna or Mexico’s National Housing Fund or even American labor unions’ unrealized plans for mutual housing as models to meet this crisis at scale. And we imagined how Vermont might become a beacon for young talent eager to get to work building a more just, sustainable and dignified world.
When Gov. Phil Scott’s executive housing team visited our class, students jumped at the chance to ask about their visions for public housing. The deputy secretary of the Agency of Human Services, Kristin McClure, responded to the premise by saying, “Vermont is not looking to become more of a landlord.” Reflecting on the quarter-billion dollars Vermont spent on emergency housing in the past few years, she added, “We did the math, and we could have housed every single homeless person had we built new units with that money.”

text:
DMACC and Ankeny Community School District have partnered to put high school students in a professional early childhood education environment. (Photo by Lourdes Balduque/Getty Images)Des Moines Area Community College is helping high school students get a jumpstart on their early childhood education training through a partnership with the Ankeny Community School District.
The Ankeny-based community college announced in a news release Wednesday it is expanding its relationship with the school district through a program allowing high school students to attend early childhood education courses at Terrace Learning Center, which houses the district’s preschool program.
According to the release, this initiative is two years in the making and transforms courses previously offered online only through the community college’s online career academy into in-person instruction and on-the-job observation of professionals.

Students who enroll in the Introduction to Early Childhood Education and Childhood Health, Safety and Nutrition courses will be taught on-site by a DMACC instructor and have opportunities to complete observation and clinical work.
“Offering the courses through DMACC faculty allows traditional college students to enroll in the same sections alongside high school students,” said DMACC early childhood education program chair Katie Champlin in the release. “As a result, both groups experience a more authentic college classroom environment while high school students benefit from learning alongside current college students.”
With this partnership, students will gain a more complete picture of what working in early childhood education looks like beyond any assumptions that having only classroom work can create, Champlin said in the release, aiding them in building confidence and establishing their “professional identities as future early childhood educators.”
The overarching goal of the district and community college’s work is to help high school students earn a certificate in early childhood education, with 13 required credits, before they earn their diploma. This certificate satisfies the education requirement for the Child Development Associate credential as well.
“Ultimately, the partnership creates a pathway,” Champlin said in the release. “An opportunity to explore the profession, develop practical skills, earn college credit and credentials, and see a clear pathway toward continued education and employment in (early childhood education).”

title: Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints
description: Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints New public portal gives Delawareans a direct way to report fraud, waste, corruption and misuse of state resources DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s Office of the Inspector General has launched a public website and complaint hotline, giving residents, state employees and others a direc[...]
text:
Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints
New public portal gives Delawareans a direct way to report fraud, waste, corruption and misuse of state resources
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s Office of the Inspector General has launched a public website and complaint hotline, giving residents, state employees and others a direct way to report suspected fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and misuse of state government resources.
The launch marks another step in establishing the independent watchdog office created by the General Assembly in 2025 and now led by Delaware’s first inspector general, Robert P. Storch.
The new website provides information about the office, its responsibilities and how it operates. It also includes an online form for submitting complaints and concerns to the inspector general.
Complaints and inquiries are kept confidential to the greatest extent possible, according to the office, and people filing reports may choose to remain anonymous.
“The public launch of the new OIG website and Hotline mark an important milestone in the development of our office,” Storch said in an announcement reported by Delaware news organizations.
Storch said the office is continuing to hire staff while giving the public more information about the agency and how concerns can be reported.
New avenue for government complaints
The Office of the Inspector General was established as an independent, nonpartisan state agency responsible for detecting and deterring fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuses of government resources that harm the public interest.
State law allows the inspector general to investigate the management and operations of state agencies and to begin investigations either on the office’s own initiative or after receiving a complaint.
Complaints may be submitted by individuals or organizations.
The law also requires the office to maintain a telephone number, website, email address and mailing address for complaints and inquiries.
The inspector general is required to remain neutral and impartial and is not intended to serve as an advocate either for the person filing a complaint or for the state agency involved.
Delaware’s first inspector general
Gov. Matt Meyer signed Senate Bill 4 in August 2025, creating the Office of the Inspector General following years of discussion about establishing an independent statewide government watchdog.
Storch was sworn in May 8 as Delaware’s first inspector general.
At the time, state officials said the office was intended to strengthen accountability, transparency and public confidence in state government.
Storch previously served as inspector general for the U.S. Department of Defense and as the first Senate-confirmed inspector general of the National Security Agency. He also held senior positions in the U.S. Department of Justice Office of Inspector General.
One of Storch’s early priorities was establishing a public website and complaint hotline so Delawareans would have a direct way to bring concerns to the new office.
What the office can investigate
The inspector general’s jurisdiction includes allegations involving fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuses of government resources.
The office may examine the management and operations of state agencies and investigate complaints involving the public interest.
The law also limits the office’s role in routine employment disputes involving state workers unless those complaints are connected to fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption or another abuse of government resources.
The inspector general also is expected to coordinate with the Delaware Department of Justice, auditor of accounts, Public Integrity Commission and other investigative or law enforcement agencies when appropriate.
State law generally requires the inspector general to issue public findings and recommendations following completed investigations.
The office also must issue an annual report outlining complaints received, investigations opened and completed, significant investigations and unresolved recommendations or concerns.
The launch of the website and hotline gives Delawareans a direct point of access to an office created specifically to investigate concerns about how state government operates and how taxpayer resources are used.

Website: https://oig.delaware.gov/
Online complaint form: https://complaint.oig.delaware.gov/
Hotline: 1-855-OIG-6998
Local phone: 302-244-DOIG
Email: OIG_Hotline@delaware.gov
Mailing address:
60 Loockerman Plaza
Dover, DE 19901
Confidentiality: Complaints and inquiries are kept confidential to the greatest extent possible. People filing complaints may also choose to report anonymously.
What it does: Investigates allegations of fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuse of Delaware government resources.
Who can file a complaint: Individuals and organizations may submit complaints.
What can be reported: Suspected fraud, corruption, misuse of taxpayer resources, serious mismanagement or other government conduct that may harm the public interest.
What it generally does not handle: Routine state employee workplace disputes unless they involve fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption or misuse of government resources.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Alert: Mississippi Blood Services seeks donors to ease shortage
description: A Mississippi Blood Services employee collects blood at the organization in Flowood on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Blood Services is calling on all eligible donors to give blood as it struggles with a severe supply shortage.
Donors of every blood type are needed.
Kasey Dickson, Mississippi Blood Services director of marketing and public relations, explained that it’s normal for donations to drop during the summer. However, MBS isn’t sure what’s causing the ongoing slowdown.
Mississippi’s blood shortage is part of a national problem. The American Red Cross, America’s Blood Centers and the Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies released a joint statement in July calling for more donations to help the nation’s strained blood supply.
MBS needs 250 blood donations and 40 platelet donations daily to maintain a healthy supply. Dickson said the amount of donations it currently receives daily is “not anywhere near that.” 
“Blood cannot be made in a tube,” Dickson said. “The only way that blood can be provided to other individuals in need is if individuals themselves donate it.”
Mississippi Blood Services provides blood products to over 50 hospitals statewide, as well as ambulance and helicopter services that transport to rural communities. This includes whole blood, platelets and more.
MBS collects products at facilities in Flowood, Oxford and with mobile collection units. 
Eligible donors can walk in or schedule an appointment. People can find information on eligibility on MBS’ website and by calling 601-981-3232. 
MBS recommends donors prepare by eating a healthy meal and drinking plenty of fluids. Donors will be given an onsite health screening, which includes a questionnaire and a mini-physical. 
Once blood is collected, it gets tested for its blood type, red blood cell antibodies and undergoes nucleic acid amplification testing. It’s also screened for infections, including HIV-1 and hepatitis B. After testing and processing, it’s ready to be delivered to hospitals in need.
MBS has been spreading the word about the need for donations, as well as holding special promotions. For Breast Cancer Awareness Donor Appreciation Week, people who donate at the Flowood and Oxford centers can receive a free T-shirt and car magnet while supplies last through Friday.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Republicans tout a gas tax cut that Democrats call an election-season desperation move
authors: Lynn Bonner, Trevon Spencer, Christine Zhu
description: As lawmakers gathered in Raleigh Wednesday to debate temporarily suspending the state gas tax, Republicans and Democrats both said they supported the idea. But while Republican leaders touted the economic relief it’ll give North Carolina drivers and businesses, Democrats say GOP leaders are motivated by election fears, not concern for their constituents.  Th[...]
text:
NC Senate leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, is surrounded by other Republican senators as he talks about a bill suspending the state's gas tax. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)As lawmakers gathered in Raleigh Wednesday to debate temporarily suspending the state gas tax, Republicans and Democrats both said they supported the idea. But while Republican leaders touted the economic relief it’ll give North Carolina drivers and businesses, Democrats say GOP leaders are motivated by election fears, not concern for their constituents. 
The bill would suspend the 41-cent gas tax until the end of November. The state uses gas tax revenue to build and maintain roads. The $362.3 million cost of suspending the tax will be backfilled by taking the money from a state reserve fund, legislators said. 
Senate leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, dismissed cutting the tax a few months ago, but now says lawmakers’ constituents need help.  
“There is great momentum to do this at this time,” Berger said at a news conference Wednesday morning. The legislature is expected to pass the bill Wednesday.
‘Election Day gimmick’? As NC lawmakers eye gas tax cut, Stein questions timing

Democrats said Republicans’ sudden decision to suspend the tax stems from fears that their candidates will lose seats in November.
Republicans could have included the gas tax suspension in the state budget the legislature passed in July, but they did not. Instead, Republican legislative leaders announced the special session last weekend, just one month before Election Day.
Senate Democratic Leader Sydney Batch said if Republicans really wanted to help constituents, they could have done it months ago.
“Republicans at this point in time are shameless, and they are cowards,” Batch said at a separate news conference. 
“They are failing to deliver for their constituents because they would rather hold on to every single ounce of power and use it as a cudgel,” the Wake County Democrat said. 
Sen. Lisa Barnes, R-Nash, also spoke at the Senate Republican news conference. Barnes is being challenged by Democrat James Gailliard, a former state House member, in what’s expected to be a close race that could decide whether Republicans maintain their veto-proof majority in the Senate. 
“This bill is an incredible lifeline for farmers and producers across our state,” she said. “Many of us are already reeling from the impact of the drought, and increased fuel costs just add another burden at exactly the wrong time.”
In May, Berger rejected the idea of repealing the gas tax, calling it “more a feel-good kind of thing than something that would actually make a whole lot of difference with reference to individuals.”
Asked about that Wednesday, Berger said, “The pressure on individual citizens is much greater now that it was then. And it still feels good.”
Under the bill, retailers won’t have to cut prices on gas they’ve already purchased and on which they’ve already paid the tax. 
Berger said he didn’t expect prices to drop immediately. 
“I’m fairly certain you’re not going to see 41 cents off tomorrow, but it should come down at some point,” Berger said. “But we’ve got to recognize that market forces also have a huge impact on what the ultimate cost of fuel is, and we’ll see.”
Drivers shop for gas, Berger said. If drivers see that one station is charging a penny less per gallon than a gas station nearby, they’ll buy the less expensive gas. 
Speaking in front of the Legislative Building, North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton criticized GOP leaders for their inaction on other pieces of legislation that address affordability. 
“I hope that nobody is buying what Republicans are trying to do right now in this legislature, which is to cover the fact that they’ve not done a thing for people across North Carolina for the last nine months or the last two years,” she said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Guckian is low on cash and altitude as Foulkes, Block soar toward Nov. 3
description: Trailing in the polls and facing public pressure to drop out, Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian has just over $7,000 in his campaign account in the final sprint toward the Nov. 3 general election, according to information filed with the Rhode Island Board of Elections late Tuesday. Meanwhile, Guckian’s two opponents, Democrat Helena Buonanno F[...]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian has $7,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5, 20206, according to his most recent campaign finance report filed with the Rhode Island Board of Elections. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Trailing in the polls and facing public pressure to drop out, Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian has just over $7,000 in his campaign account in the final sprint toward the Nov. 3 general election, according to information filed with the Rhode Island Board of Elections late Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Guckian’s two opponents, Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes and independent Ken Block, each have more than $200,000 cash on hand, having exponentially outraised and outspent Guckian, according to their campaign finance reports.
Candidates who participated in the Sept. 9 primary elections filed reports reflecting donations and expenditure from Sept. 2 to Oct. 5. Reports from candidates only participating in the Nov. 3 general election included financial activity from July 1 to Oct. 5. Both set s of reports were due by midnight on Oct. 6.
News of Guckian’s cash flow woes comes one week after he missed two gubernatorial forums to take a last-minute trip to Florida to boost his flailing campaign. Event headliners Eric and Lara Trump never showed up for the Oct. 1 private fundraiser in West Palm Beach. And mingling with deep-pocketed donors yielded not a single check for Guckian as of the Oct. 5 state campaign finance reporting period.
Also absent from his campaign accounting: travel expenses, including the private plane he took from Delaware to Florida on Sept. 30.
Guckian’s campaign plans to submit an addendum to the report detailing the in-kind donations related to his travel costs, Mike Fahey, a campaign spokesperson, confirmed Wednesday. Fahey did not know when the update would be submitted.
Guckian, an aide to former Gov. Don Carcieri and the previous head of the Rhode Island Dental Association, took a commercial flight from President Donald J. Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York Friday, Fahey said. A rental car snafu delayed his arrival in Rhode Island until late Friday night, causing him to miss a forum hosted by the Senior Agenda Coalition of Rhode Island, the Providence Journal reported. Guckian also skipped a Sept. 30 forum at Roger Williams University School of Law hosted by the League of Women Voters and the Women’s Fund of Rhode Island due to the trip, cancelling the morning of the event.
“These were truly scheduling oversights,” Fahey said.
Public pressure has mounted for Guckian to drop out following an internal poll by Block’s campaign showing Block leading Foulkes in a two-way race.
Fahey reiterated Wednesday that Guckian intends to remain in the race.
Guckian raised under $7,000 in the 33-day period that ended Oct. 5, and spent a little over $12,000. His balance includes a total of $10,500 in personal loans to his campaign earlier this year. 
Fahey was confident Guckian’s fundraising efforts would pay off. Fahey said the Florida trip was the “start of some very important conversations” but declined to name the groups or donors the campaign was speaking to.
“I don’t think we’re going to let one campaign finance report tell the whole story,” Fahey said. “We still have several weeks to Election Day.”
Guckian’s campaign has no fundraising events scheduled for the next two weeks, Fahey confirmed.
Foulkes is biggest spender
After spending more than $5 million leading up her primary against Gov. Dan McKee, Foulkes has begun to replenish her reserves, raising more than $380,000 from individuals and political action committees while spending more than $545,000 in the 33-day period that ended Oct. 5. Foulkes, a former CVS executive, also received more than $125,000 in in-kind donations from the Rhode Island Democratic State Committee, and a $500,000 independent expenditure from the Democratic Governors Association.
Foulkes’ report also includes $6,750 in combined refunds to seven donors who gave more than the $2,000 limit allowed per candidate per calendar year. The excess donations, first reported by GoLocalProv, drew rebukes from Guckian and Block. The state elections board does not intend to impose fines as long as Foulkes’ campaign returns the donations, spokesperson Christopher Hunter confirmed.
Foulkes’ account balance includes a $1.8 million loan balance from money she contributed to her 2022 gubernatorial primary campaign.
While Guckian has struggled to rally Rhode Island Republicans around his campaign after narrowly defeating Elaine Pelino in the GOP primary, Foulkes saw a surge of support from influential Democratic leaders. The 80,000-member Rhode Island AFL-CIO, which declined to endorse in the primary, threw its weight behind Foulkes for the general election, with unanimous support from the 200 union delegates who voted on Tuesday.
Also Tuesday, the Rhode Island Democratic Party held a fundraising “Unity Dinner” for candidates, including Foulkes, with tickets ranging from $150 to $2,500 per person. The event was held after the period covered by the latest state campaign reports.
Unlike his opponents, Block did not have to win a primary to advance to the Nov. 3 ballot, leaving him with more than $263,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5. Block, a software engineer and small business owner, raised just over $63,000 in individual donations during the three-month reporting period. His balance was boosted with a $190,000 personal loan. He spent just over $80,000.
Including personal loans from his two previous gubernatorial runs in 2010 and 2014, Block has a $1.2 million outstanding loan balance.
“I’m confident that we have the resources to win,” Block said in a statement Wednesday.
Foulkes’ campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The three gubernatorial candidates will meet for a live debate in the lobby of the Providence Performing Arts Center, hosted by NBC 10, at 7 p.m. Wednesday 
The race also includes two other independent candidates, Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds. Gotra, a former solar sales company owner now facing allegations of predatory and deceptive sales tactics from the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office, had just over $1,500 cash on hand, raising more than $2,800 and spending $2,400, according to his report. The campaign report for Reynolds, who works at The Capital Grille, was not available as of Wednesday morning.
Reynolds has not submitted any other mandatory campaign reports since July 2024. Reached by phone Wednesday morning, Reynolds said he was “working on it.”
Early voting begins on Oct. 14.

name: VTDigger
title: For Sam Lucci, Freedom & Unity made the path back to college a “no-brainer”
description:
“There might be a point where I have to weigh the cost of tuition against everything else,” Sam said. “But as long as there is Freedom & Unity, I can plan my life and my next semester and a path to my degree.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For Sam Lucci, Freedom & Unity made the path back to college a “no-brainer” .
text:
Sam Lucci has known for the last ten years that he wanted to finish his education but constantly found himself weighing the costs against the benefits. Feeling like he couldn’t commit until he made a plan, Sam held off, pursuing jobs he liked and loved, gaining experience in sales, and taking an opportunity for on-the-job training that let him explore the trades. 
A “circuitous route” in his career and education 
Sam took what his VSAC outreach counselor, Martha McCaughin, describes as a “circuitous route on his journey toward getting his bachelor’s degree.” Martha works in VSAC’s Educational Opportunity Center, which helps adults access college and career training. She says that his journey “makes him a great role model for others, especially other men who haven’t gone straight through to college and who use their work and life experience to inform their educational focus.” 
After he graduated from Rutland High School in 2011, Sam took a gap year. He started at the University of Vermont, took a few classes at Community College of Vermont, and then left school and started working full-time at a hostel in Burlington. He loved that job, mostly because of the interaction he had with the people and the joy of meeting travelers. 
A few years later, he found himself in a job training program that would give him the skills and licensure needed for him to sell insurance. At the time, it felt like an educational opportunity and a way for him to earn a credential. A few months in, he realized it wasn’t for him and started looking for another job. 
The good thing about the insurance job is it gave him established credibility in sales. He landed a job at VTDigger in advertising and sales and laughs when he thinks that he used to be doing digital editing on these Spotlight articles himself, and now finds himself the subject of one. 
After a few years in that role and in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, Sam was restless. “I needed to do something where I was using my body and leaving the house,” he said. He found another opportunity to do on-the-job training as a technician at a local RV dealership. Through that, he was able to sample the trades—plumbing, electrical, carpentry, and more—spend time outdoors, and interact more with folks in the community. 
Returning home to Fair Haven piqued his interest in local government 
In 2021, Sam and his partner, Hannah, bought the house Sam grew up in from his mother. They knew they wanted to be homeowners and moving home to Fair Haven, where Sam grew up, was a pathway to making that dream a reality. 
Sam, who’s always had an interest in local government, started learning more about opportunities available in the community. Through that curiosity, he found out there was an open seat on the Select Board, and no one was running to fill it. Sam stepped up, ran a write-in campaign at the last minute, and is now in his second one-year term in the role. 
Finding Freedom & Unity to finance his education
At the same time, Sam decided it was time to go back to college. He’d been considering returning to school for a while but wasn’t sure how to make it work. His father works at Vermont State Castleton (Vermont State) in student success. Sam knew that family members of employees could receive some tuition benefits but wasn’t sure if they could apply to him as an adult. He went to the registrar’s office one day to ask about it, and, while he wasn’t eligible for those benefits, the team there told him about Freedom & Unity, a program that covers tuition costs for eligible Vermonters. 
“I took them at their word that it was as easy to get Freedom & Unity as they promised it would be and applied and enrolled. I got my financial aid package and it was so much easier than I expected,” he said. 
Freedom & Unity is funded by the Vermont Legislature and administered by VSAC, in partnership with Vermont State. Open to new or returning students of any age who do not already have a bachelor’s degree, Freedom & Unity is an opportunity for Vermont students with a family income of $85,000 or less, like Sam, to attend Vermont State tuition free.
With the help of Freedom & Unity, Sam was able to enroll full-time the next semester. “Knowing the tuition was covered made it a complete no-brainer for me,” he added. “I knew I had to take advantage of this opportunity as long as it was available.”
Coupling his interest in local government with a degree in political science
Sam took asynchronous classes online so that he could still work at a local housing nonprofit. He then started working part-time at the town office as the assistant town clerk in Fair Haven. After taking a few political science classes, Sam has narrowed his focus to a major in political science. He’s leaving the door open to add another major or a minor in the future, but for now, he’s enjoying the intersection of his interest in local government and his education. 
“There are a lot of really promising careers in planning, and in municipal and regional government in Vermont,” he noted. “We need a new generation of passionate and engaged people to pursue those careers. I’m hoping I can continue my education with that in mind.”
Freedom & Unity helped make it possible 
“I have no balance on my student account after Freedom & Unity,” Sam shared. “It’s really what made this possible for me. I do have living expenses and I’m very lucky to have a partner who is supportive of me and encouraged me to go back to school and pursue this, even though it’s hard. But I think a lot of people have these juggling decisions that they’re making, especially as an adult student.” Sam has about three semesters left before he finishes his degree. 
As for his work on the Select Board, it keeps him busy. Currently, he is interviewing candidates for town manager. And the ability to serve and keep engaged locally really appeals to him and marries his interests in local government, civic engagement, and political science.
“There might be a point where I have to weigh the cost of tuition against everything else,” Sam said. “But as long as there is Freedom & Unity, I can plan my life and my next semester and a path to my degree.”

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

title: Appeals Court: Kansas mail-in ballots will be accepted for three days after November election
description: TOPEKA — Mail-in ballots arriving three days after the November general election will still count in Kansas, an appellate court ruled, citing the need to make sure no votes are lost.  It was the latest ruling in a court battle between Secretary of State Scott Schwab and Kansas Appleseed, along with Kansans who believe a […]
text:
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab lost a request to the Court of Appeals that would have allowed the state to stop counting mail-in ballots at 7 p.m. on Election Day. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Mail-in ballots arriving three days after the November general election will still count in Kansas, an appellate court ruled, citing the need to make sure no votes are lost. 
It was the latest ruling in a court battle between Secretary of State Scott Schwab and Kansas Appleseed, along with Kansans who believe a 2025 statute eliminating a three-day grace period for mail-in votes violates their constitutional rights.
“Right now, where we’re at is everything is the same as it was for the primary,” said Nicki Rose, legal director for Kansas Appleseed Center for Law and Justice.
The statute changed state law to say only advance ballots received by 7 p.m. on Election Day would be counted. 
“When considering important constitutional challenges concerning election procedure and faced with an upcoming election, courts must be careful to avoid rulings that could cause votes to be lost,” said a Friday ruling from Chief Judge Sarah Warner and Judges Stephen Hill and Kim Schroeder.  
Schwab had asked the Kansas Court of Appeals to stay an injunction that forced the state to continue accepting mail-in votes for three days after the election while the court cases proceeded. 
Douglas County District Judge Carl Folsom issued the injunction before the August midterms to stop enforcement of the new statute, based on his belief plaintiffs were “substantially likely” to succeed at trial. 
“Considering the Secretary’s preliminary showing on the merits, the State’s asserted injuries, the irreparable consequences a stay could impose on voters, the public interest, and the rapidly approaching election calendar, we conclude that the Secretary has not met his burden to demonstrate that the temporary injunction should be suspended while this appeal proceeds,” the appeals court ruling said. 
The court on Friday agreed to Schwab’s motion to fast-track the appeal but said that still wouldn’t occur on the timetable Schwab requested. He asked the court to hear arguments before Oct. 14, when mail-in ballots would be sent to voters. 
Rose said this case is important because of the potential effects on Kansas voters, especially those who live in rural areas, people who are disabled and the elderly, many of whom rely on mailing in their ballots. 
“Even Secretary Schwab said himself, prior to the passage of the law we’re dealing with here, that we have a large amount of mail-in ballots, typically, and as a state, we have handled them very well,” she said. “It’s an important access point, particularly for a state with our makeup, geographically and demographically.”

Newsweek again ranks Wilmington Hospital program among nation’s best as ChristianaCare expands rehabilitation capacity in Delaware
WILMINGTON, Del. — ChristianaCare’s Center for Rehabilitation at Wilmington Hospital has been named one of the nation’s best inpatient rehabilitation facilities for the fourth consecutive year.
Newsweek included the center among its Best Physical Rehabilitation Centers in the United States and ranked it among the leading rehabilitation facilities in Delaware.
The ranking evaluates clinical quality, professional reputation, specialized accreditation and patient experience. More than half of the score is based on quality measures from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
“We care for each patient like they are a member of our own family,” said Dr. John Cheng, medical director of the Center for Rehabilitation.
“Each patient, their family, their home situation, how they were before and how they want to be in the future, their goals and what they want to achieve in life — that’s what we focus on.”
Growing demand for rehabilitation
The Wilmington center treats patients recovering from strokes, brain and spinal cord injuries, amputations, extended hospitalizations and serious orthopedic conditions.
In fiscal year 2026, the center discharged 890 patients with an average stay of 11.6 days.
ChristianaCare also reported that 95% of patients were living back in the community 90 days after discharge, compared with a national average of 93%.
“Many medical specialties aim to add years to a patient’s life,” Cheng said. “Our aim is to add life to their years.”
Jennifer Thomas, vice president of Rehabilitation Services, said patients are increasingly arriving with complex medical needs.
“The patient always comes first,” Thomas said. “Our expert team is dedicated to providing the best rehabilitation care with compassion and respect for every patient’s unique journey.”
Preparing patients for home
Rehabilitation includes physical, occupational and speech therapy, with patients practicing everyday activities such as climbing stairs, cooking and shopping.
Families and caregivers are also encouraged to participate in therapy and receive training before patients return home.
“Since I’ve been here, it changed my life for the better,” said patient Anthony Dobrosielski, who received occupational therapy following a fall.
Major Newark expansion coming
ChristianaCare recently expanded the Wilmington center to 36 beds, allowing it to serve about 216 additional patients annually.
A much larger expansion is planned for Newark.
ChristianaCare expects to open a $75 million freestanding inpatient rehabilitation hospital at 140 Red Mill Road in 2028.
The 92,000-square-foot hospital will have 73 beds and is expected to serve about 1,000 additional patients each year.
“This transformative investment will significantly expand access to specialized rehabilitation care across Delaware,” Thomas said.
The project is part of ChristianaCare’s broader $865 million investment in Delaware and is expected to nearly double the health system’s current rehabilitation capacity.

Where: Wilmington Hospital, 501 W. 14th St., Wilmington
Services: Inpatient rehabilitation for stroke, brain and spinal cord injuries, amputations, orthopedic injuries and other complex conditions.

Coming next: A new 73-bed ChristianaCare rehabilitation hospital is scheduled to open in Newark in 2028.

title: More threats in Nolan Wells case and a lawsuit
description: The Rev. Al Sharpton, right, and former NFL player Terrell Owens, center, stand with attorney Ben Crump as Crump speaks during a press conference after Nolan Xavier Wells’ funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
An Alabama man has become the fifth person charged in federal court with making threats related to Nolan Xavier Wells’ death investigation. 
Claude Henry Bates Jr., 41, of Montomery is accused of sending death and bomb threats to the Jackson County sheriff’s and coroner’s offices on Sept. 25 — days after a Jackson County grand jury declined to indict anyone in the death of Wells, according to court records. The 18-year-old’s body was found on July 6 on Horn Island.
Also, after weeks of threatened lawsuits over alleged defamation, three friends who were with Wells on Horn Island on July 4 filed a complaint Monday in federal court against former NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens. 
In a Sept. 26 post on X, Owens shared an Instagram video featuring Wells’ friends Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour that suggested they deleted evidence from Wells’ phone after he died. Owens added the message: “Arrest them immediately!!! Like yesterday” in all capital letters. 
A day earlier, the legal team representing Wells’ family held a press conference with Andrew Garrett, the forensic expert whose company was hired to inspect Wells’ phone. Garrett said that Snapchat messages were deleted off the phone but later clarified that other users can delete or recall messages. He added that other people did not unlock Wells’ phone after he last used it. 
The friends denied the allegation in the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Mississippi. The lawsuit represents one side of a legal argument. 
“Nolan Wells’ accident death at the Island was indeed a tragedy beyond measure. However, Warren, Jax, and Morgan played no role whatsoever in Nolan’s tragic death. Any accusations or suggestions that they murder their dear friend or took steps to cover up his murder are categorically false and now an intentional lie,” the complaint reads.
Owens attended Wells’ funeral and contributed $25,000 in reward money for information that would lead to an arrest or conviction in the case. 
He was not immediately available for comment Wednesday.  
Attorneys representing the friends previously said they plan to sue other public figures who they say have defamed them, including the Rev. Al Sharpton and “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin.

description: North Dakota Gov. text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong speaks to reporters after a special session of the Legislature concluded on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong and his campaign fund have given about $430,000 in support to Republican statewide and legislative candidates this year, more than one-quarter of which went to one state officeholder he appointed.
The full scope of Armstrong’s political spending became clearer after a Friday deadline for candidates to file pre-general election campaign finance reports with the secretary of state. 
Some Republican lawmakers and candidates criticized Armstrong’s donations earlier this year as unlawful and improper influence – a criticism also lobbed at former Gov. Doug Burgum’s millions of dollars in political spending in GOP primaries in 2020 and 2022. Armstrong has said he gives money directly to candidates who then decide how to run their campaigns, no strings attached. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
“The slate of candidates I have endorsed and financially supported are focused on results-driven policies for our state,” Armstrong said in a statement this week. 
Monetary and in-kind contributions from Armstrong and his campaign coffers total $430,473 this year, including $140,000 since the June primary, according to a North Dakota Monitor analysis of filings as of Wednesday.
The in-kind support was for Armstrong’s endorsement videos and film costs in connection with the primary election, he said.
In an emailed response to Monitor questions, Armstrong said he’s “proud to support these candidates” who want to “lower property taxes, grow our economy, and reduce government spending.
“We are also supporting statewide and other legislative candidates in the fall that did not have competitive primaries. We are working hard all across the board to get Republicans elected this November,” the governor said. 
Recipients include more than two dozen legislative candidates around the state, incumbents and newcomers. Armstrong gave as much as $10,000 single donations to some of those candidates.
In May, he said the money is campaign funds he raised “from a lot of North Dakotans,” not his personal wealth.
North Dakota lawmakers, candidates trade barbs with Gov. Armstrong over campaign donations

Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, said Armstrong’s donations violate the state constitution because of improper influence. He said the governor will have the votes to kill any bill he doesn’t like.
Armstrong knows the Republican circles in North Dakota and who he can work with in the Legislature and who will be difficult, said Mark Jendrysik, a professor of political science and public administration at the University of North Dakota.
“The governor is acting in a totally rational manner to try to increase the number of people who are willing to support his agenda in the Legislature,” Jendrysik said.
Four candidates Armstrong is supporting are the subject of a North Dakota Supreme Court case challenging their eligibility. The case alleges incomplete petition information the secretary of state’s office was allowed to be corrected while other candidates or groups were rejected, according to the challengers, who include two Republicans who lost their primaries to three of the candidates. 
Armstrong is supporting at least five statewide officeholders: Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, Secretary of State Michael Howe, State Superintendent Levi Bachmeier and Public Service Commissioners Sheri Haugen-Hoffart and Jill Kringstad. 
Armstrong appointed Kringstad and Bachmeier to their positions last year. They must win in November to continue serving.
North Dakota Public Service Commission incumbents defeat Republican challengers

Kringstad has received more than $125,000 in monetary and in-kind support from Armstrong – the most of any candidate he has helped – including his single largest monetary donation of $90,000, made shortly after the June primary, according to filings. Kringstad is running against former Democratic state lawmaker Scot Kelsh in November.
“I appointed Jill. She was a first-time candidate in a competitive primary. She is doing a great job, and we were happy to support her,” Armstrong said.
Armstrong gave Bachmeier a $25,000 donation and $5,450 of in-kind support, according to filings.
Armstrong’s contributions fall far short of Burgum’s millions, but in the context of North Dakota, $430,000 can be a fair amount, Jendrysik said. For legislative races, it might be enough for more mailers, signs and campaign help, he said. 
“This could be very effective. It could be enough to really help someone run a more visible, successful campaign,” he said. 
Seventy-five of 141 seats in the Legislature are on the ballot this fall. Republicans control the House 83-11 and the Senate 42-5. 
Absentee ballots available for North Dakota voters

Absentee voting began in late September. More than 8,300 ballots had been cast as of Wednesday morning.
The general election is unlikely to have any surprises given North Dakota’s Republican dominance, Jendrysik said. 
“Since we’re a one-party state, what’s most important is the factional division inside the Republicans,” Jendrysik said. “There’s certainly a number of different divisions and factions within the Republican Party, and I’m sure the governor wants to get support for his particular positions and his faction of the party.”

title: Parents of child allegedly killed by daycare provider sue state investigators
description: The parents of an infant who police allege was killed by a daycare provider are now suing state officials over their initial handling of the investigation. Timmeri and Rylee Reeves of Madison County are suing former Iowa Department of Health and Human Services Director Kelly Garcia, as well as DHHS child-protection workers Wyatt Towne and […]
text:
Iowa's Department of Health and Human Services is responsible for investigating allegatons of child abuse. (Main image by Catherine Falls Commercial and Getty Images; logo courtesy the State of Iowa)  The parents of an infant who police allege was killed by a daycare provider are now suing state officials over their initial handling of the investigation.
Timmeri and Rylee Reeves of Madison County are suing former Iowa Department of Health and Human Services Director Kelly Garcia, as well as DHHS child-protection workers Wyatt Towne and Sadie Rhamy, and Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation agent Beth Miller, in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
The couple alleges that while their four-month-old son, Beau, “lay dying in the hospital, government officials prevented them from being at the child’s bedside,” then coerced them into consenting to the temporary removal of their daughter from their home and then failed to return their daughter even they were cleared of any wrongdoing.
According to the lawsuit, on Oct. 8, 2024, at roughly 8:15 a.m., Timmeri Reeves dropped off her son, Beau, and her 3-year-old daughter, identified in court records as “R.R.,” with an unlicensed child-care provider, Melissa Hancock, in Warren County.
About noon that day, Hancock allegedly called 911 to report that Beau was unresponsive with froth coming from his mouth and nose. Beau was transported to a hospital for emergency treatment, but shortly after his arrival, the Reeves were informed by a physician their son has sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and that when paramedics arrived at the daycare, he had no heartbeat and later showed no signs of brain activity.
The lawsuit alleges the hospital staff were instructed by DHHS officials to bar anyone, including Beau’s parents, from visiting with the child. “Timmeri and Rylee begged staff to let them see their dying son, who was 30 feet away,” the lawsuit alleges. “Timmeri and Rylee were told that hospital staff were directed by DHHS, led by Rhamy, and the DCI, led by Miller, that they were not allowed to see their son.”
The following day, the lawsuit claims, the Reeveses were approached by Rhamy and Towne, who asked them to formally consent to the temporary removal of R.R. from their home pending the completion of a criminal investigation into the cause of the injuries sustained by Beau.
“Rhamy and Towne threatened to never let Timmeri and Rylee see R.R. again if they refused to consent,” the lawsuit alleges, adding that Rhamy and Towne also asserted it was the Reeves’ duty, as parents, to “prove why you should have access to your children.”
The Reeveses gave their consent for temporary removal, and the next day, Oct. 10, R.R. was removed and placed in the home of Amanda Farlow of Madison County. The lawsuit claims that soon after, Farlow alleged R.R. was exhibiting signs of mental health issues that DHHS allegedly failed to address.
On Oct. 12, 2024, Beau was pronounced dead. About that same time, the lawsuit alleges, DHHS and the DCI had formed a multidisciplinary team to coordinate some aspects of the investigation of Beau’s death. On Oct. 28, the lawsuit alleges, the team “unanimously agreed that Timmeri and Rylee were not the perpetrators of Beau’s injuries.”
According to the lawsuit, the team documented its conclusion with a written statement that said, “The overall timeline was discussed and all parties involved agreed that based on this it would reassure the parents not being the perpetrators … All parties present agreed that these injuries would have occurred after that time that Beau was dropped off at daycare.”
Despite that finding, the lawsuit claims, DHHS retained legal custody of R.R. The girl’s grandfather then had “multiple conversations with Director Garcia” expressing concerns that nothing was being done by DHHS to return R.R. to her parents, the lawsuit alleges.
Child returned home; murder charge filed
In early November 2024, the Reeveses filed a court action seeking to revoke their consent to temporary removal, noting that “both parents have been ruled out as suspects in Beau’s injuries and subsequent death.”
The state contested that move and sought a court-issued order authorizing the removal of R.R. from her parents’ home, arguing “none of the individuals that were caregivers of (Beau) in the days leading up to Oct. 8, 2024, have been ruled out as suspects.”
The lawsuit asserts the state’s court filings also suggested the Reeveses were responsible for Beau’s injuries, stating R.R.’s continued removal from the home was in part because Beau had died “as a result of violent and traumatic injuries.”
Those claims were made despite the previous findings that “it was not medically possible” for the Reeves to have caused Beau’s injuries, the lawsuit asserts.  “At no time did DHHS or DCI inform the District Court of the multidisciplinary team’s unanimous conclusion that Timmeri and Rylee were not responsible for Beau’s injuries,” the lawsuit alleges.
On Nov. 15, 2024, the state’s application for the continued removal of R.R. was “abruptly dropped,” the lawsuit alleges, and DHHS allowed the girl to return home. The lawsuit alleges that Miller, in conversation with R.R.’s grandfather, admitted it had been her “personal call” to block DHHS from returning R.R. to her parents.
The lawsuit is seeking unspecified damages for alleged violations of the Reeves’ constitutional rights. Attorneys for state say they do not comment on pending litigation and have yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
In February 2025, Hancock, 52, was charged with first-degree murder. She has pleaded not guilty to the charge and a trial is currently scheduled for Feb. 24, 2027.
Police allege Hancock was Beau’s “sole caregiver” the day he died and that within hours of being placed in her care the child sustained a traumatic skull fracture, bilateral retinal hemorrhaging and spinal trauma consistent with blunt-force trauma.
According to the police report, “medical professionals identified both new and healing injuries to the victim’s head, neck, and spine, indicating a pattern of prior abuse.” Contemporaneous text messages from Hancock, police allege, “expressed irritation with the victim, and her conduct reflects a callous disregard for his wellbeing.”

title: ‘Not presidential,’ SC Senate candidate says about Trump’s post others called cruel and offensive
description: COLUMBIA — After President Donald Trump referred to Annie Andrews using a derogatory term for transgender people, the Democrat running to flip a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina dismissed his social media post as “definitely not presidential.” Trump, who likes to assign nicknames to people, used a slur that rhymes with Andrews’ first name […]
text:
Annie Andrews speaks to a crowd at the Columbia Bethlehem Community Center on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — After President Donald Trump referred to Annie Andrews using a derogatory term for transgender people, the Democrat running to flip a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina dismissed his social media post as “definitely not presidential.”
Trump, who likes to assign nicknames to people, used a slur that rhymes with Andrews’ first name in a post Monday reiterating his “complete and total endorsement” for Sen. Darline Graham. Appointed in July to fulfill her late brother’s term that ends in January, Graham and Andrews are competing for the next six-year term.
Trump’s endorsement of Lindsey Graham’s younger sister helped her win the GOP nomination in August to replace him on the Nov. 3 ballot.
Democrats decried the post as offensive and juvenile.
“Donald Trump is back to his old tricks but this slur is deeply offensive, untrue and stoops to a new low. Trump is weighing in on this race because Darline can’t win on her own,” Erik Polyak, director of 314 Action, said in a statement Monday night. The Washington, D.C.-based group supports Democratic scientists and health care professionals seeking office.


For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.


Others condemning the post included former GOP Gov. David Beasley.
“This is abhorrent,” he wrote on social media. “Elections don’t have to be about cruelty and lies. South Carolina deserves better.”
At a campaign event Tuesday, Andrews called it a distraction.
“If name calling would help lower gas prices and grocery prices, he can call me all the names he wants,” she told reporters at the Columbia Bethlehem Community Center, a stop on her statewide “Patients and Prices Tour” to highlight her ideas for improving access to healthcare.
“But I don’t think that’s going to get the job done,” she continued.
Andrews hasn’t asked Darline Graham to denounce the president’s statement, she said, because she’s focused on talking to voters.
In the post, Trump wrote that Andrews “is in favor of Transgender for Everyone.”
Graham’s campaign did not respond Tuesday to the SC Daily Gazette’s request for comment on Trump’s post or Andrews’ response.
But they followed the Graham campaign drawing attention to Andrews’ own past social media posts about her advocacy at the Statehouse supporting transgender youth. That includes a website titled “Dr. Annie’s Waiting Room,” which looks like a video game, that says Andrews advocated for letting “boys compete in girls’ sports” and “kids make changes they can’t undo.”
In 2022, Andrews publicly opposed the Save Women’s Sports Act. When Gov. Henry McMaster signed it into law, she called it “shameful legislation that does nothing to protect or support women or children in South Carolina.”
But on Tuesday, the pediatrician told reporters she opposes allowing transgender girls and women to compete in female sports.
“My job is to protect all children,” Andrews said. “It’s also not an issue that I’m hearing about when I’m actually campaigning, talking to voters who are struggling to fill up their gas tanks, to pay for their groceries, to keep their lights on at the end of the month. So there’s far bigger problems that we should be focused on in this Senate race.”
She also said she opposes gender-transitioning surgeries on children, which wasn’t happening in South Carolina even before the Legislature passed a law in 2024 banning it. During that legislative debate, Democrats and Republicans agreed such surgeries weren’t happening in the Palmetto State. Proponents called that part of the law preventative. Opponents called it unnecessary.
Other parts of the law banned puberty blockers and transitioning medications for minors under the age of 18.
Asked specifically about youth hormone treatments, Andrews’ campaign said the prohibitions in state law are not something she’s working to change.
“As a mom of three, Dr. Andrews understands and respects the concerns parents have about these issues,” the campaign said in an email Tuesday to the SC Daily Gazette.
Andrews, certified as a pediatrician since 2009, worked at the Medical University of South Carolina for 15 years ahead of her attempt in 2022 to oust U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace in the coastal 1st District. Much of her advocacy at the Statehouse occurred during that unsuccessful run. Legislators inserted a directive into the state budget that year requiring MUSC to end hormonal therapy for transgender youth under 16.
Following passage of the 2024 state law, Andrews’ former employer stopped providing treatments to all transgender adults too. While debate over that law focused on children under 18, it included a line barring the use of public funds “directly or indirectly for gender transition procedures.” And MUSC is a public medical university and hospital system.
Andrews called MUSC’s decision an over-interpretation of the law.
“This really boils down to an inappropriate infiltration of politics into our state’s largest medical institution,” she told WCIV-TV in Charleston in July 2024.
At the time, she was working at the Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C. That job, which she held from 2023 until June, involved conducting research and teaching, in addition to seeing patients, her campaign said.
The American Civil Liberties Union sued South Carolina over the 2024 law, arguing it violated transgender South Carolinians’ constitutional right to equal protection. But the ACLU dropped the challenge last year after the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a similar law in Tennessee.
Following criticism of his post, Trump doubled down Wednesday by reposting an ad that lampoons Andrews’ prior advocacy with a fictional scene of a man dressed in pink and wearing a pink wig approaching a child in a grocery store. It’s paid for by the Security is Strength political action committee, which backed Lindsey Graham and now Darline Graham.
