title: Public Service Commission approves review process for Alabama Power, data centers
description: The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday unanimously agreed on a new process to review electricity contracts between Alabama Power and data centers. The process will require power companies to make summaries of proposed agreements publicly available, as well as information about the project and its expected power consumption. Non-public versions that re[...]
text:
Alabama Public Service Commission President Cynthia Almond (center), flanked by commissioners Jeremy Oden (left) and Chip Beeker (right), speaks during a meeting of the commission on Oct. 6, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. The commission Tuesday approved a new process for reviewing large power agreements between Alabama Power and data centers. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

The Public Service Commission Tuesday approved a process requiring Alabama Power and data centers with which it enters contracts to deliver power to share information on their agreements.
The utility will be required to prepare a summary of agreements for the public, and filed redacted versions of contracts with the Public Service Commission and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office. The PSC will have to vote on the agreement within 90 days of Alabama Power’s submission, or it automatically takes effect.
The process, which only applies to Alabama Power, comes as data centers have become a major issue in state elections this year.




The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday unanimously agreed on a new process to review electricity contracts between Alabama Power and data centers.
The process will require power companies to make summaries of proposed agreements publicly available, as well as information about the project and its expected power consumption. Non-public versions that redact proprietary and confidential information would be filed with the PSC and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office.
The PSC would then vote to approve or reject the agreements in a public meeting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“To me, it was important because of the size of the data centers, the amount of energy they are using and all the public concern about data centers, that we take a public vote on data center contracts,” Cynthia Almond, president of the PSC, said to reporters after the meeting.
Prior to Tuesday’s vote, PSC staff reviewed contracts between Alabama Power and facilities using large amounts of electricity, like data centers, and usually recommended approval. Unless commissioners acted to intervene within 10 days of the staff’s recommendation, the agreements were approved.
The changes came amid mounting concerns about data centers, their power consumption and impacts on local communities and the environment. The issue has become prominent in state elections. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has called for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction. Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville has called for requirements for data centers to pay for their impact. Both have called for greater power for local communities over the facilities.
The vote on Tuesday ended a three-month process to align PSC policy with laws approved by the Legislature in the spring to further regulate data centers amid mounting public concern heard by lawmakers.
SB 270, sponsored by Sen. Lance Bell, R-Pell City, authorizes the PSC to consider the economic impact of data centers on communities when deciding whether to approve contracts between Alabama Power and data centers. It allows the state regulators to consider the cost to operate the facilities and determine whether they provide a benefit to the community. Rep. Neil Rafferty, D-Birmingham also filed similar legislation.
A new process
The new process only applies to agreements between Alabama Power and data centers. The public summary of the contract will list the location of the facility and information about the company, as well as the maximum amount of electricity consumed by the data center. It will also lay out a process for the utility to ensure the data center complies with public interest requirements.
A non-public filing with the PSC and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office will include the terms of the contract and exhibits, along with any analysis conducted by Alabama Power, from capacity to estimated cost and power generation. The PSC may then vote on whether to approve the contract.
Data centers emerge as top Alabama election issue as community concerns grow

An amendment introduced by Almond and approved by the commission will require the PSC to vote within 90 days from the submission of the Alabama Power filing. If commissioners do not vote, the agreement will be automatically approved.
The amendment came after Commissioner Chris V. Beeker III expressed concerns that the new rules do not require a vote within a specific time.
“There is a lot of public interest in data centers, a lot of concern about whether we are appropriately requiring them to pay their fair share at cost, and so it is important to me that we approve or disapprove these contracts out in the public and have discussion out in the public much like we did today,” Almond said.
The AG’s Office proposed that the PSC publicly vote on every data center contract, arguing the law required it. The motion drew opposition from Luke Bentley IV, the executive director of the PSC.
“The Attorney General’s Office had some comments that said the law required the Commission to vote, I want to make it clear that my recommendation is not based on that comment,” Bentley said during the meeting. “I do not agree with that assessment.”
Reaction
Renewable energy and environmental groups Tuesday said they were pleased that more information will be released about agreements between power companies and data centers but felt more needed to be done.
Jaclyn Brass, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, a legal advocacy organization that has opposed some of Alabama Power’s requests, said in a statement that she hoped the PSC would “continue this long-overdue move toward letting daylight in on how they regulate Alabama Power.”
“It’s disappointing the commission would not commit to taking public votes on all contracts. However, requiring Alabama Power to disclose basic information about these contracts, including the name of the data center and the maximum contracted electric capacity, are all important steps toward greater transparency,” the statement said.
Lowndes County residents demand transparency in hyperscale data center development

Energy Alabama, an organization that advocates for more renewable energy in the state, said it was disappointed that the PSC will not vote on all contracts.
“For three decades, rules built for manufacturers let contracts take effect without a vote of the commission. Data centers on this scale are a different animal,” said Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama. “Ninety days is better than 10, but silence still counts as yes. A contract this big should never take effect because nobody voted. Alabamians deserve to see their regulators decide in public.”
Alabama Power said in a statement that it will comply with all laws in the state.
“Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers. Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers,” the company said.
The PSC solicited comments from the public to determine the process for approving contracts but did not adopt all of them. Energy Alabama, for example, requested that a public utility provide a fixed pricing plan rulebook to data centers that are publicly available.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Three years after October 7, Jewish voters need reassurance from our Democratic leaders
description: As we approach this third anniversary of Oct. 7, 2023 — the deadliest attack on Jews since the Holocaust, followed by a war that has caused enormous Palestinian civilian suffering — American Jews are living through a period of deep trauma and dramatically elevated antisemitism here at home. For generations, American democracy has given its […]
text:
Getty ImagesAs we approach this third anniversary of Oct. 7, 2023 — the deadliest attack on Jews since the Holocaust, followed by a war that has caused enormous Palestinian civilian suffering — American Jews are living through a period of deep trauma and dramatically elevated antisemitism here at home.
For generations, American democracy has given its citizens a voice at the ballot box to help shape our country’s future. And for more than 70 percent of Jews, those decisions have largely aligned with the Democratic Party. Jewish voters like myself have helped build the progressive coalitions that protect and champion immigrants, the LGBTQ+ community, reproductive rights, and our planet.
So why are my congregants expressing such discomfort about this upcoming election?
Many of us want to support leaders like Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. His platform on healthcare, reproductive freedom, and social justice resonates deeply with our Jewish tradition. We agree with much of his domestic agenda and are not looking for a reason to walk away.
In fact, the reason I speak out is because of the serious concerns about Mike Rogers and the Republican Party, including support from a major donor who has said only Christians should hold positions of political leadership. I am concerned when I hear the rhetoric motivating Mike Rogers’ platform and believe there is far more distance between his campaign’s focuses and the Jewish community’s core concerns than there is potential in Abdul El Sayed’s campaign to begin to use language that acknowledges the Jewish community’s concerns. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
I graduated with Abdul from Andover. I know he understands what it means to live in diversity and to use language that includes everyone. I know him to be an intelligent person, and I know that he is aware of the impact of his words. Holding someone accountable is not the same as writing them off. Abdul is the candidate whose politics are much closer to my own which is precisely why I’m urging him to do better, to grow his tent in a meaningful way.
My appeal to Abdul comes from a sincere desire (dare I say prayer) to have the Jewish narrative centered on Jewish voices, and to expect any candidates who want our votes to be responsive to its potential voters’ concerns.
While antisemitism has always been a horrifying part of the Jewish experience in the U.S., antisemitic acts have skyrocketed since October 7. Criticism of the Israeli government — criticism that many Jewish Americans and Israelis share — has often crossed into the demonization of Jewish people as a whole, and has enabled people to invoke centuries-old antisemitic tropes.
When we hear candidates like Abdul describe only the country of Israel with language like “bloodthirsty” and “evil,” or when his campaign sends fundraising emails on October 7 about Israel without even mentioning Hamas’s brutal massacre or the hostages, it frankly frightens us.
For our community, this fear isn’t abstract. We have seen where the demonization and scapegoating of Jews can lead. This physical threat hit right in our own backyard in March, when a terrorist rammed his truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield and opened fire while 140 children were inside.
When antisemitic violence is happening on our doorstep, words carry enormous weight. Political leaders have a duty to model how public disagreement over Israel can happen without invoking rhetoric that Jews experience as threatening and dangerous. If our politicians won’t loudly denounce such hate and take actions as simple as speaking in defense of our community without humanizing terrorism against our community, it’s little wonder that many Jewish voters don’t know where to turn.
That is why clergy and synagogue leaders across our state have launched Nonnegotiable Michigan. We are giving political leaders — including El-Sayed — an open door and opportunity to affirm five baseline commitments to Jewish voters:

Jewish safety, including for Zionist Jews. Believing in the right of Jewish people to self-determination is not an automatic endorsement of Israel’s current government. Leaders must hold accountable those who hurl the word “Zionist” at anyone as a slur or attack.
The right of Jews to define their own identity. We reject any attempt to force us into political litmus tests or superimpose tropes of evil onto our community.
Jewish sovereignty in Israel. We reject eliminationist language that seeks to return our people to statelessness and powerlessness.
The full participation of Jews in American political life. We refuse to be excluded from protections for vulnerable groups or forced into silence just to remain included in progressive spaces.
An affirmative vision for peace. True Jewish values paint a prosperous vision for peace in the Middle East, including a two-state solution that grants both Israelis and Palestinians the right to self-determination and respective sovereignty.

We invite Abdul to sit down with our Jewish community, listen with an open heart, and show us he wants to give all of us the same dignity and protection that every other coalition in Michigan deserves. We want to be part of building a better future for Michigan and our country — and we desperately need leaders who will stand up for our safety and humanity along the way.
Our votes must be earned. But also, our community, like all Michiganders, must be kept safe. Election or no, we’re urging Dr. El-Sayed to stop using harmful language that, time and again, has led to violence and will again. It’s the most fundamental thing he can do as a leader in the party we love.

title: North Dakota special session on kratom cost $220,000
description: North Dakota’s special legislative session last month cost about $220,000, according to the Legislature’s staff agency. Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong called the special session for the GOP-led Legislature to restrict kratom products. Lawmakers met Sept. 2-4, with a policy committee meeting on Sept. 1 to take public testimony in advance of the special sessi[...]
text:
Members of the North Dakota House of Representatives participate in a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s special legislative session last month cost about $220,000, according to the Legislature’s staff agency.
Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong called the special session for the GOP-led Legislature to restrict kratom products. Lawmakers met Sept. 2-4, with a policy committee meeting on Sept. 1 to take public testimony in advance of the special session.
Expenses include: 

$137,368 for lawmakers’ daily pay
$33,881 for their lodging
$30,712 for their mileage
$14,716 for temporary session employee salaries

The Sept. 1 meeting cost $678, separate from the special session.
Legislative Budget Analyst and Auditor Allen Knudson provided the costs to the North Dakota Monitor. A few lawmakers have not yet submitted their travel expenses, estimated to be about $1,800, he said.
North Dakota bans synthetic kratom, will regulate natural products

The two-year budget for the Legislature will cover the costs, which will reduce the funding available for paying the upcoming 2027 session costs, Knudson said. Officials may have to request what is called a deficiency appropriation if the budget won’t be enough to entirely cover the next regular session, he said.
The Legislature passed two bills in the special session. One banned synthetic kratom products and allowed but restricted natural kratom. The other bill provided funding to a stalled state military museum project that paused construction in July due to a fundraising shortfall.
The Legislature killed three bills to permanently ban all forms of kratom, to temporarily ban nondisclosure agreements on industrial projects and data centers and to make a tweak to a property tax issue.
September’s special session was the second one this year. The Legislature met for three days in January to approve about $199 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds. The January session cost about $211,500.
North Dakota’s Legislature regularly meets every odd-numbered year for about four months. The next session begins in January 2027.

 Catching Our Eye

• Citizens detained by Trump. ProPublica reports, “506 U.S. Citizens Detained.”
The Trump administration says none of this is happening.
“DHS is NOT arresting U.S. citizens by mistake.” “There are no ‘indiscriminate’ stops.” Allegations of “racial profiling are disgusting, reckless and categorically FALSE.” “The pattern is NOT of law enforcement using force.” “ICE does not zip tie or restrain children.”
But that is precisely what is happening, and at a far larger scale than previously reported. We know because we have once again done what the government hasn’t:
We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent holding a citizen during the current administration. More than 500 cases. That includes:
• More than a hundred Americans held after agents questioned their citizenship. Nearly all were people of color.
• At least 70 American children and teens detained, some of whom were handcuffed.
• Of the more than 300 Americans we tracked as detained for allegedly assaulting or obstructing agents, we found fewer than half were actually charged in federal court, and many of those cases were dropped or dismissed.
• At least 63 Americans detained while recording.
• 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family.
• Roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.
• The ugliest. The New York Times reports, “This High-Profile Campaign May Be the Ugliest in the Country.”
The candidates for Ohio governor have significant policy differences, but the campaign ads have been strikingly personal, with exaggerated portrayals of one candidate as a con artist and the other as a drunk.
• Infant mortality rate. The Marietta Times Editorial Board writes, “Ohio infant mortality rate deserves full attention.”
Ohioans know our state has its challenges, but generally speaking we think of ourselves as better off than those in some other parts of the country — or world. For our youngest and most vulnerable residents, that is not always the case. Given the number of politicians who want us to believe the lives of babies are of the utmost important to them, it is astounding that the infant mortality rate here is STILL considerably above the national average.
Efforts to address the problem have made some progress. We are down to 6.6 deaths per 1,000 live births in Ohio, compared with the national average of 5.36, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
• JD Vance defends Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads praising himself. The Hill reports, “Vance argues pro-Trump campaign ads ‘are not partisan.’”
Vice President Vance said the new pro-President Trump television advertisements are “not partisan” amid criticism from both sides of the aisle.
The ads, which cost $20 million of taxpayer money, feature Trump’s voice calling for the defeat of socialism and communism while touting the “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.”
The Trump administration has claimed the ads are public service announcements, not campaign ads.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Mothers told they can’t receive WV childcare assistance and operate an LLC
description: Melissa Pearson owns and operates a cleaning business in Wheeling, West Virginia, where her team focuses on customer satisfaction while scrubbing and tidying homes and commercial properties.  A mom of two daughters, Pearson built Ready Set Clean from the ground up over the last year and a half. She relied on West Virginia’s childcare assistance […]
text:
Ashtin McCloud, 25, owns A-List Artistry, a salon, in Huntington, West Virginia. She dissolved her LLC for her business after being told she would lose childcare assistance from the state. (Photo courtesy of Ashtin McCloud)Melissa Pearson owns and operates a cleaning business in Wheeling, West Virginia, where her team focuses on customer satisfaction while scrubbing and tidying homes and commercial properties. 
A mom of two daughters, Pearson built Ready Set Clean from the ground up over the last year and a half. She relied on West Virginia’s childcare assistance program to find and afford summer care while she worked. 
But earlier this year, Pearson was forced to give up the needed financial help after being told that she couldn’t operate an LLC, which provides legal protections for her business, and receive the childcare subsidy from the state. 
“The business is doing pretty well. It’s obviously not going well enough for me to, out of the blue, come up with $3,000 for an entire summer of childcare,” said Pearson, 34.
Due to business growth, she was close to no longer needing help from the state paying for childcare.
“It prevents economic growth throughout the entire state when you hinder small businesses in this way,” Pearson said. “You don’t ever have the ability to work your way off of the system. ….  The goal was always to get away from any kind of government assistance.”
Families on average spend over $10,000 a year on childcare in West Virginia, making the state’s childcare assistance a lifeline for parents and caregivers.
More than 11,000 West Virginia children are enrolled in the childcare subsidy program, which provides financial assistance to eligible parents who are employed or in school. West Virginia funds the program through federal anti-poverty dollars.
The state pays the subsidy amount to childcare centers across the state. Many centers have said receiving the subsidy dollars were critical in the poor state to keep doors open in the tumultuous childcare economy.
The childcare subsidy policy contains specific requirements for parents whose qualifying work activity is self-employment.
Department of Human Services spokesperson Angelica Hightower said that state policy requires that self-employment approvals for the childcare subsidy are limited to qualifying contracted or sole-proprietorship arrangements. Individuals who own a business, including an LLC or certain other types of corporations, are ineligible when that business ownership is used as the sole qualifying self-employment activity for the childcare subsidy.
“Individuals in these circumstances are not disqualified from eligibility, but would have to meet the qualifying activity requirement in another manner (additional employment, educational activities, etc.),” Hightower wrote in an email.
Childcare can be hard to come by in West Virginia. More than 28,000 children currently lack access to care because West Virginia providers don’t have enough available slots. 
Ashtin McCloud works as a nail artist in Huntington, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of Ashtin McCloud)
Ashtin McCloud, 25, said she was forced to dissolve her LLC for her salon in Huntington or she would lose her state childcare assistance and care for her children. She began using the assistance program in 2025 while in cosmetology school to help locate and pay for childcare for her two toddlers while she finished school, then launched her career as a nail artist.
“I was being told that I needed to dissolve my LLC and open up a sole proprietorship instead,” said McCloud, owner of A-List Artistry. “An LLC protects you in so many ways, and I’m being forced to change the way that my business plan was and stripping away basically my protection. If somebody wanted to walk into my salon and slip and fall and say that they broke a wrist and go to the hospital, they’re not suing my business — they’re suing me.”
McCloud didn’t want to rely on the assistance but without it, she would lose her childcare. She paid nearly $400 to dissolve her LLC.
“The government claims that they want people to use them in a positive way and, you know, get the help that they need until they can get on their feet. But yet, when you’re trying to get on your feet and you’re doing all of the things the way that you’re supposed to be doing it, you’re actually getting punished … I don’t understand why I’m being punished for owning my own business,” she said. 
West Virginia’s policy regarding an LLC and the childcare subsidy has been in place since around 2007 following recommendation by the Office of the Inspector General “to ensure program integrity and reduce potential fraud and misrepresentation in accessing program benefits,” Hightower explained.
She noted that this is a separate policy from licensing requirements for childcare providers.
Hightower encouraged parents to reach out to their local Child Care Resource and Referral agency for more information on eligibility. 
“A parent should not dissolve an LLC or change the legal structure of a business solely on the basis of informal advice without first speaking with the CCR&R, and when appropriate, obtaining independent tax or legal advice,” Hightower said. 
“ … Eligibility is determined based on the family’s complete circumstances, including qualifying activity, household income, need for childcare and required documentation,” she added. 
Pearson and her boyfriend, Ben Culler, spent months appealing the loss of the childcare subsidy, basing their appeal on federal regulations and state policies they felt backed up their case. 
Those appeals were unsuccessful. 
“Ultimately, if the government’s goal is to save money, (then) save money by making a better policy and helping people advance their lives to get off of subsidy — not force them to stay small,” Culler said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Legislators said eligible Idahoans won’t lose care over work requirements. Let’s hold them to that.
description: One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very […]
text:
Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion.
We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. 
When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it.
Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work.

Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. 
Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. 
Then what?
Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? 
For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. 
Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill.
It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale.
This past session, House Bill 913 established the Jan. 1 start date for federally mandated work requirements. Medicaid proponents had requested a one-year extension to give the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and our residents more time to learn about the changes and implementation. 
That did not happen, so we hope Idaho lawmakers grasp fully their responsibility to hold true to the promises they made clearly and often during all those Boise debates over work requirements. Then, they were firm in their convictions that no eligible person would ever be stripped of healthcare. 
Policymakers should be just as committed now to making work requirement exemptions clear and accessible as they were about putting them into law. Coverage losses from work requirements usually aren’t because someone suddenly became ineligible, but because eligible people get caught in paperwork, reporting requirements, missed notices or other government bureaucracy. 
That distinction matters because it means people who are supposed to get care are forced to go without. Someone who otherwise could treat a medical condition and work, care for family members, and otherwise be active in their community could lose their coverage, get sicker until they can no longer work and be forced to a hospital and incur expensive medical debt, or worse. 
It would be dirty business to balance savings on the backs of people who qualify for coverage but can’t successfully navigate another administrative hurdle.
There is no real possibility that all eligible people who need coverage will remain on the rolls when this requirement is implemented, but simply a matter of how many will be erroneously kicked off, and what the consequences will be when they need care but cannot afford it.
More than half of Idahoans need coverage beyond their employment. Many work low-wage jobs and, for them, Medicaid expansion is a lifeline. Insured people also keep our local care providers from the financial struggles that hit when serving a population with a high number of uninsured people. 
Lawmakers and Idaho Department of Health and Welfare leadership can do a lot to help keep people covered in the coming months. They can minimize barriers to enrollment, offer robust and easily accessible educational information on the process and communicate clearly on changes coming so folks don’t get caught unaware. 
These new requirements create real challenges for many Idahoans. Lawmakers and state officials now have a responsibility to ensure implementation does not create unnecessary barriers to care for the very people these programs are intended to serve.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: When private equity came for the clinic where I worked
description: I am a licensed and registered occupational therapist, and I used to work at a pediatric therapy practice that families across Alabama trusted. When I took the job, the practice being clinician-owned mattered to me. I believed I could practice occupational therapy in a way that aligned with my values. Over time, trauma-informed and neurodiversity […]
text:
An Applied Behavior Analysis center is seen in Danville, Indiana. (Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)I am a licensed and registered occupational therapist, and I used to work at a pediatric therapy practice that families across Alabama trusted.
When I took the job, the practice being clinician-owned mattered to me. I believed I could practice occupational therapy in a way that aligned with my values. Over time, trauma-informed and neurodiversity affirming care became central to my work.
Then the company that I loved was sold to a private-equity-backed company.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The new owners told us they were different. The company described themselves as a public benefit corporation, said clinical leadership would remain important, and invited me to serve on an advisory board.
I did not understand that our clinic was part of a larger national trend. Between 2017 and 2022, private equity firms were responsible for 85% of mergers and acquisitions in the autism-services industry.
I was clear that I opposed adding Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) to our services. Yet, against my recommendation, ABA was added. ABA soon appeared to drive the company’s clinical direction. I ultimately resigned because I did not believe that direction reflected what was best for children.
ABA is not an uncontroversial pediatric therapy. Some clinicians consider it helpful, while autistic adults and self-advocacy groups described harm from approaches that reward compliance and treat appearing “less autistic” as improvement.
Neurodiversity-affirming care begins somewhere different. It recognizes that neurological differences are not deficits to extinguish. Therapy should support communication, regulation, belonging, participation, relationships, safety, and quality of life without making conformity the goal.
Some providers now promote a “new ABA” or “Today’s ABA”, even describing their approach as “trauma-sensitive”.  New language may reassure families, but it does not resolve ABA’s history or ensure that children experience genuine safety. Children need support recognizing and trusting their own body cues, communicating discomfort, and knowing their refusal will be honored.
After examining these newer models and listening to autistic self-advocates, I remain unconvinced that any version of ABA I have encountered meets a basic ethical standard.
But there is another reason to pay attention: ABA can be highly profitable.
A child may receive one to three hours of occupational, physical, or speech therapy a week.  Intensive ABA can involve dozens of hours. Much direct care is provided by lower-paid behavior technicians under a behavior analyst’s oversight. A clinic can then bill far more hours per child, at a significantly lower cost to the company, than traditional therapy services can. Multiply that by hundreds of children across clinics, and it is easy to understand why autism services attract private equity investors.
Researchers have found that investors entered most heavily in states with higher autism prevalence and more generous insurance mandates. What is presented as clinical expansion may actually be just replacing lower-volume services with a service generating more billable hours per child.
This does not mean every ABA recommendation is financially motivated. But families deserve transparency when a recommended treatment is also the company’s most profitable service. Families already navigate testing, waitlists, referrals, insurance, school services, and conflicting recommendations. They should not also need expertise in corporate finance.
Yet, with private equity takeovers so prevalent, they should now ask: Who owns this practice? Why are certain services promoted?  How were the recommended hours determined? And unfortunately, who benefits financially?
Families should also listen to autistic people, who have spent years describing harm from therapies like ABA that taught them to suppress discomfort or obey. Those of us who are not autistic cannot substitute our perspective for autistic people’s lived experience.
I loved my colleagues, families, and the work we did.  I know clinicians who still fight every day to provide care based on what is best for each child. But parents deserve to know what those clinicians may be up against, including pressure to recommend profitable services and discount autistic voices about what helps and what harms.
Autistic children are not untapped markets. Their needs are not opportunities for maximizing billable hours. Their families should never have to wonder whether a recommendation was made because it was the best choice for their child or the best return for an investor.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: As Medicaid coverage shrinks, charity care has to grow
description: H.R. 1, also known as “One Big Beautiful Bill,” may soon reduce Medicaid enrollees in West Virginia by as many as 75,000, according to the Urban Institute. This reduction in enrollment will depend mostly on how states implement new rules, including work requirements and six-month redeterminations that begin Jan. 1, 2027.
text:
As changes to both Medicaid eligibility and the provider tax loom, hospitals have warned that this will destabilize their operations. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)H.R. 1, also known as “One Big Beautiful Bill,” may soon reduce Medicaid enrollees in West Virginia by as many as 75,000, according to the Urban Institute. This reduction in enrollment will depend mostly on how states implement new rules, including work requirements and six-month redeterminations that begin Jan. 1, 2027.
While policymakers at the state and federal level grapple with how to handle this adjustment, patients in West Virginia are more concerned about what it means for their ability to access and afford care. Over 13% of West Virginia’s adults carry medical debt, half again the national rate. In rural Appalachia, 24% of the population has medical debt in collections. Worse, healthcare costs have continued to rise. West Virginia’s hospitals charge, on average, 337% of Medicare rates, the third-highest markup nationally.
For West Virginians, the high cost of care isn’t simply a risk of unaffordability, but a choice about whether to seek care at all. Medical debt is consistently associated with deferring care. With few alternatives outside of system-delivered care, lower-cost options are out of reach for many. 
Yet, many conversations around these changes — whether one agrees with H.R. 1 or not — have focused on hospital losses rather than patients’. As changes to both Medicaid eligibility and the provider tax loom, hospitals have warned that this will destabilize their operations. 
Non-profit hospitals control more than 75% of beds in West Virginia and are exempt from income, property and sales tax. As part of this exemption comes an agreement: that non-profit hospitals would provide free or reduced care for the poor and underinsured, otherwise referred to as “charity care.” However, this engagement with the non-profit hospital status has become more distorted as the years have gone on. In West Virginia, charity care averages 0.9% of net patient revenue. 
In the most recent report from the West Virginia Hospital Association’s Community Benefit numbers, they cite $79 million in charity care and $103 million in bad debt — hospitals wrote off more as unpaid bills than they forgave. In some instances, hospitals even report in their IRS 990s how much bad debt is “FAP-eligible,” or estimated to have qualified under their own financial assistance policy but was written off as debt.
These numbers often become inflated because of the broad legal standard of “community benefit,” which West Virginia hospitals claim equates to $1.19 billion annually. A closer look at this number shows that the Catholic Health Association standard the state hospital association says it follows excludes bad debt and Medicare shortfalls; WVHA tallies both. This inflates the contribution to West Virginians; less than 7% of “community benefit” is working to ease the burden of high-cost care for patients.
About $204 million of this benefit is attributable to the current provider tax, a fee that hospitals pay to draw more federal Medicaid matching, which is returned to hospitals through Medicaid payments. WVHA counts the fee as a community benefit. Meanwhile, WVHA says reduced payments from hospitals to the state under changes from H.R. 1 will further strain hospital resources. If the provider tax were a net cost to hospitals, limiting it would be a relief. WVHA calls it a loss. 
Moreover, the Catholic Health Association counts the provider tax as a Medicaid cost. In their words, “these amounts generate Medicaid revenue.” 
In truth, hospitals should be part of the solution for patients and affordable, accessible care. IRS reporting on charity care provided shows they are not. The tax exemption so many hospitals enjoy should come along with a return to patient investment and care, particularly through the moral function of hospital charity care. 
Texas and Oregon are two examples, red and blue, that have sought to correct the drift from the tax exemption’s original intent. Texas conditions tax exemption on meeting its charity care standard. Oregon requires financial screening before collection. At Oregon Health & Science University, presumptive screening raised the share of patients identified as eligible for financial assistance from 12% to 64%. At the same time, expanded financial assistance has shown no effect on hospital net patient revenue. 
Hospitals should take their financial obligation to patients more seriously. Amid significant changes to federal policy, now more than ever is a good time to do so. The upcoming legislative session offers an opportunity to stay ahead of federal changes and put patients first by requiring hospitals to deliver true charity care, not bad debt, and to screen all patients for financial assistance before any collections activity.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: It’s Banned Books Week, so find a First Amendment Library to exercise your rights
description: Three years ago, we talked a lot about banning books in Kentucky.  Back then, the wacky war on woke was gaining ground in our legislature and in our libraries. I remember talking to librarians like Erin Waller of the Daviess County Public Library, who was going through a list of 248 books that had been […]
text:
A stack of books that have been banned or challenged. (Photo illustration by Sarah Ladd)Three years ago, we talked a lot about banning books in Kentucky. 
Back then, the wacky war on woke was gaining ground in our legislature and in our libraries. I remember talking to librarians like Erin Waller of the Daviess County Public Library, who was going through a list of 248 books that had been challenged by the “Daviess County Citizens for Decency,” a local group that got mad about a drag show and decided to move their anger to the stacks.
Many of the books they challenged were about kids with two mommies, but sadly many more were about our nation’s history of racial injustice. People did not like the Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 and did not want their children reading about why we had to have them.
In Paris, Mark Adler had a similar list of 102 challenges. Apparently, the challengers had never thought that if they were offended by materials in the library, they didn’t have to check them out. Or look at them. Or even go to the library. 
Well, it’s Banned Books Week again, so I gave Adler a call. And the news was … very positive.
“We’ve had absolutely no more issues,” Adler said, “and I think in large part it was due to our very diverse community being tied together by a common belief that everyone is entitled to their freedoms, including First Amendment freedoms.”
In late 2023, the Paris-Bourbon County Public Library Board of Directors did something pretty extraordinary for a small, rural, mostly conservative place: Members voted to become the first library in Kentucky to be a “First Amendment Library,” which means a place where people have free access to read whatever they want, without anyone else choosing for them or their children.
The movement started in Chicago, where they are called First Amendment Sanctuary Libraries, but has spread around the country. Becoming a First Amendment Library has no legal teeth, of course, and people can still make their challenges. But the message, Adler said, was real and consequential.
The library’s move was supported by Judge Executive Michael Williams, who commended the library board for standing up to their oaths of office. The county’s fiscal court and Paris City Council passed resolutions supporting the designation as well.  
“Our First Amendment rights are not political,” Adler said. “Conservative people should have materials on their shelves to meet their needs, just like liberals. Everyone should be able to find themselves in books at the library.”
A better pattern
Now unfortunately, this good news has not been as widespread as we would like. According to the American Library Association, 4,235 unique titles were challenged in 2025, only five titles short of the highest number ever documented by the ALA in, you guessed it, 2023. Between 2001 and 2020, the annual average was just 273 unique titles.
But in Kentucky, the storm has mostly calmed, said King Simpson, the executive director of the Logan County Public Library and the current president of the Kentucky Public Library Association.
“There has not been nearly the number of controversies we’ve seen in years past,” Simpson said. “I don’t know if people have moved on; I would like to think people have been able to work proactively in their communities to come to understandings and encourage people to support the First Amendment.”
Back in 2023, library folks were also worried about a then-new state law that would allow county fiscal courts to have a say over who was appointed to library boards.
But that hasn’t really been a problem either, Simpson said. 
“We’ve tried to be more proactive and have encouraged our members to have those conversations and build those relationships, so officials can reach out early on, rather than when we’re butting heads,” Simpson said. 
(Photo illustration by Sarah Ladd)
It’s sad this needs to be proclaimed, but public libraries are sanctuaries: havens from boredom, ignorance, loneliness, anarchy, hatred. They provide warmth, knowledge, entertainment, enlightenment, tolerance, and yes a real live place to exercise your First Amendment rights. They are some of the finest inventions of mankind, and one of the best developments this young country ever fostered.
It’s good to know that in Kentucky at least, the fever dream of libraries as dens of iniquity has cooled so our librarians can get back to the crucially important and extremely challenging job of getting more books into all our hands. Even the banned ones.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘We want to fight for each other:’ Unionized Shelbyville tenants describe bugs, mold in housing.
description: SHELBYVILLE, Ky. — On a rainy October afternoon, Janatta Evans sat in a chair next to other tenants and described the tumultuous several months she’s had with her Shelbyville apartment.  When she first tried to move into her subsidized rental in March, there was a strong smell of urine inside. She said management at Centrebrook […]
text:
Organizers with the Kentucky Tenant Union kneel on the ground, from left to right: Amber Goldsborough and Heather Myatt. Members of the Shelbyville tenant union stand behind the organizers, from left to right: Lisa Sowder, Ashlee Nessel, Akira Jordan-Carson, Janatta Evans, Catherine Stone, Jim Toole. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)SHELBYVILLE, Ky. — On a rainy October afternoon, Janatta Evans sat in a chair next to other tenants and described the tumultuous several months she’s had with her Shelbyville apartment. 
When she first tried to move into her subsidized rental in March, there was a strong smell of urine inside. She said management at Centrebrook Apartments told her they put an ozone machine inside to address the issue, only for Evans to still find the smell inside. 
Then came the mice, a pest she’s extremely afraid of. Over the summer, she said she found mice scurrying in her apartment along with what appeared to be droppings on her stove and in her bedroom. She said management eventually told her that the mice issue was also addressed, only for her granddaughter to find “black stuff,” or droppings, on her stove and in her bed. 
“We went inside finally, and the mice were just running,” Evans said, her voice choking. “The next morning, I called an Uber and I went to stay with my daughter.” 
She eventually stopped paying rent and is staying in a hotel, unable to access her apartment recently because she said they’ve changed the locks while electrical work is being done inside. 
Tenants say they collected a sample of mold in Janatta Evans’ apartment in late September. The mold has gone in the sample dish since then. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
The apartment complex sought to evict her over not paying rent, only for the court case to be dismissed after an attorney for Evans filed a response detailing the alleged, unresolved mice infestation. She’s also been separated from her dog Diamond during the ordeal, something that’s been hard on her emotionally. 
It’s the personal stories of delayed or unresolved maintenance issues — mice, cockroaches, mold and water damage — along with other issues that have pushed Evans and other tenants at seven different Shelbyville properties to form and launch a tenant union last month. 
Their goal: a collectively bargained lease with the Lexington-based property management company Winterwood Inc. that owns or manages the seven properties including Centrebrook Apartments. The idea of a tenant union was an unknown concept to these tenants before organizers with the group Kentucky Tenant Union started knocking on their doors earlier this year; the members of the union didn’t know each other before they started organizing. 
Kentucky Tenant Union, formerly the Louisville Tenants Union, has helped organize tenant unions at apartment complexes in Louisville and Meade County previously, winning a collectively bargained lease earlier this year for some union members with a Texas-based property management company. The group said it was the first such collectively-bargained lease in the U.S. South. 
A tenant union, not unlike a labor union in a workplace, is when a group of tenants work to collectively advocate for their rights and build negotiating power with a landlord or property manager. While the right to form a tenant union is recognized in federal and state laws, tenant unions generally have fewer legal rights and recognition compared to labor unions. 
Allegations of years-long problems
Some of the claimed issues detailed by tenants at Winterwood properties have stretched over the course of several years. 
Jim Toole, a tenant union member, told the Kentucky Lantern he had been retaliated against by management at his apartment complex in past years after he requested a closer parking spot and an apartment unit to better accommodate his mobility and pain issues caused by pinched nerves. 
“Before the union. I’ve been kind of on my own battle with them for the last five years,” Toole said, sitting in a chair with a cane. “When I saw the union forming, I wanted to share some of my experience and learn some things myself, and kind of have a mutually beneficial thing there to get Winterwood to start acting right.”
Toole said in one instance, he had to get an attorney with the Kentucky Fair Housing Council involved after management denied a better parking spot despite a medical request from him. 
Art Crosby, the executive director of the Kentucky Fair Housing Council, told the Lantern he couldn’t speak on specific cases without permission from the tenant involved. Crosby said Winterwood manages a number of properties across the state and that Winterwood is “relatively receptive” to complaints.
Akira Jordan-Carson, another member of the tenant union in Shelbyville and a part of the bargaining team, told the Lantern she’s had to move to different apartments several times because of “awful” cockroach infestations. In one instance, she said was recording a video for TikTok when a cockroach fell on her stove.  
She said hearing stories of hazardous or chronic maintenance problems from other tenants at Winterwood properties in Shelbyville — ranging from sewage backing up into an apartment to broken windows to “living with black mold” — is what is motivating them. 
“We want to fight for each other,” Jordan-Carson said. “They’re elderly, and they’re disabled, and they’re low income, and don’t have the funds to fix things themselves, and they’re not being heard. It’s not right.” 
The Shelbyville tenants told the Lantern their union is meeting with Winterwood on Oct. 13 to start the bargaining process. But they also said the meeting was originally supposed to be with just the tenant union, only for the company to open the meeting to all tenants. 
In a Tuesday afternoon email, Winterwood CEO Mike Hynes said the company’s goal is to “meet with and hear from our residents.” 
Hynes also shared an email he said that he sent Tuesday to a representative of the Kentucky Tenant Union. In that email, he wrote the reasoning to have the Oct. 13 meeting open to all tenants “was simply to give an additional opportunity to hear directly from residents regarding issues affecting their communities.
“It will give everyone an opportunity to meet with my team and Winterwood leadership, if they so choose,” Hynes said in that email. “We have no issue with the tenant union and clearly you and the union are being recognized; my correspondence with you acknowledges that.”
Hynes also asked for the tenant union’s “governing documents” and documentation of the union’s representatives and officers to ensure the company is “communicating with individuals who have been duly authorized by residents to act on their behalf.”
Hynes previously told the Lantern the company takes residents’ concerns seriously, does not retaliate against tenants and is “committed to providing safe, decent and well-maintained housing.” 
The Kentucky Tenant Union and the tenants in Shelbyville have also taken issue with tax-exempt bonds given by government agencies to subsidize the construction and rehabilitation of affordable housing by Winterwood, which manages more than 14,000 apartments across eight states. 
The Kentucky Housing Corporation, a quasi-governmental agency that provides the bonds, conducts inspections of properties receiving government support “to ensure they meet federal and state requirements as well as criteria specified in funding agreements and contracts,”according to the agency’s website. 
In a statement provided to the Lantern last month through Deputy Executive Director Wendy Smith, Kentucky Housing Corporation said it has provided tax-exempt bonds to Winterwood properties totaling approximately $2,220,000 in bonds for two properties in Shelbyville,.
The corporation had not received “any outstanding complaints regarding Winterwood-owned properties in Shelbyville” but were “looking into it,” according to the statement last month. Smith said in a Tuesday email, two Winterwood properties in Shelbyville that had received bonds, Shelby Place and Shelby House, received high marks on inspections conducted in October 2024. She said the corporation isn’t scheduled to do inspections again at the properties until “later this year or the next.” 
Tenants including Jordan-Carson said there has been more maintenance and upgrades done at the properties since the union started to organize, but they want regular maintenance upgrades in a written lease to ensure it continues to happen. Evans, the tenant who faced an eviction court case, also said the apartment management didn’t start to “play ball” on addressing issues including after her attorney had filed a rebuttal in court. 
Signs advocating for the tenant union are seen at in apartment windows at Winterwood properties around Shelbyville. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Jordan-Carson said their advocacy also extends beyond the Shelbyville properties to other tenants at Winterwood properties across the state. Ashlee Nessel, one of the tenant union members, said tenants at other Winterwood properties have reached out to them.  
“We’re ready to have this set in stone that we’re gonna continue to have our maintenance fixed, not just fixed right now because the government’s coming for inspection sometimes,” Jordan-Carson said. “They’re all living in these conditions.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Constitutional: The amendment that could restore formerly incarcerated Virginians’ voting rights
description: Quadaire Patterson will vote for the first time this fall, a fact that brought a smile to his face on a recent afternoon as his 1-year-old daughter Trinity frolicked around the living room of the Henrico County home he shares with his wife.   He said he has been thinking about how future elections can shape […]
text:
Quadaire Patterson and wife Santia Nance stand with daughter Trinity on the porch of their Henrico County home in the summer of 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Quadaire Patterson will vote for the first time this fall, a fact that brought a smile to his face on a recent afternoon as his 1-year-old daughter Trinity frolicked around the living room of the Henrico County home he shares with his wife.  
He said he has been thinking about how future elections can shape Trinity’s future. But presently, he is eager to vote for a proposed amendment that could cement voting rights for former felons, like himself, into Virginia’s constitution. 
Patterson, who was incarcerated at 19 years old after committing an armed robbery, served 16 years of a 20 year sentence before being released early in 2024 through a good behavior program. 
He and wife Santia Nance joined other formerly incarcerated people and their families to advocate for the law change that allowed his early release. He has frequented the state capitol in the years since to lend insight to criminal justice legislation, despite being unable to vote for lawmakers himself.  
That changed this summer when Gov. Abigail Spanberger restored his voting rights along with more than 60,0000 formerly incarcerated Virginians. But the restoration process remains subjective; the amendment aims to make it a certainty. 
“Voting rights have been deduced down to a privilege that can be handed out and restricted,” Patterson said. “This amendment restores it back to the people.” 
Virginia’s current constitution permanently disenfranchises people with all felony convictions unless they are pardoned by a governor or successfully petition one.
Restorations trended downwards under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin. For years, it had been unclear which former felons would get their voting rights back, and the criteria guiding that decision was murky. 
After  trying unsuccessfully to pass the restoration amendment, lawmakers saw a new opportunity when Democrats gained majorities in the legislature in 2023 and tried again. 
The current amendment had to pass the General Assembly two years in a row and will appear on statewide ballots this fall, where voters will approve or reject it. 


Proposed Constitutional Amendment Question 3
Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?


Most Republican state lawmakers have consistently blocked the restoration amendment. Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, is an exception. 
Cherry sponsored an earlier version of the amendment in 2022, which failed. And when the latest attempt advanced earlier this year, he joined his Democratic colleagues in voting for it. 
He first offered adjustments that would have limited the measure’s scope: one to exclude people with violent offenses, and another mandating former felons pay restitution in full before getting their voting rights back. 
Those efforts were unsuccessful. 
In an interview with The Mercury, Cherry described his tweaks as a way “to bring some of my other colleagues along with me.” 
This was in reference to GOP lawmakers who staunchly opposed restoring rights to people convicted of murder or manslaughter.
“That’s where (some of my Republican colleagues) fall on it. They want the victims to be restored,” Cherry explained. “They don’t like the fact that someone can get their rights back if they’ve disenfranchised someone else permanently.” 
He said he understood their perspective but still supported the amendment, even without his proposed changes. 
“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” he said. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.” 
Similarly, Patterson likened the state’s disenfranchisement to “this extra sentence that carries on.” 
Other former inmates released as part of the good behavior law have gone onto serve local government commissions, become peer recovery specialists, launch nonprofit organizations, or join lobbying and advocacy groups.
Nance, Patterson’s wife, said it’s important for those experiences to gain visibility, especially for those behind bars.
“I’m big on having our story reflect what potential there is for incarcerated people currently,” she said. 
A framed sketch Quadaire Patterson made of he and wife Santia Nance to celebrate his return from prison in 2024. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Patterson said the time he spent separated from society made him eager to not just rejoin it, but help shape it. 
He and Nance have supported criminal justice reform laws like visitation standards  and probation reform. The couple is optimistic about Spanberger’s new standards for the state’s prisons and a community council that’s been set up to brainstorm ideas on how to improve corrections practices in the state. 
About 200,000 more Virginians may also be able to vote this year, after a federal judge ruled that people with certain felony convictions should never have lost their right to vote in the first place. 
A Reconstruction-era law stipulated that people convicted of felonies that were considered common law in 1870 could lose their rights.  
The state now only excludes murder and manslaughter offenses from the list, the Virginia Department of Elections announced in September. 
With congressional midterm elections and the voting rights amendment on ballots, Virginia voters will also have two other pending constitutional amendments to consider. 
The first would permanently protect reproductive rights, including access to contraception, fertility treatments and abortion.
The second would enshrine same-sex marriage protections, ensuring gay marraige would remain legal in the state even if federal standards changed.  
Though early voting has been under way since Sep. 18, Patterson plans to cast his first-ever ballot on Election Day, Nov. 3. 
Concerning the amendments, Patterson said he and his wife have already made up their minds.
“It’s a ‘yes’ all the way down the ballot for us.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: After statewide tour, Virginia Lt. Gov. Hashmi officially opposes Dominion-NextEra merger
description: The debate over whether Florida-based NextEra Energy should be allowed to acquire Dominion Energy and create the largest regulated utility in the country heated up Tuesday, with Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi pledging her opposition to the $67 billion merger. She is the first elected official at the statewide level to formally oppose the creation […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Hashmi is joined by two lawmakers in Richmond, VA on Oct. 6 2026 for a press conference announcing she is opposing the merger of Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The debate over whether Florida-based NextEra Energy should be allowed to acquire Dominion Energy and create the largest regulated utility in the country heated up Tuesday, with Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi pledging her opposition to the $67 billion merger.
She is the first elected official at the statewide level to formally oppose the creation of the energy titan.
“After engaging in discussions with experts and industry officials, after reading analyses of the proposed merger, and after listening to the perspectives of hundreds of Virginians … I’ve concluded that the proposed takeover of Dominion Energy with NextEra is not in the best interest of Virginians,” Hashmi said at a press conference at Virginia’s Capitol in Richmond.
The lieutenant governor recently completed a five-city tour across the Dominion coverage area to hear firsthand Virginians’ concerns over the merger. The clearest feedback, Hashmi said, was that citizens are worried the deal could make their utility bills skyrocket, citing increased energy costs in recent years. 
“The public wanted assurances that this most essential public good will remain safe, and will remain reliable,” Hashmi said. “They want assurances that this merger is going to bring a public benefit, rather than increased financial hardships, to our ratepayers.”
Hundreds of people at each event in Loudoun County, Norfolk, Richmond, Charlottesville, and Roanoke expressed that there are not enough protections for ratepayers who would have to bear the cost of infrastructure buildouts, Hashmi said. 
The merger will allow the companies to buy energy infrastructure in bulk, which they said would save money and increase credit ratings. That alone doesn’t prove that energy rates will remain affordable, Hashmi countered Tuesday. 
State Sen. Mike Jones, D-Richmond, also stated his opposition to the merger at Tuesday’s press conference. His stance, he said, is based on concerns that the utility companies’ priority is to serve data centers, not residents.
A recent amendment to the merger filing that expanded the companies’ promises to extend customers’ bill credits to four years and to build a headquarters office in Richmond – but Jones said those steps don’t guarantee long-term solutions for ratepayers.
“A promise and a press release is not protection on a power bill. When the commitments expire, it will not be the shareholders who pay, it will be everyday working Virginians,” Jones said
At the event, Hashmi released a report that summarized the comments and concerns from constituents at each of the listening tour stops. 
In Loudoun, residents questioned who benefits from the energy infrastructure expansion that they see from the data center buildout and who should have to pay for it. 
Norfolk residents posed queries about storm resilience and financial vulnerability. An Army Corps of Engineers study found the Hampton Roads city is at heightened risk for severe flood damage and city officials are hammering out a $6.1 billion coastal storm risk management plan.
In Richmond, residents asked about the six-month condensed timeline of the review of the merger and whether the commitments made by the two companies are enforceable. 
In Charlottesville and Roanoke residents had questions about regional cost allocation and clean energy commitments.
Ahead of the official filing for the merger, Hashmi released a list of 64 questions about the project that she urged the companies to answer. The companies have not responded to those questions, with Dominion officials stating that they believed many would be answered in the case proceedings.
Energy officials, lawmakers question NextEra’s past dealings
In a hearing of the Energy Commission of Virginia on Tuesday, lawmakers questioned NextEra Vice Chairman Armando Pimentel about past failed attempts to acquire other utilities in Texas, Hawaii, and South Carolina.
Sen. Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, brought up questions from experts that were presented to the commission in August about adequate ring fencing, or financial protections.
“One of the questions we got was that whatever the (State Corporation Commission) does, if it’s approved, it needs to make sure there’s adequate protections around things like excess dividend transfers, to make sure that NextEra or merger company affiliates don’t have undue advantage in procurement for different projects that are going to be constructed, et cetera,” Surovell said.
Pimentel responded that only one of the past acquisition attempts had questions relating to ring fencing, and that those concerns did not apply in other cases.
SCC moves forward with merger review
On Oct. 2, a SCC examiner determined that NextEra’s records concerning the company’s attempted takeover of a Florida utility company be included in the regulators official review of the case. A motion from clean energy advocacy group Clean Virginia prompted the move. 
Meanwhile, several state lawmakers and Attorney General Jay Jones have called for the SCC’s review period of the merger to be extended.
Neither Gov. Abigail Spanberger nor lawmakers have called a special session to address the review timeline for the case. 
Spanberger said she declined because she opted to be an official intervenor in the case, allowing her to partake in cross examinations and have access to confidential documents.
The General Assembly is technically still in a special session – which would allow them to call themselves back to Richmond to pass a policy that would allow the SCC to extend the timeline. But House and Senate leadership have not signaled that would happen.
The SCC recently responded to increased public interest in the merger case by adding three in-person hearings to obtain public testimony. That is in addition to the three days of telephonic testimony that will be collected and any written statements that are submitted.
State regulators have until Jan. 11 to approve or reject the deal, unless they opt to extend the review time period.
