name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Dems double down on election protection in Pa. amid Trump administration’s threats
description: The Democratic effort builds on regular election protection methods and incorporates practices and procedures that grew out of the effort to document ICE agents’ actions during the immigration surge in Minnesota this year.
text:
ÒI VotedÓ stickers at a polling place in Derry Township, Westmoreland County, May 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Claims of voter fraud, threats to assert control over state-run elections and efforts to restrict mail-in voting have prompted Democrats in Pennsylvania and elsewhere to double down on measures to ensure eligible voters have unfettered access to the polls next month.
Democratic National Committee Vice Chair Jane Kleeb spoke with the Pennsylvania Capital-Star recently about the party’s plans to help voters and alert authorities to irregularities during the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Kleeb also serves as president of the Association of State Democratic Committees. 
The Capital-Star has also extended an offer to the Republican National Committee to discuss the subject.
With an unresolved conflict in the Middle East with Iran, soaring food and fuel prices and an aggressive immigration crackdown ongoing, the midterms are expected to be both a fight for control of Congress and a referendum on President Donald Trump’s performance. . 
Trump, his administration and his associates have continued to question the 2020 election, threatened to nationalize voting and to send U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to “surround” polling places.
While the DNC mounts election protection efforts in every election, Kleeb said the party isn’t waiting to see if irregularities materialize.
Pennsylvania Republican Party spokesperson James Markley said the GOP also “takes election integrity extremely seriously.”
“We’ve invested heavily in staff throughout the Commonwealth who have been recruiting and training poll workers and monitors since before the primary election,” he said. “We are confident that we will have the ground game and legal expertise to properly deal with and eliminate  any potential issues that will arise in the 2026 general election.”
The Democratic effort builds on regular election protection methods and incorporates practices and procedures that grew out of the effort to document ICE agents’ actions during the immigration surge in Minnesota this year. The party has even hired former members of the nation’s intelligence community to guard against threats from beyond America’s shores.
This interview was edited by a Pennsylvania Capital-Star journalist for clarity. 
Q What is the DNC doing in Pennsylvania to prepare for the midterm elections?
A: We have rolled out a new program this year, all about election protection and early voting. And one of the projects specifically is called Democracy Protectors, where we are training voters all across the country to be outside of their polling location to basically be there in case Trump really does send ICE agents or insurrectionists or anybody else that we can document as well as be kind of a helpful happy face outside the polling location for our Democratic voters.
Q: Do you have indications that the threats to election integrity are greater this year?
A: We don’t know for sure, and I think we won’t know 100% until election day. But we know what the president has said, what Steve Bannon has said, what kind of the chattering class of the right is saying. We saw the move that the Georgia Board of Elections did Thursday.
Democratic National Committee Vice Chair Jane Kleeb (Photo courtesy of DNC)
And there’s lots of other signs of them trying to attack voters from abroad, trying to limit the ability of voters from abroad being able to cast their ballots as American citizens. 
So we know that the risk is real, and because we won’t know with 100% certainty what will happen on Election Day, instead of being caught flat-footed, and we also wanted to make sure that voters know that we take these risks and concerns seriously, and we’re putting a plan in place to address it. So this is, you know, us saying we are concerned that the Trump administration is so desperate and will do anything. So what can we do as state parties, to make sure that we’re playing our role to protect the vote and to make sure every vote is counted?
Q: What does this training entail?
A: We modeled part of the training off of the Minnesota Democratic Farm and Labor Party training that they did in Minnesota to train folks to be constitutional observers during the ICE raids. So it’s very similar training where we train folks on how to de-escalate. We train folks on what we need them to do when they’re documenting bad actors if there are any. For example, you have to say your name, the date that you know you’re filming, where you’re filming. So we give them very specific training on that. We’re also helping them understand what they do if they do see a problem. 
Everything we’re doing with the state parties is in conjunction with the DNC. There is a hotline that volunteers can use to call in any red flags, concerns, even if there’s long lines. We want these democracy protectors to be plugged into the chain of command and the system that we have to track all of this. 
Sometimes long lines are just long lines, right? Lots of enthusiasm. Long lines happen every election day, but sometimes it can mean that there’s a problem that we have to address. Like maybe ballots ran out, and then we need to make sure our poll observer inside is monitoring that. 
So we have systems to address red flags and problems. And from our perspective, we want more people engaged in it because we think that there are potentially going to be issues that we have to resolve on election day. We want to make sure that our democracy protectors are trained to do that. 
The other part of the training is helping them understand how to help voters. Sometimes a voter will go to the wrong polling location, and they don’t know how to look up a polling location, or they don’t understand what a provisional ballot is. And so these are all things that basically a helping hand can assist voters with outside the polling location.
Q: In recent elections, people have become increasingly wary of any activity outside of polling locations. How do you navigate that with volunteer observers?
A: We’re having our folks be happy, helpful, wear blue, so folks know how to identify them. Not to be aggressive. Not to engage in any back and forth with any potential MAGA folks that are out there trying to intimidate voters or escalate things. This, for us, is all about documenting bad behavior, but also helping voters, and I think that we can definitely find that balance.
Q: How many observers do you expect to have around the state on election day?
A: Nationally, we are attempting to train 10,000 democracy protectors.
As soon as somebody goes through training, they then go through an additional screen to make sure they’re registered Democrats or Independents that lean our way. Those names get sent to the state party’s election protection program to place them. We also know that this is not the only tool that state parties are using. State parties themselves are also recruiting folks within their state, within the county party, to help with election protection as well. But this is our way as a national association of all of our state parties to kind of help recruit people to fill some of these gaps.
Q: Do you think we’ll ever get back to a time when we don’t need to do this, or is this something that’s always been going on behind the scenes and has not been as urgent a need?
A: Even in smaller red states, the DNC has some type of election protection program. That usually meant an existing staff member within the state party was tasked with being the lead for election protection. They were helping spread the DNC’s hotline and all their voter materials, and they recruited volunteers and lawyers on election day to staff phone lines within their state party office to address any concerns that are coming in on the phone or email. The lawyers that they recruited were also there to solve any problems, often the day after election day, when you have to cure ballots, or in close elections where you have to have a legal person represented for recounts. 
In a big state like Pennsylvania or Georgia or Michigan, where they have a lot more resources for election protection, it’s always been a very robust program where they were recruiting poll workers in a nonpartisan way. So we had Democrats that were filling those lots. They were recruiting partisan poll observers to be inside the polling location-that’s a very sophisticated, you know, planned-out program with county election offices and secretaries of state-and then they would have what we call a boiler room or a war room with lawyers and election protection experts that are, you know, dealing with any red case scenarios or flags of long lines, ballots running out, that type of thing. We always do that, and we’re continuing to do that. That’s our core election protection program. Some states even do have and have had over the years people outside of the polling location, especially in kind of high priority precincts, so communities of color, or especially young voter precincts, where this is the first time a young voter is voting, so they may not know the habit of voting, may not even know what door to go in, like all that kind of stuff.
We’ve never, though, had an election cycle where we were this concerned that the White House would be coordinating to disrupt outside of the polling locations. We’ve never had a president say that they are going to send ICE agents to polling locations, or his biggest megaphone, Steve Bannon, doing that as well. That is abnormal. Do I hope after this election cycle, when we win big and we start to, you know, get norms reset, that we don’t have to do this? Sure, I’m sure we will have to do this for the presidential election, and then after that, hopefully, our country can, you know, put its shoulders down a little bit, and we can get back to normal election protection programs.
Q: What other efforts is the DNC making to ensure a fair election?
A: We’re pushing early voting as oftentimes state parties have pushed the mail-in ballots. That’s been a focus of ours over the past decade. This cycle, we’re really encouraging people to also vote early in person if they haven’t already requested a ballot by mail.
We also do have an intelligence unit. We’ve hired former CIA, FBI, Homeland Security type folks to monitor online any issues that we think that we need to be aware of, because at state parties, to be real frank, we are focused on putting out fires every day. There is always something happening at a state party that you have to do – a press conference, a canvas, a vote by mail, etc. and we don’t have time to monitor the dark web, or we don’t often have time needed to monitor Twitter and Facebook. 
We’ve hired them to watch for trends across states, so we can be better prepared. We didn’t have this, of course, in 2016 when the famous Russia hack happened, or even in 2020 when Russia used the Bernie Bro narrative, or even last cycle, when the Republicans were doing a lot of the trans attacks that weren’t coming from authentic voters, they were coming more from bots to divide people. 
Those are the types of things that our intelligence unit is monitoring and looking for, and then we’ll help state parties if something is a threat in their particular state.
The good thing is, the things that we’ve come up with so far are really kind of your traditional online scammers and phishers. There was one state party whose website was temporarily hacked into. But we’re monitoring it in case things get serious, or we really get concerned with a trend across states.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: You’re not crazy. Voting in Indiana is intimidating.
description: Voting in Indiana is not an easy process. Doing your civic duty requires optimism and nimbleness. There’s very little state voter education, and registration deadlines fall almost a month before the Nov. 3 election. We have one of the lowest voter turnout rates in the country because most races are not competitive. And, with a […]
text:
Michaela White (left) and her roommate Lee Hamersly cast a vote in the primary election May 5, 2026, at Mt. Olive Missionary Baptist Church in Indianapolis. (Photo by Brett Phelps/Mirror Indy/CatchLight Local/Report for America)
Voting in Indiana is not an easy process. Doing your civic duty requires optimism and nimbleness. There’s very little state voter education, and registration deadlines fall almost a month before the Nov. 3 election. We have one of the lowest voter turnout rates in the country because most races are not competitive. And, with a supermajority in the state legislature, many think their votes don’t matter.
Hoosiers’ hesitation is understandable when you consider the research required to articulate your political wishes. But, you shouldn’t feel guilty, stupid or uneducated because the task seems daunting. Voting can be confusing, intimidating and overwhelming. It’s not surprising that so many people who are registered give up before they cast their ballot.
The journalists in Indy newsrooms know voters in our state are not engaged. And every newsroom has a different approach to help residents feel more confident about voting. But some legwork is still up to voters. Here’s what the local press does to help voters navigate midterm elections.
Newsrooms listen to the public to create an “engaged citizenry”
At this point in the election season, most of us are familiar with the biggest issues and races in the state. The glossy political ads are out, debates are happening, and the local media has honed in on the issues that seem to be of concern to residents. This work helps voters get through about one third of their ballots. But what about lesser known races, judicial retention, school board elections and referendums?
Indy newsrooms anticipate that your knowledge will decline as you move down the ballot. Here’s what they do to try and meet voters’ needs.
(Courtesy banner)
Most of the local news outlets devote their resources to competitive statewide elections and issues that have the greatest impact on the largest number of residents. Keep in mind, there are 125 open state legislative seats and more than 200 candidates. No newsroom has the resources to cover it all.
This year, IndyStar reporters are traveling around the state for the second time to listen to residents. They’ve been to eight of Indiana’s 92 counties, collecting residents’ opinions and concerns to inform their coverage of statewide candidates, knowing that Hoosiers aren’t monolithic.
“Our second annual statewide reporting tour lets us ask Hoosiers directly which issues matter most to them, and prevents us from getting stuck in a Central Indiana bubble,” said Kaitlin Lange, IndyStar news director.
Last year, reporters at The Star learned that southern Indiana residents felt cut off from the rest of the state. They are dealing with the realities from an influx of immigrants, counties with political realignments, and the impact of property taxes.
FPI News is taking a similar approach. To avoid duplicating the work of other local news outlets, the Free Press Indiana organization is sending a reporter to areas with low voter turnout to ask residents why they don’t vote and sending another reporter statewide to learn about barriers older Hoosiers face in getting to the polls. Check out this story the outlet did on LGBTQ+ candidates in rural Owen County.
Mirror Indy tries to fill news gaps, covering the local races and issues not addressed by other news organizations. Reporters ask voters open-ended questions to learn about voter behavior, said managing editor Chris Sikich.
“We are talking to voters ahead of the election for social media stories and we will talk to them at the polls on Election Day,” he said. “We word questions in a way so as not to lead voters to an answer. We want to know what they think.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
FOX59 and CBS4 news director CJ Hoyt explained how those stations rely on voters and their reporters’ experience to drive their focus on the issues. The stations’ owner, Nexstar Media Group, Inc., partners with Boston’s Emerson College for polling, which both FOX59 and CBS4 feature in their newscasts.
“For example, for the upcoming secretary of state debate we are hosting on October 22, we have asked our viewers to send us the questions they would most like to have asked,” Hoyt said. “Beyond that, we rely on the wide spectrum of perspectives and experiences in our newsroom to identify issues that deserve coverage.”
FOX59 anchor and political director Dan Spehler interviewed all four secretary of state candidates for the newscast and the channel’s public affairs show, “IN Focus.”
Indiana Capital Chronicle Editor-in-Chief Niki Kelly said that her newsroom already knows that data centers, flock cameras and property taxes are major areas of public concern. She and her staff include questions about those issues when interviewing candidates, on top of gathering information on issues specific to the particular office.
Kelly has been reporting on the Statehouse since 1999. States Newsroom, which launched ICC in 2022, is a nationwide nonprofit news organization reporting on state capitals. Kelly remembers how in years past the focus of election coverage was more basic. Now, there is a lot more explanatory coverage, she said.
“It was a lot more of ‘here’s the race, here’s the candidates, here’s their salaries, and here’s a little bit about them,’” she said. “I think now a lot of outlets are doing more explanatory pieces on elections, and I think part of that is knowing that some people have lost trust in the election process. So I think journalists feel like we need to explain.”
Turning the tide on low voter turnout
When University of Indianapolis political science professor Laura Merrifield Wilson moved from Greene County, Alabama to Indy in 2014 she was struck by how low voter turnout was in the state.
“Alabama has really low voter turnout, but Indiana was like ‘hold-my-beer-low’ that particular year,” she said. “For all the things I can’t remember, I’ll never forget our voter turnout in that congressional midterm was 26.2%. It was in fact the lowest in the country that election cycle.”
When so few residents are responsible for electing the officials that make our laws, we are likely to get a government that is not responsive to our collective wishes.
Merrifield Wilson says the most important thing news outlets can do to create an “engaged citizenry” beyond informing and engaging the public, is share how to vote and to get residents excited about voting. She’s often tapped as a commentator on WFYI’s “Indiana Week in Review,” FOX59 and CBS4’s “IN Focus,” serves on the Indiana Debate Commission and has moderated a number of debates.
“Oftentimes there’s been a race on the ballot that people felt was close or was interesting or was important in some sort of way that it motivated them to make the choice to vote versus what is more common for us in the state of choosing not to,” Merrifield Wilson said.
Local media helps Hoosiers navigate four basic questions
So, hopefully you’ve checked your voter registration and met the October 5th deadline to register to vote. (And most of us have— Indiana has high registration but low participation.) Before you dive in, you should know that many of us aren’t completely informed about every race. It’s exhausting to try to develop fully-formed political opinions about weird land use issues or unopposed judges. The good news is that local newsrooms have anticipated your needs. Here’s what I would do to become a more confident voter.
If you need someone to walk you through your ballot:
Mirror Indy Votes’ Indiana General Election 2026 hub takes you down the ballot from national, state, and county races through judicial retention, township races and school measures. Mirror Indy explains what the people in these offices are responsible for and includes their picture and bio, if the candidate answered their questions. The hub also has related election stories.
The Indiana Capital Chronicle’s 2026 Voter Guide provides an overview of all statewide and federal races, plus the two state constitutional measures on the ballot this year. In addition to candidate bios, the news outlet provides the term limits and salaries of each position and any stories related to the candidates.
WFYI’s 2026 Voter Guide includes bios, photos, office information, and candidate interviews for secretary of state, state comptroller and state treasurer offices. It also includes all nine of Indiana’s congressional districts.
If you want to see what your ballot will look like, go to The Indiana Citizen and put in your address or select your ballot via an interactive map. The Indiana Citizen provides the most specific display of what voters will see on their ballots and links to Ballotpedia for info on how each candidate fared in the primary election.
If you want to know about the mechanics of voting:
Indiana Capital Chronicle has the best “How-To” information for applying for a mail-in ballot, finding your polling place, working the polls and voting in person. In yet another approach to the mechanics, this story by Mirror Indy service reporter Sophie Young tells you where to grab a copy of their 2026 election zine, which explains how voting works, what your rights are, and what each office does.
If you want to know about school board elections:
This voter guide produced by a collaboration that includes Chalkbeat Indiana, Mirror Indy and WFYI gives voters information about school board elections in Marion County. It includes a Q&A and background for every Indianapolis Public Schools candidate and township candidate.
If you want the best coverage of the biggest races:
Deciding what coverage is “best” is more subjective and depends on your interests, but I recommend relying on the news outlet that other outlets look to for political coverage: Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Indiana Capital Chronicle makes their content available for reprinting by any publication for free. When it first launched in 2022, they received a couple dozen story reprints per week. A weekly report from Sept. 28 showed the number at 170. The Associated Press no longer provides election coverage of Indiana that news outlets can pick up, according to Editor-in-Chief Kelly. So, newspapers, radio and TV across the state use ICC’s content.
We have to start somewhere
Indiana’s voter participation rates probably aren’t going to change dramatically, but we’ve got to start somewhere. It shouldn’t require a contentious race or policy issue to draw us to the polls. If less than 50% of the population is turning out to decide what public policy should be for the rest of us, how good can it be? The news can inform us, but you can’t complain about the policies if you’re not actively participating in democracy.



				How are you doing your research for this midterm election? I would love to look over your shoulder either in-person or virtually. If you’re open to this, hit me up by emailing me at indypubliceditor@poynter.org.

title: ‘Human error’ switches status of 67,000 Louisiana voters to inactive
description: The Louisiana Secretary of State’s office expects to restore the correct status for thousands of voters by Wednesday after a mishap during routine maintenance earlier this week switched them to inactive. Trey Williams, deputy secretary for communications, said “human error” during the process Monday night inadvertently misclassified approximately 67,000 vote[...]
text:
Routine maintenance to a state elections database Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, resulted in the accidental switch of approximately 67,000 Louisiana voters to inactive status, according to the Secretary of State. (Photo by Blair Miller/Daily Montanan)The Louisiana Secretary of State’s office expects to restore the correct status for thousands of voters by Wednesday after a mishap during routine maintenance earlier this week switched them to inactive.
Trey Williams, deputy secretary for communications, said “human error” during the process Monday night inadvertently misclassified approximately 67,000 voters statewide.  
“Our staff immediately identified the issue and began correcting it,” Williams said in an email. “We also implemented additional safeguards to prevent this from happening again.”
The temporary status glitch will not affect anyone’s eligibility or ability to vote, he added. Inactive voters are still eligible to vote under Louisiana law. 
Courtney Price, an East Baton Rouge Parish voter, told the Illuminator in an email she noticed her voting status was switched to inactive when she checked it Monday evening. She has lived at the same address for more than 10 years and described herself as a “consistent” voter. 
Price shared her email exchange telling East Baton Rouge Parish Registrar Steve Raborn about the discrepancy, and he informed Price that the problem originated with the Secretary of State.
The Secretary of State maintains a list of inactive voters, which includes voters whose addresses aren’t verified by their parish registrar of voters during their annual review of voter rolls.
Voters who’ve moved can update their registration details online if they have already updated their driver’s license or state ID with information for their new address. They can also make updates by mail or in person at their parish registrar of voters.
Voters who have not updated their registration address are still eligible to vote, but they are required to confirm their residence when voting with some form of photo ID and proof of their current address. Persons without a voter ID on Election Day will be asked to complete a voter ID affidavit form.  
Inactive voters who don’t confirm their address and do not take part in any elections may be removed from the state’s voter list after being dormant for two consecutive federal election cycles.
Voters can verify their registration information through the voter portal at Geauxvote.com or through the Geaux Vote mobile app.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Big money stirs up squabbles in Indiana secretary of state’s race
description: Big-money contributions from out of state have poured fuel into this fall’s expensive campaign for Indiana secretary of state.
text:
Indiana secretary of state candidates, from left, Democrat Beau Bayh and Republican Max Engling. (Photos provided by campaigns)Big-money contributions from out of state have poured fuel into this fall’s expensive campaign for Indiana secretary of state.
Millions of in-state dollars have also flowed into the campaign accounts, along with controversies over some donations, such as $50,000 accepted by Republican candidate Max Engling from a convicted felon.
Democrat Beau Bayh has gained more than $1 million from out-of-state donors — with some of the biggest contributors having longtime ties to his father, former U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh. 
Engling has collected far less from outside the state, although one of his largest donors so far is his old boss in Washington, former U.S. House Speaker Kevin McCarthy.
Both Bayh and Engling face barbs over some sizable deposits made into their burgeoning campaign accounts.
Bayh campaign boosted by dad’s connections
Bayh’s fundraising success has allowed him to wage the most active advertising campaign of any statewide Democratic candidate in several election cycles.
Connections through his father gave Bayh an early financial boost after he launched his campaign last year and five-figure contributions from those sources keep coming in for him.
For instance, Bayh’s largest individual donor is Connecticut billionaire Robert Johnson, who gave Bayh $300,000 last year and $100,000 more in September, according to Indiana Election Division records.


Televised debate
An hour-long debate between the four secretary of state candidates is scheduled for Wednesday evening.
The debate, sponsored by the nonprofit Indiana Debate Commission, is scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT and will be broadcast live by several public television stations across the state.

Evan Bayh joined the board of directors for one of Johnson’s businesses, RJL Lodging Trust, soon after leaving the Senate in 2011. His board member compensation last year was $250,000.
Another $100,000 Beau Bayh campaign contribution came from Andrew Bursky, co-founder of Connecticut-based private equity firm Atlas Holdings.
Bursky is a board member of the centrist political group No Labels that flopped in its attempt to find a high-profile third-party presidential candidate in 2024. Evan Bayh is a former co-national chair of the organization.
Beau Bayh said many of his out-of-state contributions have come from “people that have known me my whole life” through his father.
“When anyone’s raising resources to run a campaign, the logical place to start is people that you’ve known forever,” Bayh told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “Those are the people that know you the best, that hopefully would believe in you. So we’ve had success in reaching out to my personal network.”
Bayh also maintains that he’s had “the most fundraising success of any candidate in this race with in-state money. We have financial contributors from all 92 counties of our state.”
Bayh’s total fundraising will almost certainly top $4 million when the next state campaign finance reports are due Oct. 16. That will include $1 million contributed by the state Democratic Party over the past two weeks.
Engling bashed the out-of-state money’s role in helping Bayh’s campaign advertising that has moved beyond the secretary of state’s administrative role to advocate for tax cuts and tighter data center regulations.
“I think we can all see he’s clearly running for governor through this race,” Engling said in an interview. “Many things that he talks about on the campaign trail have nothing to do with the secretary of state’s race or the official role of the office. He’s already positioning himself to run for a different office before he even gets through the election here for the secretary of state’s office.”
Ex-House Speaker McCarthy among Engling backers 
Engling’s campaign says its fundraising has topped $2 million since he entered the race in May and defeated current Secretary of State Diego Morales for the Republican nomination.
That includes a $1 million infusion from the state Republican Party and Gov. Mike Braun’s campaign fund.
One of Engling’s largest other contributions was $50,000 from the federal campaign fund of McCarthy, the former U.S. House speaker. Engling worked as an aide to McCarthy in Washington for about four years until returning to Indiana in 2023, soon before McCarthy was ousted as House speaker in a rebellion by far-right members.
Engling, who is on leave from his job as a top staffer to Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, also has banked $55,000 from a political group affiliated with GOP Sen. Todd Young.
Engling said he saw a distinction between financial support from a current Indiana senator versus Bayh’s out-of-state contributions.
Who’s a real Hoosier? Secretary of state candidates spar over time in Indiana.

“Certainly, with former Speaker McCarthy, that is outside money, but it’s because I’ve worked directly with him,” Engling said. “He understands what I bring to the equation, knows my experience and background, and wants to be supportive of that to continue helping Indiana move ahead.”
McCarthy’s campaign fund reported no contributions to other candidates through the first six months of this year. 
McCarthy, who represented California in the U.S. House, said in an interview with the Capital Chronicle that he was impressed with Engling’s ability and believed “it’s very important that we have the very best people that are willing to run and serve.”
“When somebody of that higher quality is willing to put their name on the line and serve, I’m more than willing to help them,” McCarthy said.
Both taking heat over some big donors
Democrats have denounced Engling for accepting a $50,000 contribution last month from Noblesville businessman Michael Sherfick, who pleaded guilty in 2010 to federal bribery charges and was sentenced to 14 months in prison. 
Engling defended keeping the money.
“What we’re talking about here is somebody who is legally allowed to make a donation, who had their own challenge between 15 and 20 years ago, has paid that penalty,” Engling said. “They resolved that and have for the last decade-plus been a contributing member of society.”
Bayh links the Sherfick donation with an improper $60,000 contribution from a dark money group associated with Banks that Engling’s campaign says was refunded in July.
“His top two donors right now are Kevin McCarthy, king of the D.C. swamp, and a guy who spent time in the federal pen for bribery,” Bayh said in an online video about Engling.
Bayh, meanwhile, won the Democratic nomination in June after facing intra-party heat for accepting a $25,000 contribution from Marc Rowan, the CEO of New York-based private equity firm Apollo Global Management, where Evan Bayh became a senior adviser in 2011.
President Donald Trump appointed Rowan to his contentious Board of Peace, which drew the ire of progressives leary of Bayh’s candidacy. 
Engling criticizes Bayh for keeping Rowan’s contribution because of the billionaire’s ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. 
Department of Justice documents released in January showed Rowan and another Apollo Global executive in communication with Epstein between 2013 and 2016. Rowan hasn’t been accused of wrongdoing involving Epstein and Apollo Global said in February that Rowan did not have any “business or personal relationship” with Epstein.
More money could be coming
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings have trailed far behind Bayh and Engling in fundraising.
Shilling’s largest contribution has been $10,000 from the Libertarian National Committee, according to state campaign reports.
Ballard, meanwhile, said he expected to have some television advertising up ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3. 
He spent nearly $800,000 through June on collecting about 40,000 petition signatures to place his name on the election ballot.
What’s the Lincoln Party? Ballard’s secretary of state run could expand Indiana ballot access

That left him with about $25,000 in cash as of June 30, although he’s since had support from some major donors, including $150,000 from John Lechleiter, the former chairman and CEO of Eli Lilly and Co.
He had a fundraiser in September that collected $165,000.
Ballard, the former Republican mayor of Indianapolis, said he understood campaigns being “antsy” because of the greater attention going to the secretary of state’s race this year.
But he declined to criticize the fundraising tactics of others.
“If it’s legal, I’m not going to say anything,” Ballard said. “If they’re doing it within the campaign finance laws, what are you going to say? Campaign finance laws are the way they are right now. So you won’t hear me complaining about that.”
More outside money could pour into the race in the coming weeks for Bayh and Engling.
Evan Bayh’s federal campaign fund had a balance of more than $2.2 million at the end of June from money leftover from his unsuccessful 2016 Senate comeback bid. 
That money could be spent to boost his son’s campaign — much like Gov. Mike Braun did with his U.S. Senate campaign fund in kick-starting his 2024 run for governor.
State Democrats and the Bayh campaign, however, have avoided saying whether the Evan Bayh funding will come into play.
Political groups tied to Banks — Engling’s most-recent boss — spent millions of dollars earlier this year in support of Republican primary challengers to state senators who voted against the congressional redistricting plan pushed by President Donald Trump.
Those Banks groups have been quiet so far in the secretary of state’s race except for a recent poll released. Banks and others involved in his political groups have not responded to multiple messages seeking comment about campaign support for Engling.
When asked whether the Banks groups would be jumping into the race, Engling said he appreciated the backing he’s received from top state Republicans, including Braun and Banks.
“I do expect that there’ll be more support as we move forward from the senator — from both senators — and as we make this pitch in the last month to get across the finish line,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: How much more? Report suggests more work to be done to redo Rhode Island’s school funding formula.
description: Freshly crunched numbers for a proposed overhaul of how Rhode Island calculates the bulk of the state’s share of local school funding would increase annual state education formula aid by an additional $525 million over this year — a number which does not include new expenses the proposal was designed to shift to the state. […]
text:
A hallway in Hope High School in Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Freshly crunched numbers for a proposed overhaul of how Rhode Island calculates the bulk of the state’s share of local school funding would increase annual state education formula aid by an additional $525 million over this year — a number which does not include new expenses the proposal was designed to shift to the state.
The new report submitted Oct. 1 by the Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE) to the General Assembly “identifies several significant fiscal and policy considerations” for state lawmakers as they prepare to evaluate recommendations from the Rhode Island Foundation-led Blue Ribbon Commission.
The commission released a proposal in January crafted with the help of a research team from Brown University’s Annenberg Institute, calling for substantially increasing state investment in public education while redistributing state and local responsibility. RIDE summarized the commission’s proposal in its new analysis, undertaken with the Office of Management and Budget and Division of Municipal Finance.
A piece of legislation passed in June added a requirement to the fiscal year 2027 budget tasking education and budget officials with conducting an initial analysis of the Blue Ribbon proposal, using new and validated school financial data from fiscal year 2025.
The law set the report’s Oct. 1 due date, ahead of an Oct. 31 deadline for the first meeting of a special legislative commission that will study the feasibility of the proposal to make over Rhode Island’s roughly 16-year-old education funding system. The commission has to file its own interim report by March 2, 2027, followed by a slate of final recommendations on Sept. 1, 2027.
The 30-page RIDE report raises questions about how the Blue Ribbon Commission came up with some of its big ideas, which all revolved around the state’s education funding formula — the amount of state money Rhode Island school districts receive annually to cover baseline student costs and provide an adequate education. The commission’s original estimates noted this formula aid accounted for about $1.22 billion of the state’s $1.57 billion education budget, or about 78%, in fiscal year 2026. 
The current formula uses adjustments like demographic data to direct money to the districts where it is most needed. But the status quo was not quite equitable enough to the Blue Ribbon Commission. Central to its slate of recommendations is changing how the state calculates its education formula aid to make the distribution of state aid for so-called “core” instructional costs more equitable. 
The Blue Ribbon Commission argued the actual cost of educating children — which includes expenses like transportation or even retired teachers’ pensions — are inadequately borne by the state, forcing local school districts to pay more. 
Disagreement over ‘assertions and assumptions’
Increasing the state’s share of these costs — which would entail a redefinition of what counts as a “core” cost — is a major theme in the Blue Ribbon report.
Rhode Island Foundation spokesperson Chris Barnett said Tuesday via email that the foundation received the report “late yesterday,” and that it and the commission need time to double-check the state’s work. 
Barnett said the foundation was sharing the report with members of the Blue Ribbon Commission for “thorough review, fact-checking, and a formal response.”
“While that review is just getting started, it’s only fair to say that there are assertions and assumptions in the report that we do not agree with,” Barnett said.
Were the Blue Ribbon report’s funding recommendations pursued to the priciest scenario it modeled — which entailed about a 58% state share in this increased pool of costs — initial estimates placed the total increase to the state education budget at around $590 million, phased in over multiple years.
But RIDE’s analysis estimated the proposed formula aid would increase by about $525 million compared with the fiscal year 2027 budget: traditional public school districts would receive roughly $393 million more collectively, charter schools about $118 million more and other schools would get about $14 million. 
When updating the commission’s calculations for state-only expenses, the new RIDE analysis produced an estimate of approximately $314 million — something for which state officials are seeking clarification.
“This estimate does not seem to reflect the recommendations of the [Blue Ribbon Commission] report,” the RIDE report states, adding that the $525 million estimate “is not inclusive” of this additional tranche of funding.
Different districts, different funding
One of the most distinctive parts of the Blue Ribbon proposal was the district-by-district picture it illustrated in its hypothetical state formula aid scenarios. 
Under the commission’s modeling, only four public school districts would see lower total modeled state aid.
The report estimated 13 districts would see less formula aid than they are set to receive under this fiscal year’s budget. Of those, nine districts — Charlestown, Jamestown, Little Compton, Narragansett, Newport, New Shoreham, Portsmouth, South Kingstown and Westerly — would see their direct formula aid effectively drop to zero. 
That’s because the Blue Ribbon Commission recommended prescribing a minimum local share for municipalities’ contributions to their schools. If that local obligation covers the foundational amount assigned to it by the state formula, the Blue Ribbon panel recommended that those districts’ direct state formula aid could fall to zero. (The proposal would still have the state cover some costs now paid locally.)
The Blue Ribbon group recommended withholding further state aid from municipalities that don’t pay the minimum amount.
RIDE wondered about the consequences of enforcing this: “This approach could potentially compound the underfunding of a school district: a municipality that fails to provide its required local contribution would leave the district with insufficient local funding, while withholding state education aid in response could further reduce the total resources available to that district,” the report reads. 
The report also questioned what metrics the Blue Ribbon group used for property values when calculating municipalities’ required contributions. Also of concern was whether some costs could be counted twice and whether new reporting and oversight requirements would duplicate systems already in place.
The Blue Ribbon Commission spent more than a year developing its proposed funding system, and was co-chaired by the foundation President and CEO, David Cicilline, along with Georgetown University professor Nora Gordon.
Brenda Santos of Brown University’s Annenberg Institute — which facilitated the commission’s research and prepared its report — reiterated the worth of the Blue Ribbon findings in an email Tuesday.
“We’re proud of the Blue Ribbon Commission’s work to put forward a system for full and fair school funding, grounded in national evidence and responsive to local needs,” Santos said. “We are eager to read the report.”

name: National
title: Abortion foes plan to push pill restrictions in the states
description: As they await a federal decision on a potential nationwide ban on telehealth abortions, anti-abortion activists plan to push more states to require women to visit a doctor’s office, get an ultrasound or wait before they can get abortion pills. Under its current guidelines, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not require in-person visits, […]
text:
Under its current guidelines, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not require in-person visits, waiting periods or ultrasounds for women seeking abortion pills. Nevertheless, 10 states without total abortion bans still require them. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent)As they await a federal decision on a potential nationwide ban on telehealth abortions, anti-abortion activists plan to push more states to require women to visit a doctor’s office, get an ultrasound or wait before they can get abortion pills.
Under its current guidelines, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not require in-person visits, ultrasounds or waiting periods for women seeking abortion pills. Nevertheless, 10 states without total abortion bans still require them.
One of those states is Florida. The state only allows abortion up to six weeks — which is before many women discover they are pregnant. Under state law, women must first get an ultrasound and then wait at least 24 hours before receiving pills or a procedure. By that time, they might be beyond the six weeks threshold.
“Floridians are already under a time clock,” said Lana’e Hernandez, a case manager for the Florida Access Network, an abortion fund that helps women pay for their abortions and travel to other states if they fall outside Florida’s narrow window.
“I see a lot of clients having to then travel out of state and take even more time off of work, adding another barrier to accessing care because of those laws combined.”
Medication abortion typically involves two drugs: mifepristone and misoprostol. The FDA approved the two-drug regimen in 2000 and gradually loosened restrictions as safety reviews showed a low risk of serious and life-threatening conditions. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, the Biden administration suspended enforcement of the rule that patients had to take the medication in person, and the FDA officially removed that requirement in 2023.
But anti-abortion organizations and attorneys general have challenged these changes in ongoing federal lawsuits. And in 2025, activist groups successfully pressured the Trump administration’s FDA to review the safety data again.
On Wednesday, the FDA is expected to update the public on the progress of this review, though the agency is not expected to issue a final ruling on telehealth access to the pills. The Washington Sun recently reported that the Trump administration wants to delay any potentially controversial actions around abortion until after the midterm elections. The administration has also delayed multiple ongoing federal lawsuits until after the review.
Abortion rights advocates say reversing telehealth access to medication abortion would have a huge impact across the country. Medication abortions now account for about 65% of all abortions, and roughly 28% of all abortions are through telehealth, according to KFF, a health research group.
Critical elections
In statehouses, the midterm elections could determine whether more states will seek to restrict medication abortion.
Meanwhile, Democratic control of Congress could doom President Donald Trump’s nominee for FDA commissioner. During her confirmation hearing last month, nominee Heidi Overton would not say whether she would recommend changes to mifepristone regulation, but in the past she has expressed anti-abortion views and written that the medication is dangerous.
National anti-abortion leaders told Stateline they will not be satisfied if the FDA determines that mifepristone is safe and can be administered via telehealth.
“There are comorbidities that come with mifepristone, like ectopic pregnancies that need to be diagnosed prior to the actual provision of mifepristone, and right now under the FDA system, that’s not working,” said Bradley Kehr, vice president of legal affairs of Americans United for Life. “So states are stepping in to say that they have serious concerns, and they’re taking action for the safety of their citizens.”
Republican AGs sue abortion ‘shield law’ states in US Supreme Court

Peer-reviewed studies overwhelmingly show a low risk of serious adverse events for medication abortions up to 10 weeks’ gestation, including via telehealth. But national anti-abortion groups have pointed to examples of coercion and non-peer-reviewed white papers to argue the risks are more significant than what the FDA has reported, and that ultrasounds should be required before the pills are administered.
Hernandez of the Florida Access Network said ultrasounds might be appropriate for women who have irregular periods or are at risk for an ectopic pregnancy, but that they should not be universally mandated by lawmakers. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, for patients with regular menstrual cycles and no risk factors for ectopic pregnancy, a clinical examination or ultrasound is not necessary before taking abortion pills.
“These are conversations that you should be having with your medical professional and not the government mandating you to do one thing or another,” Hernandez said. “You should be able to trust your physician to tell you whether you need an ultrasound or not to have an abortion.”
Abortion rights advocates say abortion is being singled out even as more medical care is being delivered via telehealth.
“When it comes to telehealth for abortion care specifically, a lot of those concerns, I think are coming from a place that’s really informed by abortion stigma,” said Kimya Forouzan, the principal state policy advisor of the Guttmacher Institute, a research and policy organization that supports abortion rights. “Receiving medication abortion via telehealth is not different than any other form of telehealth care.”
Existing restrictions
In addition to Florida, Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin require ultrasounds or other in-person requirements before medication abortions. In-person requirements can include an initial in-person exam, in-person counseling, a requirement that the pills be dispensed in person or a requirement that the first dose be taken in person.
Thirteen other states (Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and West Virginia) ban all abortions.
In Alaska, Missouri and Wisconsin, plaintiffs have challenged the laws on state constitutional grounds. Wyoming last year enacted a law requiring ultrasounds and a 48-hour waiting period before medication abortions. But a state district judge overturned the law in June, ruling that it violated a constitutional amendment protecting healthcare decisions, and that the state “offered no cogent evidence illustrating that a waiting period is necessary for any purpose.”
At the federal level, plaintiffs have argued that state regulations on abortion pills should not supersede the federal guidelines.
“The FDA sets the bar, and states don’t get to impede access to an FDA-approved medication,” said Kirsten Moore, director of the Expanding Medication Abortion Access (EMMA) Project, which tracks litigation related to medication abortion.
In an ongoing federal lawsuit over North Carolina’s restrictions, the plaintiffs argue that the state law conflicts with the FDA’s regulatory authority. A federal judge in 2024 ruled that the state could not ban the mailing of abortion pills, since federal rules allow it. But the judge upheld the state’s ultrasound requirement and its waiting period.
The case is pending appeal, with oral arguments scheduled for later this month at the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which last year upheld medication abortion restrictions in West Virginia, which bans all abortions and explicitly telehealth abortions. In that case, plaintiff generic mifepristone manufacturer GenBioPro argued the state’s ban violated the federal regulation of abortion pills, but the appeals court affirmed the lower court’s decision that FDA regulations did not preempt the state’s abortion ban.
Earlier this year, Iowa also enacted a law requiring abortion-inducing medication to be prescribed in person and dispensed in a medical setting.
Beaufield Berry, executive director of the Iowa Abortion Access Fund, said that since the law went into effect, her group has gotten more calls from people asking for financial help to travel out of state. She said there are two abortion clinics left in the state, both in central Iowa, making it especially difficult on people in rural areas.
“It’s really hard for some people to be able to make an appointment to go get an ultrasound, and then if they do that, then they’re running up against that six-week clock,” Berry said.
“For an in-person visit, that’s transportation, missing work, finding childcare. And in many cases, the act of having an abortion, you may not have support,” she said. “They may be underage, and so that creates even more barriers to getting an in-person meeting.”
Different strategies
Kehr of Americans United for Life said anti-abortion state lawmakers are still figuring out their individual strategies for restricting access to abortion medication. He cited the 10th Amendment, which gives states the authority through their police power to protect their citizens, as a legal justification for mandating ultrasounds or in-clinic visits before abortion pills are dispensed.
“Other states are taking different approaches, whether it’s the ultrasound provision to check for ectopic pregnancies and things like that, or the actual consideration of abuse that’s occurring,” Kehr said.
“We’ve had multiple stories of men forcing their pregnant girlfriends or wives to take mifepristone. So looking at it from an abusive perspective or a coercive perspective, states are really looking at the gamut of options under the 10th Amendment powers.”
Model legislation developed by the National Right to Life Committee, known as the Abortion Pill Provider Liability Education (APPLE) Act, and introduced this year in New Jersey and Ohio, would require abortion-pill prescribers to inform patients about the risks of the drugs, as well as her right to sue the provider if she faces complications.
The National Right to Life Committee also supports in-person visits and mandatory ultrasounds.
“Requiring a healthcare provider to confirm, locate, and date a pregnancy before prescribing a dangerous mixture of abortion-inducing drugs is a bare-minimum safety standard, and we believe it should apply in every state,” Ingrid Duran, director of state legislation for the National Right to Life Committee, wrote in an email.
Also looming in the background are interstate fights over so-called shield law providers prescribing medication virtually. Attorneys general in Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana filed lawsuits last week targeting shield laws and in California, Massachusetts and New York, and individual doctors prescribing abortion pills to women in states with abortion bans.
“A woman can’t possibly receive fully informed consent specific to her when the dispensing provider doesn’t even know how far along she is in her pregnancy because the risk is different depending on how far along she is,” said Dr. Christina Francis, an OB-GYN based in Fort Wayne, Indiana, who is CEO of the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which has opposed abortion pills since they were first approved in 2000.
“We believe that women deserve fully informed consent, and that necessarily involves an ultrasound when we’re talking about pregnancy.”
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.
