name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: $10 diesel? One Ohio analyst says it’s possible.
description: When truck stops and gas stations erected their signs, they didn’t anticipate needing two digits before the decimal point. But an Ohio-based data analyst who used to work in the energy industry says it’s a distinct possibility that they’ll need to find one for diesel.  As President Donald Trump’s war with Iran has continued, the […]
text:
A sign at a truck stop along Interstate 70 in eastern Indiana. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)When truck stops and gas stations erected their signs, they didn’t anticipate needing two digits before the decimal point. But an Ohio-based data analyst who used to work in the energy industry says it’s a distinct possibility that they’ll need to find one for diesel. 
As President Donald Trump’s war with Iran has continued, the rising cost of diesel fuel has been felt by all consumers, even if they don’t buy diesel fuel at the pump.
That’s because 96.8% of commercial semi-trucks, nearly all U.S. freight trains, and virtually all cargo ships are powered by diesel or its distillate cousin, fuel oil. Jet fuel, too, is a “middle distillate,” and competes with diesel and fuel oil for refinery output.
So nearly all the food and consumer goods that Ohioans buy traveled most of the way to their house on the power of diesel or a related fuel. 
In Ohio on Sept. 22, diesel hit its highest average price on record — $6.80 a gallon, according to the American Automobile Association.
Those prices appear to be getting more volatile and heading generally upward at a time when diesel prices are already playing a big role in the affordability crisis that’s plaguing millions of Americans, said Dayton-based data analyst Eric Pachman. 
He built a data visualization showing that as diesel goes up, so does the fuel surcharge for everything consumers buy. 
In September 2025, the surcharge was 11% to 14%, depending on whether goods are shipped by truck or rail. By this September it was 21% to 27%. 
If diesel goes to $10 a gallon, the fuel surcharge will be 30% to 37%, according to Pachman’s model.
He now runs the nonprofit Data 4 the People, which seeks to use high-level analysis to inform journalism and public policy. He previously held senior roles doing data analysis, modeling and engineering in a number of fields, including energy, transportation and finance.
According to another data visualization Pachman built, diesel reserves are the lowest they’ve been for this time of year at least since 1980. 
That, Pachman explained, makes the entire system vulnerable to all kinds of potential problems.
One is that global demand for U.S.-produced diesel shot up because of supply disruptions caused by the war with Iran. 
Refineries are highly complex facilities and they periodically shut down to do scheduled maintenance in a process called “turnaround” that typically takes place in the spring or fall. 
Now, with global demand so high, refineries are delaying their turnarounds to take advantage of the huge profits that are available, Pachman said.
“They’re saying, ‘We’ll take our chances,'” he said. “And guess what just happened? A refinery broke down and it was one in the Midwest. When you saw a big jump in diesel prices, it was because of that. This is going on everywhere. You’re laying one risk on top of the next risk on top of the next risk.” 
He was referring to the ExxonMobile refinery in Joliet, Ill., that went offline Sept. 13 and took weeks to restart. According to the U.S. Energy Information Agency, diesel prices in the Midwest jumped from $6.25 a gallon on Sept. 14 to $6.68 a week later.
Pachman said refineries are running full bore and reserves are at an all-time low at exactly the wrong time of year — heading into winter. Particularly in the Northeast, fuel oil is widely used for heating, and demand for it will go up as temperatures go down.
“If we use more heating oil we have less diesel and that’s why refineries try to stock up, and you can clearly see from this chart going into the winter,” he said, referring to his reserve visualization. “Week 38 (of 2026) is where we try to peak out on our inventories and drop down from there.”
As the stresses in the system grow, it becomes more volatile, making progressively crazier outcomes more likely, Pachman said.
“The reason I think $10 is a distinct possibility is because things don’t move linearly,” he said. “At a certain point, people just freak out about stuff. We haven’t reached that point. Things have gradually risen as supply has drained to the lowest levels on record. There’s been no freakout yet. But I’d say it’s a distinct possibility or even a reasonable probability.”
As for finding a way to post such prices on truck-stops’ signs, Fortune on Sept. 10, reported that in California, they hadn’t. The story was titled “$9.999 and maxed out: California diesel prices overwhelm pump displays as global supply crunch worsens.”
Diesel retailers Marathon Oil, Pilot Travel Centers and BP were asked if they thought diesel could go to $10 in Ohio, and whether they planned to adjust their signs if it did. None responded.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
With no resolution of the war in sight, measures have been proposed to ease the pain at U.S. truck stops. Neither effectively addresses the underlying problem, Pachman said.
Ohio last week suspended the 47-cent-a-gallon diesel tax until Jan. 2. That means the state will lose about $725 million from gasoline and diesel taxes. 
It’s money that builds and maintains roads, bridges and waterways. The state will replace any funds local governments might lose, but that’s still public money that won’t be available for any other purpose.
That’s happening as more than 500,000 Ohioans are expected to lose health coverage due to changes at the federal level. More than 100,000 Ohioans had already lost federal food assistance by July as a consequence of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Pachman said the fuel tax holiday also warps the proper functioning of the marketplace. 
When goods become scarce, they get more expensive, and that motivates people to use less, find alternatives, or both. When the Ohio legislature artificially made diesel 47 cents cheaper, it short-circuited part of that dynamic, Pachman said.
Partly due to its refining capacity, the U.S. is the largest diesel exporter in the world. Present circumstances make that a problem.
“The war screwed all that up,” Pachman said. “Not only do we not have enough for us, we’re also still exporting it.”
Some farm-state lawmakers are still pushing an export ban on diesel even after Trump said he wouldn’t support one. Pachman said such a ban is a lot more complicated than it might sound.
“On the surface it might sound like a good idea,” he said. “But it could make everything worse because it could create such a global shortage that in Europe it could shoot prices through the roof and create chaos and raise prices here because we’re all linked.”

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



There are reasons to believe that even without a ban, diesel won’t go to $10 a gallon in the Buckeye State. But one would be bitter medicine if it happens.
Escalating global debt — due partly to spiking energy costs — is creating volatility in the bond markets. And worries are growing that the entire economy is propped up by a tech bubble that’s about to burst.
If the economy tanks due to those dynamics, diesel probably won’t reach $10, Pachman said. But it isn’t something to look forward to.
“One reason I think it might not happen is you may destroy demand,” he said. “At a certain point in time, people may stop buying because it’s too expensive.”
He added, “But that’s not a reason to celebrate — if we go into another Great Recession.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawrence launches ‘Michigan First’ constituency services plan highlighting Barrett town hall woes
description: Democratic Party-aligned constituents in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District have made U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s lack of town halls during his time in Congress a centerpiece in the campaign against his reelection prospects in the 2026 cycle — and Democratic nominee Will Lawrence is capitalizing on those concerns with a constituency services plan described as[...]
text:
Democratic Congressional candidate and political organizer William Lawrence speaks at a campaign event in Brighton Mich. on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Democratic Party-aligned constituents in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District have made U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s lack of town halls during his time in Congress a centerpiece in the campaign against his reelection prospects in the 2026 cycle — and Democratic nominee Will Lawrence is capitalizing on those concerns with a constituency services plan described as “Michigan First.”
If elected, Lawrence’s five-point plan would emphasize quarterly, unscripted and in-person town halls with residents living in the district; in-person, mobile and virtual office hours; faster response times from his prospective congressional office; and a dedicated liaison for veterans and senior concerns.
Lawrence would also endeavor to create close partnerships with community organizations as part of the plan.
“In my time as a community organizer and now as a candidate, I’ve met countless Michiganders who feel their elected officials care more about corporate donors and monied interests than working people like them,” Lawrence said in a statement. “I know that being an elected official is about more than just casting votes in Washington. It means being a constant presence in our community and looking out for our neighbors.”
Grassroots organizers delivered more than 1,800 petition signatures to the Lansing, Mich., office of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, on March 21, 2025, calling on the first-term member of Congress to hold an in-person town hall. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Lawrence, in the policy rollout announcement, said that he and other Democrats, as well as constituents of all political stripes, feel that Barrett (R-Charlotte) has failed that test.
“In response, Barrett set up a virtual town hall that was plagued with technical difficulties and left the needs of constituents unmet. Multiple residents told local news they could not sign into the event and never received confirmation,” Lawrence said. “One of our neighbors told the news that the community thinks Barrett is ‘invisible.’ The Congressman has made accessing him nearly impossible during his time in office. This is a pattern we’ve seen time and time again: politicians breaking their oath to the people they serve, shutting out the very people who elected them, and only listening to corporate donors and DC insiders. That is exactly why people have lost faith in government.”
Lawrence said his plan will “work to rebuild trust, from the bottom up.”
The Democratic nominee said that in addition to hosting in-district quarterly town halls, he would also make his office open for drop-in meetings with staff and hands-on support. Lawrence said that would include taking his office on the road at local libraries, community centers and public spaces. Those office hours would also be available for virtual appointments, Lawrence said. 
Barrett constituents deliver petition to Lansing office, demand in-person town hall meeting

Concerns from constituents would be prioritized, Lawrence added, with quick responses from his office without extended delays.
Lawrence also said he was committed to having staff assigned for veterans and seniors to expedite any issue those populations might bring to his congressional office if he wins in November. Staff in Michigan would also make regular visits to local veterans halls, senior centers and community gatherings, Lawrence noted in a breakdown of the plan.
The nominee further said that not every problem would be able to be solved by his congressional office alone, and that’s why the plan includes commitments to support community organizations specializing in housing, healthcare and public safety to connect people to vital services.
“My office will work closely with these organizations and ensure we are leveraging every possible resource for our neighbors,” Lawrence said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Election Integrity Unit finds ‘no violation’ with Ramaswamy’s campaign credit card reporting
description: Last month, the Ohio Election Integrity Unit under the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office issued a finding of “no violation” for Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign credit card reporting. Ohio state Sen. Kent Smith, D-Euclid, filed the complaint and is weighing an appeal. In June, the Ohio Capital Journal reported the Ramaswamy campaign had racked up nearly […]
text:
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. (Photo by WEWS)Last month, the Ohio Election Integrity Unit under the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office issued a finding of “no violation” for Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign credit card reporting. Ohio state Sen. Kent Smith, D-Euclid, filed the complaint and is weighing an appeal.
In June, the Ohio Capital Journal reported the Ramaswamy campaign had racked up nearly half a million dollars on a credit card without reporting details about the expenditures.
Since then, Ramaswamy’s team has revised its campaign finance reports. Expenditures previously obscured behind a single credit card reimbursement are now broken down into individual line items.
The secretary’s office has also fulfilled Ohio Capital Journal’s public records request for supporting documentation related to the campaign’s reports.
Ohio GOP candidate for governor has put $500,000 on the campaign credit card

Despite that, there’s room to quibble with the no violation finding, Smith said. The revised reports, for instance, list the payees and amounts, but instead of reporting those transactions on the date they occurred, each one is listed on the date the campaign paid its credit card statement.
Smith is also frustrated the secretary’s office still hasn’t responded to his request for correspondence with Ramaswamy’s campaign.
“There’s one of two conclusions,” Smith said. “(Ohio Secretary of State Frank) LaRose is letting the billionaire candidate skate on the rules, or LaRose and his office, to the best of their ability, are trying to make Ramaswamy come into compliance, and he’s completely ignoring it.”
“You would think that the correspondence between the offices would satisfy that curiosity,” he added.
The Capital Journal sought comment from the Secretary of State’s office and Vivek Ramaswmay’s campaign for this story. Neither responded.
The background
Starting with its very first campaign finance report in 2025, Ramaswamy’s campaign reported thousands of dollars in monthly campaign expenditures as a single credit card reimbursement.
Early on, those expenditures were relatively small. In April of 2025, for instance, the campaign reported about $6,700 on its American Express card.
A year later, the campaign reported more than $96,000 on its credit card in one month.
State law requires campaigns to report what they spent, who they paid, what they purchased and when it happened. By reporting its monthly credit card statement, the campaign was able to obscure nearly all those reporting requirements.
The Ohio Capital Journal first reported the campaign’s unusual credit card use in April ahead of the primary election and filed a public records request with the Secretary of State’s office.
The Ramaswamy campaign’s pattern of credit card use continued on its post-primary campaign finance report in June.
The Capital Journal again requested public records from the Secretary of State and asked a series of questions about his office’s efforts to correct the campaign’s reporting.
Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy holds big cash lead over Democrat Amy Acton after $25 million loan

In August, the secretary’s office responded to the records request with supporting documents for the campaign’s reports. The secretary never responded to the Ohio Capital Journal’s questions.
The complaint process
Following the Capital Journal’s story, Sen. Smith filed complaints with the Ohio Election Integrity Unit and requested correspondence between the secretary and the Ramaswamy campaign.
He described getting pushback to his complaint from the secretary’s office, explaining that Ramaswamy’s team was correcting its reports.
Smith didn’t retract his complaints, and on Sept. 16, the Ohio Election Integrity Unit sent him its findings of “no violation.”
Unlike the Ohio Elections Commission, which was a politically independent body charged with overseeing campaign finance law, the Ohio Election Integrity Unit operates within the secretary’s office.
The Ohio Elections Commission was eliminated by Republican state lawmakers and the new unit was put under the partisan elected office of the Secretary of State.
The letters emphasize the secretary’s role in the decision.
“After careful consideration of the evidence,” they read, “the Election Integrity Unit has recommended, and the Secretary of State adopted, the following finding(s).”
LaRose, who is running as the Republican candidate for state auditor this November, has endorsed Ramaswamy and appeared alongside him at several campaign events.
Catherine Turcer from the government watchdog group Common Cause Ohio, doesn’t see a problem with the unit’s finding.
The goal of campaign finance law, she explained, often isn’t to penalize committees who get their filings wrong — it’s to get them to fix the problem.
“It makes sense for the Secretary of State’s office to alert them as soon as possible,” Turcer said, “and to try to get the information as quickly as possible, so that voters actually have information when they can use it.”
Under the previous system, she said, audits or commission decisions could come a year or more after the fact. Turcer also has no immediate issue with the secretary’s role in the decision-making process.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I always appreciate when it’s honest,” she said. “It makes it very clear that at the end of the day, the secretary of state is deciding — that the unit made a recommendation, the secretary of state is making a decision.”
“What is a problem,” she added, “is that it’s not clear that the person who complained can actually appeal this to the commission.”
When lawmakers nixed the Ohio Election Commission they replaced it with a new five member Ohio Election Integrity Commission. The secretary chooses the commission chair, and majority and minority leaders in the General Assembly each get one nominee.
While the secretary’s election integrity unit investigates, and the secretary decides on fines or referrals to county prosecutors, the new commission has the final say if a complainant appeals.
The letter Smith received makes no mention of an appeal. Instead, it advises that “no further action is needed from you” and includes contact information if he has questions.
“If it’s not clear that, hey, the next step is you could go to the commission with an appeal, well that’s a problem,” Turcer said.
Appeal coming?
For Smith, the gaps in Ramaswamy’s campaign finance reports are less concerning than what those gaps might suggest.
“Has my campaign lost receipts over 25 years? Oh God, yes,” Smith said. “Has everybody lost receipts? Of course. Should any candidate be prosecuted for lost receipts? No.”
“But again,” he continued, “when the problem gets egregiously worse, that says to me the problem was never corrected. And that is either a failure of the Secretary of State’s office to tell the Ramaswamy campaign, no, you can’t do this, or the Ramaswamy campaign has been told and they’re ignoring it.”
Smith says he’s still “considering every additional option” but has yet to formally appeal the secretary’s decision.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: 2026 midterms could be the end of Pennsylvania’s split legislature, with far-reaching impacts
description: Of course, nationally the wind is at the back of Democrats. Commentators are contemplating the possibility of a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania for the first time since 1993.
text:
The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission marker outside the Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg on June 24, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
While many people are paying attention to how the 2026 midterm elections might change the balance of power in Washington, D.C., it is also a potentially pivotal election here in Pennsylvania.
Gov. Josh Shapiro is up for reelection, running against Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Who wins that race will certainly shape the state’s policy agenda for the next two years.
In the General Assembly, which is currently split – Republicans control the Senate and Democrats control the House – both chambers are also up for grabs. Democrats have been slowly eroding the Republicans’ hold over the Senate. In the House, Democrats have a three-seat majority, but Republicans could flip it.
Of course, nationally the wind is at the back of Democrats. Commentators are contemplating the possibility of a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania for the first time since 1993.
I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics. I think voters should understand not just the positions of the individual candidates on the ballot, but what the legislative priorities will be for either party if they gain control of the General Assembly.
Gov. Josh Shapiro delivers his fourth budget address Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026, during a joint session of the Pennsylvania General Assembly. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
 If Democrats control the legislature 

For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities should they keep the House and win the Senate, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate.
1. Election reform
Election reform has been a perennial priority in the commonwealth since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election. Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.
Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties to use ballot drop boxes, maintaining no-excuse mail-in voting, setting clear rules for ballot curing, instituting precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allowing independents to vote in open primary elections.
2. Marijuana
Gov. Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House even passed a legalization bill in 2025. Democrats have said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they can take the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization will remain to be worked out, even if Democrats have full control.
Democrats and Republican supporters of legalization disagree as to whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores, similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.
Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the War on Drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things like expungements of past convictions, license set-asides for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues. Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details.
3. Same-sex marriage
Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent.
Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up if they win a trifecta. They may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult, constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights.
4. Data centers and AI
The House has passed several measures to regulate AI and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs, water use, local government authority and implementing the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan. These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda.
5. Affordability
Given that this election is shaping up to be heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability, both parties have the issue on their agendas but will approach it differently.
The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.
Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it had been also passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage.
A sign opposing a data center project proposed for East Whiteland Township in Chester County on Saturday, May 9, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
 If Republicans control the General Assembly

We can turn to the current Republican-controlled Senate for insight into what will be on the party’s agenda if it resumes full control of the Assembly in 2027.
1. Election reform
Republicans have also been pushing for election law reform since 2020. In contrast to Democrats, their agenda has included repealing no-excuse absentee balloting, banning the use of ballot drop boxes and instituting stronger voter identification requirements.
2. Data centers and AI
Senate Republicans have also been active in proposing and passing AI- and data center-related legislation. A bill banning “nudification” apps, which use AI to remove the clothing from people in pictures and replace them with fake nude images, passed the Senate unanimously in late September.
There has also been bipartisan support for a Republican-proposed ban on the use of nondisclosure agreements in data center development. Republicans in the Senate also proposed designating all of Pennsylvania a Commonwealth Opportunity Zone for AI, which would fast-track data center permits and create a regulatory framework in collaboration with the industry.
While Republican AI legislation is likely to be more enabling of the emergent industry than regulating, Republicans are also concerned about privacy, transparency and costs to their constituents.
Gas prices at Shell station along Old Brodhead Road in Monaca, Beaver County May 7, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
3. Energy
Among the costs of data center development are higher energy and water prices. Republicans have already been making energy development a priority, repealing Pennsylvania’s participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative and pushing the governor on his promise of an “all of the above” energy strategy.
The stark promise of higher electric prices and poorer grid reliability due to projected data center development in a 2026 Public Utility Commission report is likely to add fuel to Republicans’ push for energy development.
4. Affordability
The affordability plan released by House Republicans in March 2026 points to the types of measures the party will pursue if it takes control of the Assembly. A cornerstone is the reduction of taxes, including lowering the personal income tax rate, a temporary elimination of energy and telecommunications taxes, and suspending the state gas tax, which is $0.576 per gallon for gasoline, $0.741 for diesel. Pennsylvania’s gasoline tax is the fifth-highest and the diesel tax is the third-highest in the United States.
A full plan with 10 bills is to be released in coming weeks, but will also include changes to zoning and construction rules to enable faster housing construction.
 

Daniel J. Mallinson is an associate professor of Public Policy and Administration, at Penn State.

title: Ohio reading scores rise. Is the science of reading working?
description: This story was originally published by The 74. Ohio students’ reading scores rose slightly last school year, the first the science of reading was mandated, but it’s too soon to say whether the phonics-based lessons are making a difference. About 63 percent of Ohio third graders — the grade educators have long considered the most […]
text:
Ohio’s third grade reading proficiency rate has bounced around since the state passed laws requiring schools to use the science of reading in 2023. (Ohio Department of Education and Workforce)This story was originally published by The 74.
Ohio students’ reading scores rose slightly last school year, the first the science of reading was mandated, but it’s too soon to say whether the phonics-based lessons are making a difference.
About 63 percent of Ohio third graders — the grade educators have long considered the most crucial for mastering reading — scored as proficient on spring 2026 state tests, up two percentage points from 61 percent in 2025.
Statewide reading proficiency also rose for all grades combined, as did proficiency for groups of students who often struggle.
That increase is cause for optimism for science of reading supporters, who cheered the progress as the state released spring 2026 test results this week. But the evidence isn’t clear yet that Ohio’s adoption of the science of reading in 2023 has students on a consistent path upward.
Third grade proficiency is still below pre-pandemic levels. It’s also below the 65 percent proficiency third graders had just two years ago in 2024 when the science of reading was being phased in. This year’s 63 percent proficiency is right in the middle of the 2024 and 2025 results.

Large changes in test scores could take a few years to show up, reading experts nationally have told The 74 since the science of reading has caught on in most states, particularly with schools needing to replace books, help teachers learn new ways to teach and then have the lessons start helping students.
Other factors could be holding scores back, including teachers not embracing the science of reading fully and still using old methods as well as Ohio’s decision to drop its hotly-contested requirement that students score well in reading to advance to fourth grade.
“It’s too early to tell in my view,” said Aaron Churchhill, Ohio research director of the Fordham Institute, a nonprofit education advocacy group that backs the science of reading. “We need to keep at it and give it a few years.”
Ohio Excels, a partnership of Ohio’s chambers of commerce, called the reading gains “encouraging” and said they suggest the science of reading is starting to take hold.
“At the same time, proficiency rates remain much too low, with nearly four in 10 students not proficient in reading,” said Ohio Excels President Lisa Gray. “We cannot be satisfied when so many students are still falling short of the skills they need to succeed.”
Ohio’s adoption of the science of reading in 2023 is a source of pride for two-term Gov. Mike DeWine, who leaves office at the end of this year. That year, Ohio became one of the earliest states to ban “cueing” — having young students figure out what a word is through context or pictures — in favor of more direct, phonics-based instruction.
The state also required all teachers to take online training in the science of reading; and for all schools to use only state-approved science of reading textbooks, workbooks and online lessons.
Though many schools had already started using science of reading methods before the law and many made the shift quickly, others moved more slowly. The 2025-26 year was the first all schools had to use it.
After third grade reading scores dropped in 2024-25, state officials and science of reading backers said last fall that spring 2026 test scores would be “pivotal.”
Backers of the change to the science of reading had several points to crow about in test results released this week. In addition to the third grade proficiency increase, the reading proficiency rate for all grades combined rose nearly two percentage points as well, to 62 percent.
And every demographic group the state measures — such as racial groups, disabled students and low-income students — also had improved reading proficiency from last year. Leading the way were Hispanic and Black students with gains of 3.5 and 3.4 percentage points and economically-disadvantaged students with a 2.7 percent gain.
“When you look at this year’s state report cards and see what has been done in a relatively short amount of time, it is a tremendous accomplishment,” DeWine said in a press release announcing the scores.
Schools that were early adopters of the science of reading also suggest that persistence in using the science of reading, and other training and ongoing coaching of teachers, can bring results.
The Elyria school district 30 miles west of Cleveland had stagnant reading results and even a decline in 2025 scores, despite receiving an award from DeWine for its science of reading efforts. But district leaders and teachers told The 74 last fall they were poised for gains in 2026.
They were right: Third grade reading proficiency in that district’s five elementary schools jumped from about 45% in 2025 to about 52% in 2026.
The district was delighted with the gains, but also cautioned keeping them going will take constant work.
“We have talked about things taking time and just what a long term process it is to implement anything, and lots of different factors we have, whether it’s staff turnover or different knowledge levels of our teachers and things like that,” said Courtney Griffiths, associate superintendent of academic services. “Yes, it’s very nice to see those results. It doesn’t mean that we back off on anything that we’re doing or we feel like it’s mission accomplished.”
Literacy specialist Andrea McKenzie said early diagnostic tests of those third graders as they started as fourth graders this school year show the improvements are persisting.
“I think it’s real,” McKenzie said. “We’re not seeing a setback… It’s really sticking in fourth grade right now too.”
There are still reasons to be unsure if the science of reading shift is bringing sustainable results, along with the third grade proficiency rate still lagging behind 2024. Multiple reasons could account for gains, including drops in chronic absenteeism over time and students having had more time to catch up from missing school because of the pandemic.
And the science of reading isn’t achieving one of its most important goals — helping the worst students read better by giving them more explicit directions on the sounds letters make and how to decode words into something they can understand.
More third graders are scoring as “limited,” the state’s lowest rating, an equivalent to an F, than before the state passed the science of reading — 21% this year, compared to 20.9% in 2025 and 19.1% in 2023.
The inability to help the students that read the worst bothers Fordham, which wants Ohio to bring back the “Third Grade Reading Guarantee” the legislature passed in 2012 requiring mandatory retention of third graders who can’t score well in reading.
Churchill said that the percentage of students scoring as limited had dropped under that law in the years before the pandemic — falling from 27% in 2016 to 14% in 2019.
“(It) pushed schools to help struggling readers —now it’s gone,” Churchill said. “The science of reading holds great promise for students, but it needs to be paired with the accountability that a retention mandate brings.”

title: What does it really cost Ohio households to lose power for a day?
description: A couple months ago, I was spending time at a friend’s family cabin in Hocking County. When we awoke in the morning, the lights would not switch on. We got a call from his mother: “Don’t open the refrigerator!” When the power goes out, people lose more than electricity. We were lucky: we were on […]
text:
An electricity meter. (Photo by Dave Cummings/States Newsroom)A couple months ago, I was spending time at a friend’s family cabin in Hocking County. When we awoke in the morning, the lights would not switch on. We got a call from his mother:
“Don’t open the refrigerator!”
When the power goes out, people lose more than electricity. We were lucky: we were on vacation with yesterday’s barbecue in the fridge. Often, people lose power and that means they can’t make it to work, they lose their week’s groceries, lose air conditioning during a heatwave, or have essential medicine go bad overnight.
When a customer pays her electricity bill, she is not only purchasing power. She is also purchasing reliable access to power. And she is making decisions based on that: what to buy, how to spend her time, trusting that when she plugs an appliance in and she flips a switch, she will have power.
Power companies don’t always have to live up to this, though. They often have to make decisions between grid reliability, service maintenance, and other priorities. And often, it is cheaper to leave customers with the costs of intermittent power outages.
Last month, a bipartisan group of 18 Ohio House members introduced a bill to change this.
Ohio House Bill 1014 would require utilities to provide electric bill credits to customers after sufficiently long outages at their homes. 
After a 16-hour outage under normal conditions, a household would receive a credit of the greater of either $50 or their monthly bill plus additional credits for additional days, plus reimbursement for lost food and medicine. Businesses would be reimbursed with a less generous formula. 
The bill also stipulates that utilities will not be able to recover those payments through higher rates to customers.
Essentially, the bill puts a price on grid reliability.
This payment is larger than some estimates of household willingness to pay to avoid outages.
According to analysis done by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, residential customers have an average willingness to pay of $57 to avoid a 24-hour blackout. The average monthly electricity bill in Ohio was $135 in 2024 and is likely higher now.
But this isn’t just about compensating households in the case of a power outage. It’s also about preventing power outages in the first place. 
If utility decision makers are mulling over whether to make grid improvements or invest in other changes, this could be a tool for encouraging prevention of power loss, which could lead to a more reliable grid overall.
Having a compensation rate at this level could also help improve equity of power outages. 
The way the compensation scheme is designed, it makes the timeline for eligibility shorter for smaller blackouts. Restoring service to isolated or difficult-to-support customers can be expensive, while much of the cost of leaving them without power falls on those customers. Under this bill, these costs would show up in a utility’s bottom line.
Excessive fees could backfire, however. If the fee level is set too high, it could give incentives for utilities to spend more preventing outages than customers value, or divert resources from other grid investments. 
Putting a price on outages, though, would give utilities a reason to account for costs that currently fall largely on customers.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms, Jackson face each other for first, and likely only, time in Georgia governor’s race
description: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night over healthcare, crime, data centers and election security in what will likely be the only opportunity for voters to see the two candidates for governor side by side.  The town hall-style debate, organized by Atlanta News First and Atlanta-based Gray Media, is the only […]
text:
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, and Republican Rick Jackson participated in a town hall-style debate Tuesday at the Atlanta News First studio. Pool photo via Atlanta News First/WANFDemocrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night over healthcare, crime, data centers and election security in what will likely be the only opportunity for voters to see the two candidates for governor side by side. 
The town hall-style debate, organized by Atlanta News First and Atlanta-based Gray Media, is the only forum where both candidates were expected to face each other. Bottoms challenged Jackson to more debates, but the Republican only agreed to the one meeting. 
But because of the town hall format, Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, and Jackson, a healthcare executive, weren’t allowed to address each other and could only respond to questions from Georgia voters who were undecided before the debate. That didn’t stop either candidate from issuing attacks in their responses, though. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bottoms introduced herself in the town hall as an advocate for Georgians.
“While my opponent is running to enrich himself and be Trump’s favorite governor, I want to be yours, Georgia,” Bottoms said.
Jackson pointed to his personal background growing up in public housing and foster care, something he does often on the campaign trail and in TV ads, before becoming a billionaire.
“I know what it means to struggle. I know what it means to get a second chance, and I’m running for governor to make sure every Georgian has that same opportunity,” Jackson said.
Healthcare, data center and election security were hot issues
The debate did become contentious at times. Bottoms repeated her push to expand Medicaid while accusing Jackson of profiting from the current system through his healthcare companies.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, participates in a town hall-style debate Tuesday at the Atlanta News First studio. Pool photo via Atlanta News First/WANF
“My opponent has made money off of this broken healthcare system. He has a staffing company that lures staff away from hospitals. It has sent many hospitals into closure because the personnel costs have skyrocketed,” Bottoms said to an undecided voter who said he did not have healthcare coverage.
Jackson was previously against Medicaid expansion but announced last month that he would pursue “intelligent” Medicaid expansion. He said Tuesday night that he would expand Medicaid without losing “$4.5 billion dollars that we’re currently getting for the state,” but he was unclear how Georgia would lose that funding, and a spokesperson for his campaign didn’t immediately respond to a follow-up question seeking clarification. Jackson quickly shifted to his other proposals to make healthcare more affordable, such as cracking down on insurance practices that deny or delay care and negotiating with pharmaceutical companies to bring the cost of prescription down.
“What we need to focus on – not only expanding Medicaid; that doesn’t solve the cost – we need to come up with solutions that actually reduce the cost of healthcare, and that’s what I’m going to do, or I’m not going to run again,” Jackson responded.
Republican Rick Jackson participates in a town hall-style debate Tuesday at the Atlanta News First studio. Pool photo via Atlanta News First/WANF
Jackson also repeatedly attacked Bottoms on her record as mayor of Atlanta, pointing to inflation and public safety in Atlanta during the pandemic.
“This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work or go to the gas store. There’s no way this should happen as a governor,” he said to a voter who asked how the candidates plan to make living more affordable.
But Bottoms pointed to her plan to provide tax relief, such as eliminating income tax for teachers and cutting taxes associated with car insurance. She also said she wants to allow local governments to have the option to suspend or eliminate sales tax on groceries.
“The average consumer or household has two cars. That would be $140 per year in savings, and also through the homeowners insurance tax that’s currently passed on to consumers, also at around 2.25%. I want to make sure that that is going back into the pockets of consumers,” she said.
Jackson offered his own tax cut pledge, saying that he has “committed to cut the income tax in half the first term, or (he) won’t run again.”
The candidates also sparred over the growth of data centers in Georgia, which has become a defining issue of the race. Bottoms is calling for a statewide pause while pointing to Jackson’s investment in a data center in Texas.  
“If he is an investor in data centers, if he builds data centers, he cannot be trusted on this, but I want a pause on all new construction until we create a path forward that best serves all of Georgia,” Bottoms said.
Jackson pushed back, saying that Bottoms approved multiple data centers in Atlanta while giving them a tax break. But Bottoms said that the only data center she approved as mayor was one at Georgia Tech that “was not a hyperscale data center (and) it was not in the middle of a residential community.”
Debate over data center growth in Georgia heats up race for governor

On the issue of automated license plate readers, Bottoms said that she would support a moratorium on new devices being installed while policies are tightened up. Jackson disagreed with halting new installations, saying it would cause crime to go up, but both candidates agreed that there should be restrictions on their use and that their use can be helpful for law enforcement.
When asked about how they would help Georgians who lost their jobs because of federal funding cuts, Bottoms took the opportunity to tie Jackson to the Trump administration, saying that she is “not running to be his favorite governor.” The Trump-endorsed Jackson, who compared himself often to Trump during the primary and who said repeatedly that he would be Trump’s “favorite governor,” has aligned himself more recently with Gov. Brian Kemp.
“I don’t owe anybody anything. Nobody’s ever told me what to do. My number one priority is Georgians. It’s you, and I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done,” Jackson said.
The candidates also tangled over election security. Bottoms accused Jackson of previously suggesting that the Georgia National Guard would be deployed to monitor Georgia’s midterm election, referring to audio obtained by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. But Jackson denied that happened.
“I’ve never suggested that we have the National Guard to come in on this election. Period. That’s just a complete falsehood,” he said.
But Bottoms maintained her stance.
“He said that the National Guard would be called in. You all can pull the tape on that,” she said.
Political observers, partisans offer initial reactions to the debate
Josh McKoon. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Both political parties praised their candidates following the debate, with Georgia Republican Party Chair Josh McKoon saying that “the contrast on the television tonight could not have been more clear.
“In Rick Jackson, Georgia will have a governor who is a problem-solver; a governor who actually has a plan and has the guts to own it,” McKoon said.
Democratic Party of Georgia Chair Charlie Bailey declared a victory for Bottoms, saying that she “dominated the debate stage by outlining her positive vision for Georgia.”
Charlie Bailey. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“Keisha held Slick Rick accountable for his long record of rigging the system against Georgians, forcing data centers on communities and pushing the president’s disastrous policies, no matter how much it hurts our families,” Bailey said.
The race between Bottoms and Jackson is virtually tied according to recent polling. Jackson has pulled slightly ahead in a recent poll, but they remain within the margin of error.
University of Georgia political communications professor David Clementson called the debate “relatively tame” compared to the negative advertising and rhetoric that is coming from both campaigns. But he said there were instances of them calling each other liars, which he said “can have the effect of further entrenching partisan viewers.”
Clementson also pointed to their nonverbal communication. He said that Jackson may have connected better with viewers as he looked directly at the camera and used more gestures, but that he also “appeared somewhat jittery and tripped up on his words more.” He said that Bottoms looked away from the camera more and “seemed less animated.”
“Their nice verbal answers were brought down by lousy nonverbals. They both offered empathic answers, sympathetic message content. But with cold delivery, monotonous tone, stiff body language,” he said.
Zachary Peskowitz, a political scientist at Emory University, said that debates don’t usually determine the results of the election. But he said gaffs and mistakes can happen, which could “definitely could be consequential” given the tight margins seen in polling.
“I think you know it could certainly affect some of those voters, and given how close it is, that could be a big part of the story for what happens in November,” Peskowitz said in an interview before the debate.
Early voting for the November election starts Oct. 13.

title: Pickens, Stegner pledge policy changes in Idaho gubernatorial candidate forum
description: Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner pledged during a gubernatorial candidate forum Tuesday night to undo many of incumbent Gov. Brad Little’s policies if they are elected Nov. 3.  Little, a Republican, did not attend the gubernatorial candidate forum, which was sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Idaho and other nonprofit organizations[...]
text:
Idaho gubernatorial candidates Terri Pickens, center, and John Stegner, right, participate in a candidate forum Oct. 6, 2026, at South Junior High in Boise. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner pledged during a gubernatorial candidate forum Tuesday night to undo many of incumbent Gov. Brad Little’s policies if they are elected Nov. 3. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Little, a Republican, did not attend the gubernatorial candidate forum, which was sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Idaho and other nonprofit organizations. 
Officials with the League of Women Voters of Idaho said Little did not respond to their invitation to participate in the forum, though they left an empty chair open for him on the stage at South Junior High School in Boise in case he decided to participate. 
Pickens, a trial attorney and small business owner, said her first action if she is elected governor will be to present a state budget that restores the tax revenue and many of the budget cuts that Little and the Idaho Legislature cut during the 2026 legislative session. 
“It’s going to restore mental health funding,” Pickens said. “It’s going to restore Medicaid expansion. It’s going to restore full funding for public education, and that is critically important because the one thing I’ve heard across this state is Idaho families and the Idaho working class are hurting.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Stegner, a retired Idaho Supreme Court justice, said his first action in office as governor would be to repeal the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit, which Little signed into law as House Bill 93 in 2025. 
“I think my first executive action would be to try to bring litigation against the vouchers as best I could,” Stegener said. 
“I continue to believe that it’s unconstitutional that we are funding private school students and homeschool students when we’re not adequately funding our own public school students,” Stegner added. 
John Stegner is running for governor in 2026. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner)
Little, Pickens, Stegner, Libertarian Paul Sand, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and independent write-in candidate named Jacob Burnett are all running for governor in the Nov. 3 general election. 
Tuesday’s candidate forum lasted 90 minutes and featured a question-and-answer format, with some questions submitted by audience members in attendance and others written by event organizers.
“This is not a debate, it is a forum, an exchange of ideas, related to the issues confronting our beautiful state of Idaho,” League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid said at the beginning of Tuesday’s forum. 
 Pickens, Stegner agree on many policy and budget issues

Pickens and Stegner largely agreed on several of the issues, from supporting Proposition 1, the ballot initiative seeking to restore the right to an abortion in Idaho, to unanimously opposing both of the Idaho Legislature’s proposed constitutional amendments, House Joint Resolution 4 and House Joint Resolution 6. 
House Joint Resolution 4 would amend the Idaho Constitution so that only the Idaho Legislature could legalize marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs. In doing so, House Joint Resolution 4 would also remove Idaho voters’ rights to run a ballot initiative to legalize marijuana, like voters in Oregon, Washington and several of Idaho’s neighboring states have done. 
House Joint Resolution 6 would amend the Idaho Constitution to make English the official language of Idaho.  
Pickens and Stegner said they will vote for Proposition 1 and implement it if it passes and will  vote against HJR 4 and HJR 6.
 Idaho gubernatorial candidate forum ends with shared history between two candidates 

During her closing remarks, during the final seconds of the forum, Pickens said a case she argued in front of the Idaho Supreme Court while Stegner was a judge had a huge impact on her. 
Terri Pickens is running for governor in the 2026. (Photo courtesy of Terri Pickens)
“In 2021 … in a published Idaho Supreme Court decision, I was called ‘brazen’ for making a legal argument that the judge disagreed with,” Pickens said, leading some members of the audience to audibly react. “Brazen.”
“That decision had such an impact on my career that I wanted to give up the practice of law, and the person that wrote that position is sitting right next to me,” Pickens said, referring to Stegner. 
Stegner had already completed his closing remarks when Pickens made the revelation, and did not get to respond. 
 



 Where do Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner stand on issues?

Immigration enforcement and 287(g) agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:
Pickens: “I don’t think we need to be providing them with state resources for Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” Pickens said, saying as an attorney she is not convinced that ICE abides by the rules of due process. “For me, there won’t be any 287(g) agreements for us to be having these discussions as to how we can support and train these folks.”
Stegner: “I would not have entered into the agreement with ICE had I been the governor,” Stegner said. “I think ICE has demonstrated in very real ways that it is a rogue agency right now. They are wearing masks, they are shooting individuals in the streets – murdering individuals in the streets – and not wearing body cameras. Unless or until they are reigned in, I would not have entered into the 287(g) agreement.”
Where do you stand on the U.S. Department of Energy’s proposed Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus in Idaho and the requirement that states that host a nuclear campus accept out-of-state shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste?
Pickens: “The (Idaho National Laboratory) is a great neighbor to Idaho,” Pickens said. “They employ thousands of Idahoans, and they have been a great neighbor. They’ve been a great neighbor because of the 1995 agreement, basically negotiated by (former Gov.) Cecil Andrus and signed by (former Gov.) Phil Batt. That 1995 agreement is the guardrail of our protection of the East Snake Plain Aquifer.”
“As soon as I am elected governor, the memorandum of understanding (to host a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus in Idaho) will no longer be,” Pickens added. 
Stegner: “It’s 66 million pounds (of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste) that would be taken by Idaho (If Idaho takes one-third of the country’s spent fuel),” Stengner said. “Another thing they’re not really saying is that it might be more. You might get one-third, you might get two-thirds. You might get all of it if you don’t stop it at its inception. So I’m not a fan of the agreement.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The Census Bureau is shutting out local data experts
description: Census Bureau staff are now banned from meeting with external partners to discuss Census 2030 preparations.
text:
Every ten years, the federal decennial census data informs two things that shape Connecticut’s future: how many seats we get in Congress and how many dollars go to our schools, roads and transit systems, and healthcare programs. 
 Right now, the U.S. Census Bureau is quietly rewriting the rules for how people will be counted in 2030. These rules will change 250 years of precedent and will disadvantage Connecticut. But instead of working with state leaders to get it right, federal officials have done something alarming:   They have stopped talking to us altogether  . 
 Our elected leaders in Hartford and Washington cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. If Gov. Ned Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, Attorney General William Tong, and our congressional delegation do not step in immediately to demand answers and transparency, Connecticut risks getting shortchanged for an entire decade. 
 Here is what is happening behind closed doors. On Sept. 10, the Census Bureau published a   proposal in the Federal Register   that could fundamentally alter “residence criteria” for the 2030 count. These rules decide where snowbirds, college students, incarcerated individuals, military members, and immigrants are counted.  
 Shift a definition by a few words, and you shift millions of dollars from Connecticut towns to other states. 
 When data experts from state data centers across the country gathered at Census headquarters in Maryland recently to ask standard technical questions, they were read a pre-scripted statement: Bureau staff were forbidden from answering any questions about the new residency rules. 
 Days later, regional meetings between Census officials and Northeast state representatives were abruptly canceled, with local experts told that Census Bureau staff are now banned from meeting with external partners to discuss Census 2030 preparations. 
 This is not routine administrative noise. It is a directive to silence the local partners tasked with making sure every Connecticut resident is counted once, only once, and in the right place. It is a deliberate assault on government transparency. 
 This is where our state’s political leadership must step in. Federal bureaucrats should not be allowed to freeze out state partners while altering the rules that dictate Connecticut’s budget and representation. 
We need our congressional delegation, Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy, alongside U.S. Reps. Rosa DeLauro, Jim Himes, John Larson, Joe Courtney, and Jahana Hayes, to demand that the Census Bureau lift this communication ban and answer basic questions about the 2030 count.
 We also need immediate state action. Gov. Lamont and Attorney General Tong should join other states in filing formal objections before the federal public comment window closes on Oct. 13. 
We also need residents, advocacy organizations, and community-based organizations to respond to the FRN and voice your concerns. (See ctdata.org for instructions on how to do it.)
 The math is simple: if Connecticut is undercounted because the rules were changed without local input, our state budget takes the hit. Local taxpayers end up footing the bill for health care, special education, housing programs, and roads that federal funding should have covered. 
 Our leaders regularly promise to fight for Connecticut’s fair share. Right now, that fight is not in a high-profile courtroom; it is in the fine print of federal notices, and time is running out. 
 The comment deadline is Oct. 13. That leaves our politicians with less than three weeks to make noise, demand accountability, and submit formal objections.   The Census Bureau may have chosen to go silent, but Connecticut’s elected officials cannot. 
It is time for our leaders to step up and defend our state’s count before the window closes.
Sarah Eisele-Dyrli is Assistant Director and Michelle Riordan-Nold is Executive Director at the CTData Collaborative, Connecticut’s lead organization in the Census State Data Center network.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll: Voters oppose redistricting ballot question when presented ‘meat of the political outcome’
description: A proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that would change the way Maryland draws congressional districts faces stiff voter opposition, a new poll shows. It's the latest sign of trouble for the ballot question backed by Democratic leaders
text:
A new poll finds that a ballot question related to eliminated state standards in congressional redistricting is confusing is hard for voters to understand even after the Supreme Court of Maryland rewrote the original question after finding it was misleading. (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that would change the way congressional districts are drawn in Maryland faces stiff voter opposition, a new poll shows.
The poll, released Tuesday by the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland Baltimore County, found 53% of those surveyed said they would vote against ballot Question 3, a proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that would lift many of the restrictions on how congressional districts are drawn in the state. Another 25% supported it and 19% were undecided.
Mileah Kromer, director of the poll, said she’s not convinced the ballot question won’t pass, despite the numbers. There is time for supporters to mount a full-court campaign for the question, which is backed by Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic party leaders.
“So I think what our numbers really show — when you look at them in comparison with the full ballot language — is that there is certainly a disconnect between when people are presented with the full ballot language, understanding what that ballot language means and what it’s asking, and the real political ramifications of it,” Kromer said.
Opposition to the question is driven by 74% of Republicans and 59% of unaffiliated voters. They were joined by 42% of Democrats.
The poll comes with four weeks left in the campaign season. Nearly 600,000 voters have already received mail-in ballots. Early voting begins Oct. 22 and ends on Oct. 29.
The survey is based on interviews with 776 Marylanders who said they were likely to vote. The survey conducted from Sept. 22 to 27 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5%.
Poll: Moore sits with a comfortable 2-1 margin over Republican challenger Cox

The survey released Wednesday is the second of three to be released by the university. A poll released Tuesday showed Moore with a 27 percentage point lead over Republican challenger Dan Cox in the race for governor. Part three is expected on Thursday and will examine the governor’s job approval numbers and voter sentiments on artificial intelligence and data centers.
The UMBC findings on Question 3 follow two polls released last month on the topic.
One, by Protect Maryland Votes, a group that opposes the ballot question, found just 28% support while another 4-in-10 opposed it. The poll was conducted by two pollsters — one that works for Democrats and another that works with Republicans.
A second, released days later by Question 3 supporters Fight Back Maryland found 40% support for the question. That poll was conducted by a pollster who works with Democratic candidates.
Both the Protect Maryland Votes and Fight Back Maryland surveys were based on asking voters to make a decision after hearing the question as it appears on the ballot. That question was rewritten by the Supreme Court of Maryland after a majority of judges found the original question was deficient.
The Fight Back Maryland poll found that many voters said they did not understand the ballot question.
Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, said there are studies “that at least appear to suggest that when voters don’t understand the question, they are more likely to vote against it or leave it blank. That’s why, to me, it really does raise the question of who’s done a better job of educating people as to what this means.”
Kromer, in her poll, took a different approach from the two other polls that surveyed likely voters after presenting them with the exact, but complicated, language that will appear on ballots. The UMBC poll presented voters with a “plain language” description of the outcome of passing the question.
“I wanted to ask something with the plain language — what the meat of the political outcome was going to be, and that is that it opens up the ability for Maryland Democrats to draw congressional district lines without constraints in the Maryland Constitution,” she said.
“At the end of the day, people recognize that drawing district lines to favor one party over another, the average voter doesn’t like that concept,” Kromer said. “I think that is when you put it in plain language, that is what you’re seeing.”
Kromer also asked voters about their feelings on the political outcome of passage of the question.
A majority, 57%, said they thought drawing districts to benefit one party over another shouldn’t be done or was the wrong thing to do. Slightly more than a third of voters said it was either “sometimes necessary” or “we should do it.”
Overall, 83% of voters surveyed identified partisan redistricting as a problem facing American democracy.
“There’s not a lot of people supporting at this point,” Kromer said.
Other concerns included:

The influence of money in politics — 88%
Declining trust in government — 88%
Misinformation on social media — 85%
The feeling that ordinary people have no say — 79%
Low voter turnout or participation — 67%
Potential for political violence — 62%
