name: Mississippi Today
title: Trial is delayed again for two former Capitol Police officers accused in shootings
description: Capitol Police at the state capitol Tuesday night, April 25, 2023.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The trial of two former Capitol Police officers accused of unlawfully opening fire on a car and shooting a passenger in the head has been delayed for at least the ninth time, Hinds County Courthouse staff said.
The white former officers, Michael Lamar Rhinewalt and Jeffery Walker Jr., each face up to two decades in prison if convicted of aggravated assault charges. They are accused of shooting at two Black people in August 2022 as they were driving through downtown Jackson, leaving passenger Sherita Harris with “permanent neurological and facial injuries,” according to a civil lawsuit she filed against them.
The officers were set to stand trial on the criminal charge Monday, but the courtroom stood locked and empty, and court records did not immediately give a reason for the delay.
Hinds County Circuit Judge Adrienne Wooten pushed the trial back at the request of the officers’ attorneys, according to De’Vone Cole, a Hinds County sheriff’s officer at the court. But at the time of the trial, the circuit clerk’s office said it had no record of the request or rescheduling. A new date had not been set for the trial in court records.
Former Capitol Police officer Michael Rhinewalt answers questions from Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson in his manslaughter trial Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in the 2022 fatal shooting of Jaylen Lewis. Credit: Jerry Mitchell/Mississippi Today
Wooten’s deputy court administrator, Tandra Thompson, initially told Mississippi Today that she wasn’t aware of anyone on staff who knew why the trial didn’t start — even though the court was responsible for setting its date under the rules issued by the state Supreme Court. Thompson then said scheduling information was confidential to the defense and prosecution, even though it is public record under state law.
The defense and prosecutors did not answer Mississippi Today’s calls to confirm why the trial did not happen. 
This will be the second criminal trial tied to a record year of shootings by Capitol Police, both against Rhinewalt. In the first trial, which was rescheduled six times before ending last week, he avoided a manslaughter conviction in the shooting and killing of a 25-year-old Black man, Jaylen Lewis, during a traffic stop a month after Harris’ shooting. 
Former Capitol Police officer Steven Frederick Jr., top, reacts on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, at the Hinds County Courthouse after a jury acquitted him of manslaughter for shooting at a Black man, Jaylen Lewis, in a 2022 traffic stop. Beside him are defense attorneys Boty McDonald, center, and Merrida Coxwell Jr. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
After the majority-Black jury deadlocked on whether Rhinewalt was guilty, the state attorney general’s office dropped the case against him, writing, “the benefit of the doubt goes to our law enforcement officers.” The jury in that trial acquitted another former Capitol Police officer, Steven Frederick Jr. 
Cole said Rhinewalt’s second trial would begin in December at the earliest — nearly two years after it was initially scheduled. Court records show the trial has been delayed at least eight other times since it was first scheduled for March 2025.
Trial previously delayed after ‘conflict of interest’
One delay came after Judge Wooten barred the attorney general’s office from prosecuting the case because of an unprecedented “conflict of interest which gravely undermines the integrity and fairness of the proceedings.”
While the attorney general’s office was pursuing a criminal case against the two officers for opening fire on Harris, it was also defending the pair against a $3 million federal lawsuit Harris filed for shooting her and violating her constitutional rights. 
“This inconsistency is not merely theoretical — it strikes at the heart of fairness and undermines the core ethical obligations owed to clients and to the judicial process,” Wooten wrote in May 2025.
Jaylen Lewis Credit: Courtesy of Arkela Lewis
The attorney general’s office argued that separate divisions were handling the cases and that there was no evidence of “improper influence” on the grand jury that indicted both officers in the shooting. But ultimately, the office of Lin Carter, the district attorney of Forrest and Perry counties, took over prosecution of the aggravated assault case.
Until the criminal case comes to an end, Harris’ lawsuit is on hold.
The case marks a rare criminal proceeding against officers for shooting at civilians. In the entire history of Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s Office reviewing these cases, the office said it has found four incidents not “justified,” including in the killing of Lewis.
In that case, the attorney general’s office still handled the prosecution against Rhinewalt, despite defending him in Harris’ lawsuit.
Why was Harris shot? Officers’ and victims’ versions sharply diverge
The former officers — who were with Capitol Police’s crime suppression Flex Unit — and the victims have given starkly different accounts of the moments that ended with a bullet in Harris’ skull.
In her lawsuit, Harris alleged that the shooting occurred after the friend she was riding with, Sinatra Jordan, “complied” with the officers’ commands to pull over while the two were waiting for a traffic light to turn green. But “shortly” after, the lawsuit stated, Rhinewalt opened fire on Jordan’s silver Nissan Rogue as it tried to drive away to “escape the constant firing of bullets.”
Rhinewalt was believed to be the officer who shot Harris in the head, according to her lawsuit, leaving her with permanent memory loss, a partially paralyzed face and damaged sight and hearing. Walker did not shoot at the car but did admit to opening fire on Jordan once he exited the vehicle, the lawsuit stated.
After the shooting, Jordan survived and was arrested. A month later, Walker admitted in a hearing that both officers opened fire on the car, but only after Jordan ran a red light, fled a traffic stop, led them on a car chase throughout downtown and then shot at them first, sparking a gun battle that ended in a residential neighborhood.



Walker testified that no bullets struck the officers’ patrol car and no gun was found in Jordan’s vehicle. He also said he saw objects being thrown from the car during the chase, but none of these items were found.
Jordan ultimately pleaded guilty to fleeing police. He was also accused of shooting at the officers and charged with aggravated assault, but that charge was dropped last year.
The shooting was one of four by Capitol Police officers in 2022 — more than any other law-enforcement agency in the state. The spike came as the Legislature expanded the force’s reach throughout Jackson in an effort to address record homicide rates.
Harris wrote in her lawsuit that the shooting left her not only with physical injuries but also “severe emotional distress” and “mental trauma,” including panic attacks, anxiety and depression. She argued that “any reasonable police officer” in Rhinewalt and Walker’s position would have known they had a “duty” to “prevent harm” to her, as an “innocent bystander.”
In response to Harris’ lawsuit, both officers denied wrongdoing, arguing that they acted “at all times” in line with “proper policing procedures” and “in good faith.”
Case continues legal trouble for both former officers
Harris’ shooting adds to the legal trouble both former officers face from their service with Capitol Police.
During last month’s manslaughter trial, Rhinewalt admitted he shot Lewis in the head during a traffic stop, killing him. He told jurors the killing was in self defense, as he believed Lewis was trying to run officers over with his Jeep Grand Cherokee.
But the passenger riding with Lewis, Selena Hayes, testified the pair didn’t know they were being stopped by officers, who were not in typical uniforms and were driving unmarked police cars. As a result, she said, Lewis was trying to drive around the officers, rather than to run them over.
Selena Hayes, a passenger with Jaylen Lewis, testifies Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Hinds County Circuit Court, responding to questions from Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson. Credit: Jerry Mitchell/Mississippi Today
While Rhinewalt avoided another trial after the attorney general’s office dropped the manslaughter case against him, he still faces a $75,000 wrongful death suit from Lewis’ family in federal court. He denied the lawsuit’s allegations.
In December, Walker pleaded guilty in federal court to violating a man’s civil rights during a traffic stop just weeks before Harris’ shooting by slamming the man’s head into his car and kicking him in the head and face while he was handcuffed and under control. But he filed a motion to withdraw his plea in August on the day he was scheduled to be sentenced — when he faced up to a decade in prison — because of “newly discovered evidence.”
His then-attorney, Arthur Calderón, wrote that the week before Walker was set to be sentenced, the former officer received pictures from Capitol Police that “contradict” federal prosecutors’ claims that he injured the man, who was identified in court records as E.S. As a result, Walker asserted his innocence and requested a trial.
In the closing arguments of the manslaughter trial of two former Capitol Police officers at the Hinds County Courthouse on Sept. 28, 2026, prosecutors presented photos showing that defendant Michael Rhinewalt was dressed in plain clothes and a tactical vest when he was accused of shooting and killing Jaylen Lewis during a 2022 traffic stop. The state attorney general’s office dropped the case against Rhinewalt after jurors could not reach a verdict. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
Federal prosecutors say the photos, which were “reportedly” provided by Rhinewalt, show E.S. handcuffed and on the ground with a swollen and discolored face. The prosecution argued Walker was still guilty, as the defense “fails entirely” to explain how the photos — which were not new evidence — demonstrated his innocence. 
U.S. District Judge Henry T. Wingate has not ruled on whether the photos are enough evidence to overcome the former officer’s guilty plea and warrant a trial.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina’s governor celebrates affordable housing project that could be model for state
description: For longtime residents of Southeast Raleigh, a lack of affordable housing and the threat of gentrification are growing concerns. But on Tuesday morning, residents were all smiles as Governor Josh Stein visited a newly constructed home built in partnership with Southeast Raleigh Promise and the City of Raleigh. Yvette Holmes, CEO of Southeast Raleigh Promise,[...]
text:
Gov. Josh Stein poses with members of the nonprofit Southeast Raleigh Promise on Oct. 6, 2026 as they celebrate the completion of one of 25 new affordable rental homes for downtown Raleigh. The entire project will be completed by the summer of 2027. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) For longtime residents of Southeast Raleigh, a lack of affordable housing and the threat of gentrification are growing concerns. But on Tuesday morning, residents were all smiles as Governor Josh Stein visited a newly constructed home built in partnership with Southeast Raleigh Promise and the City of Raleigh.
Yvette Holmes, CEO of Southeast Raleigh Promise, said the three-bedroom house just blocks from Shaw University is the first of the 25 new affordable rental homes developed through the nonprofit’s Promise of Home initiative.
“Three homes down, 22 more to go as we’re building in phases,” said Holmes. “We expect to complete this entire project by summer of 2027.”
The homes are being built across nine city-owned lots, with the Raleigh City Council leveraging public land and approving $3.3 million in gap financing.
The properties are designed to fit within existing neighborhoods, making full use of smaller parcels of land. On the remaining eight parcels, there will now be two homes, and in some cases an accessory dwelling unit will be added to the property.
“This is what missing middle housing and making room for current and future residents looks like,” said Holmes. “It is a good example of how policies that allow for greater density can result in real tangible housing solutions for growing communities.”
Governor Josh Stein said Promise 25 represents a powerful demonstration of housing done right.
“Stable housing provides a foundation for economic opportunity, but too many people of varying incomes are struggling to find the housing that they can afford,” said Stein.
Gov. Josh Stein signs executive order to tackle housing affordability

Recent studies have projected that through 2029 North Carolina is expected to be 750,000 homes short, with that housing gap growing larger as more people move to the state. In Wake County, the supply gap is anticipated to be 110,000 units.
“That’s why we must build more homes of all types to meet different families’ needs,” Stein said.
In August, the governor signed Senate Bill 445 into law, cutting red tape to help produce more houses and apartments, including accessory dwelling units (ADUs), across most of the state. Stein also signed legislation to increase flexibility for homebuilders by eliminating mandatory minimum parking spaces.
The single-family, three-bedroom home on Person Street will rent for $1,650 a month, serving households at 80% of area median income and below. That’s about $600 less than a nearby two-bedroom apartment in downtown Raleigh. High performance heating and cooling units and new insulation will also translate into savings for the new residents.
Emila Sutton, director of housing and community development for the City of Raleigh, said in communities where more housing types are available, more housing production happens, affordability increases and ultimately rents are lower.
“We also know that in those areas, the child poverty rates are in fact lower,’ said Sutton. “The importance of housing production cannot be stated enough.”
Approximately half of all renters in North Carolina spend more than 30% of their incomes on housing. North Carolina had the ninth-highest rental price increases in the country from 2024-25.





 

Gov. Josh Stein congratulates Yvette Holmes, CEO of Southeast Raleigh Promise, on the completion of the newest affordable home in downtown Raleigh. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) 







 

Governor Josh Stein said Promise 25 represents a powerful demonstration of housing done right. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)







 

Yvette Holmes, CEO of Southeast Raleigh Promise, said the three bedroom house just blocks from Shaw University was the first of the 25 new affordable rental homes developed through the nonprofit's Promise of Home initiative. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)







 

Emila Sutton, director of housing and community development for the City of Raleigh (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) 







 

Yvette Holmes, CEO of Southeast Raleigh Promise, and Gov. Josh Stein tour the new affordable rental home in Southeast Raleigh. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)







 

New appliances and a bright, modern kitchen are a signature feature of the Promise 25 affordable rental unit. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) 






 Stein: Constitutional amendments threaten progress 
Stein said state and local funding is essential to addressing the state’s shortage of affordable housing. That money could be harder to come by if voters approve the Republican-backed income tax cap amendment and property tax limit amendment on the ballot in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
“I think these constitutional amendments are really con jobs,” Stein said. “What it will end up doing is putting more burden on working people.”
Stein took aim at the income tax cap amendment, which would establish a maximum income tax rate of 3.5%. He said the cap would prevent the state from raising taxes even if the nation spun into a recession.
“Now that’s off the table,” Stein said. “They are protecting millionaires with this amendment.”
If the amendment passes, Stein said the only recourse for covering a budget gap would be to increase the sales tax.
“So every person here who was saying that we care about affordability, people who really can’t afford to pay anymore, they’re gonna be the ones who have to make it up, and not putting that extra burden on those who are doing exceptionally well,” Stein said.
Critics say NC’s property tax amendment could do more harm than good

The property tax limit amendment is a response to what GOP lawmakers say are excessively high property taxes. Seniors in particular are cost-burdened by high taxes, they say.
The amendment would give lawmakers the authority to set a limit on local governments’ ability to increase property taxes. But it doesn’t specify how or how much the limit would be. Legislators would work out the details and set the levy limit later, likely in 2027.
Local government officials, progressive advocacy groups and Democratic lawmakers who oppose the measure say state lawmakers already have the authority to do this without a constitutional amendment. They say limiting property taxes could leave local governments short of the funds they need to provide vital services.
“I think these amendments are very wrongheaded,” Stein said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: AG’s cold case unit cracks 1985 Newport murder case
description: DNA evidence collected by a special investigative unit within the Rhode Island Office of Attorney General has led to an arrest in the 1985 murder of a 22-year-old Jamestown woman in Newport. It’s a case with special meaning for Attorney General Peter Neronha, who grew up in Jamestown and knew the victim, Hillary Hellewell. “We […]
text:
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, right, speaks to reporters about the arrest of William “Billy” Morton in the 1985 murder of Hillary Hellewell at his Providence office on Oct. 6, 2026. At left is Newport Police Chief Ryan Duffy. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)DNA evidence collected by a special investigative unit within the Rhode Island Office of Attorney General has led to an arrest in the 1985 murder of a 22-year-old Jamestown woman in Newport.
It’s a case with special meaning for Attorney General Peter Neronha, who grew up in Jamestown and knew the victim, Hillary Hellewell.
“We knew each other at least from kindergarten,” Neronha told reporters at a press conference inside his Providence office Tuesday afternoon. “She was just an amazing and fun, energetic person.”
The press conference came hours after William “Billy” Morton, 61, of Smithfield, was ordered held without bail at the Adult Correctional Institutions in Cranston at his arraignment in Newport District Court on a first degree murder charge in Hellewell’s death. Judge J. Terence Houlihan referred Morton to the public defender’s office for representation.
Morton entered no plea as is customary because the felony case must be transferred to the Superior Court. Morton’s next appearance in Newport District Court is scheduled for Oct. 20.
According to an affidavit filed with the court, the body of Hellewell was found lying on the sidewalk on Anthony Street, a side street off Bowery Street near the Newport Public Library, at around 4:15 a.m. on May 19, 1985. She was wearing a sweater, white painter’s pants and socks but no shoes, and a heavily soiled blue T-shirt was found near her head. An autopsy determined that she had been strangled and raped. 
Police said Hellewell had left a party at a Friendship Street address with a male friend she had offered to walk home because he was heavily intoxicated, according to an affidavit filed in court Tuesday. Police said the man made it home but was unable to give an accurate or detailed account.
An FBI report cited in an affidavit submitted to the District Court indicates that spermatozoa was found on Hellewell’s white pants and the blue T-shirt.
“In 1985, Rhode Island did not have DNA testing capability,” reads the affidavit by Senior Cold Case Investigator Michael Naylor, who joined the AG’s cold case unit last February after retiring from Newport police as a detective captain.
In 2004, Newport police submitted biological evidence from Hellewell’s clothing to the Department of Health for testing, which found enough DNA in a sperm sample from the back seam of her pants to produce a full profile. Police collected DNA samples from several men who were close to Hellewell, including the man she escorted to his home along with others who had attended the same party on the last night she was last seen. All the men were excluded as matches to the DNA found on the pants, the affidavit said.
The DNA was uploaded to the national DNA database in 2004, but there was no match, the affidavit said.
The Newport County courthouse in Washington Square in Newport, where William Morton was arraigned on a first-degree murder charge on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)
In 2023, cold case investigators sent evidence from the case to a third-party private laboratory that specializes in reexamining DNA. The testing eventually pointed them toward a family whose DNA appeared to be related to genetic material found on the blue T-shirt and inside Hellewell’s pants. Investigators conducted surveillance and collected abandoned trash that identified two men who were only partial DNA matches. But their Y chromosome results showed they were closely related to the suspect they were searching for. During an Aug. 13, 2026, interview with another relative, investigators learned the two men had a paternal half-brother who was Morton, the affidavit stated.
Investigators began surveilling Morton in August, following him to his job in North Attleboro, Massachusetts, and later to his Smithfield home. On Aug. 21, they followed him and his fiancée to a Heart tribute concert at Woonsocket’s Stadium Theatre and entered behind them. They watched Morton drink from a water bottle and leave it on the empty seat next to him.
After Morton and his fiancée left the theater early, investigators seized the bottle he had left behind in the seat and turned it over to the Department of Health for analysis. A Sept. 24 report found that the DNA profile from the water bottle is consistent with the DNA results from the evidence on Hellewell’s pants.
At the time of her death, Hellewell’s father was chairman of the English Department at North Kingstown High School and the chairman of the Jamestown Zoning Board. Her mother was a first-grade teacher at Jamestown School.
“I know her sisters, and I knew her parents,” Neronha said. “I have my memories, but it’s really about her today and her family.”
No members of the family attended the press conference. Neronha said Hellewell’s family has requested privacy at “what for them is an extraordinarily difficult time.”
Neronha would not answer any questions about whether Morton attended the party where Hellewell was last seen or was interviewed by police in 1985. Her body was found about 1.2 miles away from the location of the party.
“Mr. Morton is entitled to the presumption of innocence,” Neronha said. “He has a right to trial and I want to be really clear about that.”
In February 1987, Morton was found guilty after a jury trial of sexual assault on a 15-year-old girl in a Newport park in June 1985. The park was only a block away from the location where Hellewell’s body was found the previous month, according to news reports.
In that case, the teen said Morton had choked her unconscious after she accepted his offer to walk her home and that she regained consciousness as he was attacking her. She had only known him for about a week, according to the affidavit. At the time of his arrest in that case, Morton told police he was living in Pawtucket but had lived in Newport until two years earlier, the affidavit said. 



Quotation







We knew each other at least from kindergarten. She was just an amazing and fun, energetic person.


– Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, who grew up with Hillary Hellewell



The AG’s cold case unit is comprised of five full-time staffers — two investigators, two prosecutors and a paralegal — and now had an annual budget of $762,308. 
The unit formed in 2024 after Neronha successfully persuaded state lawmakers to dedicate $155,000 in initial funding to dig into a backlog of over 150 unsolved crimes. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Prosecuting Cold Cases Using DNA Program awarded the AG’s office a $500,000 federal grant in September 2024.
Neronha’s office announced it had cleared its first two cases, unrelated homicides that occurred in 1984 and 2007 in North Providence, in October 2025. The victims were both women and the suspects identified in each case were dead. Then an arrest in a 2005 sexual assault case from Hopkinton was announced in August, with a bail hearing for the suspect in that case now scheduled for Oct. 14.
At the Aug. 19 press conference announcing the arrest in the Hopkinton case, Neronha expressed hope that the unit would solve “a few more” cases before he departs office in January.
Neronha is not seeking reelection because he is term-limited.
Democrat Kim Ahern and Republican Alan Gordon are running against each other to be the state’s next attorney general.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska auditor criticizes $23K ‘waste of money’ for resigning retirement director
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska State Auditor Mike Foley raised concerns over the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement System reportedly paying its departing executive director over $23,000 in salary and benefits for roughly five weeks of unperformed work. In a Tuesday press release, Foley criticized the retirement board’s response to executive director Thomas Pfeifle’s[...]
text:
Nebraska Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley testifies before the Legislature's Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. Feb. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska State Auditor Mike Foley raised concerns over the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement System reportedly paying its departing executive director over $23,000 in salary and benefits for roughly five weeks of unperformed work.
In a Tuesday press release, Foley criticized the retirement board’s response to executive director Thomas Pfeifle’s resignation. Pfeifle submitted his resignation letter on Sept. 21, as Foley put it, “walking off the job and ceasing all further interactions with the agency that day — presumably returning to his home state of Colorado.”
Though he apparently left the agency in September, turning in his state cellphone, keys, laptop and identification — according to Foley’s report — Pfeifle’s resignation letter stated his last day with the agency was Oct. 31. Foley surmised this to be “an apparently successful attempt to collect another five weeks of full pay and benefits.”
“Halloween is still weeks away, but it appears the former executive director has ghosted NPERS,” Foley wrote. “The agency got the trick, he got the treat, Nebraskans have been left holding the bag, and I am not amused.”
Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board members (from left to right): Jake Curtiss, Patrick Bourne, Gerald Clausen and Janis Elliott at a special board meeting Sept. 30, 2026. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)
The retirement board accepted Pfeifle’s resignation at a special meeting Sept. 30, as first reported in the Examiner. At the time, questions were raised about him being paid despite his absence, but those questions went unanswered. Tag Herbek, NPERS legal counsel, said the board couldn’t comment on employee personnel details.
Herbek did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Foley’s report.
Pfeifle started working for NPERS in mid-June, earning an annual salary of $205,000, equivalent to about $98 per hour, according to Foley. His employment ended an 18-month stretch of NPERS being without an executive director after the resignation of John Murante in December 2024.
Foley noted that NPERS paid a national executive search firm, Ford Webb Associates, just under $50,000 to identify Pfeifle as a candidate for the job. Foley said if the cost had been $50,000 or more, the contract would have required a competitive bid under state law.
“In addition to rewarding the former executive director to the tune of some $23,000 for not even bothering to show up for work during the last five weeks of his less-than-stellar stint, NPERS paid slightly under $50,000 to find that ‘prize hire,’ who lasted under four months with the agency,” Foley wrote.
Foley said his staff attempted to reach out to Pfeifle with no response.
Foley called it “mind-boggling” that the retirement board would be “so cavalier about spending the public money entrusted to it” given the state’s ongoing budget woes. Gov. Jim Pillen has asked all agencies to cut at least 5% from its annual spending as a result of continued projected state budget deficits.
State Budget Director Neil Sullivan did not return a request for comment.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Per Pfeifle’s employment agreement, Foley said, the board holds authority to end his payment immediately, citing this language: “This offer of employment is not a guaranty of employment for a specified period of time. Your employment may be terminated at any time by the PERB in accordance with state law.”
“It should go without saying,” Foley wrote, “that if you don’t show up for work, you lose your job. You certainly don’t get paid for playing hooky for five weeks.”
The decision to continue paying Pfeifle raised questions about the legality of his payment plan, but also had Foley questioning whether board members were following state law. Foley said the law requires board members to “act as fiduciaries when administering the retirement systems,” and tasks members “specifically with defraying only reasonable expenses.”
“How does paying an absentee official his full – albeit plainly unearned – salary comport with this explicit statutory mandate?” Foley wrote.
Foley recommended the board reconsider their decision to continue paying Pfeifle through Oct. 31. Herbek told the Examiner that the board planned to address further leadership succession issues at its next regular meeting Oct. 19.
“It’s not too late to fix this debacle and I will be watching to see if they do,” Foley wrote.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH announces $1M program to boost spotty EV charger network
description: About $1 million in grant funding for electric vehicle charging stations is up for grabs in a program the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services and Department of Business and Economic Affairs said is intended to boost the state’s economy and air quality. Locations with significance for New Hampshire’s tourism industry will be the focus […]
text:
On Tuesday, Oct. 6, state officials announced a $1 million program to boost electric vehicle charger construction across New Hampshire, where chargers are less ubiquitous than in neighboring states. A charging station was shaded by maples in a parking lot in Concord that afternoon. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)About $1 million in grant funding for electric vehicle charging stations is up for grabs in a program the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services and Department of Business and Economic Affairs said is intended to boost the state’s economy and air quality.
Locations with significance for New Hampshire’s tourism industry will be the focus of the program, according to a press release issued by the two departments on Tuesday afternoon.
“Installing public charging infrastructure at travel- and tourism-oriented locations will support the local economies of New Hampshire communities and enable EV-driving residents and visitors to feel confident in exploring all that New Hampshire has to offer,” Business and Economic Affairs Commissioner Lucy Lange said in the release.
Compared to its New England neighbors, New Hampshire has relatively few electric vehicle charging stations available to drivers. A February 2025 report from Clean Energy New Hampshire and SKI NH found that the state had the lowest total number of charging ports in the region at 597. That was about 5% of the total electric vehicle charging infrastructure in New England at the time, according to the report, which said the dearth was costing New Hampshire millions in tourism dollars.
The program will cover up to 80% of costs, up to a maximum of $10,000 per charging port, for projects to install level two, or L2, EV chargers.
The departments have also set a cap of $100,000 for projects within any one municipality, and designated a minimum of $40,000 for each of New Hampshire’s nine Regional Planning Commission zones, which together cover the whole state. That requirement is intended to ensure that the chargers funded by the program are spread across the state, according to the release.
Projects undertaken by public, private and nonprofit entities are all eligible to be funded through the program, according to the release.
Funds for what the departments have named the “Recharge the Adventure New Hampshire Grant Program” will come from the New Hampshire Volkswagen Environmental Mitigation Trust, which holds settlement funds from a Clean Air Act lawsuit against Volkswagen AG and affiliates. (New Hampshire is currently facing its own Clean Air Act lawsuit over the Legislature’s 2025 move to end vehicle inspections and emissions testing.) 
A portion of the Volkswagen funds are designated for electric vehicle infrastructure, and this is not the first grant cycle using Volkswagen trust dollars: Another program in 2021 funded about $4 million in EV charging projects on state- and local-government-owned property, according to the Clean Energy New Hampshire and SKI NH report.
“Investing in the buildout of public charging infrastructure in the Granite State not only benefits our EV-driving residents and visitors but also results in positive impacts to both New Hampshire’s economy and air quality,” Department of Environmental Services Commissioner Robert Scott said in the release.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Iran war, Trump tariffs and Michigan data centers dominate questions during Barrett-Lawrence debate
description: The reelection campaign of Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett and the progressive insurgency of Democratic nominee Will Lawerence came to a head Tuesday during the first — and potentially last — debate featuring the candidates in this year’s contest for Michigan 7th Congressional District. Hosted by WKAR-TV, the debate between Barrett (R-Charlotte) and Lawrenc[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, left, and Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence, right, face off in their first head-to-head debate at WKAR's studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)The reelection campaign of Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett and the progressive insurgency of Democratic nominee Will Lawerence came to a head Tuesday during the first — and potentially last — debate featuring the candidates in this year’s contest for Michigan 7th Congressional District.
Hosted by WKAR-TV, the debate between Barrett (R-Charlotte) and Lawrence, of Lansing, was at times heated as the candidates navigated questions including those on the Iran war and its associated costs, tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump and other price hikes, immigration and artificial intelligence data centers.
Although there was plenty of contrast between the two on some of the most pressing issues, there were a few moments of agreement over the most controversial topics in the forum, such as whether law enforcement should have unfettered access to surveillance data from Flock cameras, and on ending the Iran war in swift fashion.
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, left, and Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence, right, face off in their first head-to-head debate at WKAR’s studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)
Barrett told viewers that he ran for Congress because he wasn’t happy with the status quo in America, and that he was dedicated and committed to solving those issues during his first term in the U.S. House. Barrett said he would continue that work in Washington, D.C. if voters reelect him.
Lawrence said that he, too, was sick of the status quo on Capitol Hill and the work of the Republican-controlled Congress, which Lawrence said was dictated by President Donald Trump. Lawrence said voters could count on him to fight against the proliferation of the Iran war, and against the spread of hyperscale data centers, because he said he was not beholden to Democratic Party bosses or corporate influence.
Those comments set the stage for the back-and-forth in the battle for the 7th Congressional District, and for the kind of decision the district’s voters will have to make on Nov. 3.
Here’s how Barrett and Lawrence responded to each question, with answers edited for clarity and length.
 
How would you tackle high gas prices, mortgage rates and other increases in costs on goods?
Barrett said that gas prices were an important financial health measure because they ripple throughout the entire economy. He acknowledged that the current increase in gas prices was due to the continuation of the Iran war, which Barrett said he voted against.
“I saw friends that came home struggling after the effects of war, and I’m the only one on this stage who’s actually been to war to see these devastating effects” Barrett, a combat veteran, said of his opposition to Trump continuing to wage the conflict without authorization from Congress. “I take that responsibility very seriously. … As we wind down the war in Iran, we all know that fuel costs will come down, and the rest of the economy will recover, as well.” 
Lawrence said Barrett was right about the war needing to end, but that he was wrong in the fact that his caucus’s haphazard support of Trump’s actions was to blame for much of it.
“On the first day of the war, I was out front opposing it, while he said that his president had earned the opportunity to start this disastrous war,” Lawrence said before turning to tariffs and Barrett’s support of Trump using the economic tool in ways that have been aggressive to trading partners and have damaged the economy with price increases.
“We’ve been impacted more than any state in the country, and whether you’re a worker, a business owner, an investor, or a consumer, you know that the business conditions have been so erratic because the president wakes up in the morning and he decides what the tariff rate ought to be based on his mood that morning,” Lawrence added.
Barrett, in response, said he has been consistently against Trump continuing to wage war without the approval of Congress and that he has been consistent in calling for legislative branch oversight.
Still, Lawrence said that Trump campaigned on ending expensive “forever wars,” but the nation, instead, is writing a new chapter for one “thanks to your president.”
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, speaks during the first debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence at WKAR’s studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)
Increases in health insurance premiums and deductibles have made health care less affordable. How would you rein those prices in for consumers?
For Lawrence, the undermining of the Affordable Care and Patient Protection Act impacted insurance prices most severely for people ages 50 to 65. He said that residents on the campaign trail have told him horror stories of their premiums going from $600 a month to $2,000.
Lawrence said he would champion a single-payer healthcare system that covers an individual throughout their lifetime.
Barrett accused Lawrence of just repackaging the progressive call for Medicare for All into his single-payer plan, and that it would amount to a $40 trillion expense for taxpayers and the nation.
“What I’ve done is actually push for reform within the health insurance industry, introduce the Care Over Profits Act, which affords health insurers to actually pay more in claims for the amount of premiums that they’re taking in, premiums are far too high today for families,” Barrett said, adding that he also paid nearly $20,000 in healthcare premiums and deductibles combined last year. “I’ve rejected contributions from the health insurance PACs, and I don’t support putting a government-run program for $40 trillion onto the books when we’re already struggling with so much financing.”
Lawrence responded by noting that the nation was already spending trillions of dollars on healthcare, and that under his plan, everyone would pay less “excepting the billionaires and the wealthiest in this country who are currently not paying their fair share.” He added that Barrett’s votes in Congress have cut more people off from the ACA and are now at risk of losing their Medicare coverage.
 
What guardrails would you put in place against unfettered surveillance of residents through equipment like Flock cameras?
On mass surveillance, Barrett said he supports “robust protections of individuals” and that is why he voted against the reauthorization of warrantless surveillance.
Barrett did say, however, that he supports tools for law enforcement to better do their jobs, even though he said he would continue to advocate against using federal funds for camera surveillance to balance the constitutional protections of citizens.
Lawrence said he was glad to see people fighting back against Flock cameras and other mass surveillance methods. 
“Don’t tread on us and don’t spy on us either,” Lawrence said. “It’s a violation of the 4th Amendment. I support law enforcement and I believe in an all of the above approach to public safety, that includes police and community violence intervention, and stronger mental health services so police don’t have to be answering mental health calls and can be focused on solving violent crime.”
Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence speaks during the first debate with U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, at WKAR’s studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)
How would you manage trade woes with Canada and the Trump administration’s posturing against the nation or other allies?
The United States strained diplomatic and trade relations with Canada has taken center stage in many aspects of the 2026 cycle in Michigan, whether it’s Trump’s tariffs on that nation or posturing over the Gordie Howe International Bridge crossing.
On Trump leveling tariffs against trading partners, particularly Canada, Lawrence said it appears to him and others as if Trump was just throwing darts at a board to decide who and which country he wants to pick a fight with.
“Tom Barrett has voted to allow the president to continue changing the tariff policy each day of the week based on his mood or Lord knows what else,” Lawrence said.
Barrett said he supports tariff policies that bring investment back to the U.S. after a historic hollowing out of the nation’s manufacturing base — much of which is located in Michigan. He also said that the nation has seen Canada and other supposed trading partners disregard the needs of the U.S.
“I’ve called for predictability in our trade,” Barrett said. 
Lawrence was quick to attack Barrett on his call for predictability.
“If Tom has been calling for common stability, he hasn’t been very effective at it because what we see from this president is chaos,” Lawrence said.
 
State law stripped away an element of local control on siting issues, and that includes decisions related to AI data centers. How would you ensure local communities can make their own decisions specifically related to data centers?
In terms of the state’s decision on local control, Barrett said it was the Democratic trifecta in Lansing that stripped away that control in the pursuit of a Michigan-based Green New Deal agenda, and that residents deserved the final say in those decisions. He said that he has introduced legislation that would prohibit federal agencies from overriding or influencing local control, as well as measures to prohibit non-disclosure agreements for those involved in the process.
“I’ve voted five times against that in 12 years,” Barrett said of this state legislative and congressional record.
With the question turning to Lawrence, the Democratic nominee said he was a nationally recognized leader in the fight against data centers, and that while he was out listening to residents’ concerns, Barrett gave $80 billion in tax breaks to corporations interested in building data centers.
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, left, and Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence, right, face off in their first head-to-head debate at WKAR’s studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)
America is stretched across supporting the Ukraine war effort, Israel’s own military actions and the front in Iran. How would you manage an end to those conflicts?
Lawrence has been against the waging of “endless wars” around the world, he said, as they have made the nation less safe and weaker over the last 25 years. He accused Barrett of supporting military aid to Israel, which Lawrence said was a factor in the U.S. decision to join their costly war with Iran.
Lawrence said firmly that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza, where he said it has waged war against the Palestinian people since 2023 following the deadly Oct. 7 terrorist attacks perpetrated by Hamas against Israeli civilians. He called on the U.S. to “bring our money home” and stop funding Israel.
Barrett said he has separated himself from Trump on Iran and reiterated his call to not allow Trump to continue the war without authorization from Congress or basic congressional oversight. 
“As I pointed out earlier, the War Powers Act delegates a limited amount of authority to the president for a specific period of time before Congress has to act to decide whether or not to continue that or not. That authorization has not happened,” Barrett said. “All the way back in May of this year, I was one of the very first Republicans to vote against the continuation of the war in Iran. Now, with that being said, we definitely have a national interest in preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons. If they obtain them, it would be a disaster and one that we should prevent from happening. That doesn’t mean that we are endorsing an endless war or a furtherance of the war that we are in right now.”
A lively back and forth occurred between Barrett and Lawrence in their rebuttals on the issue of Iran and Gaza, with Barrett accusing Lawrence of agreeing with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s comments that America deserved the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attack; and with Lawrence calling on Barrett to disavow comments by Trump that, in a continued war with Iran, both the nation could lose both Los Angeles and San Diego in an attack and still carry on.
Lawrence said Piker’s commentary was “despicable,” whereas Barrett went on record and said he didn’t agree with Trump’s wartime rhetoric on potential U.S. losses.
 
What is your position on border security and funding U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement?
Lawrence was adamant that border security and support for ICE were two different matters.
“We need a secure border. We need an orderly, efficient immigration court system, and we do need to remember the words on the Statue of Liberty, which call us to higher values and remind us that we should welcome immigrants because we are immigrants,” Lawrence said. “We can never forget what we saw on the streets of Minneapolis: American citizens being shot in the face and the back, families being separated from their children. That is what this president has brought. This is so un-American.”
Barrett said that he too believes that immigration policy should be fair, firm and humane. He said one of his proudest achievements in Congress was being part of a majority that secured the nation’s borders and, as a result, has seen smuggled fentanyl deaths decline because of that work.
He warned that if Lawrence was elected, those gains, particularly on curtailing fentanyl distribution, would be in vain.
Lawrence questioned Barrett on how he could view the events that occurred in Minneapolis in the later months of 2025 and early 2026 as fair or humane.
“Your president and your Congress have failed to deliver on your own stated immigration policy in order, and I think what you want is to punish people,” Lawrence said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Madison attorney Phil Buffington announces run for state auditor
description: Voters fill out their ballots at Briarwood Presbyterian Church on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, during Mississippi’s federal primary election in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Phil Buffington, a Madison attorney involved in conservative politics and chairman of the Mississippi Tort Claims Board, announced on Tuesday that he will run for state auditor next year in the Republican primary. 
Buffington, a partner at Balch and Bingham LLP, advises financial institutions throughout the country. He said in a news release that he plans to campaign on fraud prevention, regulatory accountability and stronger cybersecurity standards for state financial systems.
Phil Buffington Credit: Special to Mississippi Today
“I’m running for Mississippi state auditor because I believe the people of Mississippi deserve a person who wants to make sure your tax dollars are not wasted or stolen and a government that is transparent, accountable, and responsible with every taxpayer dollar,” Buffington said. 
Current Auditor Shad White has said he’s considering running for governor and not planning to seek reelection as auditor. 
Sen. Daniel Sparks, a Republican from Belmont, and former Rep. Nick Bain, a Republican from Corinth, have also said they’re running for auditor. No Democratic candidate has announced a run. Party primaries for statewide offices will take place in August 2027. 
Buffington graduated from the University of Mississippi and Mississippi College School of Law, now Mississippi Christian University School of Law. He serves on the Mississippi Republican Party State Executive Committee and the Madison County Republican Executive Committee.

Nick Bain (R)

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Researchers say they’re getting closer to answers on Great Salt Lake dust
description: Two Utah researchers shed light on their efforts to find answers on Great Salt Lake dust. So did a state official, though he called it a “future issue.”
text:
Bryce Bird, director of the Utah Division of Air Quality, speaks during a panel discussion on Great Salt Lake dust at Zions Bank in Salt Lake City on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (Courtesy of the Great Salt Lake Alliance/Alex Travous) As the Great Salt Lake plunges back toward a historic low, key questions about the dust kicking up from the dry lake bed and its effects on human health remain unanswered. 



This article is published through the Great Salt Lake Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative that partners news, education and media organizations to help inform people about the plight of the Great Salt Lake — and what can be done to make a difference before it is too late.


At a Monday forum focused on solutions for the dust, two researchers said they’re working toward providing more clarity. So did a state official, though he called it a “future issue.” 
At the University of Utah, dust scientists are trying to get a good picture of how much is blowing in from the lake in the first place, as opposed to other sources such as mining. 
Derek Mallia, a research assistant professor at the university, said he and his colleagues are working on modeling that will help them account for urban emissions and pinpoint which parts of the lake are sending up the most dust. They expect to share findings from a current project early next year, he told Utah News Dispatch. 
Then there are the questions of exactly what’s in the airborne dust, including the amounts of heavy metals like arsenic and lead, and whether they pose health risks to the 2.5 million people living along the Wasatch Front. It’s less clear when Utahns will get those answers. 
When it comes to arsenic, a carcinogen, “we know it’s in the sediment,” said Bryce Bird, director of the Utah Division of Air Quality. As for how much is lifting into the air and how far it’s traveling, the division has some early data shedding insight.  
“Our initial filters that we collected on high-wind days showed that it was basically below the detection level that our laboratory could detect,” Bird said at the Monday forum hosted by the Great Salt Lake Alliance. 
“We have other air pollution concerns that I think are more pressing to us, public health-wise, than the Great Salt Lake today,” Bird said at the event. “I think the Great Salt Lake is a future issue.” 
The shores of the Great Salt Lake near Syracuse, with Antelope Island in the background, are pictured on Tuesday, May 21, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
He noted that so far this year, the Salt Lake Valley has not exceeded the federal standard for coarse PM10 pollution, which is measured over a 24-hour window. 
“We’ve exceeded the ozone standard 19 times, and so probably the more pressing effort, or issue, for me as a regulator is focusing on ground-level ozone in our urban areas, is what is actually impacting public health today.” 
The division is working to stand up more dust monitors in northern Utah after a slow start on the project that frustrated academic researchers who called for better, more comprehensive monitoring. 
Most often, when lakes across the world dry up, “the result has been it’s become unlivable and people have moved away,” Bird said during the forum. “Of course, we don’t have that option here. We are planted here, our roots go deep, and we need to find ways to address it.”
Pierce Wratten, an environmental scientist with the Utah Department of Air Quality, swaps out the filters on an air quality monitoring station at Great Salt Lake State Park in Magna on Tuesday, April 14, 2026. Although not a part ofthe Utah Dust Observation and Research Network, the station is similar to those that are. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Bird said the division plans to release information collected by the devices on a rolling basis, but it will be hard to interpret until the state determines how much of the metals are safe to breathe in a short period of time. 
There are federal standards for concentrations in soil, water, and in the air for workers cutting marble and concrete, but not for dust storms. So Utah is coming up with its own guidelines, convening environmental and public health officials to review research and coordinate with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
Bird did not have an estimate Monday for when the state guidelines would be finalized. 
Other research is ongoing. 
David Parrott, assistant director of Westminster University’s Great Salt Lake Institute, said he’s working with researchers examining microbes and heavy metals, and the effects of both on lung cells growing in culture. 
He said the multitude of research on the lake is encouraging and noted many others in the state, including lawmakers, are working on solutions to save it ahead of the Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City – now eight years away. 
“I think it’s great, but we just need to not lose momentum and say, ‘well, you know, the Olympics is 2034. We’ve got time for the lake,’” Parrott said. “We need to do it now.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ‘Dead wrong’: Lamont says changes to Head Start would make life harder for families
description: The Trump administration's proposal allows larger class sizes, reduces degree requirements for some staff and mandates teaching in English.
text:
Charles Walters was initially skeptical about enrolling his daughter in a Head Start early education program. 
But within a month of joining the program, which serves low-income children up to age 5, his daughter’s fine motor and communication skills had “jumped exponentially,” he said. 
Walters was sold. His 3-year-old daughter, Lillian, has been at LULAC Head Start in New Haven for two years. The program serves about 329 children in East Haven and New Haven, according to its executive director.
“When she’s not in my presence, I want it to be like I’m still there,” Walters, 39, said during a Tuesday press conference at LULAC’s main office. “That same care is still given. That same protection is still given. That same love is still given.”
Walters, state officials and early childhood education providers gathered Tuesday to lambast the Trump administration’s planned overhaul of Head Start, the federal program that funds childcare centers like LULAC. 
The proposed rule would allow for larger class sizes, no longer require degrees for many staff and loosen federal requirements for serving children with disabilities. It would also require unhoused families to provide documentation of their homelessness, and it would mandate that education programs be taught in English. 
If the changes are approved, Head Start would follow state and local childcare standards, which some researchers have found to be less stringent than the program’s longtime requirements.
Charles Walters, father of a child at Heard Start, speaks during a press conference regarding federal decisions around Head Start at LULAC Head Start in New Haven on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
The U.S. Department of Health Human Services, which administers Head Start, also plans to reduce the cap on administrative overhead from 15% to 5% of total program costs. According to an August press release, the agency estimates the changes could save $2.2 billion and support as many as 236,000 additional Head Start slots nationwide.
Connecticut served 4,847 children and 46 pregnant women across 22 Head Start programs during the 2024-25 school year, according to a spokesperson for the Connecticut Office of Early Childhood, or OEC.
At Tuesday’s press conference, Gov. Ned Lamont and OEC Commissioner Elena Trueworthy called on HHS to withdraw the proposed rule. 
“They’re making life a lot more burdensome, bureaucratic, expensive and impossible for our working families,” Lamont said of the agency. “I think it’s dead wrong.”
In an emailed statement, an HHS spokesperson said the proposed rule “removes duplicative regulations and red tape that have driven up the cost of the program, decreased slots, and failed to improve outcomes for children.”
The spokesperson also noted that Head Start programs are welcome to maintain the performance standards previously required by the federal program.
“It is a shame that some elected leaders … do not trust Head Start directors, teachers, and parents to make wise decisions for the children they serve but instead believe Washington must tell all 1,600 Head Start centers across the U.S. exactly how they have to run their programs,” the spokesperson said.
Lamont stressed that Connecticut will continue to support affordable childcare through initiatives like its new Early Childhood Education Endowment, which boasts more than $700 million in funding.
Starting in July 2027, a state program funded by the endowment aims to provide free childcare to eligible families earning up to $100,000 each year and cap the childcare contribution at 7% of household income for eligible families earning more than $100,000.
“But I’m not letting the federal government off by saying we’ll just make up all the shortfall,” Lamont said.
Tuesday was the last day to submit comments on the proposed rule. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, in collaboration with other states, submitted a letter condemning the proposed changes. OEC Commissioner Trueworthy did, as well.
Trueworthy worked for Head Start for almost a decade at the start of her career, she said at the press conference. “I saw firsthand how Head Start and the Head Start model transforms lives of children, families, but also individuals such as myself,” she said.
Trueworthy condemned the proposed changes that would affect homeless families and children with disabilities, as well as the English-language instruction mandate and reduced administrative overhead. 
She noted that around 7.5% of Connecticut families enrolled in Head Start are homeless, and that about 18.5% of children in the state’s programs were diagnosed with a disability this year.
“By gutting these long-term protections, this compromises overall quality and puts children and families and providers at risk,” she said.
Marsha Guthrie, who oversees the Head Start programs at the Children’s Learnings Centers of Fairfield County, also spoke at the press conference Tuesday, where she emphasized the importance of Head Start’s performance standards. 
“Maintaining these standards is essential to ensuring that Head Start continues to provide the high quality, comprehensive services that Connecticut’s children and families deserve,” she said.
Karen Pascale, the director of Connecticut’s Head Start State Collaboration Office, described Head Start as an “essential part” of Connecticut’s early childhood resources. She cited the Head Start on Housing initiative, which provides some families enrolled in Head Start with state housing assistance.
Pascale started her career as an education disabilities coordinator at LULAC Head Start, she said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Rep. Jeff Crank refused to meet with constituents related to Epstein survivor, family says
description: Family members of one of the most prominent survivors to speak out about late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein denounced U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank after he declined to meet with them.   Sky and Amanda Roberts, brother and sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, live in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District. They said at a press conference Monday […]
text:
Sky and Amanda Roberts, brother and sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, speak at a press conference Monday alongside Jessica Killin, a Democrat challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank in the 2026 election. The Roberts, who live in the 5th District, said Crank repeatedly declined to meet with them to talk about releasing the Epstein files. (Photo courtesy of Jessica Killin's campaign)Family members of one of the most prominent survivors to speak out about late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein denounced U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank after he declined to meet with them.  
Sky and Amanda Roberts, brother and sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, live in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District. They said at a press conference Monday in support of Crank’s Democratic challenger Jessica Killin that Crank, a Colorado Springs Republican, repeatedly ignored their requests to discuss the Epstein files and policy reforms to support survivors of human trafficking and sexual abuse.
“Leadership does not mean doing the right thing only after the pressure becomes too much to ignore,” Amanda said. “Leadership means standing up to what is hard when it is inconvenient, when it carries political risk, and when survivors are still waiting to be heard.”
The press conference came a day after Killin’s campaign released an ad that featured the Roberts family talking about their experience with Crank’s office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Giuffre died by suicide in April 2025 in Australia, where she had been living for several years. Giuffre emerged as one of the most prominent victims after she challenged Epstein co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell and former British royal Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, alleging they participated in her trafficking and sexual abuse.
Amanda said Giuffre’s courage to speak about her experience “came at an enormous personal cost.” Survivors live with the results of elected leaders choosing to do nothing, Sky added. Their family’s advocacy seeks to protect future victims and hold perpetrators accountable. 
“When we ask Congressman Jeff Crank to stand with survivors, we are not asking for a favor,” Amanda said. “We are asking for representation. We were asking for leadership. We are asking him to listen to the people he was elected to serve.”
The family met with Crank’s district staff in September 2025, and all messages they sent after that received no answer, they said. Their request for Crank’s support came after they traveled to Washington, D.C., to push for the Epstein Files Transparency Act. They also told Crank’s office that they met with U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican, to thank her for signing a “discharge petition” to force a floor vote on the measure. 
After a year without a response, Amanda on Monday shared a screenshot that showed Dennis Hisey, Crank’s district director, laughed with a “ha ha” emoji at one of her messages from September 2025.
Amanda Roberts, sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, shows members of the media her text exchange with U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank’s district director Dennis Hisey at a press conference on Oct. 5 alongside Jessica Killin, a Democrat challenging Republican Crank in the 2026 election. The Roberts, who live in Crank’s district, said Crank repeatedly declined to meet with them to talk about releasing the Epstein files. (Photo courtesy of Jessica Killin’s campaign)
Crank did not sign discharge petitions earlier last year to force a floor vote, but he voted in November in support of the Epstein Files Transparency Act after President Donald Trump urged Congress to pass the measure. 
Trump had a well-documented relationship with Epstein. During his 2024 campaign he promised to release the Epstein files, but supporters of the president have criticized what they view as an incomplete process of releasing the documents under Trump. 
Killin said Crank “did not have the courage to do the right thing” until Trump gave Republicans the green light. 
“He knows he had multiple opportunities to release the files. That’s been made clear. There were multiple opportunities and multiple votes before, basically, the administration’s hand was forced,” Killin said. 
An unnamed campaign spokesperson for Crank said in a statement that “it is deeply unfortunate” that Killin “is preying on a grieving family.”  
“Congressman Crank voted to release the Epstein files in the only up or down vote on the floor of the House of Representatives,” the spokesperson said. “The statements contained in this ad are intentionally vague, and are purposefully so, because the fact pattern does not support desperate Lobbyist Jessica Killin’s desired political attack.”
Sky at the press conference rejected the notion that Killin took advantage of his family. He said he still has not heard Crank directly acknowledge what his sister and other victims experienced. 
“Jeff Crank diminishing the fact that we chose to come forward is an act against us,” Sky said. “When we came forward, we came forward by choice, not by force.”
Amanda said they chose to support Killin because she sat down “to have a human conversation and meet us where we are.”
Too many politicians cover up for Trump “rather than delivering justice,” Killin said, and Crank is part of that problem. Other Republican members of Congress met with Sky and Amanda, but Crank’s refusal to meet with his own constituents “is a complete abdication of his responsibilities.”
The election is Nov. 3.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY ag commissioner applauds Trump’s move on untaxed diesel, but says Beshear can still act
description: Kentucky’s top agriculture official applauded Republican President Donald Trump for signing an executive order to defer federal taxes on red-dyed diesel through the end of the year, but says the state can still offer extra help to offset costs.  Republican Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell sent a letter to Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s office last wee[...]
text:
Gas prices have risen during the U.S. war with Iran and are averaging around $4.06 per gallon across Kentucky, up from $2.9 a year ago.  In October, diesel prices are closer to 6.19.
(Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Kentucky’s top agriculture official applauded Republican President Donald Trump for signing an executive order to defer federal taxes on red-dyed diesel through the end of the year, but says the state can still offer extra help to offset costs. 
Republican Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell sent a letter to Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s office last week asking Beshear to temporarily suspend a prohibition on using red-dyed diesel on public roads during the fall harvest season. The untaxed fuel is commonly used on farmland and for agriculture purposes. 
Shell told the Kentucky Lantern the president’s order, signed Monday, goes further than what many farmers were asking for, as it allows on-road diesel vehicles to use red-dyed diesel, through the rest of the year. 
“What he’s trying to accomplish with it is the same thing we’re trying to accomplish, which is alleviating some of this harvest pressure that we’re under right now,” Shell said. 
Shell said farmers and others in the agriculture industry should look at this “as a short-term fix,” but a long-term solution is reopening the Strait of Hormuz and looking at domestic and global energy policy. 
“We need that strait open. We need domestic and global production of oil, especially towards diesel fuel right now, to increase and be more available,” Shell said. 
The price of diesel and gas have gone up in recent months because of global political conflicts, like Trump’s war in Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supplies are transported. 
A lot of Kentucky farmers already have tanks on their farm for red-dyed diesel, so Shell expects many of them to go into “immediate use.” He added that some issues after the executive order expires, like some of the dye still being in tanks once the prohibition goes back into effect, still needs to be worked out. 
U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, another Kentucky Republican and farmer, raised questions about facing fines for the dye in a tank and order expiration on X. Massie lost his primary this year to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein. 
As for his request to Beshear, Shell said he has not received a response from the governor’s office but was aware of a spokesperson’s statement that it was being reviewed, which had been reported by the Lantern. Shell said U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins had offered to contact Beshear about the letter. 
Shell said he would still support Beshear pausing the state prohibition on untaxed diesel because the executive order only affects federal rules. Republican governors in other states like Texas, Nebraska and Louisiana, had previously paused their states’ restrictions. 
When Beshear reduced Kentucky’s gas sales tax earlier this summer, some Republicans in the legislature warned it could cost the state tax dollars for road repairs. Shell said the issue was a concern for the diesel tax, but said his office had specifically asked for use in “agriculture farm usage vehicles that are on the road during harvest season for this period of time” to minimize impact. 
“Gov. Beshear could still write it in a way that it’s not as impactful to the road fund. That’ll be up to him to make that policy decision,” Shell said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Proposed property tax elimination state question invalid, Oklahoma high court rules
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A divided Oklahoma Supreme Court has invalidated a proposed state question that sought to eliminate property taxes in three years. In a 5-4 ruling issued Monday, the state’s high court said State Question 843 “clearly and manifestly violates the Oklahoma Constitution.” The state question runs afoul of the Oklahoma Constitution because a […]
text:
The Oklahoma Supreme Court chamber is pictured Dec. 7, 2023. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A divided Oklahoma Supreme Court has invalidated a proposed state question that sought to eliminate property taxes in three years.
In a 5-4 ruling issued Monday, the state’s high court said State Question 843 “clearly and manifestly violates the Oklahoma Constitution.”
The state question runs afoul of the Oklahoma Constitution because a homestead would not be assessed in accordance with constitutional provisions governing ad valorem taxation of real property, according to the order.
Property taxes are used to fund schools, counties, public safety and other services.
Vice Chief Justice Dana Kuehn was among those dissenting.
“I do not believe this Court has jurisdiction to determine the constitutionality of an initiative petition before it has been presented to the people,” she wrote.
Former Oklahoma Rep. Mike Reynolds, R-Oklahoma City, speaks against raising lawmaker pay at a meeting on Nov. 18, 2025 at the state Capitol. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
A challenge to the proposal was filed in April.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court in June heard oral arguments on the challenge.
“We are evaluating where we want to go from here because we are not going away,” said Mike Reynolds, a proponent of the measure and former Oklahoma House member.
It is rare that the court makes a decision based on hypothetical, Reynolds said.
“It should have gone to voters where it would have passed overwhelmingly,” he said.
“They have taken power away from the people today to make decisions about what is best for them.”
