name: Mississippi Today
title: Redistricting mess: Sen. Johnny DuPree, just elected to one seat, running for another
description: Sen. Johnny DuPree, D-Hattiesburg, asks a question during a debate in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Even though state Sen. Johnny DuPree was elected last year to represent portions of Forrest and Lamar counties in the Legislature, he’s now trying to represent a new area of the state. 
DuPree announced on Monday that he’s qualifying to run in a special election in November to fill the seat vacated by Sen. Juan Barnett, a Democrat from Heidlburg who resigned last month. 
The reason DuPree is qualifying to run for a new Senate seat is that Secretary of State Michael Watson directed local election officials to revert to legislative districts adopted by the Legislature in 2022, which had been changed in 2025. 
When Barnett resigned, Gov. Tate Reeves ordered a special election to fill Barnett’s vacant seat under the 2022 district lines, which contain portions of Forrest, Jasper and Jones counties. 
A federal three-judge panel ruled in 2024 that the parts of the state’s 2022 district maps violated the federal Voting Rights Act and required the state to create more majority-Black districts.
The Legislature redrew the lines again in 2025 to comply, which created a majority-Black House district in northeastern Mississippi, a majority-Black Senate seat in Hattiesburg and a majority-Black Senate seat in DeSoto County. 
But the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the three-judge panel’s decision on the state legislative districts in light of the high court’s landmark Louisiana v. Callais decision that rolled back racial discrimination protection during redistricting, leaving the status of Mississippi’s legislative districts in flux.  
This will be the second special election in two years that DuPree has participated in because of redistricting lawsuits. 
“Here we go again,” DuPree jokingly told Mississippi Today. 
The state branch of the NAACP, represented by several civil rights legal advocacy groups, asked a three-judge panel to prevent Watson from reverting the districts to the 2022 maps, but U.S. District Judges Daniel Jordan and Sul Ozerden and U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Leslie Southwick declined. 
Now that the federal courts have cleared the way for Watson to unilaterally change legislative districts without action from the Legislature, it’s unclear what this means for a potential special legislative session to, again, redraw legislative districts. 
Gov. Tate Reeves has said he will likely call lawmakers into a special session this fall to redraw congressional, legislative and state Supreme Court districts before the end of the year, something Democrats have strongly opposed.  
DuPree’s predicament raises a range of questions about which lawmakers can participate in a potential special session and if it’s legal for legislators elected in 2025 under new maps to represent older districts drawn in 2022.
“This is not fair to the people who are going to vote to replace Sen. Barnett,” DuPree said. “It’s not fair to the people of Forrest County. Nothing about this is fair.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Head Start programs could face major changes under proposed federal rules
description: For thousands of North Carolina families, Head Start is more than a preschool program. It can mean a safe place for children to learn, eat nutritious meals and a schedule parents can rely on while they work.  But those services could look different under proposed federal changes that Gov. Josh Stein is urging the Trump […]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)For thousands of North Carolina families, Head Start is more than a preschool program. It can mean a safe place for children to learn, eat nutritious meals and a schedule parents can rely on while they work. 
But those services could look different under proposed federal changes that Gov. Josh Stein is urging the Trump administration to reconsider as the public comment period draws to a close. 
In a letter Monday to federal officials at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Stein said he supports efforts to reduce “unnecessary administrative burdens” on Head Start programs. But he argued the proposed rule would weaken standards that help ensure consistent services for children and families. 
“Flexibility should help programs respond to local conditions; it should not result in larger classes, fewer qualified staff, shorter program days, diminished health and family supports, or widely different levels of service based solely on where a child lives,” he said.  
Head Start and Early Head Start serve more than 17,600 children in North Carolina from birth to age 5. 
The programs provide health screenings, early education and services for children with disabilities and their families. They also bring more than $290 million in federal funding to the state and support more than 5,000 jobs from teachers to childcare providers. 
What would change? 
The proposed Trump administration rule would change several aspects of how Head Start programs operate, including classroom staffing, language requirements and administrative spending. 
The rule would eliminate the federal staff-to-child ratios and group-size limits that currently apply to Head Start classrooms, allowing programs to follow state requirements. 
Stein said that could result in larger classrooms in states with less stringent requirements. He argued that federal standards provide a consistent baseline for staffing and class sizes, particularly with infants and toddlers, children with disabilities and children learning English. 
The proposal would also remove current federal requirements governing how many hours and days Head Start preschool programs operate. Stein said that could allow programs to operate on schedules as short as three hours a day for 32 weeks, which could create problems for working parents. 
The rule would also lower the amount of program funding that can be spent on administrative costs from the current 15% ceiling to 5%. Stein argued the change conflicts with federal law, which establishes the ceiling. 
HHS said the changes would reduce bureaucracy, give states and local programs more flexibility, and lower administrative costs, allowing more resources to go toward children and families. 
The agency estimates the changes could save Head Start programs $2.2 billion annually once implemented. 
Why NC officials are concerned
Many North Carolina communities rely heavily on Head Start to provide early education and childcare. The programs are especially important in rural communities, where Head Start can account for a significant share of open childcare slots.
During last year’s federal government shutdown, some state Head Start programs warned they could be forced to close when federal funding was delayed. 
The East Coast Migrant Head Start Project temporarily laid off 258 employees and suspended operations at nine childcare centers. The Salisbury-Rowan Community Action Agency halted its Head Start services, leaving hundreds of children without care. 
Some Head Start programs in North Carolina poised to shut down as federal funds dry up

Last year, in a letter to Congress, Stein said more than 22 rural counties in North Carolina rely on Head Start for more than 20% of their childcare capacity. 
The proposed changes have also drawn opposition from North Carolina education leaders. 
North Carolina Superintendent of Public Instruction Mo Green said Head Start plays an important role in preparing children for kindergarten and supporting families. 
“Many Head Start classrooms sit inside our public schools or work alongside our NC Pre-K programs, so when Head Start is strong, our schools start stronger,” Green said. “Small class sizes, qualified teachers, full-day schedules and health and family supports are what make it work.”
The public comment period on this proposed rule closes Tuesday. HHS has not announced when it will issue a final rule.

name: National
title: Research suggests women living in states with abortion bans bear higher health insurance costs
description: New preliminary research from the University of Michigan shows women living in states with post-Dobbs abortion bans may be more likely to shoulder costs for employer-sponsored health insurance premiums,  with federal data reflecting a 5.4% increase in annual premium expenditures for those women after 2022, when most abortion bans went into effect. The study[...]
text:
Women practice yoga during a community yoga class in Tulsa, Okla., in 2021. New research produced by the University of Michigan finds an association between higher out-of-pocket health insurance expenses and states with abortion bans, with data showing differences were even higher for Black and Hispanic women. (Photo by Michael B. Thomas/Getty Images)New preliminary research from the University of Michigan shows women living in states with post-Dobbs abortion bans may be more likely to shoulder costs for employer-sponsored health insurance premiums,  with federal data reflecting a 5.4% increase in annual premium expenditures for those women after 2022, when most abortion bans went into effect.
The study used national data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2019-2025 Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement to compare individual medical out-of-pocket costs for women of reproductive age between 18 and 44. The study, which hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, received financial support from the Center for Reproductive Rights, an advocacy group based in Washington, D.C. 
“State abortion bans were associated with an increase in women’s likelihood of paying out-of-pocket for health insurance premiums,” the study said.
The findings also showed even higher premium expenditures for Black and Hispanic women, at 12.8% and 13.7%, respectively. The findings were not present among men, and the majority of the women in the sample had incomes above 250% of the federal poverty level.
Miscarriage patients have fewer treatment options in states with abortion bans, study shows

“Our results are suggestive that post-Dobbs abortion bans led to insurers passing more premium costs to beneficiaries,” the study said. “Our findings shed light on the more far-reaching effects of abortion bans, quantifying the extent to which they pose an economic burden to individuals and families.”
Costs associated with pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care averaged $20,416 nationally, including $2,743 in out-of-pocket expenses for women enrolled in employer plans over 2021-2023, according to previous research.
Joelle Abramowitz, an associate research scientist at the University of Michigan and co-author of the study, said the population survey — which is used to calculate poverty and health insurance coverage rates — was one of few sources that could offer recent insights. 
“What we see is, prior to the bans, the outcomes were looking comparable, and then after the bans were implemented, we see them diverge, with more women paying health insurance premiums in the ban states,” said Abramowitz, an economist and co-director of Michigan Federal Statistical Research Data Centers. .
Ten states with near-total abortion bans — Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and West Virginia — were included in the study and compared with five states that did not implement bans: Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Pennsylvania and Washington. States that expanded Medicaid during that time frame — Idaho, Missouri, Oklahoma and South Dakota — were excluded from the analysis to isolate the effects of the bans from Medicaid changes.
Abramowitz said there could be several factors increasing premium costs for female patients. One is that in states with bans, pregnancies that might have been terminated before the bans became deliveries with the potential for more complications and higher risks.
Prior research has shown that abortion bans are also associated with a higher rate of negative maternal and infant health outcomes, including admissions to a neonatal intensive care unit, as well as higher rates of  cesarean procedures, all of which can increase costs for insurers that get passed along through higher premiums. 
“I think this is an example of one way that these policies have more far-reaching effects beyond just the individuals who are directly affected by them,” Abramowitz said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico behavioral health committee meets goal of approving all 13 regional health plans
description: The committee overseeing New Mexico’s efforts to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure across the state hit an important milestone Tuesday by approving the two outstanding regional plans in the state’s 13 behavioral health regions. The two plans carry a combined price tag of nearly $13.5 million, which local officials hope will address a variety of issues[...]
text:
Members of New Mexico's Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act Executive Committee — from left to right: Violette Cloud, Alanna Dancis, Nick Boukas, Kathy Slater-Huff, Gerald “Jerry” Ortiz y Pino and Karl Reifsteck — pictured on Aug. 14, 2026. The committee on Oct. 6, 2026, passed the remaining two regional behavioral health plans. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)The committee overseeing New Mexico’s efforts to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure across the state hit an important milestone Tuesday by approving the two outstanding regional plans in the state’s 13 behavioral health regions.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Outgoing Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed Senate Bill 3, known as the Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act, into law in 2025. It established 13 behavioral health regions across the state — patterned closely after the state’s 13 judicial districts — and tasked county, city and tribal officials with identifying their communities’ biggest behavioral health needs, from treatment facilities and behavioral health workforce to transportation and strengthening youth, family, school and caregiver support.
The law sought to address issues that arose after Republican Gov. Susana Martinez accused several behavioral healthcare providers of fraud, which spurred a mass departure of providers from the state.
The Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act Executive Committee on Tuesday approved plans for regions 4 and 12, which include Mora, San Miguel and Guadalupe counties and Lincoln and Otero counties, respectively. The two plans carry a combined price tag of nearly $13.5 million. With the funding, local officials hope to address a variety of issues, including behavioral health workforce recruitment and housing.
“We have all 13 plans approved…I just want to thank everyone for their hard work,” Nick Boukas, the executive committee chair and director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, said at the meeting.
Virtually since the executive committee’s work began, it’s faced criticism from lawmakers in both parties for what they’ve described as a lack of focus and slow progress. Some local officials have voiced similar concerns, saying that they’ve often relied on “nebulous” goals when crafting their regional plans. At an August committee meeting, for example, committee members disagreed on how to address the fact that leaders from New Mexico’s pueblos, tribes and nations did not always have clarity regarding whether they were automatically included in their corresponding region’s plan.
One committee member, former state Sen. Gerald “Jerry” Ortiz y Pino, on Tuesday said some of those issues persist. He recounted how he recently met with a state lawmaker and the leaders of a state agency who were requesting workforce development funding for an alcohol and drug treatment plan.
The state lawmaker “turned to me and said, ‘Well, you’re on that SB3 committee. That’s what you’re supposed to be doing,’” Ortiz y Pino said. “The Legislature, when they passed SB3, thought we were going to be doing a lot more than we’ve been doing. They thought we were going to be taking a look at the totality of behavioral health in the state.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Vice President Vance flies to Fairbanks to stump for incumbent Alaska senator
description: Near the end of a 33-minute speech to an enthusiastic Republican crowd gathered in a Fairbanks airport hangar on Monday, Vice President JD Vance got to the point about why he was making an extraordinary campaign stop in Alaska. Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, is facing a stiff challenge in the midterm […]
text:
Vice President JD Vance delivers a speech at a campaign rally at an airport hangar in Fairbanks on Monday. Vance was in Alaska to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. Vance praised Sullivan and criticized his opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Near the end of a 33-minute speech to an enthusiastic Republican crowd gathered in a Fairbanks airport hangar on Monday, Vice President JD Vance got to the point about why he was making an extraordinary campaign stop in Alaska.
Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, is facing a stiff challenge in the midterm election, and the outcome of the Senate race in Alaska could tip control of the body to Democrats, Vance warned.
 

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at an Oct. 5, 2026, campaign rally in Fairbanks. The headliner at the rally was Vice President JD Vance, who traveled to Alaska with Sullivan on Air Force 2. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“My friends, the Democrats are obsessed with this state this cycle. AOC and Kamala Harris and the rest of them, they see the Last Frontier as their last best hope to take America in a far left direction, to impeach Donald J. Trump, to turn off the energy projects that we’re building all across this state, and to throttle this state and this country’s incredible progress,” he said, referring to Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential candidate.
Vance was in Fairbanks as part of a series of Trump administration campaign stops in red states ahead of the midterms. President Trump is expected to visit Alaska later this month. 
The Vance event drew hundreds of attendees, many of them arriving several hours before Vance stepped out of Air Force 2 onto a platform to deliver his speech.
The vice president used the occasion to blast Democrats.
“Now we all know this: They are ruthless. They will do whatever they need to do, right up to cheating, and right up to lying, right up to putting somebody on the ballot who has no reason to be there other than to help them steal an election,” he said, a reference to retired Petersburg teacher Dan J. Sullivan, the third candidate in the four-way race who has the same name and party affiliation as the incumbent.
There is no evidence that the Democratic party had any role in the candidacy of Petersburg Dan Sullivan, and the state Supreme Court has affirmed his right to run, despite Sen. Sullivan’s claims that his candidacy is fraudulent.
 

Attendees at an Oct. 5, 2026, campaign rally in Fairbanks use their phones to record the arrival of Air Force 2, which was carrying Vice President JD Vance. Vance came to Alaska to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Alaska Democrats characterized Vance’s appearance on behalf of Sullivan as a mark of desperation.
 “Sullivan sent word to his home state of Ohio to get another Ohio politician to fly in,” Alaska Democratic Party Chair Eric Croft said in a news conference held on Monday afternoon at the Fairbanks airport, before the rally started.
There is nothing wrong with people being born outside of Alaska, Croft said. “There is something inherently wrong with our U.S. Senator having no answers to Alaskans’ questions, and having to punt to Outside sources to do that,” he said.
Stuart Relay, chair of the Alaska Interior Democrats, said the rally showed that GOP leaders were fearful of losing what was once a reliably Republican state.
“The fact that Vice President Vance is coming to Alaska is an encouraging sign that our momentum is heading in the right direction,” Relay said at the news conference.
Sen. Sullivan’s main challenger is the former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat and the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. Vance spent much of his speech blasting her.

An attendee holds up a small American flag as Vice President JD Vance returns to Air Force 2 after delivering a campaign speech in Fairbanks on Oct. 5. Vance came to Fairbanks to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

He characterized her as both lazy and corrupt. He said she missed one in five votes and never passed a bill.
The claim about Peltola passing no bills during her two-year House stint is not quite correct, according to the information clearinghouse govtrack.us. Two of the bills for which she was the prime sponsor became law by being folded into other legislation.
He said she was a “failure for the state of Alaska” who allowed “boys to compete in girls’ sports” and took other Democratic stances on social issues.
“Here’s the thing, ladies and gentlemen: When the far left calls, Mary answers, and she does exactly what they tell her to do,” Vance said.
Peltola did oppose a 2023 House bill that would have barred transgender students from participating in sports in schools in Alaska and elsewhere, calling it “federal overreach.”
Vance credited Sullivan — whom he referred to as “my dear friend” and “this amazing patriot” — with a military buildup in Alaska and with bringing national attention to Alaska’s military importance.
 

A rally attendee records Vice President JD Vance as he speaks in Fairbnks on Oct. 5, 2026. Vance was in Fairbanks to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. The event drew hundreds of people to the venue, an airport hangar. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

Prior to Sullivan’s service in the Senate, Vance said, “the Pentagon, the Department of War, what we then called the Department of Defense, it treated Alaska as a strategic backwater, as something to forget and ignore.”
However, Sullivan is far from unique in stressing Alaska’s strategic importance to the nation’s defense.
The North American Aerospace Defense Command has had a regional base in Alaska since 1961. And past U.S. senators representing Alaska secured defense spending in the state and emphasized the state’s strategic importance. The late Sen. Ted Stevens, R-Alaska, famously secured funding for military operations in Alaska. He chaired the powerful Appropriations Committee from 1997 to 2005; from 1981 to 2008, he served on that committee’s defense subcommittee, A 2009 resolution passed by the Alaska legislature noted that Stevens, over his 40-year career in the Senate, “educated the national public on the geographical importance our state plays on the world stage” and secured funding and support for military operations.
Vance also credited Sullivan with numerous accomplishments for Alaska fisheries, a hot-button issue in the current Senate race, saying he blocked Russian fish exports from reaching the U.S. market. 
In reality, the ban on Russian seafood imports into the United States was accomplished by executive orders issued by then-President Joe Biden, though both Sullivan and Peltola sponsored bills seeking bans.
 

A rally attendees shows off her pro-Trump attire as she waits for the arrival of JD Vance at the Oct. 5, 2026, event in Fairbanks. Vance came to Fairbanks to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Vance credited Sullivan with the U.S. Coast Guard’s presence in waters off Alaska. “It’s thanks to Dan that our Coast Guard is now patrolling the waters, ensuring that Alaska’s fish go to Alaska’s fishermen, not to foreigners who are trying to steal from our fisheries,” the vice president said.
The U.S. Coast Guard has operated in Alaska for over 150 years.
Vance also credited Sullivan for boosting Alaska oil activity on the North Slope and pushing a long-desired natural gas megaproject proposal that would deliver stranded resources from the North Slope to markets.
“What he will tell you is that the Alaska LNG project is the single greatest priority for energy dominance in the United States of America, and we’re building it right here,” Vance said.
Trump, Sullivan and others last week falsely claimed the Republic of Korea had committed to spending more than $50 billion to build the Alaska LNG project.
Still, Vance portrayed the LNG project as a sure thing. “Dan will never stop fighting for this. And we are gonna get it done. I promise you that,” he said.
 

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, holds hands with his wife, Julie Fate Sullivan, as they walk from Air Force 2 to a stage set up for a campaign rally in a Fairbanks hangar on Oct. 5, 2026. Sullivan traveled to Fairbanks with Vice President JD Vance, who was in Alaska campaiging for the senator’s reelection. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon) 

Generally, vice presidential visits to Alaska have been in Anchorage. Sullivan, who arrived in Fairbanks with Vance on Air Force 2, said no sitting vice president had visited Fairbanks since the 1970s, when Spiro Agnew came to the city during the debate over authorization of the Trans Alaska Pipeline System and wound up casting a tie-breaker vote in 1973 that secured passage of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline Authorization Act. However, there have been more recent visits. Joe Biden, as vice president, delivered the eulogy in 2010 at the Anchorage funeral of the late Sen. Ted Stevens, and Mike Pence and Kamala Harris made stopovers in Anchorage during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration.
Sullivan spoke for slightly less time than Vance did. Like Vance, Sullivan devoted much of his speech to criticisms of Peltola and ominous descriptions of potential Democratic control of the Senate.
He led a “No Show Peltola” chant, a criticism aimed at her record of missed votes — about 18% — and what he characterized as a lack of accomplishment.
Sullivan also delivered ominous descriptions of potential Democratic control of the Senate. He repeated his frequent criticisms of the Biden administration for its environmental and climate change mitigation policies; he called former Secretary of State John Kerry, who served as a climate envoy in the Biden administration, a “knucklehead.”
“This is what Democrats do whenever they get power. It is a core element of who they are, the far left. They come to Alaska to shut down our state and try to turn us into a national park, kill thousands of jobs,” Sullivan said.
 

Protestors hold signs outside of the Fairbanks hangar where Vice President JD Vance delivered a speech at a campaign rally for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

“Here’s something that’s really important for everyone to know: The Iran conflict is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska energy and Alaska jobs,” Sullivan said.
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement, disputed Sullivan’s characterizations — and criticized him for supporting the Iran war, which has caused energy prices to spike.
“As Dan Sullivan continues to feel the fallout of his price-hiking policies and support for the war in Iran, Mary remains focused on lowering costs, fixing the rigged system in DC, and putting Alaska first. Mary will work with anyone – no matter who is in the White House – to deliver for Alaska, and that’s why Alaskans will hold Dan Sullivan accountable for his failed policies this November,” the statement said.
Before Sullivan and Vance arrived at hangar in Air Force 2, the hundreds of attendees at the Fairbanks rally mingled for hours and enjoyed pageantry.
There was loud, pulsating music, some of it from the movie Top Gun. There were attendees decked out in costumes and MAGA gear. There were speeches by Republicans Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Rep. Nick Begich III and Alaska Republican Party Chair Carmela Warfield.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, in town to visit University of Alaska Fairbanks facilities, also spoke, describing plans for human outposts on the moon and Mars. Those endeavors are “thanks to President Trump and Vice President Vance and congressional leaders like Senator Sullivan and Congressman Begich,” Isaacman said.
 

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacson speaks to reporters at the University of Alaka Fairbanks campus on Oct. 5, 2026. Next to him is U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska. Isaacson was visiting UAF’s space-related facilities. Later in the day, he spoke at a campaign rally at headlined by Vice President JD Vance. Isaacaon praised Begich and U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, both up for reelection. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There were appearances of several legislators and candidates, including all three Republican gubernatorial candidates, who are vying against Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system. 
Eric Croft, chair of the Alaska Democratic Party, questioned the gubernatorial candidates’ decision to attend the rally.
“What’s the value in that? They really don’t have any Alaskans to talk to?” he said.
But state Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake, said the rally made sense for the candidates.
“Well, they get exposure, you know,” McCabe said as attendees were filling the hangar in the hours before Vance arrived. “They’re here with the people that are going to vote for them, so they get to talk to people and shake hands, and it’s kind of a closed environment, so I don’t know how they could miss it, personally.”
McCabe shrugged off Trump’s current low approval ratings. “I don’t think he cares too much about his approval rating,” McCabe said.
State Rep. Will Stapp, R-Fairbanks, and his 8-year-old daughter Amelia pose for photos at a campaign rally held Oct. 5, 2026, in Fairbanks. The rally was headlined by Vice President JD Vance, who came to Alaska to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. Stapp was among several Alaska Republican politicians who gathered hours before Vance’s arrival at the venue, an airport hangar. Amelia Stapp later led the crowd in the Pledge of Allegiance. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

text:
The 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)Before voters receive their ballots in the mail, they should find a copy of the 2026 Montana Voter Information Pamphlet, courtesy of the Montana Secretary of State’s office.
The state-issued guide offers information on the three ballot issues that voters will decide on, and includes arguments and rebuttals for and against each issue. Those arguments come alongside information about checking voter information, finding a polling place and viewing sample ballots, tracking absentee ballots and additional resources available to Montana voters.
(You can also find information about ballot issues, candidates for federal and state offices, and additional voter information in the Daily Montanan’s voter guide.)
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“Montana’s 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet recognizes the historic moment for our country as we continue celebrating 250 years of freedom,” Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen said in a statement. “Montanans have an important civic duty to participate in our electoral process, and I encourage every eligible Montanan to review the pamphlet and be prepared to make their voice heard this General Election.”
According to the guide, 510,000 copies of the document were published at a total cost of $75,760.23.

Montanans can access the online version of the VIP by visiting https://sosmt.gov/elections/vip/. Voters can also visit the Secretary of State’s https://VoteMT.gov website to check their registration, view their sample ballot, and find additional election resources.

title: Voters to decide if Montana judiciary needs to be more political
description: Barely a month after the 2025 Legislature, multiple organizations began efforts to put nonpartisan judicial elections in Montana’s Constitution.  The groups, which eventually folded together to bring a unified nonpartisan judicial initiative to November’s ballots, were responding to a push by conservative Republicans in the state Legislature, as well as Gov.[...]
text:
The door to the old Supreme Court Chamber at the Montana Capitol. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)Barely a month after the 2025 Legislature, multiple organizations began efforts to put nonpartisan judicial elections in Montana’s Constitution. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The groups, which eventually folded together to bring a unified nonpartisan judicial initiative to November’s ballots, were responding to a push by conservative Republicans in the state Legislature, as well as Gov. Greg Gianforte, to make elections for district and supreme court justices partisan by having district judge and supreme court justice candidates state their political parties in elections.”
Eight states in the U.S. elect Supreme Court justices in partisan elections, and nine do so for at least one lower level court, but 13 other states prohibit judges from having a political affiliation on the ballot. 
Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts seeks to preserve the status quo in the state with Constitutional Initiative No. 132 which would add the following to Article VII of the state constitution:

Nonpartisan Judicial Elections. Judicial elections shall remain nonpartisan. 

In Montana, elections for district and state supreme court seats have been nonpartisan since 1936.
During the 2025 Legislature, more than a half dozen bills were debated adding degrees of political identification into the judicial process — including several that sought to change the entire process to a partisan election. 
Only one bill became law, now allowing political parties to donate directly to a candidate.
At the end of the session, Republican leaders said they laid the groundwork for further action in 2027. 
Proponents of letting judges run with a Republican or Democratic party affiliation say that the races are already partisan, and judges have their own biases; aligning with a political party gives voters more transparency and information about what are typically low-profile elected positions. 
Those supporting keeping the status quo of nonpartisan elections argue that courtrooms should focus on the law and the constitution, and politics should not enter the equation, at the risk of coloring every decision. 
In his State of the State address to the Legislature in 2025, Gianforte encouraged legislators to send a bill to his desk that “empowers Montana voters to know a judicial candidate’s political party.”
“Montanans have a right to know the values and principles of the judges they elect,” he said. “Let’s bring light to this darkness.”
At the same legislative address, Montana Supreme Court Chief Justice Cory Swanson, one of the more conservative voices on the bench, defended the nonpartisan judicial process, saying he believed a judge’s commitment should be to decide “every case based on the facts and the law of the case, not based on the party of the affiliations of the litigants.”
He said the three branches of government by necessity need to remain independent and separate to properly balance the others; and most judicial work has nothing to do with party affiliation. 
The Kalispell Chamber of Commerce recently endorsed the initiative, citing the need for businesses to have “fair, impartial and consistent” rulings. 
“Business owners depend on the consistent application of the law so they can operate in a predictable environment that helps them create jobs and keep costs down,” Chamber CEO Lorrain Clarno said. “We need to keep politics out of our courts so our businesses can continue to contribute to the economic prosperity and sustainability of our community.”
The Montana Republican Party officially opposes the initiative and passed a resolution earlier this year formalizing its stance that the current process serves “only to obscure politics.”
Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts has earned endorsements from nine former Supreme Court justices and three dozen former district court judges.
The organization has received support from state organizations including Wild Montana, Montana Conservation Voters, the Montana Trial Lawyers Association and the Montana Federation of Public Employees, which also has donated more than $100,000 to the effort. 
National groups have also poured money into backing the initiative, including the American Civil Liberties Union ($1,500,000); a democratic-leaning nonprofit organization American Opportunity Action ($700,000); National Education Association ($825,000) and others. 
The Secretary of State publishes the Montana Voter Information Pamphlet, which allows proponents and opponents of ballot initiatives to share their perspectives. 
In it, opponents of CI-132, including Derek Oestreicher with the Montana Family Foundation, and constitutional scholar Rob Natelson, pan the money coming from “out-of-state special interests” as trying to pull a fast one on Montanans. 
They say that judges are human, likely have political party preferences, and putting those in the open will help voters understand the candidates better, instead of voting “with a blindfold on.”
Proponents of the measure point out that judges handle civil and criminal cases such as traffic, family, property or employment disputes. Proponents of the measure argue mixing politics will “hurt Montanans who just want an unbiased, fair hearing.”

Constitutional Initiative No. 132 would amend the Montana Constitution to add the following to Article VII: 

Nonpartisan Judicial Elections. Judicial elections shall remain nonpartisan.  
Voting YES on the initiative will add that section to the state constitution. Voting NO on the initiative will not add it to the constitution, but will not change how elections for judicial seats take place.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s return-to-office order is an insult
description:
The order ignores the dignity, work ethic and worth of the people who do the state's work.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s return-to-office order is an insult.
text:
This commentary is by Kate Lucier, who was a state employee for nearly 14 years. She lives in Underhill.
We rarely see the perspective of public-sector employees spotlighted — or even considered — in media reports about the state workforce and the decisions impacting it, but the voices and experiences of Vermont’s state employees should have received much more attention in the past year as lives were upended and employee morale decimated. As a former Vermont state employee, I am finally free to express those thoughts and opinions without fear of reprisal.
A few years ago, I participated in the Vermont Certified Public Manager Program, a two-year program run by the state of Vermont and the University of Vermont and designed to provide additional training to current and future leaders in Vermont state and municipal government. On many occasions, including in my resignation letter, I have written glowingly 
about my experience of coming to know the members of my program cohort, employees from across Vermont’s executive branch agencies and departments, and employees of municipal government offices. The members of my cohort were engaged, dedicated, creative, compassionate and hard-working, and they participated in the program alongside their regular job duties. I have heard from members of other cohorts that the experience of being wowed by the outstanding public-sector colleagues in the program happens each time a new cohort is formed.
I begin with that particular anecdote because it stands in stark contrast to the cavalier comments often made by those who have never worked in Vermont state government. Sadly, it also contrasts sharply with state leaders’ comments and decisions about state employees’ lives and livelihoods. I have noted, as have many of my former colleagues, that state leaders have invoked “Vermonters” and “taxpayers” when discussing the order for thousands of state employees to return to commuting to their cubicles three days a week. The Vermont Supreme Court upheld the policy Sept. 25. The state leaders’ comments make clear that decision-makers have not considered the views and experiences of state employees to be those of “Vermonters” or “taxpayers,” though, of course, the vast majority of state employees are both.
It’s hard to imagine a less pro-Vermont action for leaders to take than regularly insulting employees by failing to recognize or value their dignity, work ethic, personal circumstances and worth. For those unaware of the work environments in the largest state office workplaces, in my experience, many employees sit in cubicles where speaking to others or attending virtual meetings — still the predominant meeting space for state employees — is disruptive and disallowed. So, while it is reported that the goal of the order is to improve communication and collaboration among employees, in my view it has created the opposite effect. State leaders’ decisions have decreased communication and collaboration, employee morale and productivity, and led some talented employees to leave and pursue work in more hospitable and dignified environments.

READ MORE

I want to say how impressed I’ve been by the dedication and care exhibited by most public-sector employees I’ve worked with and known. It’s extraordinarily easy, for reasons I can’t quite grasp, to stereotype those paid with taxpayer dollars as less talented, hard-working and valuable than those paid with private dollars. Vermont’s state employees are all of these things, and also often exhibit an extra dose of dedication to the common good. They live in our communities, raising families and contributing to what makes Vermont unique, and I believe Vermonters are more decent than many public and private comments about state employees would indicate.
I hope my fellow Vermonters remember that much of what makes us the Brave Little State is that we value the dignity of work and recognize that Vermont’s opportunity to flourish will always be rooted in collective effort, in looking out for one another and in being able to imagine something beyond the outdated status quo.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s return-to-office order is an insult.

title: Mental health professionals sanctioned by licensing board
description: The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals has sanctioned two central Iowa practitioners for alleged misconduct. text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing administers and oversees many of Iowa's state licensing boards. (Photo courtesy of Getty Images; logo courtesy the State of Iowa)The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals has sanctioned two central Iowa practitioners for alleged misconduct.
Bailey Luellen, 40, an Iowa-licensed, masters-level social worker since October 2024, was recently charged by the board with one count of failing to maintain sufficient, timely, and accurate documentation in client records, plus one count of deliberately falsifying client records.
According to the board, Luellen worked as an inpatient program therapist at Clive Behavioral Health in 2024 and 2025. The board alleges that at some point in 2025, suspicions arose that Luellen had documented nonexistent assessment meetings with patients — including sessions for suicide risk assessments, treatment planning and reviews of treatment plans.
Later, an internal audit at Clive Behavioral Health further raised questions as to whether Luellen’s documented patient assessments had been completed as she claimed, the board alleges.
According to the board, one patient for whom Luellen had documented as receiving a suicide-risk assessment died by suicide within 30 days of their discharge from the program.
As part of a settlement agreement with the board, Luellen recently agreed to be cited for the two counts, and agreed to repeat the completion of supervised, clinical experience work hours for licensing.  She also agreed to have her social worker’s license placed on probation for 24 months, during which time she will work as a practice monitor.
As part of the settlement, Luellen has also agreed to complete 18 hours of educational training on the topics of privacy and confidentiality, documentation and suicide risk prevention.
Ames counselor sanctioned
Separately, in an unrelated case, the board recently sanctioned another issued mental health professional, Safaa Elnour, who has been an Iowa-licensed mental health counselor since January 2024.
According to the board, Elnour was practicing in Ames in late 2025 when she “engaged in various behaviors, including terminating services with a client without providing advanced notice, transition planning, referrals or supervisory consultation; failing to contact emergency services when presented with an active self-harm client; and billing a client’s insurance for a session that did not occur.”
The board charged Elnour with a single count of deviating from the standards of learning or skill ordinarily possessed by other licensees.
In settling the case, Elnour agreed to have her license placed on probation for 12 months during which she will be required to work with a practice monitor.  She also agreed to complete 12 hours of educational training on crisis management and ethical boundaries.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach Luellen and Elnour for comment.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s congressional elections pit “thousandaires” against millionaires and “billionaire buddies”
description: One of the starkest contrasts in Alaska’s federal races for Senate and House this election season is about money. Two of the candidates, from rural Alaska and running to the left of two Republican incumbents, have few assets to their name. Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate against incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, […]
text:
Photograph for Northern Journal – Anchorage PressOne of the starkest contrasts in Alaska’s federal races for Senate and House this election season is about money.
Two of the candidates, from rural Alaska and running to the left of two Republican incumbents, have few assets to their name.
Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate against incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, reports as little as $47,000 in assets, according to the financial disclosure she was legally required to file as a candidate.
Bill Hill, an independent challenging incumbent GOP U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, reported assets valued at as little as $119,000. (Candidates are not required to report their personal residences.)
Begich and Sullivan, meanwhile, are both multi-millionaires.
The contrast is figuring into both campaigns, as progressives call out what they describe as Sullivan’s “soaring” stock portfolio and attack Begich as an “Epstein class elite” with “billionaire buddies.”
We wanted to share more of the hard facts about each candidate’s financial situation, so we dug deep into their disclosures. Here’s what we found.
For challengers, few assets but substantial income
For candidates, it’s not exactly the best look to pay yourself a salary from your campaign; donors, presumably, would rather see their money spent on stuff that translates directly into votes.
But the Federal Election Commission allows it, and both Hill and Peltola are doing so. Hill says it’s a necessity.
The only candidate who agreed to be interviewed about his finances, Hill lives in the Bristol Bay salmon hub town of Naknek, where he has a home. For the campaign, he’s relocated to Anchorage, where he acknowledged — a little reluctantly — that he’s living with one of his children to save money.

Bill Hill poses for a photo in Anchorage. (Nathaniel Herz/Northern Journal)
Paying himself a small salary, some $700 a week, was a “tough call” and something he’d prefer not to do, Hill said. Nonetheless, he added, “trying to live on the road and maintain a life back in Naknek is just not doable, with what we’re taking home.”
Hill has stressed his financial situation on the campaign trail, where he inveighs often against “the billionaires” and calls himself as a “thousandaire.” But, like Peltola, while he reports few hard assets, he did report substantial income in 2025.
That includes $244,000 from his commercial fishing operation last year, which Hill stressed was a gross figure. He paid his crew more than $100,000, he said, and there are other expenses — insurance and fuel, plus required payments on more than $200,000 in loans he took out to buy his boat and upgrade his engine.
Hill also reported an annual pension of $82,000 from his years working as a school superintendent and teacher. But he says his income only goes so far in rural Alaska, where costs are high: Gas in Naknek, he said, recently went from $6.70 a gallon to nearly $9.
“When your food prices and your fuel prices go up, we all feel it,” he said. “I think I have a clear perspective, unlike any other candidate in this race, on the impact that decisionmaking in Washington, D.C. has had on Alaska lives.”

Mary Peltola speaks at a community celebration in the Indigenous community of Metlakatla, near Ketchikan, in 2024. (Photo by Nathaniel Herz/Northern Journal)
Peltola also reported significant income on her financial disclosure, which covered 2025 and part of 2026.
That income included $342,000 from Holland & Hart, the law firm she worked at after losing her 2024 bid for re-election to the U.S. House — plus $95,000 from two different fellowships. The salary she’s collecting from her campaign is some $1,300 a week.
“Mary has spent her entire life fighting for Alaska communities, and she will continue to do so in the United States Senate,” Peltola spokesperson Harry Child said in a short prepared statement. “Mary has been taking on the rigged system in D.C. that has been propped up by Sullivan and his special interest backers.”
Incumbents push back
Both Republicans rejected the idea that their wealth puts them out of touch with the needs of everyday Alaskans.
“Congressman Begich’s personal finances have no impact on his legislative decisionmaking process,” Silver Prout, a spokesperson for Begich’s congressional office, said in an email.
A spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign, Nate Adams, said that “representing Alaskans isn’t about what’s in your bank account, it’s about what you do for theirs.” He also rejected attacks that Sullivan has personally profited from his position in the Senate, saying that “the bulk” of the senator’s investments are in mutual funds that any American can purchase.
“And, his investments have underperformed the market during his time in the Senate, which is hardly the portfolio of someone gaming the system,” Adams said.
On top of his $174,000 U.S. Senate salary, Sullivan reported roughly $100,000 in additional income largely in the form of dividends, interest and capital gains on investments.
Much of Sullivan’s wealth is tied up in RPM International, a publicly traded company founded by his grandfather in which the senator holds between $1 million and $5 million in stock, according to his financial disclosure.
The New York Times reported earlier this year that Sullivan had sold as much as $800,000 in company stock in the past eight years.

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, center, and Nick Begich III wave signs at an Anchorage intersection in August. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Begich, by contrast, reported a diverse array of investments spanning conventional stocks to cryptocurrency to holdings of gold and silver. He owns stakes worth at least $1 million in a software company that he founded, FarShore; a fund called Listen Ventures III that’s invested in companies making prepared Indian meals, an emotional wellness app and indoor hydroponic gardens; and an Austin based health-care and telehealth company.
In total, Begich’s assets are worth at least $7.4 million, according to his disclosure. He reported at least $310,000 in income in 2025, plus that he’d sold a minority stake in a construction management software company for at least $250,000.
Prout, Begich’s spokesperson, did not respond to an email requesting details about some of his holdings.
But in a previous email, she said that Begich “has not bought or sold any individual publicly traded stocks during his time in Congress, in order to expressly avoid any real or perceived benefit from his own policy work.”
“Congressman Begich believes that congressional service is an opportunity to give back and to serve the people of Alaska and the nation, not to obtain greater wealth by trading on inside information,” Prout said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gen Z women want politicians who can make the ‘American dream’ feel attainable
description: Editor’s note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th. Strike up a conversation with a Gen Z woman about politics, and affordability will likely come up within the first 30 seconds. The cost of doing anything, whether it’s renting a home, staying in […]
text:
Comedian Michelladonna interviews New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani visits Court Side Deli in the Bronx on April 7, 2026. (By Michael Appleton/New York Mayoral Office)
Editor’s note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th.
Strike up a conversation with a Gen Z woman about politics, and affordability will likely come up within the first 30 seconds.
The cost of doing anything, whether it’s renting a home, staying in college or getting a drink, is the top issue motivating young women this election cycle. In a new The 19th/YouGov poll, a majority of Gen Z women said they were worried about paying for the cost of healthcare, housing, groceries and utilities — and in each category Gen Z women were more worried than Gen Z men. Last year, 90% of Gen Z women said the cost of housing and everyday expenses was a critical or important issue — ranking it just above healthcare, abortion and immigration issues, according to a September 2025 poll by the Public Religion Research Institute and the Brookings Institution.
For politicians, it should be an easy way in — affordability is the top issue for just about every group of voters this year. But organizers around the country say the messaging around affordability is not breaking through with Gen Z women.
Reach is important if candidates want to tap into this group of engaged voters ahead of the next presidential election. Gen Z women turn out to vote at consistently higher rates than young men and in the last presidential cycle turned further to the left, creating an opportunity for Democrats.
But instead, the prevailing feeling among Gen Z women is one of disillusionment with a political establishment rarely willing to get radical with their solutions to a growing affordability crisis, young women told The 19th.
“They are fed up, I think, with the way that the political system is kind of just not doing anything for them,” said Molly Metz, a 19-year-old student leader with the political organization NextGen America at Penn State. “Especially for Gen Z women, candidates need to be more direct, and they need to take action — very concrete, very immediate action.”
When Metz talks to students on campus, they bring up how hard it is to live in State College, Pennsylvania, where the school is located. They talk about how rent averages about $2,000 for a one-bedroom apartment, and how they stock up on food when they go home during break to save on groceries.
Standard-issue political messages around lower taxes — “that does not appeal to us. It has no reason to appeal to us. We are not concerned about taxes. We’re concerned about the fact that we can’t afford to eat or pay rent,” Metz said.
There’s evidence Democrats have been trying to get less ideological and more practical when it comes to economic issues. This midterm cycle, they’ve been focusing more on tangible day-to-day issues, like the cost of groceries, because it’s an area where President Donald Trump’s approval rating has been tanking. Republicans, too, have tried to center affordability in their campaigns, but the message has been mixed; at one point, Trump called affordability a fake narrative and a “con job by the Democrats.”  The problem for both parties is that so little of that affordability message is breaking through to young people.
“A lot of candidates just kind of talk about affordability, but it’s all in very loose terms,” Metz said.
At college campuses across her state, recent graduate Sydney Ball, an organizer with the Ohio Student Association, said students bring up the cost of gas, weighing things like if it’s cheaper to commute from home and pay for the gas or live on campus. They talk about the cost of medical treatments and getting an internship. In some of the majors Gen Z women dominate, like education, students are required to do an internship to graduate but many are unpaid.
“They’re having to choose between: ‘Do I take the unpaid internship on top of the other jobs and the school that I’m doing and sacrifice some other costs in my life, whether that’s food or gas or whatever it is, or do I set myself up to not get a job post-grad?’” Ball said.
Unemployment rates for young women ages 16 to 24 have been ticking up since 2024, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In January 2024, the unemployment rate for young women got as low as 5.9% but then rose until it peaked at 10.3% in August 2025. As of September 2026, the rate was 9.9%; for working women over the age of 20, the rate is 3.6%
Over the past several years, young men have had higher unemployment rates than young women, but theirs has been coming down all year, from 11.5% at the end of 2025 to 10% in September.
Under those conditions, young women, who attend college at higher rates than men, have started to wonder if they can even bank on a good education giving them a secure future.
Cheyenne Hunt, one of the first Democratic Gen Z women to run for Congress, said for women of her generation it feels like the American Dream that was promised is slipping away, but “it doesn’t seem like people actually care.”
“We’re living the nightmare that was always used to fearmonger in politics for generations before, which was the idea that there could come a generation that is less prosperous than ours, and that is our lived reality,” said Hunt, 29. She lost in the primary for California’s 45th Congressional District in 2024, when she was 26. She is now the executive director of a nonprofit against gender bias called Reckoning Action.
In Hunt’s view, political messaging is failing to address the unique ways that young women are being affected by the current economic climate. It’s the young women bearing the majority of student loan debt, entering a labor market with a persistent gender pay gap, who are now becoming a generation of women that feels much more anxious about its financial future than men of the same age.
“They are feeling [the economic slowdown] in a unique way, and yet there’s this really strange unwillingness to acknowledge that,” Hunt said.
Affordability feels like an existential issue that politicians must address because even the simple things feel under attack, said Jessica Siles, a spokesperson for Voters of Tomorrow, a Gen-Z-led advocacy organization that promotes civic engagement.
“It really is like the cost of a drink,” said Siles, who is also Gen Z. “Young people are just really feeling priced out of day-to-day life, a night out with their friends, a concert ticket.”
On campuses, students say they want candidates who are willing to meet with young people, hear their concerns — and then meet those concerns with really specific policies. It’s much more about the individual candidate’s message than it is about the party they represent.
“This is a generation that doesn’t really believe in just blind party loyalty, and I think the two-party system has to get comfortable with being a little bit uncomfortable,” said Mary-Pat Hector, the CEO of Rise, a student-led organization focused on lowering tuition costs and expanding voter turnout.
This election cycle, there is some excitement among Gen Z women around candidates including Abdul El-Sayed, who is running to represent Michigan in the Senate on a platform that lists Medicare for All as a key pillar, and Angie Nixon, who is running to represent Florida in the Senate on a platform that includes universal childcare. Both are Democrats. But one name came up again and again over more than a dozen interviews The 19th conducted with young women and organizers: Zohran Mamdani.
What New York City’s mayor did to capture the support of 82% of young women voters in the 2025 mayoral election, compared with 65% of young men, came up repeatedly as an example of how to excite a disillusioned group.
“Mamdani is on my timeline every day. Whether it be social media or just the things he’s saying — childcare for all, that type of thing — he’s really setting an example for what people should be thinking about,” said Jasmin Lopez, 29, who works at Cisco Systems and is based in New Jersey.
Key to his success was his ability to be chronically online and reach young people on the platforms they were on. But the other part was directness: People outside New York City could cite what Mamdani wanted to do. Free buses. Free childcare. A rent freeze. His policies were not only clear, they were tangible. And he spread his message by being out in the park, on the subway, on street corners. He flew past his goal of knocking on 1 million New Yorker’s doors (with the help of volunteers). The final count was more like 3 million.
“Mamdani went to neighborhoods of people who don’t vote frequently, talked to them about issues they cared about, like how they’re going to pay their rent, how they’re going to pay their bills, how they’re going to get to work — but with free buses,” said Mariah Ross, the ballot initiative director at One Fair Wage, an organization working to raise the minimum wage to at least $25 an hour.
That is what young women want, Ross said, rather than a crop of Democratic candidates that are “trying to appeal to everyone.”
“They want to hear: ‘I have a solution for you to be able to ultimately help take care of your family,’” she said.
Of course, young women are not a group of single-issue voters, nor are they a monolith. They care about other things, like reproductive health and climate, but many can’t put their focus on other causes until their own livelihood feels secure.
When Ross talks to Gen Z women about the national push for a $25 or $30 an hour minimum wage, up from the federal wage floor of $7.25 an hour, the response is resounding, she said.
“People are like, ‘Hell yeah. Yes. I need that.’”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: US Supreme Court won’t hear company’s appeal over migrant’s wage claim
description: New Jersey’s high court said companies have to adhere to wage laws regardless of an employee’s immigrant status. The U.S. Supreme Court won’t hear the case.
text:
New Jersey’s high court said companies have to adhere to wage laws regardless of an employee’s immigrant status. The U.S. Supreme Court won’t hear the case. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)The U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up a real estate management company’s appeal of a state Supreme Court decision that found state laws governing wages and work hours apply to immigrants who are in the country illegally.
The high court declined to give certiorari to Marmic LLC’s appeal of the state court’s March decision, which found that federal law that bars employing individuals without legal permission to enter or work in the United States does not conflict with New Jersey’s Wage and Hour and Wage Payment laws.
As is its practice, the U.S. Supreme Court did not provide a reason for rejecting the appeal.
Marmic’s appeal came months after the state’s high court ruled the firm’s provision of a free apartment does not satisfy its wage obligations to Sergio Lopez, who Marmic employed as a super.
Joseph Deer, an attorney representing Marmic, did not return a call and email seeking comment.
New Jersey’s Wage and Hour law sets the state’s minimum wage and requires overtime pay for work time beyond the first 40 hours each week. The state’s Wage Payment law generally requires workers to be paid at least twice a month on a set schedule.
The state Supreme Court found neither law has broad exceptions for barter arrangements like the one for a free apartment between Lopez and Marmic, and the apartment was not proof the firm properly paid Lopez.
All a worker — even one without legal permission to be or work in the United States — has to do to establish a wage claim is show that they are an employee who performs work and does not receive proper compensation, New Jersey’s court ruled.
“A person’s immigration status is not relevant to determine those issues,” New Jersey Chief Justice Stuart Rabner wrote for a unanimous court in March.
