text:
Manifestantes de Dodge City se reúnen el 25 de septiembre de 2026 afuera de la oficina de la representante Tracey Mann, coreando: "Tracey Mann, ¿dónde estás? ¿Te necesitamos?" Protestaban contra las acciones de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. en la comunidad. (Foto de Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
DODGE CITY — Las comunidades del suroeste de Kansas que se están recuperando de la ofensiva migratoria del presidente Donald Trump —que incluyó detenciones aleatorias para verificar el estatus migratorio— buscan formas de recuperarse mientras el miedo sigue apoderándose de la gran población hispana de la zona.
Los restaurantes cerraron, los gerentes de moteles cancelaron reservaciones y las grandes instalaciones de procesamiento de carne de res en la zona acortaron o cancelaron turnos la semana pasada, ya que oficiales de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. llegaron repentinamente y empleados inmigrantes no se presentaron a trabajar.
Breanna Rutschman, maestra de segundo grado en Dodge City, dijo que siete de sus 20 estudiantes estaban ausentes el día en que llegaron los agentes. Al día siguiente, solo ocho estudiantes asistieron. La mayoría de los salones de la escuela estaban vacíos.
“Están aquí para mejorar su situación y la de sus hijos, y son trabajadores, atentos y humanos”, dijo. “Lo que está pasando es tan inhumano, cruel e innecesario. Es absolutamente innecesario.”
Agentes de ICE llegaron al área el 22 de septiembre, con el objetivo de realizar revisiones migratorias en Dodge City, Liberal y Garden City. El gobierno federal reportó más de 100 arrestos. El secretario del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional de Trump, Markwayne Mullin, dijo a través de comunicados de prensa que los agentes solo estaban arrestando a “criminales atroces”
Pero en una lista que incluye asesinos, violadores y narcotraficantes, agregó: “inmigrantes ilegales con órdenes finales de expulsión.” Mullin también dijo que los agentes de ICE, que trabajan para la Seguridad Nacional, no están deteniendo a personas en los lugares de trabajo.
Funcionarios locales y defensores dicen que eso no fue lo que ocurrió.
“No fueron solo criminales, porque he estado en contacto con varias escuelas y con las familias”, dijo Janeth Vázquez, vicealcaldesa de Liberal. “La mayoría de estas familias no tenía antecedentes penales. Eran personas trabajadoras, humildes, genuinas y buenas en nuestras comunidades.”
Los datos del censo muestran que Liberal, Dodge City y Garden City tienen poblaciones entre el 55% y el 69% de hispanos o latinos.
A medida que se difundía la presencia de ICE, dijo Vázquez, Liberal se convirtió en un “pueblo fantasma”, ya que la gente se escondía.
Funcionarios federales arrestaron a personas después de exigirles pruebas de estatus migratorio durante detenciones de tránsito y a empleados que ingresaban a plantas procesadoras de res, con base en órdenes pendientes, dijo Vázquez.
“No hablo solo de personas indocumentadas. También hablo de ciudadanos estadounidenses”, dijo. “Estaban perfilando racialmente a las personas y atacando a personas de color, así que todas esas historias se compartieron en redes sociales. La gente tenía miedo de salir de sus casas.”
 
Los voluntarios Aquilino Reyes (izquierda), Amy Soberanes (centro) y Anna Meyer cargan suministros el 24 de septiembre de 2026, donados a inmigrantes de Dodge City que temían salir de sus hogares mientras agentes de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. estaban en la ciudad. (Foto por Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Ayudando
Amy Soberanes es dueña de una pequeña tienda en Dodge City que vende jugos y lattes. Pero desde que el ICE arresta, tiene otro trabajo: organizar una red de ayuda para entregar comida y otros artículos esenciales a inmigrantes escondidos.
El porche delantero del negocio de Soberanes estaba cubierto de donaciones en los días posteriores a las búsquedas migratorias. Reunió a un equipo de conductores-voluntarios que van a sus casas para dejar pañales, fórmula para bebés, papel higiénico y víveres, una práctica comunitaria empleada en Minneapolis, Los Ángeles y otras ciudades cuando llegó ICE.
Los voluntarios son cuidadosos, dijo Soberanes. Los conductores cambian de ruta y de auto para evitar ser detectados, escriben las direcciones en un cuaderno de papel y llevan una botella de agua para arrojar el papel al agua y ocultar las direcciones en caso de que las autoridades los detengan.
La semana pasada, su teléfono sonaba constantemente mientras manejaba cajas de pañales, bolsas de fruta y rollos de papel higiénico.
“No he dormido en los últimos tres días”, dijo el viernes. “Hemos estado entregando comida hasta la medianoche y luego levantándonos a las 4 a.m. para entregarla antes de que ICE esté activo, de 8 a.m. a 6 p.m., probablemente.”
Sin embargo, Soberanes dijo que se sentía animada por todos los que se ofrecieron como voluntarios para ayudar. Incluso la cancelación de un evento comunitario latino planeado desde hace mucho tiempo, la Pachanga en la Plaza, tuvo un lado positivo, dijo.
“Lo que estamos haciendo ahora es que hemos repartido toda la comida gratis que íbamos a dar para el evento, todo el dinero que habíamos conseguido, y ahora la estamos donando a las familias”, dijo Soberanes.
 
Sufriendo, a solas
En una casa pequeña, una familia de siete personas llenó la sala la semana pasada, temerosas de irse y dependientes de las donaciones que Soberanes había dejado.
Una joven, a quien Kansas Reflector no identifica por temor a que ICE pudiera tomar represalias contra ella y su familia, abrazó a su hijo recién nacido mientras hablaba de la detención de su esposo por ICE unos días antes.
El 23 de septiembre, la mujer y su esposo iban de regreso a casa desde el hospital con su bebé recién nacido, dijo ella en español, con ayuda de un traductor. Su médico advirtió a la pareja que tuviera cuidado al regresar a casa porque afuera era “peligroso”.
A pesar de las precauciones, fueron detenidos por ICE y su esposo fue arrestado.
“Los agentes tuvieron algo de misericordia, pero fue muy poca”, dijo la mujer. “Dejó ir a mi hijo y a mí. Algo por lo que estoy increíblemente agradecida es estar aquí en casa con mis tres hijos.”
El arresto ocurrió cerca de la casa de la pareja, dijo, donde su hijo de 4 años salió y vio a su esposo ser detenido.
“No les importó mi esposo y simplemente se lo llevaron. Estoy muy triste”, dijo. Su esposo emigró a Estados Unidos con un permiso de trabajo, pero no se le renovó.
“Apeló su caso”, dijo la mujer. “Hizo todo lo que se le pidió. Vino aquí legalmente. Hizo todo. Simplemente no lo renovaron.”
Un tribunal de apelaciones confirmó la decisión de un tribunal inferior de que el asilo y una solicitud de protección bajo la Convención contra la Tortura no eran apropiados para él, según confirman los registros judiciales. El tribunal decidió que la negativa del hombre a unirse a pandillas criminales en Guatemala no era suficiente para demostrar que su vida estaba en peligro, y que su raza no influía en su miedo a ciertos “actores” en su país de origen.
“Su abogado en ese momento le dijo que solo se quedara donde estaba y que no hiciera nada”, dijo la mujer. “Así que no sabía qué hacer. Sentimos que ese abogado no nos ayudó en nada en ese momento, pero no sabíamos mucho, así que simplemente lo dejamos pasar.”
La mujer dijo que habló por teléfono con su esposo días después de que los agentes se lo llevaron. Él dijo que estaba detenido en San Diego, pero esperaba ser deportado a Guatemala.
Dijo que no ve cómo puede regresar a Guatemala.
“No puedo por mis hijos. Necesito cuidar a mis hijos. Tienen futuro aquí”, dijo. “En Guatemala, no hay futuro. No tenemos casa allá. No tenemos nada.”
La abogada actual de la pareja dijo que ya no puede ayudar porque no puede comunicarse con el esposo, dijo la mujer.
La joven se disolvió en lágrimas silenciosas al hablar de su esposo. “Él no ha hecho nada. No bebe. Toca en el grupo de la iglesia. Estas fueron las últimas palabras que me dijo: ‘Cuídate. Cuida a nuestros hijos.'”
Voluntarios, incluidos tres abogados que trabajan pro bono para inmigrantes del suroeste de Kansas, coordinarán con el hombre para ayudarlo a solicitar su regreso, dijo Soberanes. La familia no estaba segura de si firmó un acuerdo de estipulación mientras estaba detenido, un formulario comúnmente usado con detenidos inmigrantes en el que aceptan ser deportados sin pasar por el tribunal de inmigración, según el Proyecto Nacional de Inmigración.
El hombre era el sostén económico de su familia de siete miembros, que incluía a su esposa y sus tres hijos, a su propia madre y a su hermano menor, quien es sordo.
 
Manifestantes en el centro de Dodge City, el 24 de septiembre de 2026, protestan por la presencia de agentes de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. en la comunidad. (Foto de Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Protesta contra ICE
En respuesta a la presencia de ICE, cientos de personas se alinearon en la emblemática plaza del centro de Dodge City, con su toro de bronce de tamaño real y cuerno largo de Texas, el 24 de septiembre, ondeando banderas de México, Guatemala y Estados Unidos.
Llevaban carteles que instaban a la bondad y pedían que saliera ICE.
Al día siguiente, los manifestantes marcharon desde Wright Park hasta la oficina del representante republicano Tracey Mann en Dodge City, donde las puertas estaban cerradas antes de su llegada. Mann representa el vasto 1er Distrito Congresional de Kansas, que se extiende unas 400 millas de este a oeste, desde Lawrence hasta la frontera con Colorado.
Mann no respondió a las preguntas del Kansas Reflector, enviadas por correo electrónico, sobre por qué la oficina estaba cerrada o si le preocupaban las interrupciones en los negocios de Kansas.
“Las fuerzas federales de la ley tienen la responsabilidad de hacer cumplir nuestras leyes migratorias y de ayudar a mantener seguras nuestras comunidades”, dijo Mann en un mensaje enviado por correo electrónico. “También reconozco la interrupción que la operación causó a las comunidades en todo el Big First. Cuando sea posible, las autoridades federales deberían coordinarse con las locales para que las operaciones se lleven a cabo de manera segura.”
 
Ana Sánchez Ortiz comparte la historia de su madre, quien fue detenida por agentes de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU., el 23 de septiembre de 2026, en Dodge City. (Foto por Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Complicaciones de obtener la ciudadanía
No todos en el suroeste de Kansas simpatizan con las redadas de ICE.
Los residentes comentaron en redes sociales, diciendo a los inmigrantes que simplemente presentaran papeles para obtener estatus legal o se fueran, y agradecieron a ICE por su trabajo, incluso mientras otros lloraban por familias separadas.
Pero obtener la ciudadanía no es tan fácil como parece.
En 2011, el padrastro de Ana Sánchez Ortiz solicitó que ella, junto con sus hermanos y su madre, se convirtieran en ciudadanos estadounidenses.
Quince años después, la madre de Sánchez Ortiz aún no es ciudadana, y el 23 de septiembre fue detenida. Eso, a pesar de haber estado durante años en contacto con ICE, tener un trabajo en National Beef Packing Co. y mantenerse fuera de problemas, dijo Sánchez Ortiz.
Sánchez Ortiz, gerente senior de una sucursal bancaria en Dodge City, dudó al principio en hablar, temerosa de atraer la atención.
Pero los familiares frenéticos no pudieron encontrar a su madre en el sistema federal de detención durante varios días, dijo. Su madre es diabética y tiene presión arterial alta, y aunque la hermana de Sánchez Ortiz llevó apresuradamente sus medicamentos a la cárcel local, los agentes de ICE no se los entregaron a su madre.
La familia ahora sabe que su madre está detenida en California y ha viajado allí para tratar de ayudarla, dijo Sánchez Ortiz.
“Hemos hecho todo bien. Ella ha estado aquí desde que tenía 16 años”, dijo Sánchez Ortiz. “Estudió en la preparatoria aquí. Formó su familia aquí.”
Como llegó al país cuando tenía 4 años, Sánchez Ortiz se convirtió en ciudadana mediante el programa DACA, o Acción Diferida para los Llegados en la Infancia. Esta política migratoria de la era Obama permite que ciertos inmigrantes que fueron traídos a Estados Unidos cuando eran niños obtengan permisos de trabajo renovables cada dos años.
Renovó su solicitud de DACA seis veces antes de poder solicitar el estatus separado de residencia legal, que obtuvo cuando estaba en primer año de preparatoria. Pero no fue hasta los 31 años que se convirtió en ciudadana, dijo Sánchez Ortiz.
 
Julysa Barraza, activista local, explica una petición para la Ley SEAL, que crearía un camino claro para que los inmigrantes se conviertan en ciudadanos estadounidenses, durante un mitin el 24 de septiembre de 2026 en Dodge City. (Foto por Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Buscando una solución
Zac Carlton, dueño de una empresa constructora en Dodge City, dijo que sus amigos quedaron “destrozados” por las actividades de ICE la semana pasada. Todos en la zona conocen a alguien que no está aquí legalmente, dijo.
“He hablado con varios contratistas y subcontratistas, y la semana pasada todos se mantuvieron al margen, y no se estaba haciendo ningún trabajo”, dijo. “Ahora, esta semana, la gente está tratando de averiguar cómo recuperarse. Obviamente, esto ha puesto presión tanto sobre las familias afectadas por la redada como sobre los empleadores.”
El oeste de Kansas necesita inmigrantes para apoyar la construcción, la agricultura y otros negocios, dijo Carlton. Encontrar trabajadores ya es un problema en esas industrias, dijo, y seguirá siéndolo.
Carlton analizó leyes y políticas migratorias anteriores y está distribuyendo una petición para promover la Ley SEAL.
Los proyectos de reforma migratoria han fracasado varias veces en el pasado, dijo, pero espera que los políticos presten atención tras lo ocurrido en Kansas.
Vázquez ha estado librando la batalla que Carlton lleva a cabo desde hace unos 15 años, viajando a Washington, D.C., para abogar por cambios migratorios. Comenzó cuando su padre fue deportado, justo cuando ella comenzó la universidad, siendo adolescente. Hace cinco años, se convirtió en comisionada de la ciudad de Liberal, siendo la primera latina en el cargo.
Lo que sucedió en el suroeste de Kansas la semana pasada repercutirá en todo el país debido a sus efectos en el suministro de carne de res, dijo. Grupos de la industria expresaron preocupación de que los empleados que faltaron a trabajar en las instalaciones procesadoras de carne por temor a enfrentarse a ICE podrían contribuir a la desaceleración de la producción y a los precios más altos.
“Toda esta operación realmente impactó nuestra economía y todos en el suroeste de Kansas van a sufrir”, dijo Vázquez, “no solo la población indocumentada.”

title: Americans’ water bills are growing faster than groceries, overall inflation
description: Household water bills are increasing faster than inflation and income, according to a new analysis. The environmental advocacy nonprofit Food and Water Watch analyzed water bill data among the nation’s 500 largest community water providers. Those systems serve a collective 155 million people — nearly half the nation’s population. Between 2015 and 2025, water[...]
text:
Household water bills are increasing faster than inflation and income, according to a new analysis by the nonprofit Food and Water Watch. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)Household water bills are increasing faster than inflation and income, according to a new analysis.
The environmental advocacy nonprofit Food and Water Watch analyzed water bill data among the nation’s 500 largest community water providers. Those systems serve a collective 155 million people — nearly half the nation’s population.
Between 2015 and 2025, water bills increased by 62% on average across those water providers. That was faster than the overall inflation rate and more than two times the rate of grocery price increases over the same period. Food and Water Watch found that water bills increased 19% faster than household incomes, meaning people are spending a greater share of their earnings on water.
In Louisiana, Maryland, New Hampshire and West Virginia, water bills grew about twice as fast as household incomes, the analysis found.
Costs varied widely across the country: In Idaho, the average household spent $286 on water bills last year. In West Virginia, the average cost was $1,383. The analysis found for-profit water companies charge more than publicly owned water providers (Food and Water Watch advocates against private ownership of water systems).
Relief from energy bills unlikely as utilities request billions in rate hikes

The analysis projects that costs will rise further as climate-change driven drought and natural disasters threaten water supplies. It also pointed to growing infrastructure needs that are estimated to cost hundreds of billions of dollars across the country.
“Industrial pollution, aging infrastructure, and federal disinvestment are fueling a crisis for the nation’s water systems,” the report said.
The American Water Works Association, which includes more than 4,300 North American water utilities, estimates American drinking water systems will need as much as $2.4 trillion over the next 25 years to sustain and modernize infrastructure. If those costs are covered solely by users, bills could more than double by 2050, the association projected.
Aside from abandoning water system privatization, Food and Water Watch recommends that state and local governments support local control of water systems, hold polluters accountable for contamination and prevent the tech, fossil fuel and agriculture sectors from passing on costs to residential water users. The organization also calls on Congress to fund water improvement projects that can help communities meet federal water standards.
The report comes as more Americans struggle with the high costs of electricity, gas, groceries and housing.
Climate change could double household water costs in some cities, study finds

Electric bills continued to soar and millions of families that heat their homes with oil are facing a much more expensive winter. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state employees administering federal energy assistance programs, estimates that heating oil costs will be about 50% higher than last winter.
Though federal forecasters predict a warmer winter, wars in Iran and Ukraine have greatly disrupted petroleum markets, leading to quick price hikes.
Households in the Northeast, which use more than 80% of the nation’s heating oil, will be most affected. But the association projects American home heating costs will rise an average of 8.7% this winter — more than twice the rate of inflation.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

title: Alaskans still have time to appeal FEMA denials for disaster assistance, agency says
description: Alaskans who have applied for disaster assistance funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and received a denial may still appeal, according to an agency update. “This may not be the final decision as FEMA may simply require more information or additional supporting documentation from the applicant. Read your FEMA letter carefully to determine what[...]
text:
Alaska Organized Militia members, assigned to Task Force Bethel, arrive at Tuntutuliak, Alaska, for post-storm clean-up efforts during Operation Halong Response, Oct. 25, 2025. (Alaska National Guard photo by Capt. Balinda O’Neal)Alaskans who have applied for disaster assistance funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and received a denial may still appeal, according to an agency update.
 
Appeals may be submitted:
Online to DisasterAssistance.gov.
By mail: FEMA Individuals & Households Program, National Processing Center P.O. Box 10055 Hyattsville, MD 20782-8055.
By fax: (800) 827-8112, Attention: FEMA – Individuals & Households Program.
If an applicant is unable to submit their appeal, someone else can do it for them. FEMA will need the applicant’s written permission to share information about the application. Applicants can do this by completing an Authorization for the Release of Information Under the Privacy Act form and sending it to FEMA with your appeal paperwork.
Applicants will be notified in writing of the response to your appeal, either by mail or by logging into your DisasterAssistance.gov account.


“This may not be the final decision as FEMA may simply require more information or additional supporting documentation from the applicant. Read your FEMA letter carefully to determine what else may be needed,” the update said.
Alaskans seeking an appeal may provide additional documentation of damages including receipts and bills for eligible repairs, repair receipts from contractors or repair services, proof of ownership or other information to substantiate an appeal.
From there, the agency may approve additional funding. Residents are eligible for FEMA disaster assistance of up to $44,800 per household for replacement of personal property, and $44,800 for repairing homes.
“Assistance with disaster-related needs such as subsistence equipment, snowmachines, stove oil, all-terrain vehicles, initial rental expenses, continued temporary housing assistance, home repairs, vehicle damage, medical expenses, moving and storage may still be available,” the update said.
Officials with FEMA did not immediately respond to questions about how many Alaskans had been issued denials or the timeline to submit appeals. 
In the last year, Alaskans endured widespread disaster impacts with the largest and most devastating being from the remnants of Typhoon Halong that hit Western Alaska last October. The storm affected 49 communities, and caused catastrophic damage to Kipnuk and Kwigillingok. Hundreds of homes and structures were damaged or destroyed and over 1,600 people displaced. Both communities have voted to relocate.   
Following Halong, 2,511 residents applied for FEMA disaster assistance and 2,329 residents applied for state assistance. Those are the counts as of September, said Jeremy Zidek, public information officer with the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management on Monday.
As of September, FEMA has obligated more than $75 million in individual and household assistance and $8.6 million in public assistance grants to the Halong recovery effort, Zidek said.
“It never feels good to be denied, but FEMA has been a tremendous partner for us,” Zidek said. “So while there’s denials that FEMA has given us, there has been other support that has been tremendous and has made a major impact on the recovery effort and taking care of the Alaskans that have been impacted by the storm.”
As the one-year anniversary of the Western Alaska storms approaches next week, Zidek said that recovery is an incredibly complex and multilayered process with local, Tribal, federal, state and non-profit organizations involved. Officials conducted site visits, and some repairs and rebuilding took place this summer, but many residents are still displaced and long term recovery work is ongoing. 
The disaster recovery effort is funded by a 75-25 split between the Trump administration and state of Alaska, after the federal government denied the state’s request to cover 100 percent of the costs of the first 90 days after the disaster. The state appealed requesting 90 percent federal support, but its appeal was denied in May.
Zidek said FEMA has provided rental assistance for residents displaced from the disaster, totalling 189 households as of September. The assistance will be provided through April, and the state is preparing to request an extension for another year to 18 months, he said. 
FEMA also denied the state permanent housing construction funding — additional funding beyond $44,800 per household for rebuilding. The state is also planning to appeal in the coming weeks, Zidek said. “We understand that constructing a home in Alaska, or rebuilding it in rural Alaska especially — $44,000 is not sufficient if your home has been completely destroyed or had major damage,” he said. “We’re going to appeal it at the state level, and we feel that we have strong justification for it.”
Zidek said FEMA has also provided funding for crisis counseling to provide mental health support to storm survivors, as well as airfare for up to four trips to the communities of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok for residents to work on repairs, make site visits with FEMA officials and  conduct subsistence activities.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Three criminal cases involving ICE hit the Supreme Judicial Court
description: “You have to try,” said Justice Dalila Wendlandt of the Suffolk judge’s refusal to submit a corrected writ to ICE. “I’m not just making that up. I think it’s the case law.”
text:
WHEN MASSACHUSETTS’S criminal justice system collides with federal immigration actions, the fingers start pointing.  
Justices of the Supreme Judicial Court spent most of Monday’s oral arguments trying to work out whether prosecutors have any duty to tell judges if their defendants could be arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and what power, if any, state judges have to order immigration officials to bring a person back into the state so they can face trial.
If it turns into federal versus state “standoff,” as several justices put it, what then? 
Lawyers for three men detained by ICE during their Massachusetts criminal prosecutions argue that judges and prosecutors can do more to prevent immigration proceedings from derailing the normal course of justice.  
In a case that sparked a political conflagration between the Suffolk County district attorney’s office and federal prosecutors last year, Dominican national Wilson Martell-Lebron was arrested outside the courthouse mid-trial by an immigration agent who had been slated as a prosecution witness. Martell-Lebron was charged with providing false information on a license application. 
The judge in the case, Mark Summerville, accused ICE agent Brian Sullivan of violating Martell-Lebron’s rights to due process and a fair trial, and concluded that two state troopers involved in the case and communicating with the ICE agent knew about plans to detain the man. Summerville dismissed the case against Martell-Lebron, ruling there had been egregious prosecutorial misconduct. 
The Suffolk County district attorney’s office appealed Summerville’s decision. 
Justices on Monday were openly skeptical of claims that prosecutors had no special knowledge that their defendant would be detained, given that the ICE agent who directed the detention was part of the prosecution before the trial. 
“I’m not buying your argument that he’s not a member of the prosecution team after the discovery stage,” Justice Frank Gaziano said, referring to the period of time before trial where both sides exchange relevant information.  
A member of the prosecution team is not allowed to do anything to derail the prosecution — that would be prosecutorial misconduct, said Justice Gabrielle Wolohojian, who noted that the ICE agent was a member of the prosecution team “and he caused the defendant’s unavailability for trial.”  
State officials have no jurisdiction over federal immigration enforcement operations. Assistant District Attorney Elisabeth Martino told the justices that the ICE agent was conducting a “separate, sovereign, federal action.” 
Martino acknowledged that the ICE agent had said throughout the proceedings that his agency was interested in taking the defendant into custody at some point. But she claimed the understanding was that meant at the end of the trial. 
“Why wouldn’t the prosecution give the judge the information it has,” asked Chief Justice Kimberly Budd. “I understand you’re saying they have no power to do anything, but they have the power to let the court know what’s happening.” 
The district attorney’s office argued that prosecutors should not have to inform the court about possible immigration enforcement action, in part because federal agents might try to hold prosecutors responsible if they scare the defendant into fleeing. 
Under the law at the time of Martell-Lebron’s trial, the burden was on federal agents to inform the court if they plan to arrest a defendant.  
And the PROTECT Act, which was passed this year and creates new guidelines for how federal agents should operate in “sensitive locations” like courthouses or schools, does not instruct prosecutors to inform the courts if there may be an immigration action.  
There are consequences for failing to follow the new rules, like being sued by the state attorney general, but those remedies are aimed at the ICE agent rather than prosecutors. 
The Martell-Lebron case, like the two other immigration cases before the high court on Monday, also considered what power state judges have to make sure a defendant is able to appear in court. 
Once Martell-Lebron was taken into ICE custody, Martino said, prosecutors asked for a writ of habeas corpus, which is an order demanding that the government bring a detained person to court. ICE told the prosecution that the initial writ did not have the correct language, and Judge Summerville refused to issue a second one with corrected language.  
That seemed to trouble the high court. Dismissing a case with prejudice, Gaziano noted, was an “extreme remedy, and before getting there [a judge] should exhaust the process that’s available to him properly, and that didn’t happen.” 
Even if the judge was skeptical that ICE would comply, SJC justices suggested, he should have gone through the process of correcting the writ. Martino said that is “the absolute, major problem in this case.”  
In the case of Freslet Noralus, charged with assault with a dangerous weapon and taken into ICE custody in May 2025, a state district court judge wouldn’t issue a writ of habeas corpus to immigration officials at all.  
After consulting with the Fall River District Court clerk-magistrate, Judge David Sorrenti concluded he did not have the authority to issue the writ after learning that Noralus was being held at a detention facility in Kentucky. 
The court denied a motion to dismiss and issued a default — or failure to meet a legal obligation — because Noralus was not present, along with a warrant for “a man it knew was in a cell in Kentucky,” attorney David Rassoul Rangaviz said. This effectively punished him for not being there, an absence that was “guaranteed” by the court refusing to sign off on the writ of habeas corpus, Rangaviz added. 
Noralus has now been deported to Haiti. Rangaviz told the court that this means the state wants to keep the charge open indefinitely “against a man that its own inaction helped to deport.” 
Rangaviz asked the SJC to hold that the courts can issue writs of habeas corpus even if the defendant has been moved out of state and that there cannot be a default against a defendant who the court knows is absent because of being detained by ICE. He also argued that the case must be dismissed with prejudice, meaning the defendant can’t be retried, if the state does not “do the work” of trying to get the person to trial. 
The defendants’ attorney, prosecutors, and the attorney general agree that the trial judge should have issued the writ in Noralus’s case. Even though state writs can’t be enforced on the federal level, there are several instances where federal officials have respected the court order anyway, Rangaviz said. 
In a brief, the ACLU of Massachusetts said the process is well-established. A state trial court can issue a state writ to bring the person to the next court appearance, and if federal officials don’t recognize it, state prosecutors can request that the US District of Massachusetts issue a supplemental federal writ to accompany the state one. 
If ICE chooses not to comply with the writ or deports the defendants, that creates another legal quagmire. At least 30 Massachusetts criminal cases are in the same holding pattern, Rangaviz noted in his brief, with “outstanding default warrants, absent defendants, no end in sight.”  
Jaime Loredo, who was arrested on drug charges in 2025, was detained by ICE right after his family posted bail.  
Loredo is a messy example of writs in action, as he was moved from ICE detention in Massachusetts to Virgina. ICE ignored at least one state writ to have Loredo appear virtually, and honored multiple others. The state prosecutor did not file a federal writ to have him appear in person, and the federal government deported Loredo before trial. Like the Noralus case, the court similarly declined to dismiss Loredo’s charges and issued a default warrant.  
Loredo then came back into the United States and was arrested again. 
Keeping cases and defaults open can punish defendants for absences beyond their control and complicate immigration or asylum proceedings. This puts them in a “terrible limbo,” said Michaela Martin Strout, Loredo’s attorney.  
Norales and Loredo’s attorneys argued that defaults issued when someone is unable to appear due to ICE action violates defendants’ constitutional right to due process. But justices suggested in some cases, “the default serves a practical purpose for a person who doesn’t deserve to be let off scot-free,” said Justice Scott Kafker. 
Rulings from the high court are supposed to be handed down within 130 days of the oral arguments but can take longer. 
Amid the thorny questions of prosecutors reporting immigration action or the mixed incentives of defaults and open warrants targeting people well outside the state’s jurisdiction, justices appeared most clear on one takeaway — if judges can act, they should. 
“You have to try,” said Justice Dalila Wendlandt of the Suffolk judge’s refusal to submit a corrected writ to ICE. “I’m not just making that up. I think it’s the case law.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas agriculture and rural communities need immigrants, but system has failed them
description: TOPEKA — Blame for the lack of immigration reform to meet the needs of workers and the agriculture industry lies squarely with the federal government, and change must happen, one farmer said in response to September immigration raids in southwest Kansas. “This is one of those rare situations where the humanitarian and economic interests align,” […]
text:
Kansas ranchers and farmers want immigration reform because their industry is dependent on immigrant workers, a reality that affected southwest Kansas cattle operations in late September when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained immigrants and businesses had to stop or delay work because employees didn't show up. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Blame for the lack of immigration reform to meet the needs of workers and the agriculture industry lies squarely with the federal government, and change must happen, one farmer said in response to September immigration raids in southwest Kansas.
“This is one of those rare situations where the humanitarian and economic interests align,” said Brian Vulgamore, a fifth-generation farmer and Kansas businessman.
Vulgamore’s opinion about the crisis, first posted online, drew vigorous opposition from many and highlighted frustrations in the Midwestern, agriculture-based states that largely vote Republican. Immigrants are necessary to adequately operate many businesses, farms and ranches, but there isn’t a workable process to bring them to the country legally.   
Vulgamore Family Farms is a growing operation, both in size and scope, moving in the last 25 years from a couple of employees to more than 60 during busy seasons, Vulgamore wrote in an email.
“We have employees who grew up speaking six different languages, with education ranging from eighth grade to a Ph.D.,” he said. “We could not have built the operation we have today without immigrant labor.”
Brian Vulgamore, fifth-generation Kansas farmer, says the government must find a way to reform the immigration process. Immigrants benefit small Kansas towns and agriculture, he says. (Photo from Vulgamore Family Farms website)
Vulgamore’s farm employs immigrant workers through the H-2A visa program, which allows agricultural operations to apply for immigrants to work temporary and seasonal agricultural jobs. 
However, seasonal workers don’t meet the needs of much of the industry, including the beef processing plants and farm operations that need help year-round. The United States needs a legal path for workers that “doesn’t take years and cost a fortune to navigate,” Vulgamore said. 
“I also think we need to look beyond simply filling jobs,” he said. “One of the shortcomings of H-2A is that it brings us workers, but not necessarily families who can fully participate in our communities. An H-2A worker can bring a spouse and children on H-4 visas, but those family members generally can’t legally work.”
When immigrant families move to the community, both spouses can work, which strengthens struggling rural communities and fills jobs that would otherwise remain vacant, such as positions in the service industry, Vulgamore said. 
“We’re fighting to maintain our population, sustain our tax base, keep enough kids in our schools and pay for basic services,” he said. “We can’t do that without people. We need workers, but more importantly, we need families who want to live here, raise their kids here and become part of our communities.”
 
Southwest Kansas operation
U.S. Immigration and Enforcement Agents performed immigrant detention operations in southwest Kansas the week of Sept. 22, detaining about 110 people. Their presence in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal caused beef processing plants to shorten or cancel shifts when employees didn’t show up for work. 
Restaurants closed, and hotel managers said they couldn’t rent rooms because employees didn’t show up to work. 
Effects on the beef processing industry generated nationwide concern about how far behind the plants were falling and how that would raise beef prices. 
Glynn Tonsor, Kansas State University agricultural economics professor, said the week of the raids that long-term effects of a beef processing slow-down are determined by how long it lasts. 
“It’s very hard to know the duration of these events, and with that, the duration of the labor response,” he said.
Cargill and National Beef Co., which have facilities in the area that were affected, didn’t answer Kansas Reflector questions about whether they have returned to operating at full capacity. Employees in the area report that most shifts have returned. 
If the plants don’t run at full capacity for less than a week, Tonsor said, it will likely take just one or two weeks to catch up.
“The reason I’m saying that is we already have less cattle than the industry wants,” he said. “There’s extra hooks in the country, which isn’t good for margins for packers, by the way. But the system will have the capacity to catch up if the labor is there.”
However, if disruptions had occurred over a longer timeframe or if they become more frequent, then cattle and beef prices would be affected, Tonsor said. 
“The more of these disruptions and the longer these disruptions exist, lowers cattle prices and raises beef prices,” he said. “The reason for that is the cost of converting a live animal into beef is going up because the cost of labor and the uncertainty of having labor are both going up.”
Immigrant labor challenges have come along with other labor force shifts, Tonsor said. 
“Having kids later in life and having fewer per female puts us at or below replacement rate,” he said. “Then you have the immigration disruption, which is what we’re talking about here. But it’s not new. This country’s had net immigration to augment our own domestic (issues). You’ve had more aggregate labor because of it.”
The Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association released a statement noting the effects on the industry from ongoing ICE operations in the three states. 
“These disruptions come at a time of enhanced focus and pressure on the cattle and beef supply chain,” the statement said. “They are a costly and unnecessary impact to cattle producers already suffering from unwelcome political interference to both the markets as well as the physical supply chain. Frustratingly, the harm these actions cause to cattle producers last for days and weeks after such operations conclude.”
That statement was greeted with criticism from some in Kansas who support ICE operations, but it received support from others. Ashley Franklin, who works with cattle in the Pratt area, said online that they had documented workers who were afraid to come to work. 
“I’m covering 2-3 jobs as a manager just to ensure cattle’s BASIC NEEDS are met,” she wrote. “My coworkers shouldn’t have to feel threatened just because of their skin color. I will protect my employees at all costs, even if it means I come to work at 3AM and not leave until the job is done.” 
 
‘Reliable, legal workforce’
Scarlett Madinger, spokeswoman for the Kansas Livestock Association, said one of the group’s concerns about the raids was that immigrant employees working legally were scared to show up to work. 
Labor issues in agriculture aren’t new, she said. The organization’s members would like to see workers who have been present in the United States for a certain number of years — and compliant with local, state and federal laws — have the opportunity to adjust their immigration status, Madinger said. 
“Agriculture needs a reliable, legal workforce, particularly for the livestock industry,” she said. “We just need a better way to get to that legal status. And then also, there needs to be immigration policy that provides for an efficient and effective guest worker program that really accommodates year-round needs of livestock operations.”
Nine Republican state legislators from southwest Kansas sent a letter to President Donald Trump, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann, and U.S. Sens. Jerry Moran and  Roger Marshall, asking for needed immigration changes, while clarifying that they support legal processes and border security. 
The lawmakers asked to modernize agricultural and essential-worker visa program; fix immigration courts and asylum processing “so cases are resolved fairly and promptly”; create an earned legal status process for long-established residents with clean records who pay back taxes; and to “pair stronger employer accountability with enough legal-worker visas that compliance is realistic.”
“Southwest Kansas is built by people who work hard, obey the law, and contribute to their communities,” the letter said. “We stand with local law enforcement and ask for coordination that makes enforcement more effective, alongside the legal reforms needed to finish the job.”
The nine lawmakers were Sen. Ron Ryckman, Sen. Bill Clifford, Rep. Gary White, Rep. Jim Minnix, Rep. Jason W. Goetz, Rep. Lon Pishny, Rep. Bob Lewis, Rep. Marty Long and Rep. Shannon Francis.  
Changing the immigration process doesn’t mean ignoring immigration laws, Kansas farmer Vulgamore said. 
“It means recognizing the economic and demographic reality we face,” he said. “In my opinion, we’re foolish not to find a legal way to welcome and retain people who are willing to work and genuinely want to build their lives in our rural communities.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC’s next CEO can build on this critical, life-saving part of McMaster’s legacy
description: If you or someone you know is in crisis, please call, text, or chat 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Help is free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. In January, South Carolina will swear-in its first new governor in 10 years. If you’ve heard our current […]
text:
Gov. Henry McMaster speaks in Florence on June 15, 2023, to celebrate a $100 million state investment to build a regional behavioral health hub. The center that opened in August 2025 is named after the late Senate Finance Chairman Hugh Leatherman of Florence and his wife Jean. Behind McMaster are officials with McLeod Health, the Medical University of South Carolina, the state Department of Health and Human Services, and legislators. (Photo by Jeff Leieritz)If you or someone you know is in crisis, please call, text, or chat 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Help is free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
In January, South Carolina will swear-in its first new governor in 10 years.
If you’ve heard our current governor speak publicly, you’ve likely heard him beam with pride as he discusses the state’s booming economy and the $54 billion in new capital investment during his tenure. In other settings, Gov. Henry McMaster has touted raising starting teachers’ pay by 68% in South Carolina and providing funds to place a school resource officer in every public school in the state.
These are all legacy-building accomplishments.
However, the benefits of what might be McMaster’s greatest impact may never be fully known.
Mental illness, which often hides in plain sight, can be like that.
On Jan. 19, 2022, I received a call from the governor’s office advising that he was going to call on the South Carolina Department of Health and Human Services to address youth mental health.
A few hours later, in his State of the State address, McMaster declared “a mental health crisis exists in South Carolina” and tasked the agency with “an immediate review of our state’s behavioral health funding and delivery system.”
This declaration and call to action kicked off a series of actions. An audit, a study, fiscal analysis and Statehouse meetings. Within four months, policy proposals were developed to address the
state’s mental health-to-student ratio, which stood at a staggering one mental health counselor per 1,300 students.
These commonsense proposals became policy and took effect two months later.
The foundational change supporting these changes was an incentive structure that based reimbursement levels for these services on counselors’ level of licensure. This new incentive structure was coupled with a collaborative approach that made it easier for school districts to directly hire counselors and partner with licensed counselors from the private sector.
Importantly, these changes included a robust survey and data monitoring component to ensure services being billed were being delivered as authorized.
Announcing these changes came with an audacious goal: cut the ratio in half by the start of the following school year.
Mental health counselors in schools doubled since 2022, report finds

South Carolina did.
Survey data from the start of the 2023-24 school year showed a mental health counselor-to-student ratio of 1-to-653. Progress has continued as the rate improved to 1-to-567 at the start of last school year.
The state’s improvement in providing access to school-based behavioral health services led to additional, and sorely needed, investment in the state’s behavioral health system.
In June 2023, the Department of Health and Human Services awarded $45.5 million to hospitals across the state to build 13 specialized hospital-based emergency department units dedicated to behavioral health crises.
In August 2025, a collaborative effort between state agencies, hospital systems, educational partners and the city of Florence led to the opening of an innovative, $100 million-plus regional
behavioral health hub to serve the Pee Dee region.
In the Upstate, a $138 million Prisma behavioral health hospital is currently under construction in Easley.
Together, these efforts were designed to invest in infrastructure and help identify and address behavioral health issues from an early intervention system, in the case of school-based counseling, to high intensity intervention, in the case of hospital-based services.
More opportunities remain.
In 2024, an independent study described South Carolina as having the “most fragmented” health and human services system in the country.
Progress has been made on this front too.
In June 2025, McMaster signed a bill (S. 2) into law aimed at addressing that fragmentation by consolidating three adjacent state agencies into the newly created South Carolina Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities.
Bill that aims to improve services for people who ‘fall through the cracks’ advances in SC Senate

Placing these agencies and their citizen-facing programs under a common governance and single point of accountability has the potential to streamline services while also increasing efficiencies by consolidating duplicative functions.
Effective leadership of these services can (literally) be a vital difference maker.
September is recognized as National Suicide Prevention Month; as we move later into the fall, I’m reminded of another call I received about a mental health crisis. On Valentine’s Day 2015, a neighbor called to tell me my dad had died by suicide.
That call was my real introduction to the need for effective leadership and access to these critical services.
Suicide is preventable.
Under McMaster, South Carolina has made significant progress in living up to its motto: “While I breathe, I hope.”
With the newly established agency’s placement in the governor’s Cabinet, Attorney General Alan Wilson or Rep. Jermaine Johnson will have an opportunity to build on a critical, albeit less-publicized, piece of McMaster’s lasting legacy.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Pa. Republicans tout Trump accounts at state Capitol
description: This story was originally published by WITF. U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent was in Harrisburg on Monday to promote new federal savings accounts for children that the Trump administration says will help more Americans build wealth. “President Trump believes that the American dream belongs to every child and every family,” Bessent said at […]
text:
U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent visited Harrisburg to promote new federal savings accounts for children. (Haley O'Brien/WITF)This story was originally published by WITF.
U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent was in Harrisburg on Monday to promote new federal savings accounts for children that the Trump administration says will help more Americans build wealth.
“President Trump believes that the American dream belongs to every child and every family,” Bessent said at a news conference at the state Capitol. “Through Trump accounts, we are equipping the next generation to claim its rightful share of it.”
Trump accounts, created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, allow children to build a savings to use when they turn 18. Officials are encouraging parents to claim it online or by downloading the Trump accounts app.
All U.S. children are eligible for an account. But those born between 2025 and 2028 will have a one-time $1,000 contribution from the U.S. Treasury.
Adults in a child’s life, along with charities, philanthropists and employers can contribute to the accounts. Donations from friends and family will be capped at $5,000 annually.
Pa. Treasurer Stacy Garrity, the Republican nominee for Pennsylvania governor, said the accounts will pave the way to college for some.
“Trump accounts are here for education, but they go way beyond the classroom, and they can be used for a first-time home purchase to start a business or retirement,” she said.
Officials at the news conference were joined by families with young children enrolled in the program. Emily Kreps, a Harrisburg mom, said the initiative is great for middle-class families.
“We can contribute to save for our children’s future, as well as family and friends can contribute to it, and it’s been a great tool for teaching my children about saving and investing in the stock market,” she said.
“This is how we build an ownership economy in which all citizens are shareholders. Today, 38% of Americans have no exposure to our great equity markets,” he said. “Now, a generation that once might have watched American prosperity from a distance will grow up with a piece of it in their accounts.”
U. S. Congressman Scott Perry (R-10), who is running for reelection against Democrat Janelle Stelson, called the young children at the event the wealthy people of the next generation.
“These are the new people… who are going to come from Harrisburg and do great things and be great members of society because they’re going to have something,” he said.
Perry, who has a history of supporting Social Security cuts, was criticized by the Democratic party for promoting Trump’s agenda.
“With less than a month until Election Day, Scott Perry is hanging out with Scott Bessent — Trump’s Treasury Secretary who has championed privatizing Social Security and embraced the illegal tariffs raising costs for working Pennsylvanians,” Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said in a statement Monday afternoon.
Bessent said the administration does not plan to cut social security.
“Unequivocally no cuts in Social Security,” he said. “The Trump accounts are a supplement, not a substitute… if they have maintained their Trump accounts into retirement age, then they will also have a substantial nest egg that they can draw upon for their retirement needs.”

 Catching Our Eye

• Healthcare in Ohio. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler is reporting, “$2.2B Bayer plant will be Ohio’s largest-ever international healthcare project.”
A historic $2.2 billion investment is coming to central Ohio from the German pharmaceutical and biotechnology company Bayer.
The processing and manufacturing plant will make drugs to treat cancer, heart disease and other conditions. It’s the state’s largest ever international healthcare project and the largest German direct investment in Ohio history, said Gov. Mike DeWine.
“This was a big investment by New Albany, but also JobsOhio. I think JobsOhio has put $30 million in this, and you’re going to see people trained right here and there will come out and go right into Bayer,” DeWine told reporters at the company’s announcement.
Bayer is also expected to get an incentive from the Ohio Tax Credit Authority at a later date.
• Trump and data centers. The Associated Press’ Seung Min Kim is reporting, “Trump defends data centers in Ohio as he rallies to boost Jon Husted in a tight Senate race.”
President Donald Trump on Saturday defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds.
Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio to promote his administration’s action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The crowd, which had reacted enthusiastically as the president talked about other policies, was far more muted during the data centers remark.
• Education. Ideastream’s Conor Morris is reporting, “How Ohio’s educational service centers can help schools navigate tough budget times.”
With more schools dealing with financial challenges in Ohio due to rising costs, school leaders are facing a conundrum: how to provide the same, or better, education services with fewer resources.
Despite the tough times, leaders with Ohio’s Educational Service Centers, or ESCs, say they are here to help. But what is an ESC, and what is their role in Ohio education?
ESCs are regional public education agencies that are spread out across Ohio. There are 51 in total. Their main goal is to provide support services to schools.
