title: Trump effect hovers over race for Nevada attorney general
description: President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Adriana Guzmán Fralick may have helped secure her victory in the Republican primary for Nevada attorney general, but now it may be a liability heading into her general election where she faces Democratic nominee Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro. Cannizzaro, like Democrats up and down the ballot, has been campai[...]
text:
Adriana Guzmán Fralick, Nicole Cannizzaro. (Candidate photos)President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Adriana Guzmán Fralick may have helped secure her victory in the Republican primary for Nevada attorney general, but now it may be a liability heading into her general election where she faces Democratic nominee Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro.
Cannizzaro, like Democrats up and down the ballot, has been campaigning on her experience fighting Trump administration policies as a legislator.
Meanwhile, Guzmán Fralick removed from her campaign website a banner highlighting her Trump endorsement, according to archived copies. She did so sometime after her primary against Douglas County Commissioner Danny Tarkanian, whom her campaign routinely attacked as being anti-Trump.
While her campaign now downplays the Trump endorsement, Guzmán Fralick has kept up the prominent highlighting of her endorsement by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Guzmán Fralick has been described as handpicked by the governor’s camp. Lombardo, who is running for a second term and is facing Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford, has similarly been forced to navigate how to appeal to a general public seemingly souring on Trump without angering the MAGA machine and its base.
An “issues” section of Guzmán Fralick’s campaign website was also reorganized, according to internet archives. A section highlighting her commitment to “securing Nevada’s elections” and backing Trump’s SAVE Act was moved down.
Still, Guzmán Fralick has spoken highly of Trump in the interviews she has done on the campaign trail. She led the Pledge of Allegiance at Trump’s August rally in Las Vegas and later recounted to Veterans in Politics that she “almost cried” while meeting the president.
Guzmán Fralick in that interview also spoke highly of former Gov. Jim Gibbons, who is best known for personal scandals and being the only incumbent governor in Nevada to lose their primary. Gibbons gave Guzmán Fralick one of her first roles in the public sector.
Guzmán Fralick went to work for several state commissions and boards, most recently the Cannabis Compliance Board, which she chaired. Lombardo appointed her to that board.
This November she faces Cannizzaro, who has served in the Nevada State Legislature since 2016 and currently serves as Senate majority leader. She is the first woman to hold the position. Cannizzaro has championed reproductive rights, criminal justice and education bills.
Outside of the Legislature, she spent a decade as a criminal prosecutor within the Clark County District Attorney’s Office before moving to Richard Harris Personal Injury Law Firm.
She told the Current before the June primary that she sees the AG office as a natural extension of her experience as a prosecutor and legislator.
The Nevada Attorney General’s Office has more than 400 employees, including 155 attorneys and 62 investigators, according to its most recent biennial report. The office represents the state in lawsuits. That can include major nationwide litigation, like those filed against pharmaceutical companies, social media companies or the federal government. It can also be criminal cases, such as those related to Medicaid provider fraud.
The Nevada attorney general’s office has been a springboard for higher office. Brian Sandoval, a Republican, went from AG to governor in 2005. Catherine Cortez Masto, a Democrat, went from AG to the U.S. Senate in 2015. Republican Adam Laxalt, served one term as AG then ran for governor and U.S. Senate, though he was unsuccessful both times. Ford is now running for governor.
Guzmán Fralick and Cannizzaro both attended the University of Nevada Reno for undergraduate degrees, then attended UNLV’s Boyd School of Law, though not at the same time.
Both women emphasize their working class roots. Guzmán Fralick is an immigrant who says her family arrived in Northern Nevada on the Fourth of July when she was 9 years old. Cannizzaro on the campaign trail and in legislative hearings has noted her parents worked in the service industry and she became the first in her family to graduate college.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s high housing costs are driving the poverty rate, study finds
description: In CT, high housing costs are exacerbating the poverty rate. 21% of poverty can be attributed to the state's above-average housing costs.
text:
Connecticut is among 10 states in the nation with the highest average housing costs, and it’s been proven to exacerbate the state’s poverty rate.
Twenty-one percent of poverty, and 26% of child poverty, can be attributed to above-average housing costs in Connecticut, according to a new report by the Pew Charitable Trusts.
“There’s a shortage of housing, and so we’ve seen rents go up there because there just aren’t enough homes getting added,” Alex Horowitz, Pew project director, said. “Connecticut is in a long-term landlords market because tenants are competing for scarce homes instead of landlords competing for tenants.”
The report analyzed 10 states with the highest housing costs nationwide, to determine the impact housing costs have on impoverished families.
“If those states had average housing costs instead, how much of their poverty would that alleviate?” Horowitz said. “Or the converse, how much of their poverty is caused by having above average housing costs?”
Expensive housing is offsetting the financial relief many struggling families could receive from programs meant to help them, like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Housing Choice Vouchers and, for developers, Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, Horowitz said.
“Those programs are crucial, but some of the help they provide is being lost to high rents because even if someone is receiving more assistance, but then their rent keeps going up, some of that assistance they’re receiving is going away,” Horowitz said. “If our anti-poverty programs are going to be effective, that means that we need to reduce people’s expenses as well as upping their incomes, and more housing can do it.”
The state with the highest rate of poverty caused by high housing costs is Hawaii, followed by California, according to the report. Connecticut was tied for 7th.
The main way to alleviate the strain housing costs place on families is to build more housing, Horowitz said.
Passing state laws that make it easier to construct housing, including decreasing lot size requirements for homes and allowing smaller apartment buildings to have one stairwell, are some of the things that can be done to help the burden being caused by the housing crisis, according to Horowitz.
He also said zoning changes that shift from the single-family home mindset to building more townhomes, condos or apartments will balance the market.
“From 2017 to 2023, Connecticut ranked 49th in the entire United States in housing production per capita,” Horowitz said. “If you look at 2011 to 2016, all states in the U.S. combined passed an average of one law a year to allow more homes. In 2025, there were more than 100 laws passed at the state level to allow more homes.”
It needn’t just be affordable homes and apartments built either, Horowitz said. Any type of construction is beneficial.
“It may be counterintuitive that adding more new housing, even if it’s not subsidized, could help alleviate that. But the evidence is clear that it can,” Horowitz said.
This story was first published Oct. 5, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Nevada Current
title: Attorney challenging longtime Family Court judge
description: Judge Bill Henderson, who was first elected in 2008, is seeking a fourth six-year term in Clark County Family Court Department R.  Henderson came in second of three candidates in the July primary with 35% of the vote to attorney Marilyn Caston, who had 45%.  This is Caston’s second run for the bench. She lost […]
text:
Marilyn Anne Caston, Bill Henderson. (Candidate photos)Judge Bill Henderson, who was first elected in 2008, is seeking a fourth six-year term in Clark County Family Court Department R. 
Henderson came in second of three candidates in the July primary with 35% of the vote to attorney Marilyn Caston, who had 45%. 
This is Caston’s second run for the bench. She lost a 2020 primary for Family Court Dept. U with 24% of the vote.  
Henderson attended Washburn University School of Law in 1984 and was admitted to the Nevada Bar in 1987. 
Half of the 107 attorneys who evaluated Henderson in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 poll said he should be retained. Henderson’s highest score was for integrity while his lowest score was for legal ability.  
Of 38 appeals filed on Henderson’s rulings during his three terms, the judge has been in error 50% of the time, according to Our Nevada Judges, which tracks judicial records. 
Henderson did not respond to requests for an interview. His website says he’s endorsed by a variety of law enforcement associations, Veterans in Politics, the Nevada Veterans Association, the AFL-CIO of Nevada, and IATSE 720. 
As of October 1, Henderson had raised $49,000 and had $12,000 on hand. 
Caston has raised $20,800 as of July and had $3,100 in the bank. She is endorsed by a number of unions, including SEIU Nevada, Culinary Local 226, Southern Nevada Building Trades, Carpenters Local 1977, and Teamsters Nevada. She’s also endorsed by community organizations PLAN Action, Independent Black Voters, and the National Organization of Women (NOW). 
After earning a degree in Political Science from UNLV, Caston went on to obtain her law degree from Boyd School of Law, She was admitted to practice in Nevada in 2009. 
Caston says she’s running because candidates elected to Family Court in 2020 lacked “what we call general family law experience. Divorce, child custody, termination, child support – we’ve had issues in the past with judges bridging that gap from a specialized area of family law.” 
She says she’d like to see a Family Court version of business court to hear financially complicated divorce cases. “We’re dealing with the same fiduciary duties, or maybe even more complicated.” 
Henderson, in a video posted on his website, advises Family Court litigants not to forgo hiring an attorney, at least initially to get into court-ordered mediation. 
Caston notes that’s unrealistic advice for some 70% to 80% of parties who are unrepresented.
The mediation process, which is mandatory for all litigants, generally doesn’t work when an attorney gets involved, she says. 
Caston says a program spearheaded by Family Court Judge Gregory Gordon for pro se litigants is having success. 
“There are no lawyers involved. Parties can opt into this program and say ‘Here’s my evidence and all my witnesses and you ust ask whatever questions you have, Your Honor, to make your decision,’” Caston says of the program. “I’ve been on the other side of pro se litigants, and if we’re doing it the real way, and you don’t have an attorney, you are at a disadvantage.” 
Litigants who rely on artificial intelligence to write legal pleadings are creating a “nightmare,” she says. “My own clients send me stuff all the time that they ChatGPT. The robots want to please you, so they will make stuff up, and I can tell immediately that it’s not true.”
But parties, she says, can’t tell. 
“They put it into a pleading or they say it in court. They’re just losing credibility, “ says Caston, adding “a lot of attorneys are using it, too, and getting in trouble. It hallucinates cases and will misstate things.” 
Caston says that if elected, she’d make a distinction between the way she admonishes an attorney who uses AI in pleadings and an unrepresented litigant. “We’re told as attorneys that we’re always going to be held to a different standard.”
One good use of AI, she says, is for litigants to use it as a “tone monitor” by consulting it as a sounding board when they want to communicate with their ex-partner. 
“It will try to tell them how to say something more politely and get their point across without being combative or mean.” A number of co-parenting apps do the same, says Caston, who recommends parents use them. 
The way parents communicate can be crucial to a judge’s ruling, Caston contends. 
“If you’re the one perceived to be creating the conflict, it can really tip the balance,” she says, adding the judge is looking for the party who “can overlook their own emotional response” in the interest of the children. A text message that indicates otherwise and is entered as evidence can make the difference in a custody case. “A lot of times it comes down to the judge asking ‘How do you guys talk to one another?’”
Caston says if elected, she’ll advocate for earlier start times in Family Court and for better communication with parties, who she says sometimes show up for a hearing without being notified that it’s cancelled. 
Early voting begins Saturday, Oct. 17. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts can’t afford to skip natural gas pipeline upgrade
description: Project Beacon would add about 300 million cubic feet of natural gas capacity per day—roughly enough to meet the winter needs of 840,000 homes, or more than half of Massachusetts residential gas accounts.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS RESIDENTS HAVE some of the highest energy rates in the country, and costs are trending the wrong way. Since 2018, residential electricity prices have increased by 41 percent, and natural gas prices for home heating bills have increased 62 percent, costing an average family an additional $623 per year. 
A new study published by the Fiscal Alliance Foundation has found that building the proposed Project Beacon natural gas pipeline expansion project could help Massachusetts families and businesses save $367 million in heating and electric bills during an average winter. 
Proposed by Enbridge, Project Beacon would add about 300 million cubic feet of natural gas capacity per day—roughly enough to meet the winter needs of 840,000 homes, or more than half of Massachusetts residential gas accounts. The project would not break new ground either but would instead accomplish the upgrade by increasing the size of the existing pipeline and adding more compression along the line. 
This additional gas capacity would save Massachusetts residential customers $184 million per winter, on average, across both natural gas and power savings, according to the report written by Always On Energy Research. This means the average family would save $72 per winter on natural gas heating costs and $23 per winter in lower electricity costs, for total savings of $95 during an average winter. 
These savings dwarf the costs. The report estimated the pipeline would cost households $19 per winter, representing an average net savings of $76 per winter, meaning it would provide $5 in average household savings for every dollar spent on the pipeline, a return that any asset manager would be eager to achieve. 
Small businesses would also save $163 million per winter. The study found the average commercial account would save $792 per winter against a cost of $170, a net gain of $622. For a neighborhood restaurant, a dry cleaner, or a family-run shop, that’s real money: a part-time shift, a piece of equipment, or a reason not to raise prices. 
These figures represent the average per-winter savings, but the savings would be substantially higher during colder winters, with household savings reaching $173 in a winter like 2025–26, which included Winter Storm Fern, and lower during mild winters, like 2023–24, when residential customers could expect to save only $43. 
Savings are larger during the coldest winter periods because this is when natural gas demand is highest. A majority of Massachusetts homes are heated with natural gas, and natural gas is the largest source of electricity in the state. While demand rises as the mercury dips, the supply of natural gas is constrained by the size of the pipeline, much like Uber prices surge during periods of high demand. By upgrading the size of the pipeline, more gas can flow to homes, businesses, and power plants, potentially reducing the overall cost of the surge in prices. 
While Project Beacon will reduce heating and electric bills for customers, it is not a miracle worker that can completely undo the effects of costly energy policies enacted on Beacon Hill. US Energy Information Administration data show that higher natural gas prices have accounted for only a small portion of rising home-heating bills. 
Of the $623 increase in annual home heating bills since 2018, approximately $88 came from higher fuel costs, while distribution, policy, and other non-fuel charges account for roughly $535. This means that Project Beacon’s estimated $53 in net gas savings ($72 in savings minus $19 in costs) could offset roughly 60 percent of the increase attributable to fuel costs in an average winter. 
However, other cost drivers, such as Mass Save, which adds roughly $200 to $325 per year to a typical household’s natural gas bill, according to rates compiled by state Sen. Will Brownsberger, will need to be reformed to bring further energy-cost relief to Massachusetts families and businesses. 
Even the Healey administration is finding it increasingly difficult to ignore Massachusetts’s need for additional natural gas capacity. Last week, the governor called on the Trump administration to expedite its review of Enbridge’s RARE project, a smaller expansion of the same Algonquin pipeline system that would add roughly 75 million cubic feet of natural gas capacity per day.  
Healey said the project would lower costs for 600,000 customers and urged federal officials to move quickly so consumers could realize the savings. That same logic should apply to Project Beacon, which would add roughly four times as much capacity and, according to our study, deliver far greater savings to Massachusetts ratepayers. 
Project Beacon is not a choice between building infrastructure and protecting ratepayers. The numbers in the report suggest that building the infrastructure is the best way to protect ratepayers.  
Paul Craney is the executive director of the Fiscal Alliance Foundation. Isaac Orr is the vice president of research at Always On Energy Research

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Danbury mayor calls white power rally participants ‘cowards’
description: A social media psot showed masked people on a Danbury corner with a sign saying “Keep New England White.” They appear to have been outside the police dept.
text:
A video posted to social media shows about a dozen masked people on a street corner holding a sign that says “Keep New England White.” Someone can be heard yelling “White power.” 
They appear to have been just outside the city’s police headquarters.
Danbury Mayor Roberto Alvez said he respects free speech.
“But we’re also entitled to stand up against them and call them the cowards they are,” Alvez said. “This is why they come in masks. It might not be a white sheet and a white hood anymore; the KKK is a black mask and T-shirts now, but it’s the exact same thing.”
Alves said the people at the rally wore masks for a reason.
“They don’t want their families to know who they are,” he said. “They don’t want their neighbors to know who they are. They don’t want their employers to know who they are. Because they know what they’re doing is wrong and they are cowards for that. It is meant to drive fear in a diverse community, but we are not scared. We will stand united.”
Tensions have been high in Danbury this year after multiple ICE raids, including an extended operation in August where agents detained at least 70 people.
Carolina Bortoletto is with Danbury United for Immigrants. She said it’s not a coincidence.
“It’s tied to the anti-immigrant violence that we’re seeing across Connecticut and in the state,” Bortoletto said. Those folks who came to Danbury on Saturday, their goal is to strike fear into a community.”
Alves said police are investigating. He said the rallygoers appear to have shown up only for a few minutes and quickly dispersed.
This story was first published Oct. 5, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: AI may soon be in more healthcare processes in Utah under new state agreements
description: Utahns may start seeing more artificial intelligence tools in their doctors visits now that the state’s Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy signed agreements with healthcare providers to test pilots to accelerate healthcare processes through AI, including an improved medication refill system and tools to expand dermatology and postpartum offerings. The[...]
text:
Zach Boyd, Director of the Utah Office of AI Policy explains an AI in healthcare initiative at a news conference on Oct. 5, 2026. (Courtesy of the Utah Department of Commerce)Utahns may start seeing more artificial intelligence tools in their doctors visits now that the state’s Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy signed agreements with healthcare providers to test pilots to accelerate healthcare processes through AI, including an improved medication refill system and tools to expand dermatology and postpartum offerings.
The pilot programs are part of an expansion of the state’s AI regulatory sandbox capabilities. Combined with a “master agreement” with Intermountain Health and University of Utah Health, public officials hope the efforts will help shape state policy on the technology’s safety and transparency standards with oversight from third-party evaluators.
“There’s so much out there that causes a lot of doom and gloom around AI that I think we tend to sometimes overlook the promise of AI, and healthcare is one of those areas where there’s a lot of promise here,” Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, whose bill created the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, said during the initiative’s announcement on Monday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Healthcare is one of the clearest examples of why this AI policy lab approach will be amazing,” he said. “We’re going to create better access, potentially lower costs, create new innovation within the healthcare industry, and potentially even solve some of the healthcare problems that are out there.”
The office had already been overseeing some healthcare related pilots, including a first-in-the-nation program that allows an AI system to approve some prescription medication renewals in the state. The initiative was deeply criticized by members of the Utah Medical Licensing Board for not including their input before the program’s implementation.
Medical Licensing Board calls for suspension of Utah pilot program using AI to refill prescriptions

Now, the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence is bringing more stakeholders and more expertise to ensure pilots are done well and have a viable path to scale, said Zach Boyd, director of the office.
The agreement the state signed with Intermountain Health and University of Utah Health covers data privacy, AI governance and other aspects to allow the institutions to test AI tools and report back with their findings.
“We’re really hopeful and optimistic that these tools, when you bring critical evaluation and have a human in the loop, can actually allow us to provide better care for patients,” said Jim Hotaling, chief innovation officer at University of Utah Health.
Especially, he said, when healthcare leaders worry about access and the number of physicians may become insufficient to serve Utah communities.
“We’re expecting that up to 40% of the providers that deliver healthcare today won’t be here by 2035. They’ll be retired,” Dan Liljenquist, chief strategy officer Intermountain Health said during the announcement. “And the systems to train new people have not emerged quickly enough to meet the challenge, and so AI is an important tool in figuring out a bridge from an old model to a new model.”



Let us know what you think...


 


In addition to those master agreements, the state has also approved three pilot programs with individual companies — one with Nolla Health to use AI to deal with mild and moderate acne in telehealth consultations. 
“This is a very common condition relative to some other conditions. It’s comparatively low risk. We’re doing a lot to make sure we’re clearly identifying when it’s appropriate for the AI to be supporting the treatment,” Boyd said.
Another one is from Expect Fitness, another telehealth company, which came up with an “AI-enabled physical therapy pathway to support women experiencing postpartum recovery, urinary incontinence, and pelvic health issues,” according to a news release.
In that program, Boyd said, patients would receive AI-supported intake and treatment plan development support, allowing a small number of remote physical therapists to help more patients from home.
The last is August AI, a prescription refill program similar to the one that was already being tested in the state. But this one, he said, is incorporating some of the lessons learned from the previous iteration.
Some major additions are the inspection of third-party evaluators to vet the program, Boyd said, as well as better integration of electronic health records, a better accountability system for the company, and a new risk formula to determine what types of prescriptions are adequate for the program and which ones have a higher risk.
With the participation of Intermountain Health and University of Utah Health in the AI sandbox, the state expects the AI tools to have a broader reach, Margaret Busse, commissioner of the Utah Department of Commerce said. 
“As they figure out specific use cases to deploy, that’s where probably I would say most patients in Utah will see it,” Busse said. “But all patients can have access in the sense that they can participate in any of them and they can be patients of any of the businesses that have gotten regulatory mitigation from us.” 
The hope for the program as well, she said, is that the Utah AI validations can be recognized in other states as they deploy their own AI standards. 
“We’ve actually talked to our federal delegation, people in D.C.,” Cullimore said about those ambitions. “We’re very interested in this model for doing something like that at the federal level as well.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: National Newspaper Week finds some positive developments amid the doom and gloom in South Dakota
description: When I meet someone new and they find out that I’m retired, it’s only natural for them to ask what I did for a living before I entered this life of leisure. It’s with a certain amount of pride that I tell them that I was a daily newspaper editor. Hearing that bit of news, […]
text:
(Editorial cartoon by Mike English/Moonshine Ink, Truckee, California)When I meet someone new and they find out that I’m retired, it’s only natural for them to ask what I did for a living before I entered this life of leisure. It’s with a certain amount of pride that I tell them that I was a daily newspaper editor.
Hearing that bit of news, it’s only natural for them, at some point in the conversation, to say, “These aren’t very good times for newspapers.” It pains me to admit it, but that’s true.
When I was the editor in Pierre, I felt like I was part of an exclusive group. While larger papers had more than one person with the title of editor, there were only 11 of us in the state who could claim we had responsibility for managing a newsroom at a daily newspaper.
Worn down by the pandemic or hollowed out by corporate greed, many of those 11 newspapers can no longer claim to be “daily.” Some have taken to offering a printed product only once or twice a week, promising to post news online on the days when there is no print edition.
Every community needs somebody asking tough questions

The former Gannett newspapers in the state, in Sioux Falls, Watertown and Aberdeen, have drastically reduced their staffs, resulting in less local news. Let’s hope new ownership by Lee Enterprises makes some improvements.
When times started to get tough for newspapers, there was an opinion in the industry that while daily newspapers would suffer, weekly newspapers would be more likely to hold on to their readers and advertisers. Sadly, that has not always been the case. A growing number of aging publishers at weekly newspapers can’t find anyone willing to buy their publication, continue their legacy and take a chance on the future of local journalism.
Times have gotten so tough that in the past year two weekly newspapers — the Brandon Valley Journal and the Groton Independent — turned to GoFundMe campaigns to provide the working capital they needed to keep the lights on and the presses running.
Newspapers are challenged by the economy, the internet and, in South Dakota, by their own government. Newspaper publishers across the state have reported frequent, maddening delays in the delivery of their newspapers by the U.S. Postal Service. Gone are the days when your friendly neighborhood paperboy delivered the newspaper to your front porch (or your bushes or your rain gutter). Now most newspapers, even those that consider themselves dailies, rely on the Postal Service for delivery.
Some newspapers have reported to the South Dakota NewsMedia Association that they are struggling to retain subscribers because of poor mail delivery.
“All the newspapers mail us copies of their papers to the (SDNA) office here in Brookings,” said David Bordewyk, executive director of SDNA in a story about the state’s problems with postal deliveries by South Dakota News Watch. “One-hundred newspapers are sending them to us. It used to be by the end of the week, by Friday — because most weeklies would be printing and mailing on a Tuesday or Wednesday — we would see more than 90% of the newspapers. Today, by Friday, less than half of them are showing up.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
That’s quite a picture of gloom and doom to present here in the midst of National Newspaper Week. There is, however, some good news about newspapers.
As some newspapers’ corporate owners put aside their responsibility to report on local issues, others have sprung up to compete with them for readers and advertisers. The markets historically served by the Gannett newspapers are now being challenged by robust competitors: The Dakota Scout in Sioux Falls, The Watertown Current and The Aberdeen Insider. New weekly newspapers are also offering competition in Brookings and Rapid City.
These new publications, as well as others across the state that have been able to find a way to thrive in the current climate, know that there continues to be a market for what newspapers have to offer. In an age when so many news sources are shaded to the left or right, South Dakota newspapers continue to play it down the middle in their news columns. They more than live up to the motto for this year’s National Newspaper Week: Rooted in Community. Committed to Truth.



About National Newspaper Week
Since 1940, Newspaper Association Managers has sponsored and supported a week-long promotion of the newspaper industry in the United States and Canada. This year marks the 86th celebration of National Newspaper Week.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri task force seeks clearer standards for deciding when children are safe
description: A state task force created by Gov. Mike Kehoe to recommend changes to Missouri’s child welfare system convened for five hours Monday to begin  developing clearer common standards for determining whether a child is safe that can be used by abuse and neglect investigators, the courts, juvenile officers and others across the state. The Missouri […]
text:
Members of the Missouri Child Welfare Task Force discuss child safety standards on Oct. 5 in Jefferson City. Pictured from left are St. Louis County Chief Juvenile Officer Rick Gaines, Missouri State Courts Administrator Kathy Lloyd, Christian County Circuit Judge Jessica Kruse, Audrain County Associate Circuit Judge Melissa Buckman Young, Children's Division Director Sara Smith and State Rep. Melissa Schmidt (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).A state task force created by Gov. Mike Kehoe to recommend changes to Missouri’s child welfare system convened for five hours Monday to begin  developing clearer common standards for determining whether a child is safe that can be used by abuse and neglect investigators, the courts, juvenile officers and others across the state.
The Missouri Child Welfare Task Force was created the group Aug. 25 by executive order, less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative hearing examining foster care deaths, staff turnover and rising investigation backlogs in the Missouri Children’s Division.
The executive order instructs the task force to propose a statewide definition of child safety, identify gaps and contradictions in existing laws and policies, and establish processes to put the new definitions into practice.
The task force, which includes Children’s Division leaders, lawmakers, judges, law enforcement, private providers, attorneys and advocates, has a Nov. 15 deadline to recommend legislation.
But as members tried Monday to define what makes a child safe or unsafe, two longstanding problems kept intruding on the discussion: a workforce struggling with high turnover and caseloads, and gaps in services designed to keep families safely together.
The task force is using a 2009 child safety guide developed by the American Bar Association for judges and attorneys — as well as tools the division already uses to assess safety and risk, called Structured Decision Making — to guide discussions of potential definitions.
The group agreed to focus on defining three factors that go into determining whether a child is safe: threats to safety, children’s vulnerability and parents’ capacity to remove or minimize threats.
Teri Armistead, director of the department’s Division of Legal Services, said that after assessing those factors, the next step is to determine if services are available that can help a child safely stay in their home.
“The next step is looking at the resources and the services that we have in place in our communities to be able to maintain that child within the home,” Armistead said. “And if not, then it’s removal.”
 Workforce challenges

State Rep. Melissa Schmidt, a Republican from Eldridge and chair of the task force, said clear statewide criteria for assessing safety and making decisions about cases could also ease some of the pressure on frontline workers.
“A lot of the burnout and the burden of the frontline workers is that they are having to make a lot of these decisions on their own, and then they’re grappling with, was that the right decision?” Schmidt said. “…That’s why we’re losing some of them. It’s not the only reason, but those are heavy decisions to make on your own.”
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith said turnover among frontline division workers is 40%. Turnover reached 55% in fiscal year 2022, after then-Gov. Mike Parson cut almost 100 jobs in the division in 2020, citing COVID-19 budget constraints. 
Former division workers interviewed by The Independent said high caseloads and increasingly prescriptive requirements to close cases have made it more difficult to help families and contributed to burnout.
Jessica Kruse, a circuit judge for the 38th Judicial Circuit in Christian County, said she worries a recent restructuring of the division’s child abuse and neglect investigations unit could make it harder for workers to meet legally required response times — three hours for emergencies and 24 hours for most other reports.
Since the new structure went into effect Sept. 1, workers have been sent to respond to reports of possible abuse or neglect across much larger swaths of the state, instead of single circuits.
Kruse said she had heard from emergency room nurses in Branson that workers had been sent from as far as St. Louis to respond to certain types of cases.
“It’s all travel time to get to the family,” Kruse said.
Smith said the restructuring is intended to provide frontline workers with support in the field.
“You have to have people that you can call and help navigate the gray,” Smith said.
Emily van Schenkhoff, executive director of the Children’s Trust Fund of Missouri, said “the support for our child welfare workforce is not there right now in the way that it needs to be.”
“There are structural things that we can do in statute, but then there is a whole other separate issue related to our child welfare workforce,” van Schenkhoff said. “You can have all the structure and process in the world, but if you have high turnover rates, high caseloads, you’re going to still have workers that don’t screen in hotlines that they should.”
 Interagency cooperation

The task force is also charged with developing training modules for shared use by frontline division workers, juvenile officers, judges and others in the child welfare system.
Rick Gaines, chief juvenile officer for the 21st Judicial Circuit in St. Louis County, said juvenile officers generally no longer investigate reports of potential abuse or neglect. But he remembers when juvenile officers, division workers and law enforcement worked much more closely in the field.
Now, Gaines said, “it’s almost as if we’re on different planets.”
Haylee Musso, deputy legislative liaison for the division and a former frontline worker, said it was an expectation of the juvenile judge in her circuit that the “multi-disciplinary team” on each case — division workers, juvenile officers, guardians ad litem, who represent children’s interests in court, and others — would collaborate.
“I wasn’t just trained by the division,” Musso said. “I was trained by the (multi-disciplinary team).”
Gaines said he hopes the task force “can try to bridge some of the distance, if you will, between Children’s Division and the juvenile office.”
 Preventative services

Task force members also discussed whether state law should more explicitly allow courts to order services aimed at keeping children safely in their homes.
Currently, courts in some judicial circuits order some families to work with family-centered services workers from the division to receive services available in their communities. But it’s not a practice used consistently throughout the state.
Musso described court-ordered services as “both the stick and the carrot for parents,” saying, “We’re here. We’re going to help you. But the courts are also involved, so you really need to work with us.”
The expansion of court-ordered family centered services was also recommended in 2024 by the state’s Fentanyl Case Review Subcommittee, which aimed to address an increase in fentanyl-related child fatalities.
Task force members said there is a need for more basic parenting classes and in-home parenting support, as well as classes for parents of children with mental or behavioral health conditions.
Van Schenkhoff pointed to broader gaps in services available in the state as a barrier to preventing children from entering foster care.
“When we see a family that needs additional services, often we don’t have the ability to do that,” van Schenkhoff said. “And so what do we do then? We remove. We cannot get to a place that’s where we want to be as a system unless we have more supports and prevention services available statewide.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Reproductive liberty is about more than abortion
description: I am riding on the front of a train barreling into a distant land. Physically, I am at home, in an inflatable pool cushioned by warm water, entering birthland. As my son emerges, I am in awe. We are surrounded by nothing but love: my husband, my certified nurse midwife (CNM), and doula. I feel whole, and present. […]
text:
An appointment room stands empty at the Planned Parenthood in St. Louis' Central West End (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).I am riding on the front of a train barreling into a distant land. Physically, I am at home, in an inflatable pool cushioned by warm water, entering birthland. As my son emerges, I am in awe. We are surrounded by nothing but love: my husband, my certified nurse midwife (CNM), and doula. I feel whole, and present.
My hospital births nearly a decade earlier were, per my chart, textbook experiences. Yet after both, I felt hollowed out. Pushing under the deadened gaze of a resident physician and medical students hiding yawns at three in the morning felt humiliating. Two years later, an anesthesiologist shrugged off my husband and turned back to his charting after I lost consciousness.
It took years as a nurse and women’s health nurse practitioner, a clinical and quality director at Planned Parenthood, a home birth, and countless conversations to understand that hollow feeling. I wasn’t the problem. The problem is our system that too often treats birth as an economic function and reproductive care in America as a stratified risk, where access to care — and sometimes outcomes — can depend on where you live.
Despite holding a doctorate and more than a decade of experience caring for women, I cannot practice independently as an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) in Missouri. To prescribe medications and provide treatment under Missouri law, APRNs generally must work through a collaborative practice arrangement with a physician. Some APRNs pay physicians for those agreements, which also operate within geographic and prescribing restrictions.
There are also no licensed freestanding birth centers in the state, even though Missouri has a licensing framework for them. In my view, those requirements create unnecessary barriers to opening and operating one. Further, education and credentialing requirements can make entering midwifery difficult for women without the time or resources to pursue them.
Missouri, as of this year, has one doctoral certified professional midwife  program, and a handful of small, private certified professional midwife  programs. Certified professional midwife  program are not nurses, but are trained to provide pregnancy-related services. They are not licensed by the state, so they are not eligible for insurance reimbursement.
The shift away from community midwifery and toward hospital-based childbirth did not happen solely because women chose hospitals. Historians have documented how professionalization, regulation and the growth of hospital-based medicine marginalized many traditional midwives over the 20th century. Today, access to abortion, birth centers and midwifery still varies dramatically by state.
Historically, Missouri’s legal treatment of midwifery has shifted as well. In 2007, lawmakers enacted a law allowing people with qualifying national certification to provide pregnancy-related midwifery services. Physician groups immediately challenged the law, but the Missouri Supreme Court ultimately rejected the lawsuit because the groups lacked standing. Missouri still requires physician collaboration for many APRN services. APRN advocates have repeatedly sought to loosen those restrictions in the legislature, with limited success.
I learned the abortion side of this story at Planned Parenthood. I worked at the facility during some of the most tumultuous and litigious years, fighting for our license while being assailed daily by state legislators, surveyors, and protesters. Missourians voted for reproductive freedom in 2024, but many preexisting abortion regulations remained in effect while litigation continued. By the time Missouri’s abortion ban took effect in 2022, only one clinic in the state was still providing abortions. In June, a circuit judge struck down most of the abortion regulations challenged by Planned Parenthood and the ACLU, while leaving in place requirements that abortions be performed by physicians and that patients seeking medication abortion meet with a doctor in person.
The professionalization of health care also carried a racial dimension. The U.S. midwifery workforce today remains predominantly white, while historians have documented how Black midwives were marginalized as childbirth moved into hospitals and professional credentialing expanded. Those changes disproportionately affected communities that had long relied on community midwives. Birth attendance has become the province of a few highly credentialed people, while profound racial disparities in maternal health remain. In Missouri, Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at 2.5 times the rate of white women, and nearly 80% of pregnancy-related deaths in the state’s latest review were found to be preventable.
MO HealthNet covers certified nurse-midwife services and freestanding birth-center care. Yet where does a woman go when there are no freestanding birth centers, and access to midwives is limited in many communities? The result is a system that often funnels women into hospitals whether or not that is their preferred setting. This system wasn’t built with women at the table. It was built to put them on it.
Our political debate has not fully addressed reproductive liberty across the entire arc of pregnancy. Paid leave and abortion access receive sustained attention; birth autonomy gets far less. My home birth required resources that most women don’t have. Choices such as home birth, IVF or traveling out of state for miscarriage or abortion care can depend heavily on money, geography and insurance. For women who can’t afford this, their reproductive liberty ends with their paycheck.
Missouri’s fights over reproductive policy will continue in legislatures, courtrooms and elections. But reproductive liberty is broader than any single policy fight. It includes whether women can decide when to become pregnant, what providers can care for them, and where and with whom they give birth. Until those questions are treated as part of the same reproductive-health conversation, the consequences will continue to fall hardest on people with the fewest resources and the least ability to demand alternatives.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ panel mulls giving state more control over energy generation — and utility bills
description: Several New Jersey lawmakers think creating a state energy department will help them better expand energy capacity and control utility costs.
text:
Eric Miller headed former Gov. Phil Murphy’s climate action and green energy office. He testified at the Statehouse in Trenton on Oct. 5, 2026, about legislation that would create a state agency to oversee energy programs. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Some New Jersey legislators want to create a state agency to oversee energy programs, an effort intended to give the state more control to expand its energy capacity and ultimately cap soaring utility bills that have enraged residents statewide.
Members of the Assembly’s telecommunications and utilities committee heard more than two hours of testimony Monday on two bills now in the Statehouse pipeline that would create a new executive-branch department to focus solely on energy policy, procurement, and implementation to help the state expand its energy capacity. That’s a dire need, with the state now only generating two-thirds of the energy it uses and power-hungry data centers increasingly driving up demand, the bills’ supporters said.
The state Board of Public Utilities now is tasked with such work, as the only state agency overseeing energy. But its primary mission has been — and should remain — regulating electric, water, natural gas, telecommunications, and other utilities to protect residents from predatory rates, supporters said.
Safeguarding customers and expanding energy capacity are two goals that can sometimes conflict, said Assemblyman Robert Karabinchak (D-Middlesex), the chief sponsor of a bill that would create a state energy resource and development division. The other bill would establish a state Department of Energy with similar objectives. Both emphasize expanding renewable energies.
“No disrespect for BPU because I like BPU. I think they do an excellent job of protecting the ratepayers,” Karabinchak said. “However, I think there has to be some level of separation, because if your boss is saying, ‘I want you to protect the ratepayers’ at the same time he’s saying, ‘I want you to think out-of-the-box and tell me anything that you could do to increase our energy capacity that may not be cheap today, but in 10 years will be,’ I want that independence.”
New Jersey had a state department of energy until 1987, when former Gov. Tom Kean abolished it to save money and reduce bureaucracy.
While data centers were a common scapegoat at Monday’s hearing, advocates pushing for change also blamed skyrocketing utility costs on PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest electricity grid operator. PJM serves New Jersey and a dozen other states, and electric prices have repeatedly risen during its annual auctions.
“That’s what we should be doing — trying to figure out how do we break our ties with PJM and get away from that circus,” said Assemblyman Kevin Egan (D-Middlesex).
Assemblyman Paul Kanitra (R-Ocean) grilled several speakers for “throwing PJM under the bus,” blamed Democratic lawmakers’ “ideology on climate change” for spiking costs, and blasted former Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration for what he regarded as policy failures.
Murphy officials issued an energy master plan in 2019 meant to expand renewable energy and lasso rising costs, and updated it last year. But Eric Miller, who headed Murphy’s climate action office, agreed Monday that “not all of it is actionable.”
“We were setting a broad blueprint for what we think the energy system could look like and how to get there, but it is not a deep integrative resource plan,” Miller testified. “We know what type of energy we need, where we need it, how much, when we need it. All of those questions are answered.”
But, Miller added, the Board of Public Utilities does not have the broad procurement authority required to take that plan to fruition.
While some witnesses on Monday, including industry experts, agreed policymakers should act to expand energy capacity and rein in runaway costs in New Jersey, some were uncertain that creating a separate state agency is the best strategy.
“Having a Department of Energy is probably the most expensive way of doing it,” said Ray Cantor of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association. “But it may also be the way of giving it the most highlight and importance within the administration.”
Brian Lipman, director of the state Division of Rate Counsel, warned lawmakers that the bills’ focus on renewable energy could be problematic because renewable energy development is expensive and the bills contain no guardrails to insulate ratepayers from those costs.
“It’s unclear where the prudency review of these projects will be done. It is unclear who is going to be looking to make sure that these projects are within the realm of affordability,” Lipman said. 
Brian Lipman (center) is New Jersey’s Rate Payer Advocate. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Katie Mettle of Advanced Energy United urged legislators to hire consultants to examine what other states do and prescribe the best way forward for New Jersey.
The panel did not vote on the bills. The hearing was meant to help shape the state’s next steps, said Assemblyman Wayne DeAngelo (D-Mercer), the committee’s chairman.
“Listen, I think the discussion and topic of the Department of Energy, whether it’s solely by itself, whether it’s a hybrid, whether it’s revamping of the Board of Public Utilities, something needs to be done because our communication and investment into energy generation was not there,” DeAngelo said. “We were very sporadic. We’ve been sporadic for the past 25 years, going back to when we started with solar.”

name: WyoFile
title: Black-footed ferrets aren’t thriving anywhere, but in Wyoming’s Shirley Basin they’re faring OK and even dispersing
description:
The first reintroduction site following the 1981 rediscovery of the mustelid species once presumed extinct has been a rare relative success story. 
The post Black-footed ferrets aren’t thriving anywhere, but in Wyoming’s Shirley Basin they’re faring OK and even dispersing appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
SHIRLEY BASIN—From hundreds of yards away, biologist Daniel Pinneo spotted the telltale green eyes of one of North America’s rarest mammals, before the night’s mission really began.
His Wyoming Game and Fish Department counterparts were still near their trucks staging for a grueling through-the-night field shift.
Pinneo, a biologist at the Tom Thorne/Beth Williams Wildlife Research Center at Sybille, interrupted colleagues going over protocols to search for, and potentially capture the endangered species. 
“I think that’s a ferret,” he said. 
Game and Fish small carnivore biologist Andy Gygli, the research team’s leader, cast his own spotlight where Pinneo caught the green eyes. 
“I think that’s a ferret, too,” he said. “Go figure out what that is.” 
Pinneo closed the distance, striding through a prairie dog colony in the dark just west of the Little Medicine Bow River. It was the evening of Sept. 30, 2025, and he spotlighted along the way, narrating the nighttime vibrancy of the arid high desert. 
A jackrabbits’ eyes caught his attention to the right of the suspected black-footed ferret, then he noticed another critter on the move.
“That’s a fox — swift fox,” Pinneo said.  
The green glowing eyes remained. 
“See how low to the ground that thing is?” he said. “I’m almost certain.” 
Four minutes later, Pinneo was up close and staring into a prairie dog burrow. The sooty black-and-beige masked face of an inquisitive ferret kit peered his direction.
Mustela nigripes, confirmed. 
A wild non-reproducing female ferret kit awaits processing by Wyoming biologists after being captured in her Shirley Basin habitat on Sept. 30, 2025. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Although seeing a black-footed ferret anywhere is a great rarity — they were once presumed extinct — the Shirley Basin is about the best place in the world to do it. Ferrets in this ecologically rich complex of state, private and federal land southwest of the Laramie Mountains have lasted longer than any other subpopulation on Earth and they’ve fared well enough that they are even fanning out on their own unassisted. 
Wyoming wildlife managers have found pockets of ferrets near Carbon County’s Chalk Mountain and Bone Creek, a drainage northeast of Medicine Bow, where they were never reintroduced, Gygli said. And they’ve also started to detect more dispersers west of Highway 77 south of Casper.
“That’s the other spot we’ve been trying to turn into a population source,” Gygli said. “Every year we find more kits. I’m really excited about that.”
In April 2023, Gygli even learned of a road-killed ferret hit on the highway near Centennial in the eastern foothills of the Snowy Range Mountains. It was an otherwise healthy male.
“Other than the roadkill, it was in very good shape,” Gygli said. “This was a portly ferret doing very well for himself.”
The farthest dispersing black-footed ferret ever documented in Wyoming traveled over 25 straight-line miles, even crossing Interstate 80. The animal was found road-killed on the Highway 130  in the southern Laramie Plains. (Andy Gygli/Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Based on its genetics and geography, the most likely explanation is that the animal journeyed south from the Shirley Basin. While ferrets don’t have the extraordinary dispersing capabilities of their cousin, the wolverine, the Centennial ferret would have had to have traveled dozens of miles, skirted the Snowies, and it even crossed Interstate 80. 
“Every now and then, a road-killed one gets picked up,” Gygli said. “Normally, they’re in places that aren’t surprising, but who knows? We might find more Centennial-type ferrets.” 
Origins
Shirley Basin was the first place where the weasel-like carnivores were reintroduced into the wild after the species’ extraordinary rediscovery outside of Meeteetse. That moment in the fall of 1981 is etched into Wyoming lore: Shep the ranch dog brought a dead weasel-like creature home to his owners, John and Lucille Hogg, then a taxidermist identified it as a black-footed ferret and a month later federal wildlife officials found more living animals. The subsequent decade amounted to a rescue mission. The newfound population was besieged by two nonnative diseases, canine distemper and plague, and 18 remaining ferrets were plucked out of the Bighorn Basin and brought into captivity to create a reproduction program to sustain the species. By 1991, the initial 15 breeders managed to produce enough captive ferrets to give the species another chance in the wild.

This Sept. 20, 2011, file photo shows a monument to black-footed ferrets in Meeteese, where biologists released 35 black-footed ferrets July 26, 2016. Scientists thought the black-footed ferret was extinct until a dog brought a dead one home near Meeteetse in 1981. (AP Photo/Mead Gruver, File)

“We evaluated like 12 different sites before we selected Shirley Basin,” said Bob Oakleaf, a retired nongame wildlife supervisor for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department. From 1991 to 1994, more than 200 ferret kits were released in the area.
The site was selected because of the cooperation of private landowners, Oakleaf said, and its ferret-friendly attributes. In other words, there were prairie dogs. Lots of them. Today, there are over 280 square miles of active prairie dog colonies, which provide ferrets with a critical source of prey, cover and habitat. In 2024, Game and Fish surveys detected 4.24 white-tailed prairie dogs per acre, which extrapolates out to more than three quarters of a million of the chunky rodents. 
Although black-footed ferrets have maintained a presence in Shirley Basin for 35 straight years, it wasn’t always smooth sailing. Plague has been a longtime bane for prairie dogs and ferrets. Wildlife managers didn’t realize that ferrets could actually contract plague until one escaped from the Sybille research lab in the early 1990s.
“It got involved with a prairie dog that had plague, and died from it,” Oakleaf said. “About the same time that happened, plague erupted in Shirley Basin.” 
“It’s a double-edged sword,” he added. “They lose their prey, and they also die from preying.” 
Hit by the infectious disease, the population “basically crashed” in the early years and wildlife managers almost had to start over, Oakleaf said. But by the late-1990s, prairie dogs and ferrets in the region were plague-free enough that reintroductions resumed and a wild-breeding population took hold. 
“They just took off,” Oakleaf said. “We had high hopes of it being successful, and each year our optimism grew.”
There was a lot of work behind the scenes to make it work. Captively raised ferrets, like other species in similar circumstances, struggled to understand the dangers of life outside a cage.
“They were dying at a high rate early on,” said Dean Biggins, an emeritus U.S. Geological Survey scientist who’s been studying black-footed ferrets since their Meeteetse rediscovery. “Coyotes were the biggest problem, by far, but just about any predator you found on a prairie dog town would take a ferret, and that included golden eagles and great horned owls and badgers.” 
“Preconditioning pens,” where ferrets had access to prairie dog burrows they could plunge into, helped solve that problem. Captive bred and released ferrets that survived until the next breeding season increased tenfold, Biggins said, jumping from 4-5% to 40%.
“The predator kills dropped way off,” he said. “They were evading the coyotes a lot better.” 
Continued maintenance
Even as Shirley Basin ferrets survived, fanned out and started pioneering new habitats in the region on their own, the population continued to get a boost from captive-raised animals. They come from six breeding operations, including the National Black-Footed Ferret Conservation Center outside of Fort Collins, which oversees the recovery efforts. 
In 2024, ten ferrets apiece were turned loose at the newfound Chalk Mountain and Bone Creek subpopulations, according to Game and Fish’s most recent nongame species annual report. Based on spotlight surveys, they appear to be on the upswing at Chalk Mountain, but not doing so hot at Bone Creek, where just one wild born male was detected two years ago.
“They’re either not living or not sticking around,” Gygli said. 
Keeping tabs on Shirley Basin’s ferret population is an intensive annual weekslong affair. Gygli leads a crew that spotlights through the night, by truck and on foot. The nocturnal mustelid’s most active hours are 2 a.m. to 5 a.m., and the surveying biologists are often up and looking during that span for four straight days. It’s a grind on the human body, Gygli remarked on the front end of one night’s search. 
“Particularly on the last day, about 4 o’clock in the morning, sometimes I can’t continue,” he said. “I have to break for my own health.” 
Wyoming Game and Fish Department small carnivore biologist Andy Gygli examines the underside of a female black-footed ferret after capturing the animal from a Shirley Basin prairie dog burrow on Sept. 30, 2025. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Over the course of a field season, the ferret surveyors can check in on 10,000-plus acres in the Shirley Basin (in 2024, their lights combed over 11,871 acres, yielding at least 21 ferrets and four to five litters.) But even with all that effort, they’re covering just a small fraction of the 280 square miles of prairie dog colony in the basin. 
Technology could be a game changer. Ferret researchers with the Smithsonian’s Conservation Biology Institute are developing techniques that use drones and artificial intelligence to monitor populations, and they’re trying it out in Shirley Basin. 
“If it works, compared to traditional methods on the ground, at least as well, that would really save time and effort and free up tech[nicians] to do other things,” Gygli said.
There are other imperative ferret-related tasks at hand, like monitoring for plague, which remains a constant threat. 
Plague patrol
The sylvatic plague that can decimate prairie dog populations and kills ferrets is the same flea-born disease that can infect humans and caused the devastating Black Death pandemic in the 14th century. In modern times, the plague is considered endemic to places like the Shirley Basin. It can hit anytime.
“I just assume it’s always here at a low level,” Gygli said during his nighttime survey. “You just hope that the conditions never quite align.” 
With some regularity, a wet spring causes fleas to thrive, and the lethal malady flares up in one or more of the species’ dozens of attempted recovery areas. It happened at Montana’s UL Bend National Wildlife Refuge, where minimum ferret counts tumbled from 24 to one between 2017 and 2019. And it’s been a major factor in swings in western South Dakota’s Conata Basin/Badlands National Park recovery area, a rare self-sustaining population home to roughly half the wild ferrets in the world. Ferret counts there fell from 355 animals before a 2007 plague outbreak to just 49 animals six years later. Another outbreak there was detected in 2024, triggering a massive operation to fog prairie dog colonies with insecticidal dust to knock back plague-spreading fleas.
Despite the effort, around the same time the population cratered.
Unidentified park staff prepare to release black-footed ferrets in 1994 or 1995 in Badlands National Park, S.D. (NPS photo)
“In 2024, we had 250 ferrets on 17,000 acres,” said Travis Livieri, a Wisconsin-based biologist and black-footed ferret expert who’s long studied the Conata Basin/Badlands population. “Now we’re down to about 70 ferrets.” 
It wasn’t just plague, though. Crushing drought has also been a big factor in Dakota ferrets’ struggles, causing a “massive” breeding failure last year. 
“In my 30 years of doing this, I’ve never seen [drought] this bad, where prairie dogs failed to reproduce at a high rate,” Livieri said. “The prairie dogs don’t do well, the ferrets won’t do well. That’s the story of what happened in 2025.” 
Wyoming’s been hit in modern times, too. In 2018 and 19, plague hollowed out the Meeteetse ferret population, which had been reestablished with much fanfare in 2016. Between 2018 and 2020, the minimum number of ferrets detected there fell from 26 to one. There have been captive ferret infusions since then, including 18 animals in 2022, but Wyoming’s smaller recovery area has continued to barely limp along. 
“It’s not gone,” Gygli said of the Meeteetse population, “but it is not doing as well as I would like.” 
During the 2025 surveys, his team found a single animal in two weeks of looking. 
“Hopefully, we just happened to miss seeing them,” Gygli said. “Even though we only saw one, chances are there’s more out there.” 
In Shirley Basin, Gygli hasn‘t seen a major plague outbreak since he came aboard in 2017. But there have been some scares. In July 2025, a dead prairie dog tested positive to the west of the newfound Chalk Mountain subpopulation. It immediately became a top priority for Game and Fish, and its federal ferret recovery partners. 
“We put together an effort to treat [1,000 acres] where our ferret litters are near Chalk Mountain,” Gygli said. “My desperate hope is that we never actually know if our efforts did anything. If things just continue as normal, that’s what I’m hoping for.” 
Is this success?
The great lengths Wyoming Game and Fish and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service go to keep black-footed ferrets alive in the Shirley Basin is one of the most successful efforts to bring back the native species.
Black-footed ferrets were declared an “endangered species” in 1967, before the Endangered Species Act even existed (they were grandfathered in when the ESA passed in 1973). There are historical estimates of more than 5 million ferrets in the late 1800s, and although biologists believe they were always a low-density species they co-evolved with prairie dogs and have been a part of western ecosystems for over 100,000 years.
Today, verified ferrets in the wild number in the hundreds. The sorry state of the species is inextricably linked to its primary prey, the much-maligned prairie dog, which is simultaneously managed as nongame wildlife and an unprotected pest in Wyoming. The Territorial Legislature classified prairie dogs as a nuisance in Wyoming before the state even existed. As long as prairie dogs aren’t thriving, ferrets won’t either. 
“By and large, prairie dogs are not well liked,” said Biggins, the USGS retiree who’s studied ferrets for 45 years. “That’s been a problem in most of the places where we work.” 
For black-footed ferrets, the picture of success in the modern era is simply weeks of intense through-the-night monitoring every summer and fall, occasional releases of vaccinated captive ferrets and quick action — and lots of resources on hand — anytime there’s any plague detected. 
Members of a Wyoming Game and Fish Department-led black-footed ferret surveillance team transfer a young female from a cage trap to a black tubing from which she’ll be released.  (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Just having ferrets continuously on the landscape is a feat in itself. 
“Shirley basin has been pretty well occupied the whole time,” said Livieri, the Wisconsin-based black-footed ferret expert.
Most ferret reintroduction sites fail. Out of 35 locations in eight states where Mustela nigripes have been turned loose, only about 15 still actively have ferrets, Livieri said.
Livieri marveled in particular at the geographic enormity of the south-central Wyoming population. Even though the Conata Basin/Badlands population is the largest going by headcount, it’s confined in a much smaller area that he can drive across in a couple hours. And it would have blinked out if not for aggressive annual plague control. 
An advantageous and unique feature of the Shirley Basin population is that it’s so spread out — a dynamic that’s continuing as animals disperse. 
“Shirley Basin has kind of that metapopulation feel,” Livieri said. “When you only got one basket, and the eggs are all breaking, that’s bad. But when you’ve got a big, big yard with a whole bunch of baskets, if some baskets don’t do well, that’s okay.” 
It may be that, even in a place like Shirley Basin, intensive management is necessary forever to ensure the species’ persistence. The reason is plague, said Biggins. It’s a persistent organism that’s put wildlife managers between a rock and a hard place, he said. 
“I don’t like these schemes we’ve got for plague management,” Biggins said. “But you have a hard choice to make: You want ferrets, or don’t you?” 
Captured
After Pinneo cornered the ferret in the burrow at the onset of the Sept. 30, 2025 survey, Gygli and the ferret surveyors promptly began implementing their capture protocols. 
Plastic cups — flagged so they got collected later on — were thrust into nearby burrow openings, so the animal couldn’t surreptitiously escape. A long, rectangular cage trap was jammed into the main entrance and a blanket cast over it, a ferret safety measure that’ll ensure a trapped animal stays warm. 
Then it’s time to wait. 
“Every now and then, when you walk away, you’ll hear it slam shut and you’ll have a ferret,” Gygli said. “That has not happened this year.”
The trap stayed silent as they walked away. An hour later, Pinneo’s voice emerged from a hand-held radio as Gygli spotlighted from his pickup truck. 
“I got a ferret in a trap,” Pinneo said. 


All wild ferrets handled in Wyoming receive inoculations for distemper and plague, two nonnative diseases that have the potential to devastate fragile populations. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)


A chiller-than-normal ferret is released into a prairie dog burrow entrance after being processed by Wyoming researchers in September 2025. The small mustelids can be feisty when captured, but this one stayed subdued throughout her brief time being handled. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)


Minutes later, the team of ferret surveyors began a routine examination. The young-of-the-year ferret kit had been born in the wild, and weighed in at just 2.3 pounds. She received two inoculations: one for distemper, the other for plague. 
Although trapped ferrets can be plenty irascible, this one was notably subdued. Nevertheless, the research team communicated in whispers to not frighten the animal and wore masks to keep her safe (ferrets can catch COVID-19 from humans). 
“She’s behaving very well,” Gygli said. “Just keep doing you, lady.” 
Moments later, the ferret kit was gently shaken free from a transfer tube and scurried away into a prairie dog burrow. She was back in the wild in Shirley Basin, site a black-footed ferret success story, even if it houses a population that will likely always be on shaky footing.
The post Black-footed ferrets aren’t thriving anywhere, but in Wyoming’s Shirley Basin they’re faring OK and even dispersing appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: A universally panned Grand Teton ballpark plan is dead. Let’s keep it buried.
description:
People who love national parks and major league baseball were justifiably horrified at the thought of the two being combined, writes columnist Kerry Drake.
The post A universally panned Grand Teton ballpark plan is dead. Let’s keep it buried. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

Until someone in Major League Baseball recently came up with the knuckleheaded idea to build a stadium in Grand Teton National Park, I thought the worst national park proposal in Wyoming’s history was a 1991 plan to build a monorail in Yellowstone.
The Yellowstone monorail, the brainchild of former Wyoming U.S. Sen Malcolm Wallop, had people laughing at the thought of turning the first national park into Disney World.
But unlike the MLB’s weird Grand Teton proposal, which was universally panned, at least some monorail proponents had a reason behind the idea. The plan was born from frustration with the terrible condition of Yellowstone’s roads, which were causing traffic jams and a plethora of complaints from tourists.
As you’ve probably noticed, there is no Yellowstone monorail. That’s because while it would have unclogged the roads, it came at a big price: at the time fixing roads in the park cost an average of $1 million per mile, while building a monorail would cost anywhere between $15 million and $50 million per mile.
Hopefully, we successfully dodged ever breaking down the estimated cost to build a temporary baseball stadium in Grand Teton National Park. It was dropped like a hot potato by Major League Baseball and the Trump administration when people were either outraged or found it laughable.
When I first learned about the proposal — “Grand Teton National Ballpark? Visitors Call It a Field of Nightmares” — for a few seconds I thought I must be reading The Onion, America’s best satirical website.
But no, WyoFile’s account of what park visitors thought about the plan was the cold, hard and unvarnished truth.
Building Wyoming’s equivalent to the “Field of Dreams,” where two major league teams square off once a year in a permanent stadium built in the cornfields of Iowa, was immediately branded a horrible idea by, well, everyone.
“MLB, you should know that Grand Teton National Park, home to free ranging wildlife, including grizzly bears, bison, wolves, moose, cougars and elk, is not an appropriate or safe venue for your baseball fantasy,” said Joan Anzelmo, former superintendent of Colorado National Monument, said in a statement.
I expected that perfectly reasonable reaction from national park visitors. But what about baseball fans? Did they have any dreams of attending a game with the majestic mountains in the background?
What did Wyoming baseball fans think of the idea when it was first announced, and then squashed? 
To find out I went to the state’s most dedicated followers of baseball I know: the Wyoming Rotisserie Baseball League, the oldest fantasy baseball league in the state. Its first season was in 1989.
Full disclosure: I’m a proud member of the WRBL, having joined in 2002. I own the “Wolf Blitzers.” 
I asked our commissioner, Dan Neal of Casper, an Idaho native whose team is the “Russets,” if the league would like to make a statement. It did.
The league officially condemned the “dangerous idea” that it said should never have been explored. But after the Trump administration listened to the pitch from Rob Manfred, MLB commissioner, it decided to give life to the nutty notion by actually wasting time and money to send Interior Department officials to the park to check out three potential stadium sites.
“President Trump always resorts to chaos to distract people from the issues/matters he fears. This is simply another stir of that pot,” the WRBL stated. “They’re using the prospect of defiling one of the National Parks system’s great Nature parks to make people forget the Iran War, the Trump-Epstein files, and the rise in the cost of living.”
Neal said members of the league love both baseball and our national parks.
“I suspect a minimum of 95 percent of our players over the past years enjoyed the beauty of GTNP,” he said. “They’ve enjoyed it for many things: skiing; hunting; hiking; exploring; and seeing its abundant wildlife.”
Neal said Manfred and most MLB owners “have a thirst for money that their mere monopoly of the sport cannot slake.”
“They continue to strive to broaden the market across the world and in the country,” Neal said. “The president, I’m sure, will be willing to help them if they agree to pay a few million dollars in ‘campaign contributions.’”
The president, who I can see naming the ballpark the “Donald J. Trump Stadium” and covering it in tacky fake gold, bailed on the idea. I agree with Neal and my fellow WRBL owners, it was a smokescreen to try to hide everything else that was blowing up during Trump’s monumentally addled second term.
But another WRBL member, “Grinning Dogs” owner Russ Dahlgren of Cheyenne, had a different opinion of this project. He told me, with his tongue firmly planted in his cheek, that he’s not sure this is such a bad idea. 
“Sitting in a new stadium with a cold adult beverage in my hand, looking out over the green grass field with the Tetons in the background, I could think of worse places to be,” Dahlgreen said.
That much, I’ll concede, is true. Wherever humans get together to enjoy the thrill of watching tremendous athletes launch mammoth homers or turn perfect double plays, I’d rather be there than any other place on Earth. But in this case, not at the expense of disturbing one of the world’s wonders.
Dahlgreen added that he thinks all revenue from the new stadium should go to beautification projects in Washington, D.C.
“Sounds like a great deal for us ‘mericans that we can all get behind,” Dahlgren joked. “The stadium, of course, will be paid by private funds, hopefully money from Russian oligarchs.
“We could have Grand rule doubles, Teewinot triples, Mount Moran homers,” he added. “The Cascade Canyon power alley in left field, Leigh Canyon the right field power alley. The Rockchuck section would be the cheap seats.”
Upon learning that the Grand Teton plan is now dead, Neal reminded opponents to be vigilant. “It’s an idea that has its appeal to the greedy, so like a bad penny, we can expect to see it again,” he said. 
He’s right. And his advice should extend to any pathetic plan this administration tries to lead off first base. Wyoming, we’re the pitcher, and we need to be ready for the pickoff throw.
