name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Passing HJR 4 would give Idaho Legislature sole authority to legalize marijuana, other drugs
description: Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and […]
text:
A voter casts his ballot in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. 
First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. 
Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. 
Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. 
House Joint Resolution 4  is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. 
If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. 
If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. 
Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. 
People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Passing HJR 4 would mean Idahoans voluntarily give up rights to ballot initiative process, Idaho constitutional scholar says

David Adler, president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls, says passing HJR 4 would mean voters are agreeing to give up their own rights and freedoms. 
David Adler is president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls. (Photo courtesy of David Adler)
Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities and has spoken about HJR 4 this fall. 
“The more I speak on it, the more I realize people generally are of the belief that this is about regulating marijuana and they don’t understand that it has a far broader impact on their ability to resort to the initiative to exercise their rights,” Adler said. 
“Really, HJR 4 asks Idahoans to surrender both their rights and their powers to shape their future,” Adler said. 
He said a ballot initiative is a tool of democracy that the public has used to improve the state since the 1930s. Different ballot initiatives in Idaho have created the nonpartisan Idaho Fish and Game Commission, regulated dredge mining to protect clean water and created sunshine and transparency laws that provide for the disclosure of campaign finance reports and lobbying activity, Adler said 
Idaho voters should not give that power up permanently when nobody knows what future medical discoveries could come from drugs or psychoactive substances, Adler said, adding that coffee and tea are considered psychoactive substances. 
HJR 4 is also another example of the Idaho Legislature trying to restrict access to ballot initiatives or make the requirements to qualify a ballot initiative more difficult, Adler said. 
 Idaho legislators says HJR 4 protects Idaho from special interests trying to force legalization

Almost all Republicans in the Idaho Legislature support HJR 4 and oppose the legalization of recreational or medical marijuana. 
Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who co-sponsored HJR 4, said the constitutional amendment is necessary to ensure that special interest groups don’t run expensive political campaigns designed to manipulate the public into legalizing drugs at the ballot box. 
Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“When ballot initiatives run for marijuana or other psychoactive drugs like they did in Oregon, there is a lot of money that comes in on the pro side to legalize the drugs because special interests are trying to make money selling the drugs,” Grow said. “It is difficult to get money to fight it, and that’s the same thing we are seeing with HJR 4. It is difficult to get money to make the public aware of what it is because there is no money to be made by those of us pushing HJR 4. We’re just trying to help the citizens understand that the status quo is the Legislature has the power currently. We just want to prevent special interests from convincing people to pass legislation that would give money to those special interest groups.”
Grow said passing HJR 4 does not grant any additional power to the Idaho Legislature, which already has the ability to regulate and legalize drugs. Grow said the public has the opportunity to participate and make its voice heard through the committee and public hearing process in the Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate. 
“I would say the citizens have the full opportunity to be involved in the process,” Grow said. 
Republicans in the Idaho Legislature introduced and adopted HJR 4 during the 2025 legislative session. With near unanimous Republican support and opposition from Democrats, HJR 4 passed 58-10 in the Idaho House of Representatives and 29-6 in the Idaho Senate.

title: Jones, Tuberville nearly even in September fundraising; Tuberville maintains funding lead
description: Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville raised almost identical amounts of money in September, though Tuberville retained an edge in spending and cash on hand. According to campaign finance documents filed Friday, Republican candidates for Alabama’s constitutional offices generally outraised Democrati[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones (left) and Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville (right) were evenly matched with funding in September according to campaign finance reports. (Jones photo by Andrea Tinker /Alabama Reflector; Tuberville photo by Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector; Graphic by Andrea Tinker Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville reported nearly identical fundraising in September, though Tuberville had a clear edge in cash on hand and expenditures.
The race for commissioner of agriculture and industries also saw fundraising parity between Republican nominee Corey Hill and Democratic nominee Ron Sparks. Sparks outspent Hill, who retains a cash-on-hand advantage.
Republicans in most other races outraised and outspent their Democratic opponents.




Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville raised almost identical amounts of money in September, though Tuberville retained an edge in spending and cash on hand.
According to campaign finance documents filed Friday, Republican candidates for Alabama’s constitutional offices generally outraised Democratic nominees last month, though spending within individual races varied significantly.
 Governor 
According to campaign finance reports, Jones raised $1.12 million to Tuberville’s $1.13 million during September. However, Tuberville remains ahead of Jones with cash on hand with $6.5 million to Jones’ $2.2 million. Tuberville also outspent Jones last month, putting down $4 million while Jones spent $1.5 million.
Malloy Jaspers, communications director for the Tuberville campaign, said in a statement Monday afternoon that “Coach continues to raise and spend money at a record pace to make sure Alabama candidates up and down the ballot win on Nov. 3.”
Jones criticized one of Tuberville’s donations in a Substack post Sunday.
“We just found out that toward the end of September, Tommy Tuberville accepted yet another massive contribution from a data center company, this time for $20,000,” the post said. “We are in just about the opposite position from Tommy Tuberville. We’re still behind in fundraising, but we have an extraordinary grassroots movement behind us, and the energy on the ground is like nothing I’ve ever seen.”
Campaign finance records show that Tuberville received $20,000 from TCBC Development Company, a computer systems design company in Cottonwood.
Both candidates received money from political action committees. Jones received $1,500 from the Chilton County Democratic Party; $1,000 from the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers & Trainmen; $3,000 from March On PAC and $1,000 from New Direction PAC. Tuberville received $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors Political Action Committee.
The fundraising numbers were closer than gubernatorial campaigns of recent years. In September 2018, Republican Gov. Kay Ivey, then seeking her first full term in office, raised a little over $735,000. Tuscaloosa Mayor Walt Maddox, the Democratic nominee for the office, raised just over $373,000 that month. 
 Commissioner of Agriculture & Industries 
The two candidates for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries were evenly matched in fundraising in September. Corey Hill, the Republican nominee for commissioner of agriculture and industries, raised $58,900 to Sparks’ $55,200. Sparks spent $36,200 while Hill only spent $2,200.
Hill said in a text message Monday afternoon “I continue to be grateful for the outpouring of support from people from all over Alabama.”
Sparks said in an interview Monday afternoon he was proud of the money he raised and the amount spent was to help amplify the campaign’s message.
“We wanted to get our message out, and that was our strategy: to try to get as much out as we could, so people will start listening to the commissioner of agriculture race and not other races,” Sparks said.
Corey Hill, Ron Sparks face off in race for commissioner of Agriculture and Industries

Hill maintains the edge in cash on hand with $142,600 to Sparks’ $119,500. 
Both received money from PACs. Hill received $1,000 from Reaching For A Brighter America PAC; $1,500 from Montgomery County GOP Executive PAC; $10,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC and $7,500 from Progress PAC.
Sparks received $5,250 from Persist PAC; $1,500 from BIZ PAC; $5,000 from Persist PAC; $500 from March On PAC and $5,000 from the Poarch Creek Indian PAC.
 Lieutenant Governor 
In the lieutenant governor race, Republican nominee John Wahl has been consistently outraisng his Democratic opponent Phillip Ensler. Last month, Wahl raised $155,100 and Ensler raised $81,500. However Ensler spent more than Wahl, dropping $32,800 to Wahl’s $25,000.
Ensler in a statement Monday said he had received contributions “from nearly 600 donors” since Aug. 1, while Wahl “has received contributions from about 30 — meaning nearly 20 times as many people have chosen to financially support Phillip’s campaign.” 
A message seeking comment was left with Wahl Monday. The Alabama Secretary of State’s website lists 34 separate contributions to Wahl’s campaign between Aug. 1 and Sept. 30, to about 544 for Ensler. It was not clear how many of those were single donors and how many were repeat.
“We are proud of the broad grassroots support we have built visiting over 60 of Alabama’s 67 counties, and we will continue aggressively raising the resources necessary to communicate with voters across Alabama through Election Day,” Ensler’s statement said.
Both candidates received PAC money. Wahl received $50,000 from the Alabama Realtors Political Action Committee; $20,000 from the Alabama Credit Union Legislative Action Council; $5,000 from SAVEPAC; $5,000 from FAXPAC; $5,000 from TELPAC; $5,000 from Bradley Arant Boult Cummings LLP; $1,000 from the Cullman County Republican Women PAC; $5,000 from the Petroleum & Convenience Marketers of Alabama PAC; $25,000 from ALAPAC and $5,000 from the Republican State Leadership Committee.
Ensler received $1,000 from the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers & Trainmen PAC Fund; $5,000 from IBEW PAC and $8,000 from Persistence PAC.
Wahl retains the lead with cash on hand with $348,300. Ensler has $154,700 on hand.
 Attorney General 
Republican nominee Katherine Robertson once again raised and spent more than her Democratic opponent Jeff McLaughlin. Robertson raised $241,200 to McLaughlin’s $21,200 and spent $24,200. McLaughlin spent $14,800.
A message seeking comment was left with Robertson Monday. McLaughlin said in an interview Monday he’s going “to take what money I’ve received from individuals and buy whatever time I can with it, and try to get my message out.” 
Alabama’s attorney general can intervene in power rate hearings. Will AG candidates do so?

McLaughlin has not taken any PAC money throughout his entire campaign. Last month, Robertson received $1,000 from the Alabama CPA PAC; $10,000 from the Retailers of Alabama PAC; $10,000 from the Alabama Beverage Association PAC; $1,000 from the Wallace, Jordan, Ratliff and Brandt PAC; $25,000 from Trust Representing Involved Alabama Lawyers (TRIAL); $25,000 from ALAPAC; $5,000 from the Home Depot Action Committee; $25,000 from Alabama Builders PAC; $2,500 from AT&T Alabama PAC; $10,000 from PROG Holdings, Inc. PAC and $1,000 from ARDA-Resort Owners Coalition PAC. 
McLaughlin has long shunned PAC money, and said Monday that he thought “it’s important to know who’s behind a candidate (and with) a lot of PACs, it’s hard to sort that out.”
“I’ve always thought if you can accept campaign contributions, accept them from the people and from individuals only,” he said.
Robertson also remains far ahead of McLaughin in cash on hand, with $4.4 million to McLaughlin’s $20,300.
 Secretary of State 
Republican secretary of state nominee Caroleene Dobson outraised her opponent Wayne Rogers last month with $42,200 to Rogers’ $5,600. Dobson spent $13,400 to Rogers’ $5,000.
Messages seeking comment were left with Dobson and Rogers Monday. 
Rogers did not accept PAC money last month. Dobson received $2,000 from the Alabama Federation of Republican Women; $10,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC; $25,000 from ALAPAC and $5,000 from Bradley Arant Boult Cummings PAC.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: An assault on freedom and the Constitution in southeastern North Carolina
description: One of the most important distinguishing characteristics of a free society is what former Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis described simply and eloquently nearly a century ago as “the right to be let alone.”  Like a lot of Americans who came of age in the latter part of the 20th century, I remember absorbing this […]
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall, a detention center, in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. Employing new tactics, ICE arrested more people in July than in any previous month of the Trump administration. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)One of the most important distinguishing characteristics of a free society is what former Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis described simply and eloquently nearly a century ago as “the right to be let alone.” 
Like a lot of Americans who came of age in the latter part of the 20th century, I remember absorbing this fundamental idea of the U.S. Constitution and having it brought home to me while consuming any number of classic films and books that showed the frightening reality of life in Nazi Germany, Soviet-dominated Eastern Europe, and other totalitarian states.
One of the best things about the country in which I grew up, I learned, was that we Americans don’t have to line up passively like sheep to prove who we are to government officials merely because we’re traversing a public thoroughfare. Indeed, it was this simple fact – perhaps more than any other – that made our lives were so clearly and powerfully distinguishable from that of the unlucky millions stuck behind “the iron curtain.” 
Of course, I learned later that there had been frequently some big and disturbing exceptions to this fundamental freedom in American history – most notably the evil and discriminatory treatment of Black Americans that was inaugurated under slavery and continued in many places into the present. And then, in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, there was the complete and sobering overhaul of American air travel that forced us to surrender a sizable measure of our privacy and personal dignity in the name of combating terrorism.
All that said, the basic idea that, doggone it, government employees – be they law enforcement officers, immigration officials, safety inspectors, or some other unidentified bureaucrat – should not and cannot invade our space or privacy without a very specific and darn good reason remains at the heart of the American experiment. Indeed, for all our imperfections in enforcing and executing it, this idea is one that still remains a shared north star for millions of people across the political spectrum. 
Unfortunately, and tragically, this fundamental right is currently under a terrible and sustained assault throughout the country right now as the Trump administration and its allies in state and local government pursue their unconstitutional and un-American anti-immigrant pogrom. 
North Carolinians were reminded of this sobering fact yet again recently when it was reported that law enforcement officers of some ilk had established a “license checkpoint” on a public road in Columbus County and arrested or detained 10 people.
As NC Newsline journalist Trevon Spencer detailed in a September 25 story, the immigrant rights advocacy group Siembra NC reported that at least 10 people were arrested or detained.
According to witnesses, drivers and passengers alike were questioned about their immigration status and asked to provide citizenship documents. This is from Spencer’s report:

Javier Carbajal, an electrician who encountered the checkpoint while driving home with his coworkers, said he presented his driver’s license but was ordered out of his car and patted down by a sheriff’s deputy. 
He said a passenger in his car was also questioned about his documents and was arrested after he couldn’t produce them. 
‘We are electricians. We were just coming home after a long day of work,’ he said. 
Carbajal also reported seeing multiple other people put inside a van. Two other witnesses told Siembra NC they saw Latino men on the side of the road with their hands in zip ties.     
All of this would be bad enough if the arrested individuals were booked in public in a court of law, apprised of their rights, allowed to contact family members and post bail, and provided with legal representation.
But according to the report, family members were unable to contact those who were arrested or even to find out who it was that had arrested them. 
Spencer reported further that the Columbus County Sheriff’s Office, which participates in the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency’s 287(g) Task Force, declined to confirm the checkpoint or the arrests. The office said it could not release information because it was part of an ongoing investigation.
In other words, at least 10 people on an American street minding their own business not only had their privacy wrongfully and unconstitutionally violated, but they were also quite literally “disappeared” by unidentified individuals who were presumably officers of our government. 
This is the kind of beyond deplorable and unacceptable action that’s right out of the playbook of the Gestapo, the KGB and the white supremacist vigilantes of the Jim Crow era.       
Yes, it may be true that some of the arrested individuals had or have immigration or other legal issues. Millions of people do, both citizens and noncitizens.
But when taxpayer-funded officials are empowered to randomly stop people on the street and secret them off to undisclosed locales – whoever they are and whatever their alleged offenses – our nation has taken a huge and disturbing step toward abandoning one of its cornerstone principles. 
And all of us – whatever our status, race, wealth, affiliations, or beliefs – are significantly less free as a result.

title: Affordability, healthcare, accountability center of heated race for central Arkansas US House seat
description: Running for a seventh term, Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill is focusing on what he’s done for his central Arkansas district in the past 12 years. But his Democratic opponent, Chris Jones, is emphasizing what Hill hasn’t done and what Jones would do for the district if he wins in November. One thing Jones would […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill face Democrat Chris Jones in the 2026 election for Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District. (Photos courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)Running for a seventh term, Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill is focusing on what he’s done for his central Arkansas district in the past 12 years.
But his Democratic opponent, Chris Jones, is emphasizing what Hill hasn’t done and what Jones would do for the district if he wins in November.
One thing Jones would do is ensure he is available to the public as much as possible, even from Washington D.C., he told potential constituents at a Conway sandwich shop in September.
“It is not French Hill’s seat — it’s your seat, and every two years you get to choose who you want to be in that seat,” Jones said.


Election day is Nov. 3, and early voting begins Oct. 19. More information about voting locations and registration is available on the Arkansas secretary of state’s website. 


In a September interview, Hill said his decades of business and banking experience make him more than qualified to keep his seat.
“I’ve tried to take all those economic lessons and management lessons and deliver for the people in central Arkansas on concrete, practical things to help make this a better place,” Hill said.
Jones said it’s time for someone new to represent the 2nd Congressional District, comprising all or part of eight counties, including part of Little Rock, where Jones and Hill both live.
If he wins, Jones would be Arkansas’ first Black member of Congress. He has never held elected office, and his first foray into politics was his 2022 run for governor, which he lost to Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Democrats face long odds in a state where Republicans have held every statewide and federal office since 2014, the year Hill first won his seat.
A 2021 redistricting plan approved by the majority-Republican Legislature moved some Pulaski County voters into other districts and made the 2nd District more favorable to the GOP. Hill won his sixth term in 2024 with 59% of the vote.
Even before redistricting, Democrats’ nationally watched efforts to unseat Hill, including by state Sen. Clarke Tucker in 2018 and former state Sen. Joyce Elliott in 2020, were unsuccessful.
But in August, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the 2nd District to its list of GOP seats it aims to flip, and on Monday it added the race to its “Red to Blue” program, a targeted fundraising effort for races deemed competitive.
An August Talk Business & Politics poll indicated Jones had a slim lead over Hill within the margin of error. Political forecaster Larry Sabato earlier this year moved the race from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican,” while the Cook Political Report classifies it as “solid Republican.”

Chris Jones (left), the Democratic candidate for Arkansas 2nd Congressional District, speaks to supporters on Sept. 17, 2026 at Cross Creek Sandwiches in Conway. Former U.S. Rep. Joe Kennedy III of Massachusetts (right) expressed his support for Jones. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Jones has drawn attention from national Democratic figures: former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed him, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg headlined a Jones rally in Little Rock. Former U.S. Rep. Joe Kennedy III of Massachusetts spoke at Jones’ Sept. 17 event, and a political action committee started by Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has placed TV ad buys supporting Jones’ bid. 
Hill’s campaign has outraised and outspent Jones, and the GOP lawmaker has also drawn support from top Republicans. Ohio U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan, who chairs the House Judiciary Committee, is scheduled to headline a rally for Hill in Benton later this month.
Two cryptocurrency-focused super PACs have thrown their support behind Hill. Defend American Jobs spent heavily earlier this year supporting Hill during the GOP primary, which he won with 76% of the vote over challenger Chase McDowell.
The Associated Press reported that Fairshake will direct $1 million each to three incumbent Republicans, including Hill, and three Democrats.
DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said Monday that Republican super PACs spending millions of dollars in safe GOP districts is a sign that voters are moving toward Democratic candidates.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Affordability

Jones’ concerns about affordability in Arkansas include the looming cuts to low-income people’s health insurance and nutrition assistance under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year and Hill supported.
The law is expected to cut rural Medicaid spending by $15.5 billion per year over the next decade. More than 800,000 low-income or disabled Arkansans rely on Medicaid.
Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion faces an uncertain future after the Trump administration rejected its renewal in July. Jones said members of Congress should work with the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to meet Arkansas’ healthcare needs. Hill agreed that part of his job is to be a liaison to federal agencies.
Low reimbursement rates force Arkansas hospitals to scale back services

Both Jones and Hill expressed frustration that Arkansas hospitals have been cutting services due to low reimbursement rates from Medicaid and from private insurers. Specifically in the 2nd District, Jacksonville’s Unity Health closed its emergency room in April.
Jones noted that low-income people tend to use emergency rooms as primary care providers in the absence of a robust hospital system, and he said elected officials should be at least partly responsible for plans to replace health services that get cut.
Hill said Arkansas’ low reimbursement rates are “repugnant” and require a joint effort between state and federal officials to address the issue.
“It systematically discriminates against health providers in the state, and then by virtue of that, has an impact on patients,” Hill said.
On other affordability matters, Hill has touted his votes for reestablishing the federal child tax credit and for eliminating taxes on tips and overtime pay.
Hill also sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan bill that became law in July without President Donald Trump’s signature, removing some of the regulations on housing manufacturing and bank loans for homebuyers.
The policy changes are meant to bolster housing supply and increase investment in housing by banks, which will help reduce the Little Rock Housing Authority’s waitlist for public and affordable housing units, Hill said in March. The waitlist exceeded 5,000 at the time, and the agency oversees 1,100 housing units.
The House Financial Services Committee, which Hill chairs, met in Little Rock in March to discuss the housing legislation and the Little Rock Housing Authority’s history of financial and management issues. Hill said in September that holding the agency accountable is a point of pride in his sixth term.
Jones said the ROAD to Housing Act is a step in the right direction. Further steps would be to increase access not just to mortgages but to homeownership itself by ensuring Arkansans can afford necessities like food and healthcare, he said.

Hill says House, Senate need to resolve ‘distinct differences’ on housing bills


 Accountability

Jones has criticized Hill for not voting to end the war in Iran that Trump started in February. He said central Arkansans regularly tell him how frustrated they are about the conflict, which has cost the federal government billions of dollars per week and raised the cost of gasoline.
“Military families, veterans, current service members — they’re watching a war that Congress has never voted on, and they’re watching French Hill abdicate his congressional duty and responsibility,” said Jones, whose wife is an Air Force veteran.
Hill clarified that he has specifically voted “against poorly drafted amendments that are sloppy [and] encourage all American forces to be withdrawn from the Middle East.”
“I do think the conduct of how we eliminate that Iranian nuclear and military threat could have been done more with an allied approach,” Hill said.
Hill’s voting record has almost always aligned with Trump’s priorities. Jones and other Democrats have made an effort to associate incumbent Republicans with Trump, whose approval rating in Arkansas and nationwide has been declining.
Hill has split with Trump on some issues, including opposing the president’s plan to allow more beef imports into the U.S. 
Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

Arkansas Republicans have been less inclined to tie themselves to Trump than to tie their opponents to Harris and other prominent Democrats.
The Republican Party of Arkansas announced Wednesday that it would file a complaint with the Federal Election Commission against Jones for not filing a required financial disclosure report by the Aug. 13 deadline.
“Chris Jones’ refusal to disclose his personal finances begs the question: what does he have to hide?” state GOP Chairman Joseph Wood said in a news release.
In an interview, Jones called the state GOP’s complaint and statement against him a “very unfortunate” effort to “play on people’s fear.” He said he was dealing with a personal tragedy in August and plans to pay the $200 fine to the FEC for missing the filing deadline.
Jones also said 2nd District residents have expressed “frustrations and hope” in his months campaigning for their support.
“They’re frustrated with where things are, but [they have] a real hopefulness about where things can be,” Jones said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Diaper Bank offers pocketbook relief to local families in need
description: As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. […]
text:
Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank)As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child.
And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet.
Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit.
“People who need diapers need our help,” she said.
There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting.
“Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives.
Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian, one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers.
“SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said.
Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.”
Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors.
“We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.”
The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month.
“This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.”
As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges.
“The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said.
“Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.”
One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives.
“Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.”
The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Annual free health care day returns to Charleston clinic; increased demand expected
description: A free and charitable clinic in Charleston, West Virginia, will offer a full day of medical, dental and vision care to the public this month at no cost and with no income restrictions. This is the third year for West Virginia Health Right’s #WeCareWV Day. This year’s event will be from 8 a.m. until 5 […]
text:
Patients line the sidewalk outside West Virginia Health Right during #WeCareWV Day 2024. More than 500 people got free medical, vision and dental care during the popup clinic. (Photo courtesy of 84 Agency)A free and charitable clinic in Charleston, West Virginia, will offer a full day of medical, dental and vision care to the public this month at no cost and with no income restrictions.
This is the third year for West Virginia Health Right’s #WeCareWV Day. This year’s event will be from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17  at West Virginia Health Right, 1520 Washington Street East in Charleston. 
Prior to starting the event in 2024, Health Right partnered with Tennessee-based Remote Area Medical for an annual free walk-in clinic. 
CEO Angie Settle said Health Right has the capacity to treat 500 patients on #WeCareWV Day. She expects a bigger demand for services this year, as the costs of health care, food, gas and other things have risen. 
“We’ve seen a big increase in our patient numbers as prices go up,” Settle said. “People have to make decisions between paying their utility bills, putting gas in their car to get to work, and see if they can buy glasses or pay for dentists because a lot of people, they don’t have that insurance.”
Thousands of West Virginians dropped their health insurance plans through the Affordable Care Act this year after premiums spiked when subsidies ended. State and local government workers on the Public Employees Insurance Agency also saw their health care costs increase in July. 
Gas prices average around $4.27 per gallon in West Virginia, up from about $3 a year ago, according to AAA. 
Health Right patients are generally required to show proof of their annual income to be sure they meet federal poverty level guidelines. The clinic typically treats uninsured people, Medicaid and Medicare recipients, Settle said.
On #WeCareWV Day, the clinic may see patients who may have health insurance with high deductibles and co-pays, she said. 
“We want to be sure we try to remove any barriers, and those people can get that preventive care that they need,” Settle said. “So that’s one day we don’t ask any of the qualifying questions. Anybody that’s willing to come and wait, we’re going to see them.”
Beginning in January, some Medicaid recipients must meet new work requirements in order to keep getting health care. Settle said Health Right, which has 48,000 patients now, expects to see an even bigger need for health care once the requirements take effect. 
“It’s just a challenge for us, budgetary wise, because we’re still trying to buy the medicines and provide the care to as many people,” Settle said. “It’s just trying to do more for less.”
The one-day clinic usually has around 300 volunteers, ranging from healthcare professionals and support staff to lay people to help with parking and patient intake, Settle said. 
She said the clinic is a great opportunity for medical students to gain experience treating people who are in need, which is important for any health care professional.
“I think it’s so important to expose people going into the medical field or dental field early about people in need, so that when they’re out and they’re in practice, even if they don’t end up doing something like we do here, like a free and charitable clinic… they always keep in mind that there are people out there that if you hand them the prescription or whatever, you need to make sure that they actually can get it filled,” Settle said.
“It’s not just enough to say goodbye in the exam room,” she said. “You really need to be thinking through if they can access that care or not.”
Settle said the clinic could use more volunteers, especially from the dental field, for the event. Anyone interested in volunteering may contact Settle at 304-414-5931, or sign up on the clinic’s website, wvhealthright.org. 
For more information, see Health Right’s website at wvhealthright.org.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee lawmakers began hearings on medical marijuana program. TBI rep calls weed “dangerous drug”
description: ​Tennessee lawmakers held hearings to discuss implementing a limited medical marijuana program, but the state’s top law enforcement group remains the most vocal opposition. Representatives from the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, TBI, emerged as the strongest opponents, stating there were no circumstances in which they thought medical marijuana should be[...]
text:
Sen. Ferrell Haile, a Gallatin Republican, right, is leading the charge for a narrow medical marijuana program in Tennessee. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)​Tennessee lawmakers held hearings to discuss implementing a limited medical marijuana program, but the state’s top law enforcement group remains the most vocal opposition.
Representatives from the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, TBI, emerged as the strongest opponents, stating there were no circumstances in which they thought medical marijuana should be allowed in Tennessee.
“Marijuana is in fact a dangerous drug, whose use poses a significant threat to public safety, and whose cultivation poses a threat to the environment,” said Erica Stephens, a TBI agent working on the bureau’s Dangerous Drugs Task Force, to lawmakers during the hearing. “In the state of Tennessee, marijuana is the number one drug associated with criminal activity, including violent crime.”
​Lawmakers held nearly six hours of hearings last week to discuss the program, with much of the discussion focused on how Tennessee should address marijuana use considering it is either fully legalized or legal for medical use in 41 other states, and widely available on the black market.
TBI and other law enforcement representatives repeatedly brought up Oklahoma’s medical marijuana program as the most prominent failure of a medical program.
Sen. Ferrell ​Haile, a Gallatin Republican, said during the hearing that Oklahoma’s program, which included smokable products, was “nowhere near comparable” to the program Tennessee lawmakers were studying.
​“It’s apples to oranges,” Haile said.
The bureau’s adamant opposition appeared to rankle several lawmakers.



Quotation







California and Colorado have significantly lower violent crime rates than Tennessee. We are a state that has no legal marijuana program, and we have some of the highest violent crime rates in the country.


– Sen. London Lamar, D-Memphis


State Sen. Todd Gardenhire, a Chattanooga Republican, told committee members that law enforcement’s testimony had “drifted” the conversation away from what was important.
“This is a way to keep people from having to go to the illicit market,” Gardenhire said. “It’s a way to get them the help they need in a legal way.”
State Sen. London Lamar, a Memphis Democrat, said the correlation between marijuana use and violent crime was “inaccurate.”
“Crime is an issue for all of us,” Lamar said. “California and Colorado have significantly lower violent crime rates than Tennessee. We are a state that has no legal marijuana program, and we have some of the highest violent crime rates in the country.”
After the federal government reclassified marijuana as having potential medical benefits in April. Tennessee lawmakers agreed to hear recommendations from the state’s cannabis commission on creating a limited medical marijuana program that doesn’t include smokable products and is only obtainable for a narrow set of conditions.
​The state cannabis commission is proposing allowing medical marijuana for those suffering from Alzheimer’s, ALS, cancer, Crohn’s disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, HIV/AIDS and sickle cell disease.
Banning of THCA potentially blows $110 million hole in Tennessee’s budget

Over the past decade, medical and legal marijuana programs have swept across the nation as the federal government has let states decide how to regulate the product. Most of Tennessee’s neighboring states have either legal or medical marijuana programs.
This proliferation has made enforcing a state ban difficult, as many Tennesseans can drive across state borders to places where they can legally buy it.
For several years, Tennessee’s legalization of hemp-derived cannabinoid products served as a loophole to the state’s marijuana laws. But lawmakers banned smokable hemp products, all but killing the market in July.
Christina Flatt, a Nashville pharmacist, said during the hearing that Tennessee’s potential medical marijuana program doesn’t go far enough and should include medical conditions like post-traumatic stress disorder for veterans and hospice patients.
“Cannabis has medical value, and the United States government recognizes it,” Flatt said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Lawmakers renew contract auditing ADOC compliance with federal sexual assault laws
description: A state legislative committee Thursday approved a contract to audit Alabama’s prisons’ compliance with the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act. The contract between the Alabama Department of Corrections and Texas-based Corrections Consulting Services, was renewed through November 2027 and increased by $58,400, bringing the total amount to more than $164,000.[...]
text:
A gate opens at Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore, Alabama on October 22, 2019. Members of the Contract Review Committee Thursday approved a contract renewal between the Alabama Department of Corrections and auditors to determine compliance with the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act. (File)A state legislative committee Thursday approved a contract to audit Alabama’s prisons’ compliance with the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act.
The contract between the Alabama Department of Corrections and Texas-based Corrections Consulting Services, was renewed through November 2027 and increased by $58,400, bringing the total amount to more than $164,000.
“This is the vendor that does that,” said Mandy Speirs, assistant general counsel for the ADOC. “It audits each facility every three years, so it rotates. It audits a third of our facilities every year.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
PREA, passed in 2003, requires facilities to provide resources to reduce sexual assaults in prisons. Corrections Consulting Services employs auditors who are certified with the U.S. DOJ to conduct audits of facilities to determine if they meet the standards set by the department.
The ADOC opened 153 investigations related to sexual abuse and harassment across its facilities for the first three months of the year, according to the quarterly report on the ADOC website. ADOC opened another 139 investigations for the next three months leading up to the end of June.
ADOC listed most of the results from the investigations as either “unfounded” or “unsubstantiated.” In the first three months of the year, for example, only 11 of the 153 investigations that were closed were substantiated. For the three months leading up to June, only 3 of the 142 closed investigations into sexual assault and harassment were substantiated. Critics have charged the department underreports sexual assaults.
In 2019 and 2020, the U.S. Department of Justice released a series of reports detailing physical and sexual assaults on inmates in Alabama’s prisons, which led to a federal lawsuit against the state late in 2020.
In August, members of the Contract Review Committee delayed a contract awarded by ADOC for an additional $30 million to Bill Lunsford of Butler Snow to defend ADOC in the lawsuit.
Last month, the U.S. DOJ filed a request for summary judgment in the lawsuit, which alleges that the conditions in Alabama’s men’s correctional facilities violate their Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The motion for summary judgment said some of the sexual violence is committed behind sheets draped over bunks, which leads to a lack of reporting. The motion also alleged corrections staff are not present to address the problem.
The motion for summary judgment also quoted former ADOC Commissioner John Hamm saying he did not monitor information about the incidents of sexual assault or receive reports of overdose deaths.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: The Trump train runs out of steam
description: The Donald Trump who took the stage in Mobile Friday night was not the man who catapulted onto the political scene in the same city in 2015. Eleven years ago, he strode into Ladd-Peebles Stadium on a warm August night looking crisp, tan, and tieless, wearing a white shirt, khakis and a navy blazer. On […]
text:
President Donald Trump waves to the crowd after speaking at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026.  The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)The Donald Trump who took the stage in Mobile Friday night was not the man who catapulted onto the political scene in the same city in 2015.
Eleven years ago, he strode into Ladd-Peebles Stadium on a warm August night looking crisp, tan, and tieless, wearing a white shirt, khakis and a navy blazer. On his head perched an O.G. “Make America Great Again” hat,  the only red hat in sight. The people cheering behind him wore regular clothes; Trump merch hadn’t yet become ubiquitous.
“I’m a non-politician,” he declared back then. “The other day I served jury duty. I told you — they had ‘occupation.’ I refused to put down ‘politician.’”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 30,000-odd people in attendance ate it up. That night launched the Trump Train, full steam ahead. Who among us, in the ensuing decade, has managed to go an entire week without thinking, reading, or speaking the word “Trump”? If you have, tell me your secret.
But a decade at the center of America’s political orbit has sucked Trump into the very swamp he promised to drain. He has become the thing he ran against.
Compare that fizzy August night in 2015 to last Friday, as gray clouds hung thick in the sky and lines of Trump die-hards trooped into the 10,000-seat Mitchell Center on the campus of the University of South Alabama. 
The former “non-politician” returned to Mobile to stump for Republicans in the midterms. “It’s the most important midterm election we’ve ever had,” he said. “Close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot.”
He promised that if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November, every adult citizen will get a check for $5,000. I guess if the GOP keeps both chambers, we can add that trillion-dollar payout to Trump’s tab, alongside the promised DOGE checks and tariff dividends.
He seemed subdued as he ticked through all his boilerplate talking points: “radical left dumbocrats,” “hottest country in the world,” “fake news media,” etc., etc. Empty seats dotted the uppermost sections of the stadium.
He looked faded, his bronzed cheeks a few shades paler than usual, his suit a little loose on his diminished figure. Normally a charming showman, he wasn’t really selling it on Friday night
Eleven years will do that to a person. There’s a marked difference between a 69-year-old man and an 80-year-old man. 
There’s also a difference between a salesman confident in his untested ability to run a country, and a leader who’s had to live through the grind of governing.
The Trump of 2015 was a dynamic speaker who exuded enthusiasm about his vision for the country. Many voters didn’t care for his brand of optimism, but he sold his idea of a gold-plated future with a heart and soul that had not yet calcified into bitterness against his enemies. In the open air of Ladd-Peebles Stadium, he held forth on the corrupting power of lobbyists, outlined how he’d fix America’s flagging manufacturing sector. He signed an attendee’s copy of “The Art of the Deal” and crowed about his successes in real estate. He was buoyant; his future held nothing but upside.
Sure, he talked about the “dummies” running the government. But his bite didn’t have the same vicious edge that it does now. “We have people that don’t have a clue,” he said in 2015. “And I don’t know, some people say they’re bad people. I don’t think they’re bad people. I think they’re incompetent people.”
He has now had six years as president to prove his own competence. For the last two years, he has enjoyed a Republican trifecta in all three branches of government. 
And last Friday, ever the salesman, he trotted out a line off the teleprompter declaring that we’re living in a “golden age” even as “communists” try to tear down the country. But Americans are no longer buying what he’s selling. With gas above $4 a gallon, diesel hitting all-time highs, inflation still pummeling household budgets, and Democrats shut out from power (and therefore blame), his approval rating is scraping the bottom of the barrel.
(He might also want to check that “golden age” message with gubernatorial candidate Tommy Tuberville, who glad-handed him onstage on Friday and who, just last week, said that Alabama’s major cities are so dangerous, it might require deploying the National Guard if he’s elected.)
Toward the end of his speech — his attention flagging as he churned through his canned lines — Trump put the cherry on top by mispronouncing “Mobile.” Twice.
Ouch. Such a rookie mistake.
And so Mobile, the launchpad for his meteoric rise, is now also sealed as a symbol of his decline. How fitting that the same town should serve as bookends for his relevance.
He still has two more years in the Oval Office. Who knows what national monuments he might decide to tear down in that time, what novel ways he might find to diminish America’s global standing and commit human rights abuses? He will maintain access to the nuclear launch codes, God help us.
The damage he has wrought will be generational. 
But last Friday showed that he is well and truly past his peak. If Democrats eke out a majority in one or both chambers of Congress in November, he will become the lamest of lame ducks.
I can almost see the glimmer of the next era peeking around the corner — an era when we’ll go days or weeks without thinking or speaking his name. 
At a rally in Ohio on Saturday, he mused about the impending end of his presidency: “Perhaps I’ll try a couple of years of being nonconsequential, if you don’t mind.”
Be my guest, sir.

title: Democrats more trusted on healthcare costs, survey shows
text: WASHINGTON — Democrats are more motivated to vote in November’s midterm elections than Republicans, potentially giving the party an advantage to flip at least one chamber of Congress, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonpartisan health organization KFF.Democratic candidates also held an edge with voter confidence in their ability to address the rising cost of healthcare and everyday goods as well as abortion policy, though the parties were mostly tied when it came to addressing fraud in government programs. Republicans are trusted “to do a better job handling” immigration. “Of all the cost-of-living worries hitting voters now, a big health care bill is the least predictable, and that’s a big reason why health care costs are right up there with gas prices and the costs of food and housing on voters’ minds,” KFF President and CEO Dr. Drew Altman said in a statement. A majority of respondents, 66%, said they favor a candidate who supports a national health plan, which Democrats often refer to as Medicare-for-all. That support, however, fluctuates depending on how the question was asked. Seventy-six percent of those polled said they support a nationwide health plan when told it would “guarantee health insurance for all Americans.” The level of support was about the same, 75%, when people were told it would “eliminate all insurance premiums and reduce out-of-pocket costs for most Americans.” A slight majority, 52%, of respondents said they’d support a Medicare-for-all type plan when told it would “eliminate private health insurance companies.” Approval dropped to 38% when those polled were told it could “threaten the current Medicare program” and then to 35% when informed it would “require most Americans to pay more in taxes.” Support for a nationwide health plan decreased to 24% when those polled were told it could “lead to delays in people getting some medical tests and treatments.”When broken down by political party, far more Democrats, 84%, than Republicans, 35%, supported a nationwide health plan like Medicare-for-all.  Voters seek changeRegardless of which party secures control of the U.S. House and Senate following the November midterm elections, a significant number of those polled want to see lawmakers work to change the country’s healthcare system. Forty-nine percent said that “there are some good things about our healthcare system, but major changes are needed.” An additional 36% said “there is so much wrong with our healthcare system that it needs to be completely overhauled.” Another 13% said the country’s health system “works pretty well, but minor changes are needed.” And just 2% said there should be no changes. When asked what motivates people to vote in this year’s election, 20% of those polled said they wanted to bring about change, 19% said to stop President Donald Trump, 15% said they believe the country is in a crisis, 11% said the rising cost of living, 10% said to vote out Republicans, 9% said to protect democracy, 8% said to keep Democrats out of power, 7% said to end corruption and 6% said it was due to concerns about socialism or communism. Dems hold enthusiasm edgeForty-seven percent of those polled said they were more motivated to vote in this year’s elections than they were in the past, while 41% said they were about as motivated and 12% said they were less motivated. Democrats had a clear motivation advantage over Republicans with 63% of Democratic supporters saying they were more motivated and 28% saying they were about as motivated as they were during earlier elections. Thirty-eight percent of Republicans are more motivated and 53% said they were about as motivated as past elections. KFF polled 1,328 U.S. adults, including 1,013 voters, in English and in Spanish between Sept. 16 and Sept. 21. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey’s administration now competing with Justice’s for title of least transparent
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey bragged about how transparent he was with the press when he first took office. But he should answer to the people and the press.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey speaks at a news conference about foster care on May 28, 2025. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)Gov. Patrick Morrisey bragged a lot about how transparent he was with the press when he first took office. He’d take questions from reporters at in-person news conferences, which felt like an improvement after Gov. Jim Justice, who only did virtual press conferences and didn’t allow follow up questions from the few reporters he took questions from. But that really is the bare minimum. The government should answer to the people and the press.
In September, the governor took questions at only three of the 25 press events that are archived on his YouTube channel.
When media are invited to a press conference, it gives them the opportunity to take photos or video, and ask follow up questions to the governor’s announcement of a new initiative or policy. Typically a couple of hours after the presser, Morrisey’s office will email a news release with the information, and a few quotes from the governor. Allowing reporters to ask questions during the event gives the governor and his staff the opportunity to answer questions once instead of multiple times when the release may have had confusing wording or left out certain information. 
If he’s not going to take questions at his events, why should a reporter waste one to two hours of their day attending the event when they’ll have the same information in a news release just a few hours later?
At the end of a news conference, Morrisey used to ask the media if they had any questions for him or other officials who might have been present. Sometimes he’d ask the media to keep their questions related to the current announcement, but this is a great opportunity for reporters to get a quote straight from the governor instead of his spokesperson. So yes, they want to ask questions about other issues as well.
Not only has he stopped taking questions, but it seems Morrisey’s office doesn’t want the media to be able to plan to attend his pressers. Often, his office announces an event the morning of the speech or the night before, after 5 p.m.
Ogden reporter Steven Allen Adams posted on X last week that Morrisey was “preparing to have a last-minute press conference announcing home energy rebate programs.”
The governor responded to the post that the presser had “been scheduled for some time so it’s not last minute.” However, as Adams pointed out, the email announcing the press conference was sent at 7:16 a.m., less than three hours before the event. That doesn’t leave time for reporters to plan to attend.
This has become a strange pattern with Morrisey. He won’t take questions, his office won’t respond to comments, but he’ll respond to reporters on social media if they don’t reach out to his office.
Just last week, he attacked the reporting of Gazette-Mail reporter Mike Tony over his coverage of West Virginia’s application to become a nuclear development hub.
Morrisey lashed out at the Gazette-Mail and Tony on X: “The Gazette got it wrong. This Friday’s story intentionally misrepresented my administration’s energy plans without giving me a chance to address their claims and slanted coverage.” 
Tony obtained the state’s application through a public records request, and it stated that the state offered to store nuclear waste and listed potential sites in Boone, Jackson and Jefferson counties.
Morrisey’s post continued, “But West Virginia will not be a dumping ground for nuclear waste. Period.”
Which is true, because the Morrisey’s administration quietly withdrew its application Wednesday night, according to reporting by Adams.
When reporters can’t get officials to respond to them, they often turn to public records requests, and the Morrisey administration’s handling of these is even more frustrating than the lack of comments. 
Under the Freedom of Information Act, everyone has the right to request a copy of any public record of any public body in West Virginia. The state then has a maximum of five days, not including weekends or holidays, to provide the documents or give a reason for denying the request.
It’s not uncommon for the Morrisey administration to respond to a reporter’s FOIA request with a notice that their response will be delayed.
It took West Virginia Watch reporter Amelia Ferrell Knisely months to write a story on the state piloting a new system for how Child Protective Services workers make decisions about foster children’s cases because the state took 77 business days to respond to her request. She sent her original request on Nov. 19, 2025, and received the documents on March 13, 2026.
Lori Kersey waited three weeks on a records request before giving up and reporting a story about Aaron Siri, a lawyer who represented the plaintiff in the state’s vaccine lawsuit, who also represented RFK Jr. and an anti-vaccine group. Eight months after the story was published, she received the documents, which didn’t include anything worth using. If she had waited, the story would have been delayed eight months for no reason.
WV MetroNews reporter Brad McElhinny showed exactly how maddening the cycle is in his story about what happened with the state’s SNAP waiver for hot, healthy foods.
On Aug. 21, 2025, McElhinny sent his first FOIA request to the West Virginia Department of Human Services, Bureau for Family Assistance, asking for copies of public records related to the state’s waiver request allowing for hot, healthy foods to qualify as SNAP purchases.
The state responded the next day to say they expected to have a formal response to him no later than Sept. 29, 2025.
“But then, every month for the past 12 months, the state has responded with an email saying, ‘We are still researching to determine if we are in custody of any responsive documents regarding your request.’” McElhinny wrote. “That was the response last September, then in October, twice in November, a break for December, turned the calendar to January, blustered through February, blew into March, poured into April, then May, June, July and finally circled back to a year in August.”
There are so many stories that reporters want to write, but they can’t because they can’t get the supporting documents from the state. I’ve seen questions from people wondering why the media isn’t covering a certain subject and in most cases, this is why. 
We’re working on so much, and we get so many tips, but when the governor and his administration don’t cooperate with us, it makes it very difficult to report. 
Government transparency is necessary for the press to be able to tell the stories of how decisions made by our government officials are affecting or could affect West Virginians. Unfortunately, Gov. Morrisey and his administration rarely cooperate with us, making it very difficult to publish these important reports. Please know that we’re persevering.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: It’s time to celebrate the sacred rite of voting in America
description: It was an early November day, cold and snowy. My father, Walter, was 85 and recovering from cataract surgery gone bad. He did the things an 85-year-old did – he read his newspaper daily despite an 8th grade education, told WWII stories, and doted on his grandchildren. But there was one more thing he did […]
text:
Kentuckians will got to the polls again on Nov. 3, 2026. (Austin Anthony for The Kentucky Lantern)It was an early November day, cold and snowy. My father, Walter, was 85 and recovering from cataract surgery gone bad. He did the things an 85-year-old did – he read his newspaper daily despite an 8th grade education, told WWII stories, and doted on his grandchildren. But there was one more thing he did on that cold, snowy November morning.
 Moving slowly with a patch securely over his left eye, he sat down at the dining room table as I arrived. 
“Daddy, it’s time to go vote,” I said. 
“I don’t think I can this time,” he replied. 
His answer was not unexpected but shocking nonetheless. I pondered for the longest moment and came up with this: “if you don’t vote, daddy, your guys won’t win”!  He looked at me for a moment with a look of deep concern and a sudden sense of urgency.  Slowly, he rose from his chair and headed toward the door. As if there was never a moment of hesitation, he walked past me at the door with these words, “What are you waiting for?”
 Looking back, it was a teaching moment that voting was something the weather or a bad eye could not stop. It was that important. We are reminded that democracy is sustained not only by historic figures and grand speeches, it is the stuff of ordinary people who put on their coats, learn about the candidates and the issues, and go vote.
 In honor of people like my dad and the most sacred rite of freedom, voting, The League of Women Voters of Lexington, Global Lex, and CivicLex are launching “Make Democracy Social,” and “Celebrate Democracy,” a two-part, nonpartisan voter engagement initiative, designed to help Fayette County residents become informed voters, make a plan to vote, and build community around civic participation.
The initiative, launched this September, will provide a toolkit where information instructs on how to conduct and host Democracy Potlucks. The potlucks will feature community forums where citizens gather to make democracy social with a meal and conversation. Community groups, churches, neighborhood associations, clubs, workplaces, language communities and friend groups are encouraged to consider hosting a Democracy Potluck before early voting begins. Sponsoring organizations will provide nonpartisan resources to help people research what is on their ballot, understand the offices being elected, and make a voting plan.
 Following these activities, all will be invited to Democracy Celebration opportunities where voters gather after voting to celebrate community participation.
 Visit www.lwvlexington.com for more information and look out for League of Women Voters of Lexington, Global Lex, CivicLex, and partner organizations out in the community throughout the fall.
 Let’s remember that our fundamental freedoms were the result of sparks of passion and the act of voting that underpins our most basic freedoms. They include freedom to worship as you wish and separation of church and state, freedom of speech to voice opposing opinions and enjoy a free press, due process and the right to counsel sparked by one man who spoke up and demanded representation in our courts (Gideon vs. Wainright, 1963).
 Let us remember that our most fundamental right to speak up and vote lay at the root of all our freedoms. The many battles throughout American history were ones of expanding the right to vote through many means including constitutional amendments that afforded voting status without discrimination regardless of gender, race, and age.
 Let’s honor the legacy of those who have gone before us. Voting is not something my dad did when convenient, when weather cooperated, or when he felt particularly inspired. It was a part of being a citizen and fighting hard every day to be informed and go vote. It is the act that not only preserves democracy but something we should celebrate. Let’s celebrate democracy together!

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Workforce training program earns another No.1 ranking for Virginia
description: Virginia’s workforce training program has earned another No. 1 national ranking as the commonwealth competes for companies looking for workers trained for specialized jobs. Area Development, a major national trade publication, ranked Virginia first for workforce training programs in its 2026 Top States for Doing Business report. The recognition highlights th[...]
text:
The Virginia Economic Development Partnership oversees the Talent Accelerator Program, which provides customized recruitment and training services at no cost to qualifying employers. Virginia ranked first for workforce training programs in Area Development’s 2026 business rankings. (Photo courtesy of VDEP)Virginia’s workforce training program has earned another No. 1 national ranking as the commonwealth competes for companies looking for workers trained for specialized jobs.
Area Development, a major national trade publication, ranked Virginia first for workforce training programs in its 2026 Top States for Doing Business report. The recognition highlights the Virginia Talent Accelerator Program, which provides customized recruitment and training at no cost to qualifying companies opening or expanding operations in the commonwealth. 
Since its launch in 2019, the program has supported projects representing more than 22,000 announced jobs across the state, according to Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration. 
Virginia placed eighth overall in Area Development’s nationwide rankings and also finished fifth for innovation and research, sixth for site readiness programs and seventh for logistics and transportation infrastructure. 
The workforce recognition comes after Business Facilities ranked Virginia first for customized workforce training for the fourth consecutive year this summer.
“Workforce is one of the most important factors in any company’s location decision, and Virginia continues to distinguish itself nationally,” Virginia Secretary of Commerce and Trade Carrie Chenery said in a statement Monday. 
“The Virginia Talent Accelerator Program is a clear competitive advantage because it drives business growth by customizing talent solutions. This recognition reinforces that the commonwealth is not only attracting investment but also preparing Virginians for the jobs those investments create.” 
Created by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership in collaboration with the Virginia Community College System, the Talent Accelerator receives funding support from the governor’s administration and the General Assembly. Its services are offered as an incentive for companies creating jobs in Virginia. 
The work varies from project to project. Before training begins, the Talent Accelerator assesses a company’s recruitment processes and workforce needs. That can lead to assistance before an employee is even hired, including brief training sessions and assessments that give applicants a look at the work while allowing employers to evaluate potential hires. 
Recruitment help can include digital advertising and campaigns on streaming and podcast platforms. The program’s in-house team also produces videos, websites and 3D animations to help companies recruit workers and demonstrate workplace tasks. 
Once workers are hired, training can range from safety and basic skills to detailed instruction on production processes and individual jobs. Teamwork, conflict resolution and leadership training are also available. 
Manufacturing projects are paired with a regional community college, while the program also works with universities, including historically Black colleges, according to VEDP. 
Spanberger said Virginia’s latest rank shows the value of connecting economic development with workforce preparation. 
“Virginia is building the best workforce in America, and industry is taking notice,” Spanberger said in a statement. “The Virginia Talent Accelerator Program gives businesses a powerful reason to choose the commonwealth by delivering customized training that prepares Virginians to succeed from day one.”
Area Development has covered corporate site selection and relocation since 1965. Its 2026 rankings are based on a survey of 50 site consultants who evaluated states across 20 categories affecting corporate location and investment decisions. 
The magazine then weighted those results based on the importance of each factor in corporate site selection.
Virginia finished behind Georgia, Texas, Tennessee, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Alabama in the overall ranking. But it took the top spot for workforce training, ahead of Georgia and South Carolina. 
VEDP President and CEO Jason El Koubi said the Talent Accelerator’s value lies in building recruitment and training around an employer’s particular operation rather than offering a standard package. 
“Our team works directly with companies to design recruitment and training strategies that reflect their operations, culture and long-term growth plans,” El Koubi said in a statement. “Area Development’s recognition underscores the program’s impact and the value Virginia delivers to companies creating jobs across the commonwealth.” 
Several companies that announced Virginia projects this year are using the program.
Avio USA plans a roughly $500 million manufacturing facility in Hurt that is expected to create more than 1,000 jobs. RINGANA, an Austrian skincare and nutritional products company, announced an $85 million U.S. headquarters, production and distribution operation in Roanoke with 435 jobs. Jabil plans a manufacturing facility in Prince George County expected to create 352 jobs. 
Merck & Co. also plans to use Talent Accelerator as part of its $3 billion expansion in Elkton. The project is expected to create 500 jobs and will serve as the company’s Center of Excellence for Pharmaceutical Ingredients and Small Molecule Manufacturing. 
The Spanberger administration’s figure of more than 22,000 jobs reflects announced positions associated with projects supported by the Talent Accelerator. It does not indicate how many of those jobs have been filled or how many workers have completed training through the program.

title: Virginia Board of Education reinstates adult education advisory committee after 3 years
description: The Virginia Board of Education recently reestablished its adult education advisory committee after a three-year hiatus to guide how the state uses resources to improve its adult education and literacy program. The programs combine education and job training that can help enrollees earn recognized industry credentials and provide academic and parenting suppo[...]
text:
A college student leaving a lecture hall. (Photo by Getty Images / ferrantraite) The Virginia Board of Education recently reestablished its adult education advisory committee after a three-year hiatus to guide how the state uses resources to improve its adult education and literacy program.
The programs combine education and job training that can help enrollees earn recognized industry credentials and provide academic and parenting support for adults and their children. They also help learners strengthen English proficiency, develop civic and workplace skills, and improve basic academic skills through in-person or remote classes.
The committee’s return follows a three-month listening tour led by Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration, where educators, school leaders and parents spoke about strengthening Virginia’s K-12 system. 
At the board’s Aug. 27 business meeting, Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway said the committee helps the board by gathering feedback from stakeholders, considering adult learners’ access to rigorous programs and making effective use of funding, while keeping adult education and literacy moving forward. 
The board voted to re-establish the committee on Sept. 24.
“We can’t always have all those folks represented here on the board, and so we welcome reestablishing this committee to think through how we make sure that these students are having access to sort of equal rigor,” said Conway.
She added, “We want to make the most of every dollar, and we want to make the dollars go as far as possible.”
Virginia serves over 17,000 adults annually and has awarded $18 million to local adult-education providers for 2026-27 program year, according to the Virginia Department of Education.
Over the past three years, the agency said recipients reported over 52,000 student enrollments, and 7,400 secondary and industry-recognized credentials have been earned.
On June 20, 2001, a previous board created the first 14-member committee. However, the agency said the board’s action did not specify seat requirements, meaning seats could be added or taken away in future years.
Staff recommended no changes to the number of members, but asked that the ex officio role be reserved for the Adult Student of the Year, chosen through the Virginia Association of Adult and Continuing Education.
VDOE said it will seek nominations using the agency’s form and processes, review them for a balance of stakeholder groups and geographic representation, and then the board will review and approve recommendations.
The agency did not immediately respond to questions about the reason for the committee’s three-year break.
