name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds unveils proposal to protect Florida waterways
description: INDIAN SHORES — While the environment has not taken much prominence in the race for governor, public opinion surveys have consistently shown Floridians place high value on issues like marine protected areas and clean waterways. Declaring that the issue is important to him, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds unveiled a “Florida’s Coastal Corrido[...]
text:
Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaking at Caddy's in Indian Shores on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)INDIAN SHORES — While the environment has not taken much prominence in the race for governor, public opinion surveys have consistently shown Floridians place high value on issues like marine protected areas and clean waterways.
Declaring that the issue is important to him, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds unveiled a “Florida’s Coastal Corridor” proposal Monday that he promised to enact if he gets elected next month. He calls it the marine equivalent of Florida’s Wildlife Corridor, which state lawmakers passed in 2021 to preserve migration paths for animals like the Florida panther.
“Where the Wildlife Corridor connects inland habitats from the north to the south, the Coastal Corridor links and protects our coastal waterways along the Gulf of America and the Atlantic Ocean. It connects them to inland watersheds that feed them,” Donalds announced at Caddy’s in Indian Shores, a waterfront bar and restaurant with clear views on the Intracoastal Waterway in Pinellas County.
The “Gulf of America” is Donald Trump’s preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico.
Donalds said the proposal doesn’t add layers of bureaucracy or regulations and won’t restrict fishing on public access. “Instead, it brings our existing agencies and existing programs and existing authorities under one coordinated, operational plan,” he said.
As announced on Monday, the proposal would:

Using Florida’s Seafloor Mapping Initiative and state habitat monitors, “target every taxpayer dollar where it delivers the highest ecological and economic return.”
Execute scientifically sound habitat investments, deploying artificial reefs, rebuilding oyster bars, replanting seagrass beds, restoring living shorelines, and propagating coral. “These projects restore fish habitat while building natural storm protection for our coastal communities,” he said.
Future land conservation to protect coastal headwaters would be 100% voluntary, “working through willing sellers to sell the easements under proven tools like Florida Forever.”

Florida Forever has been considered the state’s biggest conservation and recreational lands acquisition program, established by the Florida Forever Act of 1999. Since it began in 2000, it has allowed the state to purchase more than 1 million acres of land.
However, the Legislature declined to provide any funding for the program this year. Instead, lawmakers redirected millions of dollars previously dedicated to land acquisition in the Florida Wildlife Corridor towards other projects, including $425 million for the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program, which allows agriculture landowners to permanently preserve their land from development but doesn’t require public access.
Citizens’ initiative blocked 
Concerns about the state’s waterways is what has led a group of environmental advocates to push for a proposed “Right to Clean and Healthy Waters” constitutional amendment. Efforts to get that proposal on the 2026 ballot were scuttled in 2025 following passage of legislation (HB 1205). That law created major barriers to citizen-led initiatives gathering the required signatures, the result being that no citizen-led constitutional amendments made it to the November 2026 statewide ballot.
The campaign behind the Right to Clean and Healthy Waters says participants hope to regroup to restart a similar campaign for the 2028 fall election.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly has spelled out some of his plans for those who live in coastal communities and Florida’s water quality crisis on his campaign website. It says his plan “ties water quality to broader environmental investment.”
“Blue-green algae crises are addressed by reducing discharges of nutrient pollution to our coastal waters, and springs degradation is addressed through septic to sewer conversations, agriculture runoff rules, and groundwater protection. Protecting Florida’s coast requires changing what flows into it.”
A number of mostly Pinellas-based state and federal lawmakers joined Donalds at his press conference, including U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, state Sen. Nick DiCeglie, and state House members Berny Jacques and Toby Overdorf.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: The rocky road to more manageable healthcare costs in NC
description: As it seeks ways to make healthcare in North Carolina more affordable, a group of some of the state’s main decision-makers in medical care, payments, and policy highlighted the challenges of developing and agreeing on ideas that will lead to lower costs and better health.  In on the discussions are the state’s big insurers, including […]
text:
The NC commission coming up with ideas to lower healthcare costs met Oct. 2, 2026. From left: independent practitioner Dr. Karen Smith, facilitator Barak Richman, NC DHHS Secretary Dev Sangvai, state Treasurer Brad Briner and Mark McClellan, director of the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy. As it seeks ways to make healthcare in North Carolina more affordable, a group of some of the state’s main decision-makers in medical care, payments, and policy highlighted the challenges of developing and agreeing on ideas that will lead to lower costs and better health. 
In on the discussions are the state’s big insurers, including state Treasurer Brad Briner, who oversees the State Employee Health Plan; the CEO of Blue Cross Blue Shield, the state’s largest insurer; the state Health and Human Services secretary, who runs Medicaid; and doctors, nurses, hospital administrators, and academics. 
Gov. Josh Stein appointed the bipartisan Health Care Affordability Commission in June. The goal is to come up with suggestions for reducing the share of household income that state residents spend on healthcare while improving quality.
Legislators and state government officials are voting members. The advisory members represent healthcare providers, businesses, and nonprofits. 
“We’re trying to move a large and complicated system in a different direction,” said Barak D. Richman, the commission facilitator, at the commission’s Friday meeting. ”We’re trying to change a lot of interlocking parts at once.”
The commission is considering how to invest in primary care as a way to lower overall patient cost and improve health. The idea is to keep people healthy or catch problems early before they become harder and more expensive to treat. 
One option is setting annual spending targets for primary care for both public and private insurers. However, leaning more heavily on primary care is a challenge because the state doesn’t have enough doctors in rural counties. 
“We just don’t have enough docs,” said Dr. Tunde Sotunde, Blue Cross North Carolina president and CEO. The state is short about 2,000 doctors, he said. 
 “At the end of the day, we have to solve for this,” Sotunde said.  “Status quo is not going to work. We have to come up with creative solutions. The bottom line is that we are facing a significant access issue in our rural and underserved parts of the state.”
Dr. Karen Smith, an independent primary care doctor with an office in Raeford, likened talk of different ways of paying doctors to performing CPR on a patient that is bleeding to death. 
“Right now, independent primary care practices are hemorrhaging,” she said, because they can’t afford to stay open. 
Lawsuit over doctors supervising nurse practitioners adds new twist to long NC debate

Another suggestion that nurse practitioners be empowered to treat patients without supervision from doctors revealed the familiar fault lines between advanced practice nurses who want independence and doctors who oppose it. 
“Advanced practice registered nurses have known for many, many years they could be doing more for the people of North Carolina, but have been restricted by a 1970s-era regulatory structure,” said Tina Gordon, CEO of the North Carolina Nurses Association. 
“This has never been about what nurses want,” she said. “This is about what nurses can do, and what patients need.”
Steve Keene, CEO of the North Carolina Medical Society, representing the doctors, said physician supervision for advanced practice nurses is an important safety feature. 
“I do not think we are in a position to say conclusively that it’s time to change,” Keene said. 
Legislators have filed bills to allow advanced practice nurses to work without doctors’ supervision, but they have not become law. Last month, a nurse practitioner filed a lawsuit to overturn the requirement. 
Expensive medical bills are stressing North Carolina households, recent polls have shown.
A poll from earlier this year found that 75% of respondents said they were concerned about costs, and 57% said their medical bills were too high but they paid anyway,

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Diamond urges House leaders not to allow skill games deadline to pass without a solution
description: At the start of the General Assembly’s last session week before midterm elections, Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said he offered to work with Democrats to amend his legislation to also provide additional funding for public transportation agencies.
text:
State Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) speaks at a news conference where he urged House leaders to keep working on a measure to make skill games legal. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)A state lawmaker sponsoring two bills that he said would save skill games while providing new revenue for tax relief and more blamed Democratic House leaders Monday for inaction on the topic.
At the start of the General Assembly’s last session week before midterm elections, Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said he offered to work with Democrats to amend his legislation to also provide additional funding for public transportation agencies.
“But their leadership’s stubborn insistence that any action on skill games must originate in the Senate … stands in the way,” Diamond said at a state Capitol news conference with business owners who rely on the income skill games generate.
Elizabeth Rementer, a spokesperson for House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery), noted Senate Republicans pushed to take the lead on skill games, but have been unable to pass their own members’ bills.
“House Democrats stand willing and eager to come to a reasonable resolution to the skill game issue that would both bring in new revenue and ensure a safe and equitable skill games framework,” she said. “But first Senate Republicans must prove their ability to pass something.”
Rep. Diamond proposes gaming reform to save skill games and boost tax relief

Skill games resemble casino slot machines but they can be found throughout the commonwealth in small businesses, private clubs and volunteer fire companies instead of casinos. Until this year, state courts had ruled they were distinct from gambling devices because they incorporated an element of skill by which players could recoup their bets.
But the state Supreme Court ruled in June that skill games are, in fact, gambling devices that are illegal to own and operate without a license from the state Gaming Control Board. The decision ended more than a decade in which skill games proliferated in a legal gray area without state oversight or taxation.
Recognizing the potential for its ruling to upend a segment of the commonwealth’s economy, the Supreme Court delayed the effect of its ruling until Oct. 15. On that date, state law enforcement agencies warn, all skill game machines must be removed from unlicensed establishments.
George Lewis, co-owner of Atlantis ATM in Allentown, supplies skill games along with jukeboxes, pool tables and other coin-operated amusements. He said the share of revenue from skill games that host establishments collect saved many nonprofit organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic, after they were forced to close. 
Now, many rely on the cash they make from skill games to pay for building repairs and replace equipment. Many also make donations to pay for children’s gifts at Christmas time and other charitable endeavors.
But Lewis said he was wary of the uncertain status the skill games industry held. 
“When we first started doing the skill games. I didn’t think it was going to last, and I actually told all my customers. I said, ‘Listen, this is just extra money. Take it now … but don’t depend on it,” he said.
Like his customers, Lewis said he now relies on the revenue skill games produce.
“I hired more employees, you know, getting more vehicles, insurance. I had to depend on that money more myself,” he said.”Our jukeboxes and our ATMs, we can live off of it. But in order to flourish and then help all of our employees … we had to depend on the money.”
While lawmakers have been working since before the ruling to reach consensus on a taxing and regulatory scheme for the devices, none of the proposals have passed both chambers of the General Assembly to move on to Gov. Josh Shapiro’s desk. Shapiro has indicated support for a plan to tax the games by including revenue in his last two budget proposals. 
House Gaming Oversight Committee Chairperson Patrick Harkins (D-Erie) said last week lawmakers in the lower chamber have been working to formulate a proposal while pressuring Senate Republicans to secure the votes they need to pass a measure.
“I turn it back to the Senate Republican leadership, who has told us for four years that they have no intention and they have no ability to get the votes for anything at this point in time. It’s difficult to negotiate by ourselves,” Harkins said during a Gaming Oversight Committee meeting.
Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman, meanwhile, told reporters at a Pennsylvania Press Club luncheon last month that “various stakeholders” had rejected “in no uncertain terms” a Senate proposal to place skill games under the auspices of the Gaming Control Board.
Diamond said Monday that the General Assembly should stop at nothing to get the job done.
“The people of Pennsylvania elected all of us with an expectation that we’d actually get things done,” noting the Pennsylvania legislature is supposed to be full-time but has been in voting session only about three dozen times this year. “We spent those days unwilling to tackle the big issues.” 
He urged House Speaker Joanna McClinton (D-Philadelphia) keep the chamber in session as long as necessary to develop a solid bipartisan solution, adding that passing his proposals would accomplish that. 
The alternative could have broad electoral repercussions, warned Diamond, who began his political career with a campaign to unseat state lawmakers who voted to give themselves a middle-of-the-night pay raise in 2005.
“That money is going to go away, and I don’t think anybody in this Capitol actually understands what happens when you take money out of people’s mouths,” he said. “I think it’s dangerous. I’ve been around when people in Pennsylvania get mad at the entire General Assembly, and it’s not pretty.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democrats accuse Senate Republicans of violating AI campaign law on misinformation
description: The New Mexico Democratic Party has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate whether state Senate Republicans’ use of AI-generated images in recent social media posts violate a 2024 state law aimed at curbing political misinformation.
text:
New Mexico Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho), along with other Senate Republicans, is facing a State Ethics Commission complaint over an AI-generated mugshot he shared on social media of Senate Pro Tem Sen. Mimi Stewart (D-Albuquerque) on Sept. 22, 2026. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The New Mexico Democratic Party has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate whether state Senate Republicans’ use of AI-generated images in recent social media posts violate a 2024 state law aimed at curbing political misinformation.
The Senate Republicans and state Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) have published or shared artificially generated images of Democrats in recent weeks as part of a campaign accusing the majority Democrats of being corrupt. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Some of the images include a fake jail mugshot of Senate Pro Tem Sen. Mimi Stewart (D-Albuquerque), House Speaker Javier Martinez (D-Albuquerque) wearing a hammer-and-sickle lapel pin and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland embracing an unspecified man in an orange prison jumpsuit.
The fake mugshot suggests Stewart was charged with “hit and run,” a reference to an automobile crash between Stewart and a pedestrian in 2024 that has recently surfaced in news reports. Stewart was never issued a citation or booked into jail, and she stayed on scene until police arrived, interim Santa Fe Police Department Chief told the Santa Fe New Mexican. 
In a complaint to the ethics commission the Democrats provided Friday, DPNM Chair Sara Attleson said the images violate House Bill 182, which imposes strict disclaimer requirements on AI-generated campaign materials. The law requires artificially generated images to carry conspicuous disclaimers with the following text: “This image has been manipulated or generated by artificial intelligence.”
In a statement, Attleson called on the Ethics Commission to investigate and impose any penalties as quickly as possible. State law provides for $1,000 fines for each violation. 
“Voters should not be misled by public officials or their official offices about what is or isn’t real,” Attleson said. “We are asking the Ethics Commission to enforce the law that is meant to protect faith in our elections.”
None of the images on social media carried the required disclaimer, though Facebook has since labeled both as AI generated. Block, who originally posted the fake mugshot of Stewart, also noted that his image was AI-generated at the end of a lengthy Facebook post Sept. 22. 
Block told Source NM on Monday that the SEC complaint is Democrats’ effort to distract from the real corruption the images seek to highlight.  He also defended his post as protected speech under the First Amendment. 
Deepfake disclosure bill passes NM House

“I can’t believe they’re crying over that when they refuse to hold themselves accountable,” Block said of Democrats. “It’s called free speech.” 
Late Friday, after New Mexico Democrats announced they’d filed the ethics complaint, Senate Republicans republished their post with the contested images along with the required disclaimer. 
Still, Sen. Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington), in a statement, called the matter “funny.”
“The Democrat Party, that consistently fails to hold their own members to account when it comes to breaking the law and violating ethical standards, is taking exception to our efforts to expose their failed leadership and lack of accountability,” he said.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Autism-treatment task force inches closer to finalizing recommendations
description: A blue-ribbon panel will hold two more meetings before it adopts the final list of recommendations to the Legislature on how best to use state dollars to treat children with autism. Those recommendations could include requiring businesses that provide applied behavior analysis (ABA) services to be licensed, not just the providers working for those companies;[...]
text:
Autism awareness bracelet worn by an audience member at the Aug. 31, 2026, ABA Task Force meeting in Tallahassee. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)A blue-ribbon panel will hold two more meetings before it adopts the final list of recommendations to the Legislature on how best to use state dollars to treat children with autism.
Those recommendations could include requiring businesses that provide applied behavior analysis (ABA) services to be licensed, not just the providers working for those companies; tying Medicaid reimbursements to annual licensed provider surveys; and offering parents access to more than just applied behavior analysis.
Those were some ideas members of the ABA Task Force heard Monday and discussed during a near all-day meeting.
Centria Autism is not an ABA provider in Florida but purports to provide more Medicaid ABA services than any other provider nationwide and operates in 11 states.
Its CEO, David Harbour, told ABA task force members that Centria thinks some of the concerns about the high costs of  providing ABA services and the effectiveness of the services could be resolved in part through licensure. He recommended the  state consider regulating ABA providers similarly to how it licenses home healthcare providers, which requires licensure and ongoing surveys for re-licensure.
The licensure requirement, he said, could help to “create standardization around the services,” whether provided in facilities or in people’s homes.
The surveys could be used to determine whether the ABA providers are following treatment plans.
Results of the surveys, he said, could be tied to an ABA provider’s reimbursement rates.
“Failed surveys should carry a Medicaid reimbursement penalty,” Harbour said, acknowledging that “no state has done this yet.”
“Think of the carrot and the stick. Do the right thing, pass the surveys, and you get to keep your rate. If you don’t, then you have to take the 10% reduction for the rectification time period.”
‘Interesting’
Agency for Health Care Administration Secretary and task force member Shevaun Harris said she found it “interesting” an ABA provider was advocating for facility licensure.
“I just want to note our agency has been very intrigued by that concept,” she said, noting that AHCA is in charge of licensing most of the health care facilities in the state, from abortion providers to nursing homes to hospitals to home healthcare agencies.
“We’ve had the same conversation here at the agency, around you have individuals going into people’s homes of very vulnerable kids,” she said. Although AHCA conducts on-site inspection as part of the Medicaid application process, it’s “not the same as a  licensure process, and so we, I found it interesting that that was included in your presentation,” she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harbour said Centria also would like to see states require Medicaid patients to attend ABA appointments to continue to receive the services.
“There’s a lot of them who do not show up to their clinically recommended hours,” he said. He acknowledged “this is a really hard thing to do,” but said “some states” require it and specifically named Texas.
Texas, he said, has a “minimum attendance that the family has to attend, or they could lose their services.”
During public testimony, Mariel Fernandez, a Dallas resident and vice president for government affairs for the Council on Autism Service Providers, clarified the policy, telling board members Texas Medicaid requires 85% utilization of scheduled parent training sessions but doesn’t require minimum participation per month.
She said lack of parent or caregiver involvement doesn’t mean ABA services will be denied.
“However, parent or caregiver involvement may affect the effectiveness, durability, and generalization to natural settings of the treatment and may be considered when making determinations regarding effectiveness of the treatment requested,” she said, reading directly from the Texas Medicaid Provider Procedures Manual.
ABA isn’t the only option
Applied behavior analysis uses structured interventions to decrease maladaptive behaviors and reinforce appropriate ones.
ABA is common in the treatment of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), traumatic brain injuries, and intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The ABA Task Force kicked off the meeting with a presentation from certified speech pathologist Sheryl Rosin, who said the task force could consider alternative therapies to ABA.
“So, there is evidence across this continuum of care, no single approach has definitely settled that this is the right treatment for autism. We have lots of different treatments out there, not even autism-specific but like speech language pathology and occupational therapy. So, the research filed as a whole is still accumulating the evidence across all these models, including ABA.
She said New Jersey has started using what’s called DIR FloorTime, which, according to its website, was developed in the 1980s and emphasizes social-emotional development through meaningful relationships and nurturing interactions.
“It’s already being done in multiple states,” she said, noting that DIR FloorTime is an option families in North Carolina can tap into in addition to ABA.
Similar to ABA, she said, a child needs a physician referral and confirmed diagnosis to receive care and must undergo progress reviews.
“This is just another way of thinking about alternative models,” she said.
Meeting dates not finalized
The Legislature established the 10-member task force as part of fiscal year 2026-27 budget negotiations.
Harris, who chairs the task force but cannot vote on any of the recommendations, said during the first meeting she’d like the panel to finalize its recommendation during October. But the group was unable to firm up when to meet again.
AHCA is required to post meeting dates at least seven days in advance.
The review comes after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released the State Medicaid and CHIP Applied Behavior Analysis Toolkit, a 173-page document meant to “support state Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) agencies in making decisions regarding ABA service provision for Medicaid and CHIP.”
The DeSantis administration announced in June that it was cracking down on fraud, waste, and abuse in Florida’s $38 billion healthcare safety net program. That initiative was launched after CMS sent a letter to Florida, as well as California, Maine, and New York, seeking information about Medicaid integrity and oversight and after CMS Director Mehmet Oz said on social media that “Florida has been a hotspot for health care fraud for years.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Surgeon accused of sexually assaulting Illinois patient now seeks Iowa license
description: A physician sanctioned in other states for sexual misconduct involving a patient is now seeking licensure in Iowa. According to the Iowa Board of Medicine, Dr. Shaun A. Kink submitted an application for permanent medical licensure in Iowa in October 2025. In June 2026, the board issued a preliminary notice informing Kink that it intended […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) A physician sanctioned in other states for sexual misconduct involving a patient is now seeking licensure in Iowa.
According to the Iowa Board of Medicine, Dr. Shaun A. Kink submitted an application for permanent medical licensure in Iowa in October 2025. In June 2026, the board issued a preliminary notice informing Kink that it intended to deny him licensure for reasons the board has opted not to publicly disclose.
Kink then asked for a hearing on the matter, which is currently scheduled for Nov. 12, 2026.
Massachusetts Board of Registration in Medicine records indicate that while working in Illinois in August 2019, Kink began treating a female patient. Later that year, Kink reportedly engaged in sexual conduct with the woman, and in January 2020, he was indicted by a grand jury and charged with aggravated criminal sexual assault, criminal sexual assault, aggravated criminal sexual abuse and criminal sexual abuse.
At the time, prosecutors alleged that Kink, a surgeon who specializes in foot and ankle issues, had sexually assaulted the woman in the hospital and then did so again, after her discharge, at the woman’s home.
In February 2020, Illinois’ Division of Professional Regulation temporarily suspended Kink’s license, alleging he posed an immediate danger to the public.
In 2022, the criminal charges against Kink were amended to include solicitation of a sexual act. While the case was pending, prosecutors sought to introduce evidence alleging three other female patients had also accused Kink of sexual misconduct.
On Dec. 27, 2022, Kink entered into an agreement whereby he pleaded guilty to the solicitation charge and the original four charges were dismissed. He was sentenced to 120 days in jail and 18 months of probation.
In 2024, the Massachusetts licensing board revoked Kink’s physician license in that state, citing his Illinois criminal conviction for solicitation as well as “his admitted sexual relationship with the patient.”
More Board of Medicine actions
Other physicians facing sanctions from the Iowa Board of Medicine include:
— Dr. Brett Olson of Spirit Lake, who is charged by the board with professional incompetence. The board has disclosed no information as to the circumstances or alleged conduct that gave rise to the charge. The charge against Olson, while approved by the board in June 2026, was only recently made public by the board. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for March 25, 2027. According to the board, Olson is a family-practice physician in Spirit Lake.
— Dr. Mona Alqulali of Clinton, who specializes in obstetrics and gynecology, was charged by the board with improper management of medical records and improperly prescribing drugs for her father without an examination.
According to the board, Alqulali initially denied prescribing her father any drugs, telling the board, “I never gave my father anything outside of what his treating doctors had prescribed or agreed upon.” The board alleged those denials were false and alleged that subpoenaed records show five instances of Alqulali prescribing her father drugs in 2024.
Citing what it called “other instances of her writing prescriptions to family and her denying this until pressed by the board,” the board recently imposed a $5,000 civil penalty against Alqulali and placed her Iowa license on probation for three years while also requiring her to complete two educational courses.
Alqulali’s attorney, Mike Sellers, said he recently filed an emergency motion in Polk County District Court to stay the board’s enforcement of its order since it would temporarily restrict her ability to write prescriptions.
“The issues now are the life or death of Dr. Alqulali’s career and/or her practice,” Sellers told the court in a filing last week. “Every day that goes by, the board’s ruling imposing a restriction on prescribing controlled substances — which has always been involved in most areas of (Alqulali’s) practice — until she can finish two courses chokes more of the remaining breath out of what is left of Dr. Alqulali’s practice.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach Kink or Olson for comment on their cases.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota National Guard helps with more than 1,000 deportations since July 2025, governor says
description: The South Dakota National Guard has helped process 1,013 deportations for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement since July 2025. Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office included the figure on Monday in a news release announcing his decision to extend his order for cooperation with ICE in paperwork processing, a task assigned to seven National Guard members. The […]
text:
Gov. Larry Rhoden, of South Dakota, meets with soldiers with the South Dakota National Guard, Georgia National Guard and Alabama National Guard in support of Joint Task Force-District of Columbia in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2025. About 2,300 National Guard members were supporting the D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission providing support to the D.C. Metropolitan Police Department. (U.S. Army National Guard photo by Sgt. Tyler O’Connell)The South Dakota National Guard has helped process 1,013 deportations for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement since July 2025.
Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office included the figure on Monday in a news release announcing his decision to extend his order for cooperation with ICE in paperwork processing, a task assigned to seven National Guard members. The extension will run through September 2027.
It’s unclear how many of the 1,013 people were residing in South Dakota, because some of them could have been passing through the state. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the federal agency that oversees ICE, did not provide the number to South Dakota Searchlight when asked.
Highway Patrol reimbursement
Rhoden’s release also said the Trump administration will pay the South Dakota Highway Patrol $480,000 for its continued work under a cooperative agreement with ICE. Under the terms of that agreement, signed in 2025, 38 state troopers have been trained and are enabled to question people about their immigration status and detain people on ICE’s behalf.
Earlier this summer, Rhoden said the state got $150,418 from ICE to compensate the Highway Patrol for its work. 
Rhoden’s Monday news release said the combined $630,418 goes toward “personnel payroll, specialized field equipment, and information technology stipends to support the agency’s coordinated enforcement efforts.”
Troopers have been involved in “261 immigration-related arrests involving individuals unlawfully present in the United States who were encountered during routine patrols across South Dakota,” according to the press release.
Prison, parole cooperation
The state Department of Corrections has also helped ICE deport people since Rhoden’s pledge of state aid for immigration enforcement efforts began last year.
The prison agency has an agreement under which its officers can question inmates about their immigration status. 
The state has also paroled inmates who are in the U.S. without legal status into ICE custody. Since July 2025, the state has done that to 38 people. 
Some of those inmates were released on presumptive parole. That means they were in line for an automatic early exit from prison because they had followed the rules there and completed the in-custody programming assigned to them upon arrival.
Broader cooperation
In total, there are 11 state or local agencies in South Dakota that have 287(g) program agreements with ICE, under which the agencies are trained and empowered to conduct certain tasks related to immigration enforcement. 
The Department of Corrections has two agreements.
The power to question inmates comes through a “Jail Enforcement Model” agreement. The second agreement is a “Warrant Service Officer” model, which lets corrections staff serve immigration warrants to inmates in state prison custody.
South Dakota Attorney General clarifies scope of immigration enforcement agreement

The Highway Patrol has a “Task Force Model” agreement, acting on ICE’s behalf to ask questions and detain people encountered in the normal course of state trooper business.
The Minnehaha and Pennington county sheriff’s offices, both of which operate jails, have warrant service officer agreements. The Grant County Sheriff’s Office has two agreements: one for jail enforcement, and another that lets its deputies question and detain as state troopers do.
Centerville and Viborg are the only cities in South Dakota that have 287(g) agreements with ICE. 
The other agencies that have agreements with ICE are the sheriff’s offices in Corson, Edmunds and Hughes counties, and the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation.
Tony Mangan, spokesperson for the division, said there hasn’t been remuneration for its work with ICE, which is more limited in scope than the work of the Highway Patrol. Mangan also provided a statement from Marty Jackley, who oversees the division as South Dakota’s attorney general and entered into its agreement with ICE.  
“I limited the Division of Criminal Investigation’s agreement with ICE to only violent criminals and drug dealers,” Jackley said. “That mission has not changed.”
Local chief hopes assistance helps bring new funding
Centerville Police Chief Lon Hatcher said he signed a task force agreement with ICE in the interest of making sure he and his fellow officer in the department of two are “evaluating who we’re dealing with to make sure that we’re safe, and the community remains safe.”
“We don’t have a huge amount of demand because our community is smaller,” Hatcher said. “We’re sitting between 900 and 950 people, roughly.”
Centerville is about 40 miles southwest of Sioux Falls. Hatcher’s task force agreement also involves welfare checks for unaccompanied minors.
Under that part of the agreement, Hatcher is empowered to help ICE visit children who entered the U.S. without a parent or guardian and are placed with adult “sponsors” by the Department of Homeland Security. Last November, the department announced its plans to leverage local agencies with 287(g) agreements to help locate and vet sponsors for 450,000 such children.
Hatcher said he’s been called out to assist in one such welfare check, in Sioux Falls.
Centerville is reimbursed for its time and equipment use, but Hatcher said he also hopes the agreement will help the department receive favorable treatment when applying for federal grants.

title: Trump drops longtime aversion to mail-in voting with GOP trailing in polls
text:
President Donald Trump wants to sharply curtail mail ballots. He’s called them “inherently corrupt” and baselessly condemned them as a major source of fraud.But with Republicans falling behind in the polls, the president is now urging his supporters to vote in the midterm elections any way they can, including by mail.The White House has also sent emails through a government account promoting voter registration in recent days and Trump is continuing a string of campaign rallies in typically conservative states, including Nebraska on Monday night. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has directed that members of the military, who tend to support Republicans, have a day off to vote.“If your state has early voting, do not wait. Go out and vote. Vote early, vote by mail, or vote in person on Election Day, November 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left ‘Dumocrats’ in a midterm victory that is too big to rig,” Trump said in a social media video over the weekend, using a derogatory term for Democrats.The about-face by the president is familiar. Trump encouraged his voters to cast their ballots by mail in 2024 and has repeatedly voted by mail himself, despite a long record of attacking the practice.Republicans battle against loss of majoritiesThe latest comments — along with the red-state rallies — underscore the political peril that analysts see facing Republicans and Trump. If Republicans lose control of either the House or Senate, Democrats are likely to launch investigations into the White House that could complicate the president’s final two years in office. A Democratic House would face pressure from the base to pursue impeachment against Trump or other administration officials.Democrats enjoy an 11-point advantage over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot, according to a nonpartisan September national poll by Emerson College. The poll also found Democrats more enthusiastic, with 78% “very excited” to vote compared to 66% of Republicans. A poll by The New York Times and Siena College, released Saturday, found Democrats ahead or tied in Senate races in several GOP-leaning states, including Alaska, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. Several of those same states — including Alaska, Kansas and Ohio — allow voters to cast a ballot by mail without providing an excuse. Iowa also features a highly competitive Senate race and has no-excuse absentee voting, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.Vice President JD Vance was visiting Alaska on Monday to campaign for the Republican Senate candidate, while Trump was scheduled to hold a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where the incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts faces a competitive challenge from independent Dan Osborn. ‘We seem to have no choice’Republicans are scrambling to find ways to turn out their base voters, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston. The immediate objective for the party is maximizing voter turnout among their supporters, he said, adding that discouraging them from using legal methods to vote would be an obvious electoral disadvantage.“The overriding concern for the White House is turnout, not consistency,” Rottinghaus said. “The political messaging has been inconsistent on this. But all of that aside, the need to get Republicans to come vote is paramount for Republicans.”Trump at the White House on Monday said that he prefers voters to cast their ballots in person but that they can “vote by mail if they want because we seem to have no choice.” Without offering evidence, he alleged significant cheating in voting by mail.Pressed by reporters for evidence, the president pointed to California. The blue state, where all voters receive a ballot in the mail, has drawn his ire in the past for a vote-counting process that can last weeks, in part because of ballots that arrive in the mail after Election Day. But a slow count isn’t evidence of fraud.When asked about Trump’s shifting stance, the White House referred States Newsroom to the president’s Monday remarks.Supreme Court blocked TrumpTrump’s decision to again tout voting by mail — while also attacking it — came after he spent months pursuing a high-stakes effort to impose restrictions on mail ballots. In August 2025, Trump promised to lead a movement to eliminate mail-in voting. Less than a year later, he signed an executive order directing the U.S. Postal Service to require states, at least 90 days before a federal election, to notify the Postal Service whether they intended to allow ballots to be sent through the mail. States would have then had to submit to USPS a list of voters planning to vote by mail at least 60 days before the election.

 






A portion of an email from the White House urging Americans to vote, including by mail. (States Newsroom photo)

Postmaster General David Steiner had said that the Postal Service wouldn’t deliver ballots for states that refused to comply with the rule. Democrats and other opponents said it would have given the Postal Service unprecedented and unconstitutional authority over elections, which are administered by the states under the Constitution.The U.S. Supreme Court blocked the rule from taking effect in a one-paragraph order that upheld a lower court decision halting it. Election officials and voting rights advocates had warned that implementing the requirements so close to the election would have caused chaos.Trump railed against the decision at the time, calling it a “big loss” for Republicans and alleging it would make cheating by Democrats on mail-in ballots much easier. “And now they have open field to do so,” he wrote on social media when the order was issued in mid-September.On Monday, League of Women Voters President and CEO Celina Stewart emphasized that the Trump administration had spent months attacking voting by mail. She said in a statement that while Trump sought to impose restrictions through an executive order — which the League sued over — “the President does not have the authority to unilaterally dictate how states administer elections.”“A shift in rhetoric does not undo those actions, nor does it erase the need for the League to take this fight to court. We will judge this administration by its actions, not by its latest statement,” Stewart said.Trump’s attacks on voting by mailTrump’s attacks on voting by mail stretch back to the 2020 election, when mail voting surged amid the pandemic. At that time, he characterized mail ballots arriving after Election Day as fraudulent, even though late-arriving ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day — indicating that voters made their choices before the close of polls. The Supreme Court this year upheld the authority of states to count mailed ballots that arrive after Election Day.Six years later, mail-in voting remains a major way for Americans to cast their ballots. Nearly a third of U.S. voters cast a ballot by mail in 2024, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. This year, nearly 1 million people have already voted by mail in the general election, with more than 52 million mail ballots requested, according to data compiled by the University of Florida Election Lab.For campaigns, every ballot a supporter casts by mail represents a “bird in the hand,” said Rottinghaus. By contrast, voters who wait until Election Day remain potential voters, with the risk that something will come up that keeps them from voting.Campaigns build whole persuasion operations around mail voting, he said, adding that demonizing the practice takes away a weapon some campaigns rely on.“This is a top-down effort from the most vocal and visible Republican that can create a lot of complications for Republicans down ballot who may rely on mail voting for a big part of their strategy,” Rottinghaus said.

(Courtesy of Holiday Market)LINCOLN — The state’s tourism commission has announced its Nebraska Holiday Passport selections for 2026 — two dozen places ranging from a flower farm in Glenvil to the Draw Bar in Valentine.
The commission, also known as Visit Nebraska, on Monday said travelers will have from Nov. 13 to Jan. 10 to visit and collect passport stamps from the 24 “festive” locations, which are a mix of  holiday-themed stores, coffee shops and outdoor destinations. Many of those stops will offer special deals.
The 2026 Nebraska Holiday Passport booklet is out for travelers to see. (Courtesy of Visit Nebraska)
This year marks the fifth year of the holiday passport program. It is a supplement to the popular Nebraska Passport program, which started 17 years ago and this past year highlighted 70 stops across the state for travelers to visit May 1 through Sept. 30. 
The passport program aims to help travelers discover what Visit Nebraska describes as hidden gems. 
“We are looking forward to getting Nebraskans and visitors alike out and exploring new parts of the state during the holiday season and seeing what Nebraska has to offer,” holiday passport program coordinator Lilly Uhlmann said in a statement.
Participants can earn prizes based on the number of stamps they collect on the visits. People can request a holiday passport booklet to learn more about the recommended stops.

title: Republican TN state senator spurns party, backs independent candidate Hatley
description: ​A Tennessee Republican state senator is backing a conservative independent candidate for governor, spurning her party and leading to speculation about her future. ​State Sen. Janice Bowling, a Tullahoma Republican, endorsed independent gubernatorial candidate David Hatley in a social media post Saturday. ​“A lot of the people in my district wanted me to mee[...]
text:
Tennessee state Sen. Janice Bowling, a Tullahoma Republican, endorsed a conservative independent candidate for governor rather than  Republican Party nominee U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn. (Photo: John Partipilo)​A Tennessee Republican state senator is backing a conservative independent candidate for governor, spurning her party and leading to speculation about her future.
​State Sen. Janice Bowling, a Tullahoma Republican, endorsed independent gubernatorial candidate David Hatley in a social media post Saturday.
​“A lot of the people in my district wanted me to meet [Hatley],” said Bowling in a video posted on Hatley for Governor’s Facebook page, adding she met with him privately and was “pleased” to endorse him.
​Tennessee will elect a new governor in November to replace term-limited Gov. Bill Lee. In August, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn won a three-way contested Republican primary, and Memphis city council member Jerri Green won the Democratic primary for governor.

Hatley and Lauren Pinkston are the two most prominent independent candidates running for Tennessee’s top job.
​Hatley, a Washington County businessman, has described himself as “very conservative,” but because of a past felony conviction, he never met the bona fide requirements to run as a Republican.
​Hatley has invested at least $7 million of his own money in the race, running on an outsider message.
​Bowling, 79, has served in the Tennessee Senate since 2013 and won reelection in 2024.
​The Tennessee Republican Party’s rules prevent a Republican from endorsing anyone besides the party’s candidates after the primary, leaving open the possibility that Bowling could become ineligible to receive the GOP nomination if she runs for reelection in 2028.
Scott Golden, the chair of the Tennessee Republican Party, said in a statement that failure to stand behind the party’s nominees “absolutely endangers” any Republican’s good standing with the party.
“We encourage Republicans to compete in the primaries and expect differences, but after the primary, we come together as one family to support the winner,” Golden said.
Bowling could also be removed from the state Senate caucus, impacting the succession fight as Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, an Oak Ridge Republican, steps down as state Senate speaker later this year.
​The race to replace McNally pits Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, a Franklin Republican, against Sen. Paul Bailey, a Sparta Republican. Neither man has appeared to lock up enough votes so far to lead the chamber.
J. Holly McCall contributed to this story.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bridgeport residents rally behind Police Chief Roderick Porter amid union dispute
description: Bridgeport residents expressed their support for Police Chief Roderick Porter at a rally as the police union calls for his removal.
text:
As members of the Bridgeport police union continue to call for Police Chief Roderick Porter’s removal, residents, faith leaders, elected officials and retired officers gathered Saturday to make their own position clear: They support him.
The rally outside Bridgeport’s Government Center brought together longtime residents and community leaders who said Porter’s accessibility and presence in the community have earned their trust. Their support comes as some union members have raised concerns about Porter’s leadership and working conditions within the department.
Longtime Bridgeport resident and community activist John Marshall Lee said Porter’s willingness to communicate with residents is a major reason he supports him. Lee said Porter regularly makes himself available to the public, takes questions and connects residents with other officers when needed.
“People are happy because they look for that from governments that care,” Lee said.
Carmen Serrano, who has lived in Bridgeport since 1985, said Porter has brought people together in ways she has not seen from other leaders. “He has changed our community,” Serrano said. “He has brought a lot of people together that other people have not done.”
The public show of support contrasts with concerns raised by members of the police union, who have accused Porter of unfair labor practices and raised broader concerns about his leadership and the department’s working environment. 
Union representatives have called for an investigation and questioned whether Porter should remain in charge. Mayor Joe Ganim has agreed to engage an outside investigator, while declining to remove Porter.
For retired Bridgeport police Sgt. Dawud Moss, the rally was also an opportunity to push back against the perception that all of the Bridgeport Guardians, a group of minority officers within the department, oppose Porter. Last month, Officer Carlos Pabon, president of the Guardians, expressed support for the union’s complaints against Porter.
Moss said he supports Porter because he knows the chief personally and respects his integrity, intellect and commitment to police service.
“There’s a perception out there that the Bridgeport Guardians are opposed to Porter’s leadership,” Moss said. “Nothing can be further from the truth.”
Moss said the Guardians have spent decades pushing for reforms within the department and described Porter as a continuation of that work.

Retired Bridgeport police officer Ted Meekins and retired Sgt. JoAnne Meekins attend Saturday’s rally in support of Police Chief Roderick Porter. Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror

Retired officer Ted Meekins was one of the early members of the Guardians and a leader in the group’s success in diversifying the workforce after a judge found widespread discrimination and imposed a special master to oversee the department in the 1970s.
He connected Porter’s leadership to the group’s history of pushing for greater opportunities for Black officers. Meekins said Porter, who was hired as a Bridgeport officer in 1993, is a product of those efforts and has continued the organization’s mission of community engagement.
Meekins’ wife, retired Sgt. JoAnne Meekins, who worked with Porter when he was a captain, said she supports him because she believes he is fair and cares about officers and residents.
“He’s just a good person,” she said.
“He cares about that department and those officers, and he cares about this city of Bridgeport,” she said.
Michael Salemme, president of AFSCME Local 1159, disputed the level of community support for Porter, noting roughly 50 to 60 attended the weekend rally. He said the turnout was small compared with Bridgeport’s population of more than 150,000 residents. 
Salemme also pointed to more than 20 complaints filed by Bridgeport officers with the state Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities and several federal lawsuits as evidence of what he described as “major problems caused by Chief Porter.” 
He said residents should want police officers to work in good conditions because it ultimately affects the quality of service and the costs taxpayers will bear.
Sen. Herron Gaston, D-Bridgeport, said at the Saturday rally that strong leaders can face resistance when they try to change an existing culture. He said Porter is responsive to residents and that the community should continue standing behind him.
Gaston also connected the dispute to race and Bridgeport’s history of racial inequality, saying those issues continue to affect institutions today.
City Councilmember Mary McBride-Lee, who helped organize the rally, said Porter’s presence in the community is one reason she supports him. She recalled an incident when she was attacked and said Porter responded himself rather than sending another officer.
McBride-Lee also praised what she described as the diversity of the department under Porter’s leadership.
Bridgeport residents and supporters listen to speakers during a rally Saturday in support of Police Chief Roderick Porter. Credit: Reginald David / CT Mirror
Margaret Judge, president of the Stratfield Historic District Association, said she supports Porter because of his connection to residents.
“He’s a good man and good person and a man of the community,” Judge said. “He’s always there for us, and we want to be here for him.”
Porter said he was “obviously very appreciative” of the community support and said the rally reflected relationships he has built with residents throughout his career and during his time as chief. 
The community supporters at Saturday’s rally said concerns raised by the union do not reflect their experiences with Porter.
For Lee, the divide between the union’s criticism and the community’s support has created confusion, but he said residents should continue to have opportunities to engage directly with their leaders.
Serrano said her reason for supporting Porter is simple.
“He cares about his community,” she said. “He cares about his people.”
Moss said the rally was about more than one chief. He said it was also about recognizing the history of reform within Bridgeport’s police department.
“We know that,” Moss said of Porter’s connection to those reforms. “And that’s why we’re here.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: National Park Service should investigate Nolan Wells’ death, congresswomen say
description: Christine Wonsley, mother of Nolan Xavier Wells, stands with attorney Ben Crump, from left, her husband Elmore Wonsley, and the Rev. Al Sharpton as they pray during her son’s funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
Members of Congress are asking the National Park Service to investigate the death of Mississippi Gulf Coast teenager Nolan Xavier Wells, adding to calls for federal intervention to help his family better understand what happened to him. 
Rep. Frederica Willson, a Democrat from Florida, wrote to the agency Sept. 28, requesting a “prompt and exhaustive investigation.” Wells, 18, was last seen on July 4 at Horn Island, a barrier island that is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore administered by the park service. His body was found there two days later, and a Jackson County grand jury concluded he probably drowned.
Florida Rep. Frederica Wilson Credit: Frederica Wilson home page
“The full resources and investigative authority of the National Park Service must be brought to bear,” Wilson wrote in the letter, which was also addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. 
“ … Nolan cannot speak for himself. We have a duty to ensure his death is met with the seriousness it deserves,” she wrote.
The letter comes several weeks after the Congressional Black Caucus sent its own letter asking for the U.S. Department of Justice and FBI to step in and investigate. Over 60 representatives and senators are part of that group, including Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson and Wilson. 
On Monday, civil rights attorney Ben Crump joined Wells’ parents at a news conference at Center of Hope church in Inglewood, California, to renew calls for a federal investigation and push for answers for the family.
The family’s legal team has continued to raise questions about his death, including how water was not found in Wells’ lungs, airway and stomach – where water is typically found in drowning incidents. They also raised questions about what caused blunt-force trauma injuries to the back of his head. 
Rep. Maxine Waters, a Democrat from California who is also part of the Congressional Black Caucus, was unable to attend the news conference. Crump said she joined Rep. Wilson’s letter asking for the Park Service to investigate. 
At the news conference, Christine Wonsley said the Jackson County grand jury’s decision not to indict anyone for her son’s death has left her and her husband with more questions and heartbreak than answers. 
“In fact no one has given us any answers other than ‘consistent with accidental drowning’,” she said. “That’s all our Black and Asian child received.”
Through his mother, Wells was Black and Filipino. 
Cynthia Choi, executive director of the national group Stop AAPI Hate, also spoke at the news conference and joined calls for a federal investigation into Wells’ death. She also condemned “patterns of harassment and intimidation” his family has faced, including those directed at Christine Wonsley’s workplace. 
Stop AAPI Hate was formed in 2020 during a surge in incidents of anti-Asian hate during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Christine Wonsley gives a speech in remembrance of her son during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026. Credit: Jackson Ranger/The Sun Herald
Christine and Elmore Wonsley were in California over the weekend where she was honored by the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum, which hosted its 30th anniversary celebration and showed support for their family. 
At the event, Christine Wonsley received the “Voice of Courage Award” for seeking answers and transparency about what happened to her son. She was also recognized for a career of caring for others as a nurse practitioner. 
“I never thought I would be in this position,” Wonsley said Monday about receiving the award and her advocacy. “I never thought I would be someone who was giving a voice to so many who feel like they have none because our justice system has told us to just take the answers you have been given.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ACLU seeks ‘deterrent’ against election problems by training observers across South Dakota
description: Citizen observers could play an especially important role in the Nov. 3 general election, according to the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota. “They are a deterrent against bad behavior,” said Samantha Chapman, the organization’s advocacy manager. The group plans to deploy trained, volunteer observers in Aberdeen, Rapid City and Sioux Falls on El[...]
text:
An American Civil Liberties Union observer watches election workers count absentee ballots for Minnehaha County on Nov. 5, 2024, in the county administration building in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/100526-Election-Observer-Training-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
Citizen observers could play an especially important role in the Nov. 3 general election, according to the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota.
“They are a deterrent against bad behavior,” said Samantha Chapman, the organization’s advocacy manager.
The group plans to deploy trained, volunteer observers in Aberdeen, Rapid City and Sioux Falls on Election Day, and is inviting the public to receive training this month in those cities and online.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Observers will document anything out of the ordinary, Chapman said, including instances of voter intimidation, inaccessible polling places, long lines, precincts running out of ballots, or challenges to voters’ registration.
With the control of Congress at stake, President Donald Trump and his aides have refused to rule out interfering in the elections. In an interview with TIME magazine published recently, when Trump was asked about sending Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to conduct enforcement actions at the polls, he said only that he hadn’t thought of it. He also addressed whether he’d declare a national emergency to impose regulations on the election.
“I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see,” Trump said.


For broadcasters

Produced 1 minute, 8 second audio story with host intro script.



New South Dakota laws that impact elections and voting rights also make an observer’s presence more urgent than previous elections, Chapman said. Those include laws that designate registered voters as “federal only” — meaning they can only vote on federal contests, not state and local ones — if they failed to prove their South Dakota residency or U.S. citizenship. Another new law allows voters to challenge another voter’s citizenship.
“With all of those big sweeping changes, we also think it’s critically important to have our election observers there to make sure that no one is being disenfranchised because they don’t understand what these new laws do or do not require,” Chapman said.
During the 2024 general election, the ACLU deployed 40 trained observers to polls in the state’s three largest cities, where observers documented that “our elections are being administered freely and fairly,” Chapman said.
Early voting for the Nov. 3 general election is underway and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.



Election observer training
The ACLU of South Dakota invites the public to the following election observer training sessions:

Virtual: 7 to 8:30 p.m. Central time, Oct. 7.
Aberdeen: 5:30 to 7 p.m. Central, Oct. 13, K.O. Lee Aberdeen Public Library.
Sioux Falls: 3:30 to 5 p.m. Central, Oct. 18, Siouxland Libraries Downtown Library.
Rapid City: 5:30 to 7 p.m. Mountain, Oct. 22, Rapid City Public Library.

The ACLU will also host an informational session from 2 to 4 p.m. Mountain on Oct. 10 at the Catalyst Theater in Rapid City about what voters should know when they’re at the polls, and what to do if they face problems while voting.
For information and to RSVP for any of the events, visit aclusd.org/events.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Baker joins Patrick in bipartisan all-party primary support
authors: Michael P. Norton I State House News Service
description: The Massachusetts Democratic Party and the Massachusetts Republican Party both oppose Question 3, which has drawn support from former Republican Lt. Gov. Kerry Healey and former MassGOP Chair Jennifer Nassour as well as Democrat Auditor Diana DiZoglio, former State Treasurer and MassDems Chair Steve Grossman and former US Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a Democrat.
text:
THEY RAN AGAINST each other in 2010. They each served two terms as governor. They led their parties. And now they are both supporting a ballot question that strips Democrats and Republicans of guaranteed candidates in general elections.
The Yes on 3 campaign announced Monday that former Republican Gov. Charlie Baker has joined former Democratic Gov. Deval Patrick in endorsing the election reform. Patrick’s lieutenant governor, Tim Murray, is also on board. 
“The opportunity to hold public office is a tremendous privilege, but even greater than that honor is the profound responsibility it carries to serve the community that elected you, regardless of party politics,” Baker said in a statement. “As governor, I worked hard to listen to different points of view because that’s the only way for leaders to find the best ideas and reach common ground to get important stuff done. Massachusetts is at its best when we put good ideas and good government ahead of politics, because the real work begins after campaigns end.”
Despite his electoral success here, Baker late in his second term and since fell out of favor within some corners of the Republican Party as it shifted its own abacus before and during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The Massachusetts Democratic Party and the Massachusetts Republican Party both oppose Question 3, which has drawn support from former Republican Lt. Gov. Kerry Healey and former MassGOP Chair Jennifer Nassour as well as Democrat Auditor Diana DiZoglio, former State Treasurer and MassDems Chair Steve Grossman and former US Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a Democrat. 
“All-party primaries will give voters more choice and our elected officials will have to reach across the aisle to voters from other parties if they want to be successful. That’s why I believe Question 3 will return the focus to what matters most: delivering meaningful results for the people of our Commonwealth,” said Baker. 
Added Patrick: “Politics nowadays is less about ‘red’ versus ‘blue’ than about insiders versus outsiders. Elections ought to be a competition of ideas, experience and character than about who has the better structural advantage. All-party primaries can enable more good people to compete, and encourage more office holders to deliver results once elected.”
The Yes on 3 campaign says the reform, which would require all candidates to compete in a single primary with the top two vote-getters advancing, would end “convention gatekeeping,” whereby candidates must secure the support of 15% of delegates during election-year party conventions. That requirement derailed the 2022 gubernatorial campaign of Danielle Allen, who had hoped to challenge Maura Healey for the Democratic nomination. 
Democrat House Speaker Ron Mariano last month called the proposal “ridiculous” while Senate President Karen Spilka, also a Democrat, said she has “concerns about it, that those with the most money will be the ones coming out on top.”
Democratic Party Chair Steve Kerrigan has also claimed that Question 3 will make primary elections more about money.
“It becomes what everybody talks about: these smoke-filled back rooms of folks start putting their thumb on the scale in September for candidates, and then in order for a party or party activists to try to push one person or another, it becomes a money primary only, and not an activist primary,” Kerrigan said.

name: VTDigger
title: Not every job needs to be done in the office
description:
The return-to-office order could drive out workers Vermont can't afford to lose.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Not every job needs to be done in the office.
text:
This commentary is by Latimer Hoke, a paramedic and ski patroller in northern Vermont.
I work as a paramedic. It would be pretty difficult to do my job remotely, what with carrying patients, starting intravenous lines and administering medications. Similar story for plow truck drivers, police and corrections officers, teachers, cooks, delivery drivers, mechanics and many other jobs that require a physical presence. But some jobs can and should be performed remotely.
The recent pandemic illustrated that a job that can be completed with equal or greater efficiency without maintaining a central office space should be performed remotely. Maintaining unnecessary centralized office space is wasteful. Much of the private sector has embraced this reality.
Gov. Phil Scott demanded that all Vermont state employees return to the office at least three days a week. The Vermont Supreme Court just gave Scott his lollipop. Cool. The governor can take the win over the Vermont State Employees’ Association, but there are many problems with forcing this return to the office fully six years after much of Vermont’s state workforce retreated to home. 
Many state employees were hired remotely after the pandemic and have never even lived in Vermont; presumably they’re doing a fine job wherever they are. Similarly, some remote state employees have since left Vermont because it’s too expensive to live here. Others have moved within the state and no longer live within commuting distance of their assigned offices. For remote employees hired in the last six years, this isn’t a return to the office, but a demand to start working in a state office.
And about those offices? Yeah, some of them don’t exist anymore. With the recent consolidations, there simply isn’t room for everyone to return to the office. Someone who was originally hired to work in Burlington may now need to commute to Waterbury or Montpelier.
This requirement will decrease the quality of life for those who can commute and for their families. They’ll have less time with family and less money with all of the expenses that come with commuting, including the priciest gas in years and salty goop that melts cars. Those who cannot commute may need to quit.

READ MORE

Forcing a return to the office may well cost Vermont’s taxpayers more money with the purchase or rental of office space, and hiring new employees to replace those who inevitably cannot afford to move close enough to their newly assigned offices.
Unless Scott plans to eliminate the many layers of Vermont bureaucracy — that’s an essay for another day — I find it hard to believe that we can afford to lose everyone who will have to resign.
For those complaining along the lines of, “But I have to commute to work; so should everyone else,” I hear you, but you sound like a whiny toddler. I also have to go to work, but that’s because I want to do work that requires my physical presence. Frankly, I’d go insane with any job that can be done remotely, but if you want to work from home, what’s stopping you from finding a remote job?
I’m truly grateful for all of the people who can tolerate doing computer- and phone-based work from home, or from anywhere. Scott still has a chance to show some appreciation for our remote state workforce and for taxpayers.
